# THE RUDOLPHINE
# TABLES.

->WHICH CONTAIN THE RESTORATION OF ASTRONOMICAL SCIENCE,<-
->which had collapsed over the long passage of time;<-

->By that Phoenix of Astronomers,<-

# TYCHO

->Born of the Illustrious and Noble family of BRAHE in the Kingdom of DENMARK, a Knight,<-

->FIRST CONCEIVED IN HIS MIND AND INTENDED IN THE YEAR OF<-
->CHRIST 1564: THEREAFTER SERIOUSLY PURSUED THROUGH THE MOST ACCURATE<-
->OBSERVATIONS OF THE STARS, ESPECIALLY AFTER THE YEAR 1572, IN WHICH A NEW STAR<-
->SHONE FORTH IN THE CONSTELLATION OF CASSIOPEIA <note>This refers to the famous supernova of 1572, which proved the heavens were not unchanging.</note>; AND THROUGH VARIOUS WORKS, BOTH<-
->mechanical and literary, at the expense of a most ample patrimony, with the addition of the support of FREDERICK II,<-
->KING OF DENMARK, worthy of royal magnificence, carried on for 25 years, chiefly on the Island of the SOUND,<-
->HVEN, and in the castle of URANIBORG <note>Tycho's famous observatory, "The Castle of the Heavens."</note>, built from its foundations for these purposes:<-

->FINALLY BROUGHT INTO GERMANY, AND INTO THE COURT AND<-
->Name of EMPEROR RUDOLPH in the year 1598.<-

---

->THESE VERY TABLES, ALREADY BOTH NAMED AND BEGUN, BUT<-
->LEFT UNFINISHED BY THE DEATH OF THEIR AUTHOR IN THE YEAR 1601,<-

->RELYING ON THE COMMAND AND PATRONAGE OF THREE EMPERORS,<-
->RUDOLPH, MATTHIAS, AND FERDINAND,<-

->WITH THE BRAHE HEIRS STRIVING TOWARD THE SAME END; FROM THE FOUNDATIONS<-
->of the remaining observations; following the example of the parts already constructed; through the continuous<-
->speculations and computations of many years, first at PRAGUE of the Bohemians he continued them; then at LINZ,<-
->the Metropolis of Upper Austria, aided also by the subsidies of the Illustrious Provincials, he perfected, completed,<-
->and brought them to a formula of causes and perennial calculation:<-

## JOHANNES KEPLER,

->First joined to TYCHO by Emperor RUDOLPH II as an assistant of calculation; and thereafter<-
->Mathematician to the three Emperors in succession:<-

->Who likewise, by the special mandate of EMPEROR FERDINAND II,<-
->at the request and urging of the Heirs,<-

->Brought forth this work for the use of present and future generations, in type, with his own numbers, and other<-
->materials from the press of JONAS SAUR, Printer of the Republic of Ulm, and was present at ULM as the<-
->overseer of the typographic work.<-

### IN THE YEAR 1627.

It credits the patronage of three Holy Roman Emperors and the King of Denmark, detailing the work's journey from the island of Hven to Prague, Linz, and finally its printing in Ulm.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the formal dedication of the Rudolphine Tables to Emperor Ferdinand II. It establishes the lineage of the work from Tycho Brahe through the patronage of Rudolf II.</meta>

<image-desc>An ornate horizontal woodcut banner featuring symmetrical, intricate scrollwork, acanthus leaves, and floral motifs.</image-desc>

# TO LORD FERDINAND II.
## EMPEROR OF THE ROMANS,
### FOREVER AUGUST,
## OF GERMANY,
## HUNGARY, BOHEMIA, &c.
### KING,
## ARCHDUKE OF AUSTRIA,
### MOST MERCIFUL LORD AND MASTER.

---

->MOST AUGUST, MOST POTENT, AND UNCONQUERED<-
->EMPEROR.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'C' set within a square frame, surrounded by intricate foliage and scrollwork engraving.</image-desc>

When, twenty-six years ago, our parent <term>Tycho Brahe</term> <note>The famous Danish astronomer (1546–1601) whose precise observations provided the data for Kepler's laws.</note> was snatched from us by an untimely death, although we his heirs—six in number, along with our widowed mother—were most deeply afflicted, we were nonetheless not as anxious for our own welfare as we were for the studies left behind by him. We were concerned specifically for the books of <term>Celestial Observations</term> <note>original: "Observationum coelestium"</note>, gathered by him over thirty-eight years, and for the structure of the <term>Astronomical Tables</term> <note>The "Rudolphine Tables," which this volume contains.</note> begun and founded upon them. For since it was clear to us that his inclination toward the study of Astronomy was regarded as a divine inspiration by all others who had some knowledge of the art, we did not think it becoming for us, his offspring, to feel more humbly about our progenitor than others did. We felt we should not turn our eyes away from this patrimony left to us, which he himself had valued most highly, to look askance at the riches commonly celebrated, which he had always despised as fleeting and soiled with mud. We felt we should not despise, neglect, or cast away his supreme labors and works, upon which he had expended no common wealth and his entire life; nor, finally, should we fail the public desire of the learned. But since there was no resource in us to advance those works, the Emperor <term>Rudolf II</term> <note>Holy Roman Emperor (reigned 1576–1612) and Tycho's great patron.</note> of most celebrated memory—as he was by his very nature a great lover of all the arts—so too did he look with favor upon our vows and reminders;

<summary>The heirs of Tycho Brahe dedicate this astronomical work to Emperor Ferdinand II, recounting how they preserved Tycho's lifelong celestial observations after his death in 1601 with the support of Emperor Rudolf II.</summary>
<keywords>Ferdinand II, Tycho Brahe, Rudolf II, Celestial Observations, Astronomical Tables, patronage, scientific inheritance, astronomy</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal dedication of the Rudolphine Tables, likely following a description of the initial support provided by Emperor Rudolph II and the transition of the project after Tycho Brahe's death.</meta>

# D E D I C A T I O N

<note>original: "DEDICATIO"</note>

...he sustained the wavering fortune of the **Tables**, and appointed overseers to bring the work to completion. Indeed, he appointed from among us, and in place of us all, a Director of the work: **Franz Gansneb**, called **Tengnagel**, our brother-in-law. One other, who had already spent two years within our Father’s household dedicated to his astronomical labors—**Johannes Kepler**, a man of powerful intellect—he received into his courtly service and assigned a salary. However, not long after, Tengnagel was admitted among the Counselors of the **Emperor** <note>Referring to Rudolph II</note>; having undertaken political affairs and embassies, he was drawn away from the care of the Work. As for **Kepler**, besides the fact that he was left alone, the turmoils that arose throughout the **Emperor's** Kingdoms and provinces, and most ruinous internal wars, hindered him in various ways. And so, against our will and despite our vain hopes for better circumstances, the completion of the Work was dragged out from year to year. Now at last, these Tables having been brought to a conclusion by divine Will, and after the most Merciful will and Mandate of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty <note>The dedication here shifts to the current Emperor, Ferdinand II</note> intervened that they should be published: We, the heirs of **Tycho Brahe**, offer with the most humble veneration this work of the **Rudolphine Tables**, begun and named by our Father, constructed from our Father’s observations (which Kepler received into his hands in good faith). We offer it in our name to Your Sacred Imperial Majesty, who was the Heir in the Austrian Kingdoms and Dominions and the Successor in the Empire to the late **Emperor Rudolph** (from whom, by his consent, the Tables drew their name), and who both promoted the ripening of the work with Imperial munificence and commanded its publication. We sincerely wish from our hearts that this may be happy and auspicious, and that it may yield great utility—of which we have no doubt—to the learned living under Your Majesty’s Empire and the dominions of other Great Lords, and indeed to the whole world and posterity. At the same time, we most humbly commend ourselves—to whom this is the sole patrimony remaining from our father—to Your Majesty’s Mercy and Kindness, upon which the rest of our hopes recline.

Your Sacred Imperial Majesty’s

->*Most Humble and Obedient*<-

->**T H E   C H I L D R E N   A N D   H E I R S**<-
->**O F   T Y C H O   B R A H E.**<-

->To the same,<-

# AUGUST EMPEROR,
## LORD,

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring floral patterns and a small figure within the square frame.</image-desc>

INDEED, most sacred Caesar, since the Dedication of this Work—over which I have toiled for twenty-six years—has already been made to Your Majesty, I may seem like one traveling on another’s ship, bound to make my landing on the same shore where the vessel has docked. Yet I have private reasons by which I am moved; even if the choice had been mine alone, I would have directed my sails into this very same harbor. I had as Patrons Your Majesty’s predecessors of most sacred memory, **Rudolph and Matthias**. If I now return to their Successor the accounts of the duties entrusted to me—accounts I could not render while they lived—I believe this is done rightly and in proper order. What do I not owe to Him <note>Referring to the current Emperor, Ferdinand II</note> who even paid the old wages owed by his predecessors? What do I not owe to Him under whose Empire I have woven together, finished, and perfected these Tables, which had remained incomplete since the death of **Tycho**? What do I not owe to Him who ratified the proposals of myself and **Tycho’s** heirs regarding the publication of the Tables and sanctioned them with his authority; Who demonstrated his desire for a most timely publication by tempering his Majesty with kindness in his inquiries; Who, with Imperial liberality, most magnificently commanded that the expenses necessary for the work be paid to me?

These matters are recent; I shall turn to older things, and trace the very origin of the cares and speculations I contributed to these Tables back to the very egg <note>original: "ab ipso... ovo" - a Latin idiom meaning from the very beginning</note>.

When twenty-nine years ago at **Graz in Styria**—which at that time promised the Archduke **Ferdinand** to the people as their future Emperor—I offered some small astronomical gift: I remember that I, full of confidence in my success in this faculty (such was the power of the then-recent discovery of the single *Cosmographic Mystery* <note>Kepler's first major work, *Mysterium Cosmographicum* (1596)</note>), asked this one thing of Your Serenity: that you might stretch out a helping hand to me as I sought reliable observations of the stars. At that time, **Tycho** had not yet begun sending his letters to me; he had not yet ascended into **Bohemia**. Surely my prayers carried some sense of the fate even then looming. Not quite two years had passed when I gained possession of **Tycho’s** Observations (to which none are equal in reliability and precision) and of **Tycho** himself, having set out to join him in **Bohemia**. I conceived this vow at the very beginning of Your Serenity’s governance, as if under your auspices; I brought my hopes before your most Serene eyes. Why then should I not present and dedicate the happy outcome, which has now at last followed, to that same gaze? For those fateful delays seem to have reserved it plainly for this very time, which was to see the Archduke **Ferdinand** placed at the summit of affairs, shining with Imperial Majesty.

To be sure, I was ignorant of the plan by which the Arbiter and Lord of Fates had snatched that supreme craftsman <note>Tycho Brahe</note> from us in the year 1601, and had checked this heaven-flying chariot of our studies, widowed of its charioteer and guide. I, undeserving...

<summary>Kepler justifies dedicating the Rudolphine Tables to Emperor Ferdinand II, citing the Emperor's financial support and a prophetic meeting in Graz decades earlier. He frames the long delay in finishing Tycho Brahe's work as a matter of divine timing.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Kepler, Tycho Brahe, Rudolph II, Matthias, Ferdinand II, Graz, Styria, Bohemia, Rudolphine Tables, Mysterium Cosmographicum, patronage, astronomy</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues Kepler’s explanation of the delays he faced in completing the Rudolphine Tables, transitioning from the death of Tycho Brahe to the political and personal upheavals of the early 17th century.</meta>

## D E D I C A T I O N.

The reliability of the Court Chamber <note>original: "fides aulicæ Cameræ"; the administrative body responsible for the Emperor's finances</note> and the undeserved pensions of the officials, viewed with squinting eyes through the years 1602 and 1603, were not a hindrance to our progress, but rather the fate of our work itself was an impediment to them. I did an injustice to the fortune of **Tycho Brahe’s** heirs when I blamed it for deserting us; that fortune succumbed to greater Divine powers. I erred gravely by snarling at the stones cast into our orbit—while fate additionally hurled them at us—when Hungary was in turmoil in the year 1604; when the Imperial armies, retreating from Transylvania, afflicted Austria and disturbed the peace of the Imperial court in the year [16]05; when the plague dispersed the courtly gathering through the towns of Bohemia in the year [16]07; when the Hungarians, joined with the Austrians, led an army into Bohemia in the year [16]08; when riots, stirred in the name of religion, terrified Prague in the year [16]09; when a convention of certain Princes of the Empire was held in Prague in the year [16]10; and when the soldiery, called "the Passauers," hostiley invaded Prague in the year [16]11. <note>The "Passauers" were troops of Archduke Leopold V who invaded Prague in a failed attempt to support Emperor Rudolph II against his brother Matthias.</note>

And now I also free from blame my domestic calamities: having then lost my wife, the mother of our common children, the care for whom persuaded my departure from the Court. At that time, I sought in vain why the most magnificent decrees of **EMPEROR RUDOLPH** toward me—by which I was retained at Prague—should result in no outcome; why I spent both money and time in vain, knocking now at the doors of the Silesian Chamber, now at the Imperial Treasury. Meanwhile, following the example of the August patron in human affairs <note>Referring to the death of Emperor Rudolph II in January 1612</note> in the year [16]12, I again burdened public fortune with unjust complaints about my private hindrance. For indeed, it was so destined in the fates that the labors of astronomical leisure were still awaiting their Patron, who was approaching from afar.

Why then did I complain afterward about the move to Austria in that same year—a move truly full of business—with my children (bereft of their mother), with my library furniture, under the new **EMPEROR MATTHIAS**? Why complain of the departure from **Brahe’s** books of Observations? Why the troublesome journeys and the waste of time in patching up that rupture? Why the long bereavement of my house in a foreign place? For what fault was in all these delays that your looming succession, **CAESAR FERDINAND**, did not take upon itself? It was for this succession, of course, that the hidden genius of the astronomical art was deferring the success of these studies.

I believe the speculations themselves felt the vicinity of Styria, their first homeland; <note>Kepler began his career as a teacher in Graz, Styria, before being exiled for his Lutheran faith.</note> they felt their own more prosperous fortune rising in it under the hope of the imminent **FERDINAND**. Reinvigorated by this feeling, as soon as I returned from Regensburg to Linz in the company of his Emperor in the year [16]14, and as soon as peace was restored to that place by the departure of the court and my house was settled, the studies progressed through the following two years toward some form of the whole work. Finally, by the same steps by which **FERDINAND** strove toward his kingdoms and Austrian domains, the Tables themselves strove toward their own perfection.

And so, in that very year when the Crown of Bohemia was placed upon Your brow, I, having been called to Prague, brought and exhibited the first Ephemeris <note>term: Ephemeris (a table providing the daily positions of celestial bodies)</note> computed from these Tables. Having been approved, I published it the following year, using types <note>Printing types or fonts</note> suitable for the work, prepared at my own expense and direction; with these same types, these very Tables are now described and communicated to the cultivators of the art.

The Oaks of the heir and the tall Elms easily forgive the weak vines if they are made equal to their own height; <note>A metaphor comparing the strength of the Emperor (Oaks/Elms) to the dependence of the scientist (vines).</note> no greater or more pleasing worship comes even to God than from a man who refers all his fortunes back to Him. And I also, having once dared to enter this comparison, proceed with that constancy which a belief in the greatest veneration confirms. For I believe you were then destining public peace for the peoples who would be under your empire; but a peace conformable to your judgment, which God established as the arbiter of affairs; a peace...
<meta>catchword: incom-</meta>

<summary>Kepler recounts the decade of political instability, war, plague, and personal tragedy (the death of his wife and Emperor Rudolph II) that delayed the Rudolphine Tables, eventually finding the necessary stability for their completion under the rise of Emperor Ferdinand II.</summary>
<keywords>Thirty Years' War, Passau invasion, Styria, Linz, astronomical calculations, Imperial Treasury, patronage, 1604-1614, Ephemeris</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the formal dedication of the Rudolphine Tables to the Holy Roman Emperor, likely Ferdinand II, following the initial address. The tone is one of humble petition, linking the completion of astronomical work to the restoration of peace in the Empire.</meta>

# DEDICATION

free from the inconveniences which you judged ought to be driven away: a peace of this kind you have not yet been able to obtain, having now been exercised for an entire decade by the dire contention of studies <note>original: "studiorum contentione," likely referring here to the intense legal and political disputes of the era</note>, and by defections and most mournful internal wars. And for me also, aspiring continually from that time toward the completion of the work of the Tables, one blemish after another was subsequently discovered, which had to be washed away or cut out, and the scar covered over: in turn, one shortcut for the solemn calculation after another, one beautiful discovery after another occurred, which could not be associated, joined, or refined with the work unless the whole labor was recalled to the anvil and transformed. Grant pardon, **EMPEROR**, to your fortune; grant it to the condition of these studies; which, since they are the ornaments of peace, have waited for peace in your empire until now. Nor do they go out into public with any other confidence even now—although summoned by the commands of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty—than that they trust they carry and bring forth an omen of a peace even now to be concluded. Although they can strengthen this persuasion neither by facts nor by causes; indeed, they even now willingly confess the same ignorance of these things by which they were held until now: nevertheless, they both love this persuasion in themselves, fascinated by the zeal of Your Majesty and by pity for the fatherland, and they suspect it to be consistent with the truth, being reminded of it by the very progress of this comparison undertaken.

For indeed, these Tables both contain and publicly confess some imperfections detected in the very subject of the celestial motions, which are not warrantable or surmountable by any human art (especially before the sufficient experience of future ages): but Your Majesty—what you might think to grant to the condition of mortal affairs, what crooked and intercepted things you might pass over so that peace may be reached by a shortcut, how much severity may suffice for your August office, and finally what you might think to leave to be corrected by successors—these Tables, pining with a desire for peace, in which alone the joy of their use may blossom with increments, most anxiously await.

**GOD**, in whose hand is the supreme power of Princes and peoples, through whom Kings command and leaders of war conquer; **GOD**, who knows how to use His instruments, sometimes even when they are ignorant of the counsels of their Mover, and in places where they are doing something else; who, having uprooted evil customs, is accustomed to impose a limit on affairs and an end to calamities; that **GOD** of Gods, I say, may He prolong, protect, and prosper the Life, Health, and Empire of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty: to the Son of the same, the King, and to the other children born to the highest station, and to the August partner of your Life and Empire, and thus to the whole House of Austria, may He, appeased and propitious, bestow all-encompassing happiness, in which my safety and that of my people is contained; whom, that He may do this and wish it ratified, I venerate with most humble prayer.

But now I suppliantly pray Your Sacred Imperial Majesty, that with these **RUDOLPHINE** Tables, which are offered and dedicated to Him by the heirs of **BRAHE** <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose observations provided the data for these tables</note>, the first namer of them, He might also receive with a serene countenance my labors of so many years spent in finishing and perfecting them; and most mercifully deign to grant His Imperial patronage to me, his most humble little client, and to my family.

->Of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty<-

->*the humble servant hired*<-
->*for the cultivation of Mathematics,*<-

->**JOHANNES KEPLER.**<-

<summary>Kepler concludes his dedication by linking the long-delayed publication of the Rudolphine Tables to the ongoing turmoil of the Thirty Years' War, praying for imperial peace and divine favor. He acknowledges the work's imperfections while formally presenting it as the fulfillment of Tycho Brahe's legacy under the Emperor's patronage.</summary>

<keywords>Johannes Kepler, Tycho Brahe, Rudolphine Tables, Holy Roman Empire, Thirty Years' War, astronomy, patronage, House of Austria</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page serves as the poetic frontispiece to Johannes Kepler’s Rudolphine Tables (1627). The poem, an "Idyllion" by Johann Baptista Hebenstreit, describes the famous engraved title page which depicts a "Temple of Astronomy."</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece consisting of a repeating horizontal pattern of floral rosettes and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>

# ON THE KEPLERIAN STAR-ADORNED TOWER,
### THE ORIGIN AND PROGRESS OF ASTRONOMY UNTO OUR OWN AGE;
### AND THE NEW, LONG-DESIRED, AND INCOMPARABLE
# WORK OF THE TABLES
->exhibited in a depiction;<-
## BY JOHANN BAPTISTA HEBENSTREIT, OF AUGSBURG.
->AN IDYLL.<-

Does something stand here at the very edge of an Apellean <note>Apelles was the most renowned painter of ancient Greece; his name is used here to signify supreme artistic skill.</note> curl, a work of blossoming genius? Tell me, O Goddess, leader of the Aonian sisters <note>The Muses.</note>, you who took your name from heaven itself, Urania! If you hold those sublime theaters in such high esteem, where the quiet throng of Gods dwells, and from whence come the successions of labors to mortal fields: let it not be a shame to have taught the imitations of such great things in drawn forms.

And so, behold for yourself, admirer of the earth and the ethereal globe! Do you see the temples of the Gods rising in new splendor, which the diverse care of earlier men raised up, and left to be polished in our own age? If these things perhaps seem too wonderful to you, and you stand silent, fixed in a single gaze, I will now reveal them, with the Goddess opening the way. If you lend your ears, you will see all obscure things become clear, as if by the torches of Phoebus <note>The Sun god.</note>. DO YOU SEE how the roofs shine, supported by twelve columns, to be known by as many signs <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note>? How the columns hold their own supports, adorned with five small tablets? I see them, you say: but what does this reversed order mean?

<margin>Why are the fixed stars at the lowest place?</margin>
Whatever lights seem fixed in the ethereal hollow in other lofty stations, those are now, by art, engraved upon the pavement: is the pole mixed with the ground? Has the ether yielded from its own seat? Whoever you are asking these things: Heaven remains immutable. But by the genius of the Poets, and the guidance of the learned Apelles, and by the law of the Astronomer, those thresholds are placed beneath sublime columns, like the sacred foundations of the masters of the art. Therefore, the floor provides the stars for you, where the area is strewn everywhere with the twelve Signs. In no other way could watchful eyes lead down Olympus: or with skillful investigation track the wondrous

<margin>By observations.</margin>
paths of the Wanderers <note>The planets; from the Greek 'planētai' meaning wanderers.</note>, and the seven crossroads. Happy souls! whose relentless labor distinguished the starry host and the flames themselves in order from the deep Orb, and painted the various forms of both things and men. Among these, why do you, Aratus <note>A Greek poet (c. 315–240 BCE) famous for his poem on the stars.</note>, hide behind the back of a Column? Is it not enough that you are praised for having distinguished the regions of Heaven with Pierian melody, and for having

<margin>The armillary sphere of Aratus.</margin>
entwined orbs within orbs? Does fortune fail your labor? Did the virtue of Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who produced the first systematic star catalog.</note> sweat more on the Pharian shores? We do not all obtain the same gifts: there are a thousand types of men: industry is of different colors: the very law of fate varies: nor is the highest strength in genius present at one time. Hipparchus, better than Aratus (both Greeks), allowed a Dane <note>Referring to Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer.</note> to arise as a better heir to his captured works. Behold the seat! He bequeaths it to the Gods with marked tablets, if anyone, in the mature lapse of years, should replace them with better foundations. At last, after the exact winding of the ages, that which those men

<margin>Tycho perfected the Catalog of fixed stars.</margin>
scattered more roughly, TYCHO collected, and raised for certain uses, so that the whole area might shine more splendidly, and now show its fires more learnedly, arranged with immense zeal through nearly eight lustra <note>A lustrum is a five-year period; eight lustra equals forty years.</note>. Therefore, when the individual stars had obtained their own seats, then the COLUMNS, as supports, lift the roof more uprightly, and strengthen the gables of the lofty temple. # D E D I C A T I O N.

# EMPEROR AUGUSTUS,
## L O R D.

I indeed, Most Sacred Caesar <note>original: "Cæsar Sacratissime". A traditional formal address for the Holy Roman Emperor, linking his office to the ancient Roman Emperors.</note>, now that the dedication of this work—over which I have toiled for twenty-six years—has been made to Your Majesty, seem necessarily to make my landing upon the same shore where the ship has arrived, much like one who is carried in another’s vessel. Nevertheless, I have my own private reasons by which I am moved; even if the choice had been mine alone, I would have directed my sails into this same harbor. I had as patrons Your Majesty’s predecessors of most sacred memory, **RUDOLPH** and **MATTHIAS**. If I now render the accounts of the duties and tasks entrusted to me by them—accounts I could not give while they remained among the living—to their Successor, I believe this is done rightly and in proper order. What do I not owe to Him who even paid the old stipends <note>Kepler struggled with chronic underpayment from the imperial treasury; Ferdinand II eventually authorized payments to settle these long-standing debts.</note> owed by his predecessors? What do I not owe to Him under whose Empire I have woven together, consummated, and perfected these Tables, which had remained incomplete since the death of **TYCHO**? What do I not owe to Him who ratified the proposals of myself and the heirs of **TYCHO** regarding the publication of the Tables and sanctioned them with his support? Who demonstrated his desire for the earliest possible publication through inquiries, tempering his Majesty with kindness; and who most magnificently commanded that the expenses necessary for the work be paid to me from the Imperial liberality?

These matters are recent; I shall turn to older things, and seek the very origin of the cares and speculations which I contributed to these Tables, going back to the very beginning <note>original: "ab ipso... ovo", literally "from the egg itself," a Latin idiom meaning to start from the absolute commencement of a story.</note>.

Twenty-nine years ago at **GRAZ IN STYRIA**, when the Court was then promising the Archduke **FERDINAND** as Emperor to the people, I was offering some astronomical gift or other; I remember that I, full of confidence in my success in this field (so great was the recent discovery of the single *Secret of the Universe* <note>original: "Mysterii Cosmographici". This refers to Kepler's first major book, published in 1596, which attempted to explain the spacing of the planets using the five Platonic solids.</note>), asked this one thing from Your Serenity: that you might extend a helping hand to me as I sought reliable observations of the stars. At that time, **TYCHO** had not yet begun sending his letters to me; he had not yet ascended into **BOHEMIA**. Surely my prayers bore some sense of the fate that was even then imminent. Not a full two years had passed when I gained possession of **TYCHO’S** observations (which are matched by none in reliability and precision) and of **TYCHO** himself, having set out to join him in Bohemia. I conceived this vow at the very beginning of Your Serenity’s government, as if under your auspices; I brought my hopes before your most serene eyes. Why, then, should I not also present and dedicate the happy outcome, which has now finally followed, to that same sight? since

# D E D I C A T I O N.

)( 3

...it seems those fatal delays reserved [this work] plainly for this very time, which would see the Archduke **FERDINAND** placed at the summit of affairs, shining with Imperial Majesty.

Truly, I was unaware of the plan by which the Arbiter and Lord of Fates had snatched away the supreme artist <note>Refers to Tycho Brahe, who died in 1601.</note> from us in the year 1601, and had halted this heaven-roaming chariot of our studies, deprived of its driver and moderator. I stared with sideways glances <note>original: "limis confixi oculis"; an expression meaning to look upon someone with suspicion, resentment, or envy.</note> at the undeserving Presidents of the Court Chamber and the undeserving Masters of Pensions through the years 1602 and 1603: it was not their lack of favor toward our progress, but the fate of our work itself that was an obstacle to them. I did an injustice to the fortune of Tycho Brahe’s heirs while I accused it of deserting us; it succumbed to greater Divine Powers. I erred gravely by biting at the stones thrown into our path—ignoring the one who hurled them—when Hungary was in turmoil in 1604; when the Imperial armies, retreating from Transylvania, afflicted Austria and disturbed the peace of the Imperial court in 1605; when the plague dispersed the courtly gathering through the towns of Bohemia in 1607; when the Hungarians, joined with the Austrians, led an army into Bohemia in 1608; when disturbances, stirred up in the name of religion, terrified Prague in 1609; when a meeting of certain Princes of the Empire was held in Prague in 1610; when the soldiers, known as the Passauers <note>The "Passauers" were an irregular army raised by Archduke Leopold that invaded Prague in 1611, causing significant chaos.</note>, hostily invaded Prague in 1611. 

And now I also free my domestic calamities from blame—the loss of my wife at that time, the mother of our common children, whose care persuaded me to depart from the Court. I sought in vain then why the most munificent decrees of **EMPEROR RUDOLPH II** concerning me, by which I was retained at Prague, resulted in no outcome; why I spent both expense and time in vain, knocking now at the doors of the Silesian Chamber, now the Imperial Treasury. 

Meanwhile, when my August patron was removed from human affairs in the year 1612 <note>Emperor Rudolph II died in January 1612.</note>, I again burdened public fortune with unjust complaints about private obstacles. Indeed, it was destined that astronomical labors should take a holiday while their Patron was still approaching from afar. What then did I complain of next: the transition into Austria in that same year—quite a busy one—with the children, the mother of the orphans <note>original: "matre orbis"; likely referring to his second wife, Susanna Reuttinger, who cared for the children of his deceased first wife.</note>, and with my library furniture, under the new Emperor **MATTHIAS**? Why the departure from Tycho Brahe’s books of Observations? Why the troublesome journeys and the expense of time to mend that breach? Why the long-lasting bereavement of my house in a foreign place? 

For what fault was there in all those delays that Your imminent succession, **CAESAR FERDINAND**, does not take entirely upon itself? It was for this that the hidden genius of the Astronomical art postponed the success of these studies. I believe the speculations themselves felt the vicinity of Styria, their first homeland <note>Kepler began his professional career as a teacher and mathematician in Graz, Styria.</note>; they felt their own more prosperous fortune rising there under the imminent hope of **FERDINAND**. Restored by this feeling, as soon as I returned from Regensburg to Linz in the Emperor's retinue in the year 1614, and as soon as peace was restored to that place by the departure of the court and my home was settled, they [the Tables] progressed through the following two years toward some form of the whole work. Finally, by the same steps with which **FERDINAND** advanced toward the kingdoms and Austrian domains, the Tables themselves strove toward their perfection. And so, in that very year when the Crown of Bohemia was placed upon Your brow, I, having been called to Prague, brought the first Ephemeris <term>Ephemeris</term><note>A table giving the calculated positions of a celestial body at regular intervals, used by astronomers and navigators.</note> calculated from these Tables and presented it to be seen. And having been approved, I published it the following year, printed at...

<summary>Kepler recounts the two decades of political upheaval, war, and personal tragedy—including the death of his wife and two Emperors—that delayed the completion of the Rudolphine Tables, ultimately framing these delays as a divine preparation for the patronage of Ferdinand II.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Johannes Kepler’s dedication of the *Rudolphine Tables* to Emperor Ferdinand II. Having previously detailed the external political turmoils and personal losses that delayed the project, Kepler now describes the internal scientific struggles and the metaphorical parallels between the Emperor's search for political peace and the astronomer’s search for "celestial peace" (accuracy).</meta>

# D E D I C A T I O N

...the work having been prepared by suitable means, provided at my own expense and by my own direction: by which same means these very **Tables**, now finally described, are shared with the practitioners of the art <note>The "art" refers to the science of astronomy.</note>.

Oaks easily forgive the ivy, and tall elms the weak vines, if the latter measure themselves against the height of the former; no greater or more pleasing worship—not even to God—comes from a man than when he refers all his fortunes back to Him. And I also, having once entered upon this bold comparison, proceed with that constancy which a belief in the greatest reverence confirms. You intended, I believe, public peace for the peoples about to be under your rule, but a peace conforming to Your judgment, whom God has appointed as the arbiter of affairs; a peace lacking the hardships which you judged ought to be repelled. Yet for a whole decade now, though exercised by a dread struggle of studies, by defections, and by most mournful internal wars <note>original: "bellis intestinis"; a reference to the devastating Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) which was raging as Kepler wrote this.</note>, you have not yet been able to obtain it.

And for me also, from that time, as I constantly aspired toward the completion of the work of the Tables, one blemish after another was detected, and had to be washed away or cut out, and the scar covered over. In turn, one shortcut of formal calculation <note>original: "calculi solennis compendium"; likely a reference to Kepler's revolutionary use of logarithms to speed up astronomical math.</note> after another, one beautiful discovery after another occurred, which could not be joined, committed, or refined unless the whole work was recalled to the anvil and transformed. Grant pardon, **EMPEROR**, to your fortune; grant it to the condition of these studies, which, since they are the ornaments of peace, have until now waited for peace in your empire. Nor do they go out into the public even now with any other confidence—though summoned by the commands of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty—than that they trust they carry and offer an omen of a peace now on the verge of being concluded. Even if they cannot strengthen this persuasion with facts or causes—indeed, they freely confess the same ignorance of these matters by which they were held until now—nevertheless, they love this persuasion in themselves, fascinated by the zeal of Your Majesty and by pity for the fatherland; they suspect it to be consistent with the truth, reminded by the very progress of this comparison I have begun.

For indeed, these Tables both contain and publicly confess certain imperfections detected in the very subject of the celestial motions, which are not excusable or surmountable by any human art (especially before sufficient experience of future ages is gained). But Your Majesty: what you think to overlook in the condition of mortal affairs—what crooked and obstructed paths you might pass by so that peace may be reached by a shortcut, how much severity suffices for your August office, and finally, what you think to leave to be corrected by your successors—these Tables themselves, wasting away with a desire for peace (in which alone the use of their happy fruits might flourish), most anxiously await.

**GOD**, in whose hand is the supreme power of Princes and peoples, through whom Kings rule and leaders of war conquer; **GOD**, who knows how to use His instruments, sometimes even when they are unaware of the plans of their Mover, and sometimes when they are doing something else entirely; who, having uprooted evil customs, is accustomed to impose a limit on affairs and an end to calamities; that God of Gods, I say, may He prolong, protect, and prosper the Life, Health, and Empire of Your Sacred Imperial Majesty. May He, appeased and propitious, grant all manner of happiness—in which the safety of me and mine is contained—to your son the King, to your other children born for the highest things, to your August partner in life and Empire <note>Refers to Empress Eleonora Gonzaga.</note>, and indeed to the entire House of Austria. That He may do this, and wish it to be ratified, I pray with most humble prayer.

# D E D I C A T I O N

But I humbly pray Your Most Sacred Imperial Majesty <note>original: "Sam verò Cam Mtem Vam," an abbreviation for *Sacratissimam vero Caesaream Maiestatem Vestram*.</note> that you look upon these **RUDOLPHINE** tables with a serene countenance—those which are offered and dedicated to Your Majesty by the heirs of BRAHE <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used; the tables were named "Rudolphine" after their original patron, Emperor Rudolf II.</note>, who first gave them their name—and that you also recognize my own labors of so many years spent in completing and correcting them; and that You might most mercifully deign to grant Your Imperial patronage to me, your most humble little client, and to my household.

# UPON THE KEPLERIAN STAR-ADORNED TEMPLE,
## SHOWING THE BIRTH AND PROGRESS OF ASTRONOMY EVEN UNTO OUR OWN AGE;
### AND THE HITHERTO LONG-DESIRED, INCOMPARABLE, AND NEW
# WORK OF THE TABLES,
## presented in illustration;
### AN IDYLL BY JOHANNES BAPTISTA HEBENSTREITT, OF AUGSBURG.

Does some hair-fine curl of Apelles <note>original: "Apellæi cinni." Apelles was the most celebrated painter of ancient Greece, often used to signify supreme artistic skill.</note> stand upon the first margin of the **BOOK OF KEPLER**? Speak, O Divine chief of the Aonian sisters <note>The Muses, specifically referring to Urania, the Muse of Astronomy.</note>, who took your name from heaven itself, Urania! If you hold those sublime theaters in such high regard—the quiet dwellings of the crowd of Gods, from whence come the changes of tasks for weary mortals—then let it not be a shame to have taught the imitations of such great things in drawn forms.
   And so, behold for yourself the admirer of the earth and the ethereal world! Do you see the temples of the Gods rising with new elegance, which the differing care of earlier men raised up, and left to be polished in our own age? If these things perhaps seem too marvelous to you, and you stand silently fixed in a single gaze, I shall now reveal them, with the Goddess opening the way. If you lend your ears, you shall see all obscure things become clear as if by the torches of Phoebus <note>Apollo, the sun-god.</note>. DO YOU SEE how the roofs shine, supported by twelve Columns, recognizable by as many signs <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note>? How the columns hold their own supports adorned with five small tablets? I see, you say: but what does this reversed order mean?
<margin>The fixed stars; why in the lowest place?</margin> Whatever lights seem fixed in the ethereal Hollow in high stations elsewhere, those are now carved by art into the pavement: is the pole mixed with the soil? Has the ether yielded from its seats? Whoever you are asking these things: the Heaven remains immutable. <gloss>of Apelles,</gloss>
But by the genius of the Poets, and by the guidance of the learned, and by the law of the Astronomer, those thresholds are placed beneath the sublime columns as the foundations of the sacred art of the Dictators <note>Referring here to the masters of the science.</note>. Therefore, the base shows you the stars, where the floor is spread on all sides with the twelve Signs. In no other way could watchful eyes bring down Olympus, or investigate the wondrous

<column-break/>

paths and crossroads of the seven Wanderers <note>The seven planets known to the ancients.</note> with skillful searching.
Happy souls! whose tireless labor distinguished the Star-bearing Orb and the flames themselves in order, and painted the various forms of things and men. <margin>Because they are for the foundation of Observation.</margin> Why do you, Aratus <note>An ancient Greek poet famous for his poem on the stars.</note>, hide behind the back of a Column among these? Is it not enough that you are praised for having distinguished the regions of the Heaven with Pierian melody <note>Poetic song.</note>, and for having entwined spheres within spheres? <margin>An armillary sphere.</margin> Does fortune fail your labor? Did the virtue of Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer often cited as the father of trigonometry and discoverer of the precession of the equinoxes.</note> sweat more on the shores of Pharos <note>Alexandria, Egypt.</note>? <margin>Of Hipparchus.</margin> We do not all obtain the same gifts: there are a thousand kinds of men; industry is of different colors; the law of fate itself varies; nor is the greatest strength always in geniuses at one time. Hipparchus, better than Aratus (both Greeks), suffered a better Dane <note>Tycho Brahe, who was Danish.</note> to arise as the heir of his captured works. <margin>Tycho completed the Catalog of the fixed stars.</margin> Behold his seat! Let him bequeath the Gods to marked tablets, if someone might replace them with better foundations after the mature passing of years. At last, through the exact winding of the ages, TYCHO collected what those others had scattered more roughly, and raised it for certain uses, so that the whole area might shine more splendidly, and more learnedly show its fires, arranged with immense zeal through nearly eight lustra <note>A "lustrum" is a period of five years; Tycho spent nearly forty years on his observations.</note>. So great a task it was to discern the divine body in its spaces, and to compose the once-wandering ranks of stars into an exact measure in a certain position! Therefore, when the individual stars have each obtained their own seat, then their supports, the COLUMNS, raise the roof more rightly and strengthen the summits of the high temple. What else shall I call these, if not OBSERVATIONS refined by a wise mind, when experience created the art? <margin>The Columns signify the Observations.</note> Lest it escape him whom the heat of learning urges, what the face of the World is: whether it is forced to remain the same, or whether each part sustains its own days in order, and changes something while the mobile year...

<margin>Epoch.</margin> He has finished his course, or the notable weaving of a long destiny. Here, too, both the matters of heaven and the works of Craftsmen are accustomed to proceed from unequal starting points; hence, leaning upon those columns, <margin>The observations of Tycho Brahe.</margin> gleaming in his precious fur robe, he reclines to show his refinement and the honor of a perfected art. <margin>Certainty above all others.</margin> Does not the head of the pillar stand out, conspicuous with Corinthian acanthus? Do you see how the instruments, cast from yellow metal, shine as eternal monuments to Tycho? <margin>Quadrant and sextant.</margin> By these stairs he climbed the great and turning temple of the World, about to increase his fame with things seen and written, and to scatter it into future ages. For such great merits, O Rudolph <note>Emperor Rudolph II, the patron of Tycho Brahe and Johannes Kepler.</note>, you cherish him as he departs from the Danish land, allowing him to be more free for heavenly things and to bring an end to his great endeavors; you command him to grow in honor in your August court. <margin>Next to those of Copernicus and Regiomontanus.</margin> From the opposite side, COPERNICUS stands out, one of better renown (although you know that more things of Tycho survive); <margin>His Hypotheses.</margin> he brought forth wonderful thoughts unknown to the common crowd. From these, Brahe is seen to depart only a little, and to assign the primary place to his own discovery. <margin>And Tycho Brahe's.</margin> Therefore he chides the Prussian <note>Copernicus, who was from Royal Prussia.</note>, and of his own accord rebukes him with such words: **WHAT IF IT BE THUS?** <note>original: "QUID SI SIC?" This was Tycho Brahe's personal motto, expressing his skepticism and his own geo-heliocentric model.</note> There is not only one way to the azure temples of heaven; what if, having progressed by a nobler path through our discoveries, he joins himself to a closer Olympus? Copernicus, not unlike one struggling, remains unmoving, so much so that he would sooner have the weight of the Earth turned in a circle than change his mind. Therefore he sits, supported by his own suspended column; <margin>Jacob's Staff.</margin> he praises the instruments, specifically the cross-shaped staff <note>term: <term>Jacob's staff</term> (radius astronomicus), a tool used to measure the angle between two stars.</note> and the joined beams, by which the wonders of the heavens are brought into <margin>Parallactic Ruler.</margin> true account, even if the distance mocks our eyes and a careless error deceives us. Here and there one can see the other supports of the temple, different in their decoration, <margin>The cruder observations of the ancients.</margin> built of squared stone, but full of cracks and bare of lime mortar. This is the not-unskilled ignorance of the ancient way, when neither Hipparchus, nor Aratus the author of the poem, nor others yet knew the more certain teachings of our art; <margin>Hipparchus, Aratus, Ptolemy the Astronomer and Geographer.</margin> among these, Ptolemy once shone with a face of honor, reshaping things above and on the earth. <margin>His Astrolabe.</margin> He also more confidently built a wonderful Sphere, marked with networks <note>A reference to the "rete" or star-map on an astrolabe.</note>, where the transverse ruler shows the path of the Sun, and through the mouth of a small sight-hole, he strives to reveal more miracles of the Gods. Behold! with his laboring right hand he draws diagrams, and with his head covered by his ancestral crown, <margin>Chords subtended by arcs of a circle.</margin> he fits straight lines—no futile task—to the arcs; through these, he brings that which is curved (and which of itself rejects all measurement) under the yoke of number and measure. <margin>Eccentrics and epicycles for demonstrating the motions of the Planets.</margin> Behind him reclines a beautiful Table, providing the desired aid to one searching the seven wandering bodies <note>The "seven wanderers" are the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, to see if they can be joined to a certain part among the stars scattered in the vault

<column-break/>

<margin>of those stars for past and future times.</margin> above, whether that part has already been marked, or is to be marked hereafter for posterity. O arts of a most wealthy genius! <margin>Meton's nineteen-year cycle, reconciling the lunar year with the tropical year.</margin> From here, an instrument hangs from the neighboring stones, which the learned Meton once found in Cecropian Athens. By this cycle of ten and nine years, he shows the Great Year <note>term: <term>Metonic cycle</term>, a period of 19 years after which the moon's phases recur on the same days of the solar year.</note> that arises for the nations: whereby the path of Phoebus [the Sun] would not be foreign to the winding path of his sister Phoebe [the Moon], if the golden bearer of Helle <note>The zodiac sign Aries.</note> and the Balance <note>The zodiac sign Libra.</note> divide the middle of the sphere between shadows and light; or if winter and summer be separated by the solstices. These inventions found their own applause, because previously hearts had struggled, drawn away into various cares, when the appearance of the sky, with its returning stars, was not yet perceived within the complete boundaries of the year. <margin>Other columns clearly of a crude beginning.</margin> Although Leostratus sought suitable inventions from Tenedos, these inventions, however (like a huge and monstrous mass of stone, full of danger in its very structure, when some stones lie upon others and the edges rub against each other with a light touch, nor has any mortar or lime-sand bound the nodding lips of the falling rock), do not deserve to be considered illustrious. <margin>Wooden columns from tree trunks.</margin> Finally, even the forest gives supports to our heights, namely the branches of the aged mountain ash, and the oak sacred to Jupiter. Alas! do you also, wooden aids to the supreme Goddess [Astronomy]—if not entirely made of fig-wood <note>Fig-wood was proverbially weak and useless for construction.</note>—raise up trunks and support the imposed crown of the Roof? But however we may bear this, honor is also given to the logs, which the learned adze has not yet rightly formed into a graceful shape. And behold, how the intractable wood stiffens with knots! How it raises itself up! It does not yet touch the paneled ceilings, but in a shorter way sighs toward the ether of the seven wanderers! And certainly it could bring ruin to the inner sanctuary, unless a dutiful hand, such as Kepler's, fills the spaces with inserted wedges. <margin>The crude custom of the Chaldeans for observing the stars.</margin> But who is that obscure father, stretching out his arms far? Does he dare to measure the stars by the span of his extended thumb and forefinger? He who is nearest to the wooden logs likewise proves with what rudeness he noted the things seen in high Olympus. Refer here, then, to those who professed more rugged decrees, the pupils of great Babylon; yet they are not to be despised: glory is due also to first attempts. Just as the Tirynthian hero <note>Hercules.</note> gave a specimen of his power while not yet a hero, when—while Alcmena trembled—he seized the great throats of the dragons in his tender palms and dashed them to the ground. If there had been more aids for the Chaldeans, they would have polished our arts more beautifully. <margin>The ROOF resting upon the columns.</margin> But now we have come to the ROOF. The Roof has embraced all things far and wide that are suited to your powers, <margin>The necessity of the ancient observations.</margin> O Divine Urania; for the new structures alone could not fulfill the mind's desire, nor provide full supports for the ancient Roof.

It was fitting to bring forth bodies solidified from the ancient age, of whatever sort they were, and to have conveyed them with zeal. From this, indeed, how great a task it was to make the ancient go together with the recent, and to have established disparate columns in an equal row! But through trial, use has conquered, and labor sharpened the wit so that those things which you denied could be completed now strike your eyes with clear light.

Therefore you see that whatever mortals have ever hoped for up to this point is played out there in no vain image. Following the heir of Hipparchus <note>original: "Hipparchi heredem," referring to Tycho Brahe, who was considered the new Hipparchus for his observational accuracy.</note> by a fated law, Kepler <note>original: "Kepleriades," literally 'son of Kepler' or the Keplerian successor.</note> arises: to him the Courtyard yields, and from there the columns, born under severe laws, submit. To touch, it touches with a leap, licking the slopes. Just as when an iron plate is struck against an anvil, and one sees it both bend and lose its proper alignment, if someone should cast their eyes from the top of the iron to the bottom. But although the rays of light waver like spears

and gladly receives them to be fully formed.

May the caretaker Kepler <note>original: "Kepleriades," meaning "son of Kepler" or "the Keplerian," here referring to Kepler himself</note> refine it with his file, and reshape the body into an excellent form, with all its limbs beautifully fitted.

<margin>The Tables were completed and printed at the printing house in Ulm.</margin>
The region to the right shows how, after Kepler departed from the Austrian borders and reached the Swabian countryside, the final day arrived for the Tables to finally come forth into the light of day. Behold! For the **PRINTING HOUSE** <note>original: "CHALCOGRAPHIÔN," literally a place for copper engraving or printing</note> at **ULM** loves to perform the duty of Lucina <note>The goddess of childbirth, used here as a metaphor for the birth of the book</note>, so that this great advancement for the world may fly forth into the lands.

The presses are hot; the weary limbs of the workers flow with sweat. From this, the workers are thirsty, and water does not give those thirsty men enough; the liquor of beer <note>original: "Zythi," an ancient term for beer</note> and the pure drink of Bacchus <note>Wine</note> refreshes their bodies tired from their duties and restores them for labor. The furthest wall places under the light

<margin>Where Kepler also contributed his own typefaces.</margin>
a case divided into small compartments, in which all the offspring of Cadmus <note>A mythological reference to the alphabet; Cadmus was said to have brought letters to Greece</note>—even the pugnacious ones—are abundantly distributed as if in various inns. Kepler himself, lest they breathe forth battles with too much swollen pride, mixes in his own troops from the race of **Numbers**. And so that he might join these talents in a friendly treaty,

<margin>Serving only the reading of the typesetter.</margin>
the builder from Nuremberg <note>original: "Noricus exstructor," likely referring to the skilled craftsmen or typesetters from the printing centers of Germany</note>, his limbs stretched by constant labor, performed his daily measures with every kind of gesture: now looking at the woven text with a squinting eye, now pressing his belly into the curved bends [of the desk],

<margin>Return to the Goal and the peak of the Roof.</margin>
while his right hand snatched from the boxes and his left hand caught what, when inserted into the rule <note>A composing stick used by printers to align type</note>, would produce straight lines. All these emblems <note>referring to the decorative elements of the temple frontispiece</note> which I have gladly painted together,

<margin>The Triumph of restored ASTRONOMY.</margin>
the spectator sees Queen **Urania** assume in joyful triumph. Do you see how, from the highest Peak <note>original: "Meta," the conical finish at the top of the temple</note>, that most holy goddess leaps out, and rushing closer, sends forth her herald-signs: the lamp of a cloud dripping with heavenly light: just as Aurora <note>The Dawn</note> rising again from the chambers of the Ocean, when she scatters rosy flames through the thin clouds? And now the goddess shows herself in the midst of the Divine ones at the very summit, and sends back her applause to bright Olympus. Why should I describe her finery? Why her gestures worthy of the heavens?

<column-break/>

Veiled in a purple robe, she stands out upon her high throne: she has placed rays of light upon her hair, and the stars of the Gods; everything glitters with gold and with fire-stones <note>original: "pyropos," a red bronze or gemstone like garnet</note> that mimic flames.

She herself carries in her right hand a laurel, which she tosses toward the sky, about to pray to the winged armor-bearer of highest Jove <note>The Imperial Eagle, symbol of the Holy Roman Empire</note>. If she seeks to make the required monuments eternal enough, let her turn her eyes here; let her turn her scepters kindly here: let her say that the omens were long ago taken by the great **Brahe**, whom the Father of things withdrew from the lowly earth so that, as a cultivator of the heavens, he might enjoy the gift of heaven; then that those things begun were sufficiently increased by **Kepler** in polished ways to reach the desired goal. From here, those ornaments which could not be prepared by the ancients are handed over, most beautiful, to the new world.

<margin>The three Imperial Patrons of the restoration.</margin>
She says that the divine **RUDOLPH** munificently favored these things; that **MATTHIAS** was moved by equal nods of approval to promote these heavenly works; yet, because mortal hearts hold these as their highest prayers before they pass away, both fell before the end; and finally, that the laurel is owed to this man, **FERDINAND**; to him, if it is permitted for any to rejoice, the triumphs are due.

<margin>Privileges granted to Kepler.</margin>
With these words from the Queen, soon the other Queen of Birds <note>The Imperial Eagle</note> more mercifully spreads her pious wings and nods to the work with her golden scepter, as they were hesitating. Nor does she only promise Kings, or Dukes, or worldly gifts according to merits, and the commissions of fame, and a defense against the "gaping mouths" of writers <note>A reference to copyright protection and "privileges" against literary pirates</note>; but she also shows the propitious and ever-memorable power of the **AUGUSTUS** <note>The Emperor Ferdinand II</note>, in whose court the bird sits.

<margin>Imperial munificence.</margin>
She scatters the most certain proofs of the matter: coins, marked with the Imperial faces, masses of silver and ductile gold, the solaces of a meager gathering. It was a joy to have played <note>in poetry</note> upon these things above the **TEMPLE OF URANIA**, where **KEPLER** now burns joyful incense.

O, would that the Hours, moved by divine command, might allow my Muse Thalia to meditate on brave things after these wounds <note>Likely referring to the hardships of the Thirty Years' War</note>!

# PREFACE TO THE RUDOL-
## PHINE TABLES.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap initial 'D' depicting a landscape with trees and a building.</image-desc> *The science of the Stars has two parts: the former is concerning the Motions, and the latter is concerning the Effects of the Stars in the sublunary <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earthly world below the Moon, which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the "immutable" heavens.</note> nature. The Ancients were accustomed to call both by the common term, Astrology. But since there is a vast difference between these parts in terms of their certainty, later usage has succeeded in distinguishing them by names; so that the teaching of motions might be called Astronomy instead, because the laws of motion are immutable and consistent with the highest reason. The other part, however, being occupied with conjectures, held the formerly common name of Astrology as its own private title; for this part first created a place in the minds of men, who are ever looking to the future, for the contemplations of celestial things. For just as in man—the most excellent work of the entire Universe, indeed the Lord of all things and the image of God the creator—the principles of his origin are weak, trifles, and (having already contracted a stain <note>A reference to original sin or the perceived "lowliness" of biological beginnings.</note>) almost shameful: a tiny fluid and menstrual blood; a place in the lowliest part of the whole maternal body; for food when newly born, milk; for work, either sleep or wailing;*
<margin>Job 10:10 <note>This verse describes the formation of a fetus: "Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?"</note></margin>
*life is but grime, and clothing but a tangle: yet from this workshop, as it were, those come forth to us who build cities, who dig out harbors, who cut through mountains, who pave over straits with bridges; Princes, Kings, and Monarchs come forth. In the same way, that discipline capable of understanding the celestial machine—conceived first from the imagination of horrible eclipses of the sun and moon, and of long-haired stars <note>Comets.</note>, which appearances were followed by the most sorrowful misfortunes of the human race—thence drawing its very thin and obscure beginnings of formation, through beliefs about the stars and various figures of the constellations, and a desire for the future, it first conceived a certain vital force, as it were. Relying on this, it erupted openly into the light from the hiding places of thought and began to be boasted of publicly among men. Then, having been nurtured by the dreams and trifles of horoscopic <note>original: "Genethliacarum," referring to the casting of birth charts or nativities.</note> predictions, it gradually grew up; and at last, leaving behind its toys <note>original: "nucibus relictis," literally "leaving behind walnuts," a Roman idiom for leaving childhood games behind for the business of adulthood.</note> as they say, with manly daring, through the accustomed exercises of celestial Meditations, it passed into many uses of life, into admirable mechanical devices, and into the providing for necessary things; it even strives more and more, as if by certain steps, toward the improvement of morals, and indeed toward the knowledge of GOD the creator himself.*
<margin>Astronomy is the mother of Astrology. <note>The text later argues the reverse, suggesting Astrology was the "nurse" that funded and birthed the rigorous science of Astronomy.</note></margin>

*Nevertheless, just as the years appear in the bark <note>original: "libris," referring to the inner bark or rings of a tree.</note> of trees, so in the whole composition of this most divine art certain lineaments of this origin appear; so that the daughter and pupil, Astronomy, cannot deny her Mother and Nurse, Astrology. Its chief parts are held to be Observations, Hypotheses, Mechanics, and Calculation or Tables: each of which is directed toward predictions. A care looking to the future taught us to observe the positions of the Stars, as well as the rising of the Dog Star <note>Sirius, whose rising predicted the flooding of the Nile.</note> for fear of the Nile's floods. Craftsmen established Hypotheses so that, once the causes of the observed variations were placed in the open, not only could the Grain Supply <note>original: "Annona," the Roman concept of the yearly grain harvest and its price.</note> be foreseen from the Stars, but the Stars themselves could be foreseen from the Hypotheses, and there might be signs of future things in the mind before they were in the world. For this use, Arithmetic supplied Calculations and Tables, expressing the power of the Hypotheses; Mechanics supplied Circles, Theories, and Sundials <note>original: "Sciaterica."</note>; so that in the part where the weary mind might succumb, the hands might provide aid; and that in every way the path might be open and smoothed, leading straight to the present, past, or future position of the stars; so that by its gaze, clearly, the fates of those being born could be fashioned.*
<margin>The origin of Tables from Astrology.</margin>

*But in truth, these parts of the art—received from a childhood that was surely deep and foolish—were all approved, strengthened, and consolidated by the succeeding more mature age of practice and a more sublime and blameless end; so that henceforth the philosophy of the stars cannot do without them. He would go so far as to remove the Sun from the world, who would order Astronomical tables to be exiled from Philosophy and the pulpits of the learned.*
<margin>The end or use is nonetheless highly necessary.</margin>

<summary>In this preface, Kepler argues that although astronomy originated from the "foolish" and superstitious practices of astrology, it has matured into a vital, rigorous science that reveals the mind of God. He compares the development of the science to the growth of a child into a king, justifying the use of astronomical tables as essential tools for philosophy.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy vs astrology, celestial mechanics, Rudolphine Tables, history of science, Kepler, sublunary realm, hypotheses, grain supply prediction</keywords>
