<meta>This page continues the Preface of the Rudolphine Tables. On the previous page, Kepler began comparing the humble biological beginnings of humanity to the development of the science of the stars. Here, he pivots to the immense utility of astronomy and begins a chronological history of how astronomical tables "matured" from infancy to youth.</meta>

# ON THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES.

<meta>catchword: as if</meta>

<margin>Psalm 19.</margin> For even if I say nothing of the necessities of daily life, and of the arts that serve these principles—those which have been polished by Astronomy and must be repeatedly repaired and perfected; of Chronology, of the calculation of Feasts, of Agriculture, of Medicine, of Geography, and of Seafaring—let us instead look upon Metaphysics itself and Theology. If it is true, as all Philosophers and all Theologians of every age cry out, and as all the Saints inspired by the divine declare, that "the heavens declare the glory of GOD, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands" <note>original: "coeli & enarrant gloriam DEI, & opera manuum ejus annunciat firmamentum"</note>: by what part of ourselves do we perceive this more clearly? Is it with the eyes of our body, or the eyes of our mind? Indeed, we literate men share our physical eyes with the unlearned, and even with the beasts; though both the learned and unlearned gaze upon the admirable variety and beauty of the stars together, we do not perceive the inner adornment of the work—the order, consistency, and perpetuity of the celestial revolutions—with the naked eyes alone. Here, there is a need for the mind <note>original: "mente"</note>, for the memory of past observations, and the comparison of present ones; and finally, for the prediction of future positions. Thus, if we represent through the art of writing those things observed at any time, and see that those things we further predict happen in the same way, we are confirmed with the fullest persuasion regarding the immutable nature of the supreme mover <note>A common philosophical term for God as the "Prime Mover" who sets the universe in motion.</note>, and regarding the most provident governance of the world—concerning things, I say, that do not immediately strike the eyes and are widely called into great doubt. He who would cast aside these Astronomical Tables—the aid of memory, the product of studious midnight labor—would reduce the eyes of man to blindness, reduce the observations of the stars to those of brute beasts, and turn an undertaking worthy of man, taught by the succession of ages and the greatest labors of craftsmen concerning the most excellent matters, back into the cradle of ancient ignorance.

<column-break/>

<margin>All the ages of the Tables in exact Astrology.</margin>
But the same association of distinct goals, which gave Astronomy its first sublime origin, has persisted even in the perfection of the art; and the discipline has retained, through memory, the study of divination as an admonition to be emended through the ages. For to say nothing of the institutions of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia, famous for early sky-watching and astrology.</note>, obscured by the length of time so that barely a thin rumor of them survives to us: in the Parapegmata <note>term: <term>Parapegmata</term> (Ancient Greek almanacs or calendars, often inscribed on stone, used to track astronomical events and weather changes.)</note> of the Greeks, one may certainly see a sort of image of its childhood. You can see this in the celestial fixed year of Dionysius; when he perceived that the annual storms returned consistently to their days neither with the wandering meanders of the nineteen-year cycle <note>original: "Erradecaeteridis." This refers to the Metonic cycle used to align solar and lunar years.</note>, nor with the risings and settings of the Assyrian stars, he began to suspect the five "Wanderers" <note>original: "Errones," referring to the five planets visible to the naked eye (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn).</note>. 

<margin>Infancy in physics.</margin>
Here, the Greeks began to lend an ear to the Chaldeans, to whom the Greek Astronomers began to travel under the Seleucid kings. They began to join the appearances and disappearances of the Wanderers, and their acronychal <note>term: <term>acronychal</term> (The rising of a star or planet in the east at the exact moment the sun sets in the west.)</note> risings and settings, with the appearances of the fixed stars and the moon, and to record them in the Parapegmata of past years for the sake of memory, alongside the changes of the air. Nor does there exist anything older among these Greeks, or more precise among the Chaldeans themselves before they were brought under the power of the Macedonians, than the thought that an exact prediction of the motions of the five Planets could be grasped by art; they judged that this method itself should be aided by the artistic descriptions of their observations through circles and their fixed stars. For even though they saw that each of them observed certain cycles of years, the perpetual variety in that matter seemed to testify that those laws of revolutions were joined with much liberty—just as in a Republic there are fixed intervals for magistrates, or among the Romans, where the consulship was accustomed to be repeated after ten years. 

<margin>Not by Magic Chaldeans.</margin>
From this comes that word <term>μεσαυχρεπκή</term> <note>original: "mesaüchrepkē" (Likely a corruption of a Greek term meaning "self-directed" or "arbitrary").</note> taken from Cleomedes: "arbitrary motion," which we call "Proper Motion." From this came the opinion of divinity in the planets and power over human affairs; from this came those things in Chaldean Astrology, such as the casting of lots for magistrates: who is the lord of the birth <note>original: "dominus geniturae"</note>, the lord of the ascendant? Who presides over which day, which hour? How many votes does each one win? All these things savor of the opinion of liberty in the motions, and they lead to a neglect of exact determination and the approach to certain fixed stars.

<margin>The adolescence of the Tables under Hipparchus.</margin>
The later Hipparchus <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek astronomer, often considered the father of trigonometry.</note> took up and organized these Greek observations of the planets and compared them with the experience of his own time; he published a sort of rough draft of Tables, from which the temporal periods of each planet could be constructed, and the times of stations and retrogradations could be predefined by a looser calculation. This can be considered the "adolescence" of the Tables.

<margin>Youth under Ptolemy.</margin>
Ptolemy was the first who, having gathered into one the aids of the ancients (especially Hipparchus) and the motions of his own time, published a complete work of Tables...

<summary>Kepler argues for the theological and practical necessity of astronomical tables, framing the history of astronomy as a human life stage progressing from "infancy" in ancient Greece to "adolescence" under Hipparchus.</summary>
<keywords>Astronomy, Theology, Psalm 19, Parapegmata, Chaldeans, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, planets, proper motion, history of science</keywords>

--- Page 31 ---
<meta>This page continues the Preface of the Rudolphine Tables. The previous page discussed the philosophical and theological foundations of astronomy. Kepler now transitions into a historical narrative, tracing the "growth" of the science from its Greek maturity through its decline in the Middle Ages and its preservation in the Arabic-speaking world, finally leading to its rebirth in Europe and the work of German reformers like Regiomontanus.</meta>

### PREFACE.

<margin>He who was an Astrologer.</margin> ...as if he were establishing the youth of a science that had reached full stature. For although he everywhere brings forth thoughts in his great work pertaining to the Highest Philosophy, and expressly refers the <term>Astronomic art</term><note>Here meaning the mathematical study of the stars.</note> to its perfection, as was fitting: he was the same man who, besides his "Great Work" on motions <note>The *Almagest*, Ptolemy's foundational text on planetary motion.</note>, also published the "Four-part Work" on the Effects of the stars <note>The *Tetrabiblos*, Ptolemy's primary work on astrology.</note>. In both works, he addresses the same Syrus; and among the goals of his great work, he assigns a significant place to <term>Genethliac</term><note>original: "Genethliacis"; refers to the casting of nativities or birth charts (natal astrology).</note> predictions, which his other four-part work encompasses. In that work, you may see many of the 
<margin>And a Physicist.</margin> trifles of the Chaldeans <note>The ancient Babylonians, often associated with the origins of astrology.</note> reduced into a kind of systematic form; so that that previously most futile infancy of conjectural Astrology began, under this Master, to learn its first basic elements.

<margin>Astronomy's service departs to Africa.</margin> **BUT** Philosophy fell into difficult times during the age of Ptolemy and his successors. Greece was enslaved to the Romans, and along with her liberty, that ancient vigor of intellect had collapsed; right reason was no less contaminated by superstitions than her noble spirit was by a public, slavish patience. Indeed, even the people who professed **CHRIST**, then spreading throughout the whole world, because they were despised by the Philosophers of that time, in turn categorized the astrological art among the pagan arts. Because it was thoroughly stained with superstitions and soothsaying injurious to **GOD**, they sometimes dared to condemn it entirely; so much so that there were those who preferred to desert the science itself rather than their Christian identity. On the other side, new nations and empires arose: here the Huns and Goths, there the Arabs. The former were barbaric and dull-witted; the latter were indeed ingenious, but most superstitious. Therefore, driven out of Europe by the former and tumbling down to the latter in Africa, the discipline of the stars served a most foul slavery under horoscopists, sorcerers, magi, and interrogators, giving answers to anyone who asked, as if from the Tripod 
<margin>The correction of the Tables is neglected.</margin> in the place of oracles. For these men, seeking only profit and bound by impiety, the observation of the stars, the certainty of the Tables, and comparison with the heavens were not a concern at all for several centuries.

<margin>Resumed.</margin> Until at last, in the ninth and tenth centuries after Christ, both the Goths and Franks began to shed their barbarism, and the Saracens their superstition, as the former established empires and the latter propagated theirs far and wide. Then the Europeans also gradually began to reclaim a doctrine full of Divinity; and the Arabs, as well as learned Jews, began to pity its imperfections and took up the care of its correction. As the centuries proceeded, it finally happened—amidst the growing influence of **FREDERICK II** of the **HOUSE OF SWABIA**, 
<margin>As Astronomy returns to Europe, Astrology accompanies it.</margin> and **ALFONSO** of Spain, Emperors of the Romans—through trade with the Saracens in Palestine, Sicily, Italy, and Spain, that the practice and care of the art passed to the Christians of the West. Many books were translated from the Arabic into the Latin language, both many on astrology and even the "Great Work" of Ptolemy itself, which the Arabs were accustomed to call the *Almagest*, as if to say "The Greatest" <note>original: "τὸ μέγιστον" (to megiston).</note>. And although the clearly royal care of this **ALFONSO** soon shone forth—a care to be commended to all posterity—in the preparation of the Tables, which from him we call the **ALFONSINE TABLES**; yet the King himself, in the preface prefixed to some copies, takes the beginning of his speech from the connection of sublunary things with the motion of the stars, and displays a great presumption regarding the <term>Genethliac art</term><note>Natal astrology.</note>. Thus Astronomy never forgets its own milk, nor, though fully grown, can it entirely abstain from it.

<margin>Astronomy's transition into adulthood.</margin> A fortunate age for literature followed the **TABLES** corrected under Alfonso, in which many new Universities were awakened across Europe from a few ancient ones. These now established a kind of manly age for Astronomy; superstitions were more and more wiped away from the knowledge of most excellent things, and the discipline was recalled to its supreme goal and its utilities in common life: to Geography and the Art of Navigation. This art has since 
<margin>Its achievements.</margin> opened a New World, joined the East to the West externally, and united nearly the whole of both under one Empire. There was also added an internal concern arising from religion: that of correcting the Feast of Easter, the errors of 
<margin>The Germans attempt the correction of the Alfonsine Tables.</margin> which were brought more clearly into view through the propagation of the art. Thus they themselves, and their disciples throughout Germany and Italy—Walther at Nuremberg, Domenico Maria at Bologna—applied themselves more diligently to the observation of the stars and recorded them, either for their own use or for posterity. They also brought to light the ancient monuments of Ptolemy, Albategnius <note>Al-Battani, a 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note>, Geber <note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century Andalusian astronomer.</note>, and Alfonso, aiding them with explanations, correcting them, and preparing all parts of the doctrine of the Sphere with new auxiliary tables for the easier use of the art. <meta>This page continues the historical narrative from page 3, moving from the preservation of astronomy in the Greek and Arabic traditions to its renewal in Northern Europe. It focuses on the transition from the work of Copernicus to the more user-friendly "Prutenic Tables" of Erasmus Reinhold, while discussing the practical and philosophical relationship between astronomy and astrology during the 16th century.</meta>

### TO THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES

...he would have been equal to the task had his life not been cut short by an untimely fate. Nevertheless, the care of this reformation fell to **NICOLAUS COPERNICUS**, a Canon of <term>Warmia</term><note>A region in Poland; Copernicus spent most of his life here as a church official.</note> and a Prussian, who was a disciple of **DOMENICO MARIA** <note>Domenico Maria Novara (1454–1504), an astronomer at Bologna who influenced Copernicus.</note>. He was a man of the greatest genius and—what is of great importance in this pursuit—of a free mind. For twenty-seven whole years, he kept his work *On the Revolutions of the Planets* (which encompassed a reformation of the Tables and was prepared with immense labor in a new form) hidden away in his desk. Finally, as he was treading upon the very threshold of death, he sent it to Nuremberg to be published.

<margin>The origin of the Prutenic Tables.</margin>
Although this work contains Tables added to the explanations of his proofs, there is no one today, as far as I know, who employs them for calculation. For in the years following, **ERASMUS REINHOLD** succeeded him. Reinhold was a man most highly accomplished in every branch of learning, but especially fashioned by nature for the mathematical arts, possessing an admirable clarity and ease in explaining abstruse matters. He undertook the transformation of this work of the Tables by the then-deceased Copernicus, and he named them the **PRUTENIC TABLES** <note>original: "Prutenicas"; Prussian Tables.</note>, either after Copernicus the Prussian, or after his own **PATRON** <note>original: "Moecenate"; a reference to Gaius Maecenas, the Roman patron of the arts.</note>, the Duke of Prussia, and he based them on a chosen local <term>Meridian</term><note>The longitudinal line used as a reference point for time and planetary positions.</note>. For the "Royal Mountain" <note>Königsberg (modern Kaliningrad).</note> to which the <term>Epochs</term><note>Reference dates for astronomical calculations.</note> of the Prutenic Tables are adapted is not that one in Eastern Franconia which was the homeland of Regiomontanus, but rather the other town in the Duchy of Prussia on the shore of the Baltic Sea.

The reasons **REINHOLD** gives for taking up this task can be seen in his own writing, though he seems to hide two of them. First, while Tables ought to be <term>handy manuals</term><note>original: "πρόχειροι" (procheiroi); meaning "at hand" or ready for use.</note> prepared for practical use—as the **ALPHONSINE** <note>The standard astronomical tables of the Middle Ages, commissioned by Alfonso X of Castile.</note> and other authors of Tables had aided this manual use by the very form of their books, presenting the tables of numbers in a single sequence with very brief instructions at the start—**COPERNICUS**, by contrast, has his Tables scattered throughout the text of his proofs, just like the **PTOLEMAIC** *Syntaxis* <note>Better known as the *Almagest*.</note>. Thus, for those seeking speculation in the text and practical use in the Table, the mind is distracted, and the work itself is deprived of its primary utility. Secondly, **COPERNICUS** insisted upon absurd hypotheses <note>A reference to the sun-centered (heliocentric) model, which many 16th-century scholars found physically "absurd" even if mathematically useful.</note>, which **REINHOLD** believed would frighten off offended readers. He therefore decided he must do this: omitting any mention of those marvelous suppositions, and omitting the long and tedious proofs, he would provide the Tables themselves separately in a manual, corrected and calculated more diligently, so that they might more exactly represent the fundamental observations upon which they had been built by **COPERNICUS**.

<margin>His acquaintance with Astrology.</margin>
Having taken this course, **REINHOLD** indicates that in attacking the work, he had exhausted himself with an immense and unpleasant labor. If you ask about its purpose, it is indeed praiseworthy: the certain knowledge of motions; the measurement and boundaries of the year, equinoxes, solstices, eclipses, and great conjunctions; so that from the most fitting order of these things, the wisdom and goodness of the **CREATOR** might shine forth. Yet, at the same time, the author does not hide his study of predictions. In few but pregnant words, he hints at what he attributes to the <term>Genethliac art</term><note>Natal astrology (casting birth charts).</note>, asserting that events in this lower nature are either caused or signified by the motions and positions of the stars, and can thus be predicted.

<margin>Whence Astronomy derives its livelihood.</margin>
Why say more? With a different mental perspective, he would more rightly have made the one who was hitherto the mother into the grandmother, and the daughter into the mother; from whom is born a granddaughter reflecting the face of the grandmother: **Astrology** again. As I once wrote on this subject: foolish daughter Astrology supports and sustains her mother, the most wise but very poor Astronomy, by an income that is not equally approved of by everyone. And the author [Reinhold] seems to concede this very point even while appearing to deny it. For while he denies that he preferred divinations over the learned and useful labor of the Tables, he nonetheless indicates he was well-versed in this kind of exercise and confesses to giving it the second place of importance.

**NEVERTHELESS**, lest anyone think this implies that I consider this most learned man to be numbered among those superstitious Arabs whose only care was for profit and none for Philosophy: I exhort readers to read his preface to the *Theories of Peurbach* <note>Georg von Peurbach (1423–1461), an astronomer whose textbook was standard for decades.</note>, which he composed in the year 1542 in a most pure and pleasant style. For in it, blossoms breathe from the innermost gardens of Philosophy with an admirable fragrance that ravishes the very mind of the reader; so much so that even if someone were to deny that human events depend on the stars, they would certainly be compelled to recognize some effects of the stars in human affairs. Refer to page 178 of that Commentary on Peurbach, and also to page 197.

<margin>The maturity of the Tables.</margin>
**BUT** let our discourse return to where it digressed; and let it now assign to Astronomy—now that she has been brought among men—her own maturity and consistent age. For regarding what **Reinhold** affirms about the **ALPHONSINE** Tables, experts know that they no longer [agree] with the phenomena...

### PREFACE OF THE AUTHOR.

...agree: the same must also be said of these *Prutenic Tables* <note>The astronomical tables published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551, based on the theories of Copernicus.</note>, about which many men most experienced in observations have complained. This very year, **1625**, served as the most evident proof: throughout the entire year, the star **MARS** was observed in the heavens to be much further advanced than the *Prutenic* calculation had predicted. This discrepancy grew during the months of *August, September, and October*, reaching a magnitude of four, and nearly five, degrees. For as it happens, *Reinhold*—following conjectures drawn from only a few instances since sufficient observations had not yet been recorded by anyone—judged that while the "file" of correction <note>Kepler uses the metaphor of a "file" (limæ) to mean the fine-tuning or smoothing out of mathematical errors.</note> might be needed for the mean motions, the tables of **prosthaphæreses** <term>prosthaphæresis</term><note>A technical term in pre-Keplerian astronomy referring to the geometric correction added to or subtracted from a planet's mean position to find its true position.</note> would serve usefully both backward and forward for the entire duration of the world. In this example, he is found to have been deceived in both respects. For in the mean motion of **MARS**, only a very small change was required; however, the entire error of this year arose from flaws in the *Prutenic prosthaphæreses*.

<margin>Tycho Brahe undertakes to emend the *Prutenic Tables*.</margin>
**Therefore**, when learned men experienced in the observation of the stars detected such aberrations in the *Prutenic Tables* from the time they were first published—among whom must be mentioned for his supreme merit as a leader, the Most Illustrious **WILLIAM, Prince of the Hessians** <note>William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel (1532–1592), a pioneering patron of observational astronomy.</note>—there finally arose **TYCHO BRAHE**. Born of the highest nobility of the Kingdom of *Denmark*, he disregarded the typical pursuits of his peers and embraced the *restoration of Astronomy* with a great soul. He chose this as his sole work in which to spend his life and to expend the splendid ancestral wealth with which he was supported. And what I count as the foremost part of his glory: he did this with a mind free from all astrological superstitions, directed toward that one supreme end of all *Philosophy*—the knowledge of both **GOD** and **himself**. This he made most manifest with a very constant steadiness, both in the writings and poems in which he took delight, and in his daily conversations.

<margin>A despiser of Astrology, while preserving physics.</margin>
Indeed, he was accustomed to greatly mock and detest the vanity, laziness, ignorance, and filth of the *Astrologers*. He did so, however, in such a way that he by no means denied the effects of the stars upon sublunary things—a most excellent part of *Philosophy*—without compromising physics. He was skilled at distinguishing those general effects of the stars from the actual events in individual human affairs by a most accurate judgment. Since the common crowd of men could not grasp this—being credulous toward miraculous predictions and prompt to spread false rumors, and thus most vain in both respects—they sometimes exposed this most innocent man to the oblique talk and envy of the Great Lords through an inept zeal for his fame.

<margin>The first author of the *Rudolphine Tables*.</margin>
**He**, therefore, is the first namer of the **RUDOLPHINE TABLES**; he is the arranger of the thousand **Fixed Stars**, the explorer of the motions of the *Sun and Moon*, and the observer of all the planets through **38** years—and of these, through the latter **20** continuous years—surpassing all human belief in his diligence, circumspection, patience, and constancy.

<margin>*Christian Severin Longimontanus*, Tycho’s calculator. *Kepler’s* association with *Tycho*.</margin>
**But** what he achieved in the motions of each of the remaining planets beyond what has already been said, I prefer the reader to learn from the *Danish Astronomy* of **Christian Severin Longimontanus** rather than from my own report. For he lived with **TYCHO** for ten continuous years; I lived with him for barely a few months of his final two years. For in the year **1600**, in the month of *February*, I first came to **TYCHO** at *Benatek* <note>Benátky nad Jizerou, near Prague, where Tycho had his observatory.</note>, while *Longimontanus* was present. I had been frequently summoned by letters from **TYCHO** out of *Styria* <note>The region in modern-day Austria where Kepler had been teaching.</note>, the opportunity having been provided by the publication of my *Cosmographic Mystery*. Having made a pact with him, I returned to *Styria* in the month of *June* to fetch my family and my library. In *October* of that same year, when *Longimontanus* had already departed, I presented myself to **TYCHO** with my family at *Prague*, but I was useless: for a quartan fever <note>A form of malaria characterized by paroxysms that occur every fourth day.</note> had seized me on the journey and held me until the solstice of the following year. Nor did it leave me until I had hurried back to *Graz* <note>Latin: Gratium.</note> on account of an inheritance. Having returned to *Prague* in the month of *September*, I was able to enjoy the conversation of **TYCHO** for no more than two months before death snatched him away on the 24th day of the next *November*, New Style.

<margin>Which parts of the *Rudolphine Tables* have existed for a long time.</margin>
**Therefore**, as to which parts of the **RUDOLPHINE TABLES** **TYCHO** completed while he survived, and what aids or instructions he left behind for completing what remained: *Longimontanus* would be the most proper witness. He reports those corrections of *Tycho* **in their general outline** <note>original: "ὁλοσχερῶς" (holoscheros); meaning completely or in broad strokes.</note> for all the planets, and he employed them as trustworthy foundations in computing his own tables. Although I also indicated some things in the *Commentaries on MARS* <note>Kepler’s *Astronomia Nova* (1609).</note>, and there exists my letter on these matters written in the year **1601** from *Graz* to *Giovanni Antonio Magini*, Professor of Mathematics in the Acad—

# ON THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES

...recorded at the University of Padua; which he <note>Referring to the astronomer Giovanni Antonio Magini.</note> first published twelve years ago, without my knowledge, at Bologna in his supplement to the *Ephemerides*; and this work of his was reprinted with my letter in the year **1614** at Frankfurt.

Since, however, I published my aforementioned *Commentaries* on the motions of the star **MARS** <note>Kepler’s *Astronomia Nova* (1609), where he first proposed elliptical orbits.</note>—first begun at Benatky <note>Tycho's observatory near Prague.</note> as part of the work of the Tables left by **TYCHO BRAHE**—eight years after Tycho's death: Magini, impatient of the delays, calculated the Tables of the **prosthaphæreses** <term>prosthaphæresis</term><note>A geometric correction used to find a planet's true position; Magini adapted Kepler's new findings into the older, more familiar table format.</note> of **MARS** from that work, based indeed on the foundations I had laid, yet in the customary form, and made them part of his supplement; he also repeated the Tables of the motions of the sun and moon from Volume I of the *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho’s *Exercises in the Restoration of Astronomy*.</note>. Indeed, **TYCHO BRAHE** had completed the full catalogue of a thousand fixed stars before he came to Bohemia, and he sent manuscript copies far and wide to the libraries of Kings and Princes. I myself was the bearer of the one sent to Vienna when, in the year **1600**, leaving Benatky in Bohemia and heading into Styria, I passed through Vienna. From one of these copies, I believe Johannes Gruenperger of the Society of Jesus <note>The Jesuits.</note> derived these thousand fixed stars for his Roman edition on the fixed stars; for the numbers agree. Longomontanus <note>Christian Longomontanus, Tycho’s long-term assistant.</note> inserted the same thousand fixed stars into his *Danish Astronomy*, differing only by a single minute of longitude.

<margin>What Kepler contributed to the RUDOLPHINE TABLES.</margin>
Thus, it has long been that from this "shipwreck" of **BRAHE’S** astronomy, everyone attaches the salvaged tables to their own boat. It is well known to students of astronomy by the testimony of many which parts of these Tables are the genuine work of **TYCHO BRAHE**, and which, in turn, are mine—or to which I have given a new form. Certainly, wherever possible, I have selected the fundamental observations of the present age from **BRAHE** alone; I have adopted those of others and a few of my own only for the sake of agreement, or because Tycho's observations were not available to me for the specific days I needed.

But regarding each of these points, something has been said in the introduction to my *Ephemerides*, and there will be another place for saying more. For manual tables <note>Reference books meant for daily use by astronomers.</note> ought to be free from the weight that would come to them from long-winded commentaries. Meanwhile, the reader has the theoretical part of the *Epitome of Astronomy* published by me in the year **1621**: in which book you will find both the forms of the particular hypotheses—for the general hypothesis, as I demonstrated in the *Commentaries on MARS*, is common to **PTOLEMY**, **COPERNICUS**, and **TYCHO**—and the method of calculating each and every part of these Tables from them.

<margin>Causes for the composition of the RUDOLPHINE TABLES taking so long. Indeed, now the twenty-sixth year.</margin>
Here, before I finish, the place reminds me to excuse the so very long delays in the publication of these Tables; for this is the twenty-fourth year <note>Kepler notes in the margin that it is actually now the twenty-sixth year.</note> since the death of **TYCHO BRAHE**; during all of which time I have earned the courtly salaries of three Austrian **EMPERORS**: to which was added in later years also the annual stipend of the Lords of the Archduchy of Upper Austria. But if time long since lost cannot be compensated for otherwise than by the expenditure of both present time and effort: let us therefore rather hold onto the present and leave the elapsed time to criticism. Although it is neither necessary to recount the difficulties of courtly obstacles—especially with intervening wars—to the experienced, nor easy to persuade the ignorant. What, however, I have achieved in the meantime through constant meditation, having overcome those difficulties—what benefits have redounded to the perfection of celestial philosophy from the efforts of meditation interposed during the delays—both my books will speak, which I have meanwhile presented for public use; and the very method of philosophizing, the novelty of the discoveries, and the unexpected transformation of the entire Astronomy, from fictitious circles <note>The "circles" refer to epicycles and eccentrics, the abstract geometric tools used by previous astronomers.</note> to natural causes, most profound to investigate, and most difficult to explain and calculate in my first attempt: these things, I say, and similar ones, will render a most sufficient account of the time to those who understand.

<margin>Defense of the innovation regarding the rejection of real circles and the introduction of physical causes.</margin>
**FORTASSE** <note>original: "Perhaps"</note> verò <note>original: "but/indeed"</note> this delay I mentioned, spent in unearthing the natural causes of motions, will seem to some unnecessary, troublesome, and even useless. To such thoughts I have already opposed other suitable considerations long ago, both in the introduction to the *Ephemerides* (where I respond to David Fabricius) and in the *Epitome of Astronomy* in the chapter on the causes of Hypotheses, and in the preface to Book IV. Even if that defense alone could suffice for me: that what **TYCHO BRAHE** first conceived in his mind while establishing the theory of the moon, and pronounced publicly—that it seemed the causes of motions were physical; which indeed cannot seem otherwise to one who rejects the solidity of the spheres <note>The ancient belief that planets were embedded in physical, crystal shells.</note>: these things, I say, I have both demonstrated with no unhappy effort to be the case for all the planets, and have taught how to reduce them to calculations; and by that means, I have both asserted and strengthened the suppositions and sayings of the first author of the *RUDOLPHINE TABLES*, my Master, according to the capacity of my talent.

<summary>Kepler accounts for the long delay in publishing the Tables, citing courtly duties and wars, but primarily his revolutionary work in replacing abstract geometric circles with physical laws of motion. He defends his contributions as a fulfillment of Tycho Brahe's own suspicions that celestial movements were driven by physical forces.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Kepler’s justification for his revolutionary approach to astronomy. Having previously discussed the "wreckage" of Tycho Brahe’s data and the work of Magini, Kepler now addresses his critics—specifically those who believe physics (the study of physical causes) has no place in the geometry of the heavens.</meta>

# PREFACE ON PHYSICS

But there will also be those who, disregarding these warnings, will try to overwhelm me with the authority of the man I praised above, **ERASMUS REINHOLD**, the astronomer and philosopher. In his commentary on Peurbach <note>Georg von Peurbach, author of the standard medieval textbook on planetary theory.</note>, Reinhold did not think physical disputes should be stuffed into the work, as others have done. He asks: what is more foolish than to disturb and harass Geometric discoveries with the conjectures of the Physicists? Yet, whoever reads those words, I would wish you to consider the goal toward which Reinhold directed them. He is not arguing with *Ptolemy*, nor with *Aristotle*, nor with himself, for in the final preface to his *Theories* he uses these words: *Perhaps,* he says, *these seven luminous bodies <note>The Sun, Moon, and five visible planets.</note>, even without the kind of orbs <note>The traditional "crystalline spheres" thought to carry the planets.</note> which art—or rather the weakness of our intellect—asks to be granted to it, possess a divinely implanted power so that each maintains its own law and perpetual harmony amidst the variety and irregularity of its motions;* yet for us, without all these many orbs, it would be very difficult to grasp that "harmony of irregularity" (if I may call it so) with the mind or to follow it in thought. By these words, he does not repel, but rather silently invites the man who brings forward such forms of motion, natural instruments, and kindred magnetic forces <note>Kepler’s own theory that planets are moved by physical, magnetic-like forces from the Sun.</note> that are not only more rational than those many vast orbs, but also offer the mind a way to grasp the apparent irregularities of motion easily, making them far more efficient for calculation than the orbs themselves. And so I have made this attempt, following even the persuasion of *Ptolemy* himself (lest anyone think I lack an authority from the ancients), who commands us to devise hypotheses that are as simple and probable as possible.

<margin>
Added to this were two years during which the work, though long completed, waited for publication. During this time, besides other calamities shaking the province where I had made my home with continuous assaults, it was finally utterly disturbed and ruined by the Peasant War <note>The Upper Austrian Peasant War of 1626, which occurred while Kepler was trying to print these Tables in Linz.</note>—a true "Iliad of evils"—so that I had to resume the task with new expenses, new plans, and new journeys.
</margin>

As for Reinhold’s excuse for omitting physical disputes, it is easy for anyone who has read *Cremonensis* <note>Gerard of Sabbioneta, a medieval commentator.</note> or other commentators on the *Sphere* to judge what he meant. Those authors turned a great part of Physics and Metaphysics into a discussion of the "orbs" introduced by astronomers, treating them as if they were a fully explored reality. By searching everywhere for many arguments to support conflicting opinions, they created a useless and infinite chaos of ridiculous questions. They had no care for directing those disputes toward the instruction or ease of calculation, or for explaining the reasons for what appears among the stars. Consequently, the calculations stood on their own even when those useless disputes were cut away, even if the practitioner doubted the reality of the orbs entirely—which has just now been established regarding Reinhold from his own confession, and which *Ptolemy* himself made very clear throughout his *Great Work* <note>The Almagest.</note>. This is surely what Reinhold meant by "harassing and disturbing Geometric discoveries" (which have their own proofs) with the tricks of conjecture. This same thing might happen to me: some insolent boaster of the art might arise and, having no regard for the celestial appearances which these tables represent, deny ironically <note>original: "κατ' ἀντίφρασιν" (kat’ antiphrasin)</note> that they are true and consider them overturned, if he should undertake to demonstrate that the physical principles I lay down are false. But even if I hope to defend the principles on which I rely before other tribunals, in this art I consider it enough if, through them, I set the necessary definitions and rules before the eyes of the calculator more clearly than through solid orbs. On that account, I consider both my replacement of solid orbs with physical causes of motion to be defended, and the cause of such great delays to be now fully explained. Therefore, returning to that common saying, *soon enough if well enough*, I proclaim the highest praise to the immortal GOD, who has prolonged the flexible course of my mortal life to this very day, on which I finally lay the finishing hand upon the work destined for His praise and for human use, triumphing over all difficulties by His gracious help.

<margin>
How great is the certainty of the Rudolphine Tables?
</margin>

As for the certainty of the calculation, the observations of the present times will bear witness, especially those of **BRAHE**. Regarding future times, however, we can presume no more than what either the observations of the ancients (which I have used) or the condition of the "mean motions" themselves (not yet fully explored) and the concurrence of physical causes can provide. For the observations of Regiomontanus and Walther <note>15th-century astronomers whose data helped bridge the gap between antiquity and Tycho Brahe.</note> testify that we must certainly think about "secular equations" <note>Corrections for very long-term changes in planetary orbits.</note>, as I shall demonstrate in a special booklet in due time. However, what kind and how great these equations are cannot be defined by the human race before the passing of many centuries and the observations of those yet to be born. See the beautiful comments on this opinion by *Willebrord Snell* at the end of the observations of the *Landgrave* <note>William IV of Hesse-Kassel.</note> and some of *Tycho’s*. Moreover, you have below, in the doctrine of Eclipses, clear evidence even from current observations that the motions of the sun, moon, and the first mover <note>The "Primum Mobile," the outermost sphere in traditional cosmology.</note> are not equal according to a strict mathematical "ruler," but are subject to minor physical intensifications and remissions <note>speeding up and slowing down</note> outside the normal order.

<summary>Kepler defends his "physical" approach to astronomy against critics who prefer pure geometry, arguing that his theories of physical forces are more rational and practical than the traditional belief in solid celestial spheres. He also notes the delays caused by the 1626 Peasant War and acknowledges that the long-term accuracy of astronomical tables depends on observations spanning many centuries.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from Kepler's defense of his physical theories to a formal acknowledgement of his patrons. Having just finished arguing that his "magnetic" astronomy is a valid pursuit, he now turns to credit the House of Austria (the Habsburgs) for providing the resources and continuity required to complete the Tables across three different reigns.</meta>

# PREFACE TO THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES

Whatever utility might flow from this work of Tables—whether to students of Astronomy or even to Philosophers and Theologians, both present and future—let them remember that it is all to be credited to the benefit of my patrons, whom I have commemorated above. Therefore, let everyone join me in lifting up with the highest praise (as they deserve) **AUSTRIA**, and the family of Princes who, with God guiding their success, ascended from the possession of that land from which they take their name to the dominion of the whole world. Finally, let them praise three most August <note>In this context, "August" (Latin: *Augustissimus*) is a formal title for the Holy Roman Emperor, referencing the majesty of the first Roman Emperor, Augustus.</note> Emperors from that house:

First, **RUDOLPH II**, who called Tycho Brahe <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a Danish nobleman and the most famous observational astronomer of the era; his massive collection of data formed the basis for Kepler's work.</note> from his homeland of Denmark into Germany under the most splendid conditions, worthy of his illustrious origin. It was he who gave me to Tycho as an assistant while he lived, and appointed me as his successor for this part of the work after his death; he who accepted and ratified the title **RUDOLPHINE**, which had been proposed by Brahe while he was still alive; and he who, during his lifetime, designated the funds suitable for these editions.

Next, **MATTHIAS I**, who, along with the provinces, kingdoms, and the Roman Empire, also took upon himself from his brother the care of this art and my own patronage.

Finally, **FERDINAND II**, who, in addition to continuing all the same support, actually provided the designated funds, increased them with a new liberality, and commanded that the Tables be published. I say, let everyone freely join me in praising them as they deserve, and let everyone offer prayers for the well-being of this entire most August House.

### CHAPTER I.

## ON LOGISTIC ARITHMETIC, NECESSARY FOR THESE TABLES.

Reinhold <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), author of the Prutenic Tables, which were the standard astronomical tables before Kepler’s.</note> and Magini <note>Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), an Italian astronomer and contemporary of Kepler.</note> (in his revised works) place the art of calculating "logistic" numbers <note>term: Logistic Arithmetic — The system of calculating with sexagesimal fractions (base-60), which are still used today for degrees, minutes, and seconds.</note> at the very beginning of the Prutenic Tables. I presuppose that this art ought to be known, especially to those who do not wish to adopt the use of Logarithms. Therefore, if anyone has forgotten these logistic rules or needs to learn them anew, let them return to the Prutenic Tables or to other mathematicians who either hand down the rules of logistics or provide their proofs; among the Greeks, Barlaam the Monk <note>Barlaam of Seminara (c. 1290–1348), a Byzantine scholar who wrote a significant treatise on logistic arithmetic.</note> is numbered among them.

<margin>Why the Table of Sixties was omitted.</margin>
The reader will find in the aforementioned authors a "Table of Sixties" <note>original: "Canon Hexacontádon"</note>, by whose aid logistic multiplications, divisions, and the extraction of roots are performed. I decided that this Table should not be included among the present Tables for this very reason: it serves the old way of calculating. In these Tables, a new method is taught—without the Table of Sixties, without mental fatigue, and even with a saving of time—for multiplying and dividing logistically with as much accuracy and precision as the purpose of the Tables requires.

## ON NUMERATION.

<margin>The numbering of intervals.</margin>
<margin>Where logistic numbering is applied.</margin>
As far as logistic numeration is concerned, the calculator must be advised in a single word that, following the custom of the first author, Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, whose data Kepler used.</note>, a distinction is observed in these Tables: the intervals <note>distances</note> of the Planets are expressed in "absolute" numbers, using a scale where the mean distance between the Sun and the Earth is 100,000. However, the positions of longitude and latitude, their mean motions, the equations <note>original: "Prosthaphæreses" — corrections applied to mean planetary positions to find the true position.</note>, and the anomalies are expressed in "figured" or logistic numbers based on the sexagesimal system <note>units of 60</note>, just as in the tables of other authors—at least in two types, namely Minutes and Seconds. These logistic numbers inserted into the text I have mostly marked with their own strokes or indices of their type <note>i.e., ' and ''.</note>.

<margin>How whole units are completed.</margin>
<margin>What a Sign is.</margin>
The only difference is in the grouping of whole units. Here, sixty whole parts or degrees are rarely collected into one "sixty" <note>original: "sexagena"</note>; instead, thirty degrees are collected into one Sign of the Zodiac. Furthermore, where the numbering does not begin with the Zodiac, we mostly count in a continuous series from one whole unit up to 180° for a semicircle, or to 360° for a full circle, without grouping the whole numbers into Signs or sixties.

The reason for this is that the use of long and difficult logistic multiplications and divisions—which require grouping into sixties—is almost non-existent now that the tables are finished. Everything is performed much more easily, even if you are only moderately

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

attentive, by using the common division of the Zodiac into twelve signs.

For this purpose, the Epochs <note>the reference dates for astronomical positions</note> or the "roots" of the motions are expressed not in "physical" signs (as others call the groups of sixty), but in the "usual" signs <note>the 12 signs of the Zodiac</note>, following the custom that Brahe held in the first volume of his *Progymnasmata*. The mean motions are treated similarly.

<margin>Where is the symbol of the current sign used?</margin>
It also pertains to this that the positions in the Zodiac of the Apogees <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> and Aphelions <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the Sun</note>, as well as the nodes of the five planets, are not marked by the number of signs completed from the start of the Zodiac because of their very slow motion. Instead, they are marked by the symbol <note>e.g., ♈, ♉</note> of the sign in which each of them is currently located; though the degrees, minutes, and seconds are understood as being completed.

<margin>Grouping of whole hours into days, not sixties.</margin>
Similar things must be said about hours. Although each hour is worth 60 minutes, and a minute 60 seconds, etc., sixty hours are not treated as one "sixty"; rather, 24 hours are treated as one natural day.

<margin>The distinction of times.</margin>
Regarding other time units, such as days, months, and years, it is necessary to note whether they are understood as "current" <note>elapsed time plus the one in progress</note> or "completed."

<margin>The numbering of Logarithms.</margin>
It remains for me to speak also of the Logarithms, which are inserted here and there in the planetary tables. These are written just like the intervals of the Planets, in a continuous order of digits without punctuation when they are in use, according to the custom of common and simple Arithmetic.

<margin>Negative values.</margin>
They have this peculiarity, however: some of them are positive, and others are negative <note>original: "privativi"</note>. The positive ones are those to which either no sign is added or to which this sign + should be prefixed; the negative ones are those that must have this sign — prefixed. These signs are mostly placed at the top of the columns in which the Logarithms are inserted. To distinguish a Logarithm from an absolute number more easily, I have seen to it that all Logarithms, when they are mixed with absolute numbers in the same column, are expressed in lowercase <note>small-print</note> characters.

The method for writing "Mesologarithms" <note>Kepler’s term for logarithms of sines or other trigonometric functions</note> is the same, insofar as they serve the latitudes of the planets.

Regarding the punctuation of the "Heptacosian" Logarithms <note>Kepler’s base-100/7 logarithms</note> and the Antilogarithms (which we indeed need for Eclipses), instructions will follow in Chapter XI; and regarding the counting of "scruples" <note>small fractions</note> in the Table of the Rising Angle, by parts of the "As" <note>a Roman unit divided into 12 parts</note>, in Chapter XIV.

# RUDOLPHINE TABLES

<margin>RULE I. On the handling of whole numbers and parts.</margin>

<note>The first paragraph is about addition of figures in tables.</note>
**RULE I.** Regarding both whole and fractional <note>original: "figuratis seu logisticis"</note> numbers. In the **Addition** of these figures, specifically for the use of these tables, whether they be whole numbers or parts of the numbering system explained previously, there is this one caution: whenever the sum of two or more figures results in a sum or degree of 360°, that amount should be cast away, and only the remainder should be kept as the Total.

<note>The next paragraph discusses subtraction.</note>
Conversely, in **Subtraction** (taking one from another), first attend to this carefully: if the number to be subtracted is presumed to be larger than the one from which it is being taken, then a unit of the next higher rank must be added to the left-side degree; thus the sum will not be less than 360° (or in this case, 12 signs, which equals one full circle).

<note>This paragraph continues on addition principles.</note>
Whenever in **Addition** it happens that the sum of one member or species exceeds 30° (for signs) or 24 hours (for days)—the first being composed of zodiac signs and the latter of days—you must subtract those 30° or 24 hours and increase the preceding rank of the sum by one unit.

<note>This paragraph further explains subtraction principles.</note>
In **Subtraction**, if the number to be subtracted in any rank is clearly larger than the one it is being taken from, it cannot be removed unless a unit is taken <note>or "borrowed"</note> from the preceding rank and resolved into the units of the rank being subtracted. Diligent care must be taken so that you do not forget: one Prime <note>minute</note> is worth 60 Seconds, and one whole degree (or figure) is worth one Prime. Furthermore, one sign is worth 30 degrees, one day is worth 24 hours, and one year is worth 365 days (or 366 in a leap year). Here, the drowsy calculator often trips up.

<note>This paragraph explains how to handle numbers not yet fully formed or complete.</note>
If in either of the numbers to be added or subtracted there is expressed a "current" month or a symbol for a "sign" not yet completed: in their place, one must take the number of all the days in the months completed *before* the current one. Likewise, for signs, take the number of signs already traversed before the current one. This number of completed figures must then be resolved into degrees. If these are combined with the remaining days or degrees (which are beyond the whole units), they must be cast into a single sum, provided the first species of the other number on the left is also in days or degrees.

<note>This paragraph addresses calculations for incomplete periods like years, days, or months.</note>
This method of working through "completed" units is universal and therefore safe. But even without formal instruction, daily experience will provide it; it will also be easy for the calculator to observe shortcuts <margin>Special rules and cautions in the addition and subtraction of incomplete values.</margin> such as this: whenever a number of whole days or years is added to an "incomplete" sign, day, or year, the resulting sum will have its last unit incomplete. The same observation holds true in subtraction, especially if the number to be subtracted is small; by taking the number of completed units from the "current" number, the remainder remains a "current" number. But never should "current" values be added to "current" values, nor one subtracted from the other, unless we wish the remainders to be "completed" units.

<column-break/>

It is not worth the effort to provide examples for these observations, as they are very easy and will be repeatedly emphasized in the following instructions.

### CHAPTER III.
### *ON LOGISTIC MULTIPLICATION AND DIVISION, AS PREPARED FOR THESE TABLES, AND ON THE HEPTACOSIADE, BY WHOSE AID WE ARE SUPPORTED AND RELIEVED.*

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'E' adorns the beginning of the paragraph. It features intricate scrollwork and possibly a small face or figure within its design.</image-desc>

**E**ven as the doctrine, as mentioned above, is left in its proper place in these Tables, the calculator may seek it from the named authors. From them, one learns that the entire operation cannot be performed unless numbering is established through a perpetual Sexagenary <note>base-60</note> collection. Although the sum of one Sexagena <note>sixty</note> of wholes is then used for 2 usual signs, one should write it as a "sixty" or a sign, as <margin>Physical sign.</margin> follows. Therefore, nothing should hinder the calculator of the tables who wishes to subtract, whether he follows the Tychonic method <note>referring to Tycho Brahe</note> or the one observed here in the Tables.

<note>This paragraph explains difficulties in calculations and the use of the Heptacosiade.</note>
Because those old "logistic" <note>sexagesimal</note> additions and divisions involve a great deal of labor and trouble even for the most experienced, and since the primary purpose of these Tables is to reduce the labor of computing, to spare the powers of the intent mind, and to save time: I made this decision six years ago to introduce Napierian Logarithms into logistics as a great supplement. I gave some specimen of this matter in the *Chilias* <note>Kepler's "Table of 1000 Logarithms," published in 1624</note> written four years ago, but because of the desire for its supplementary instructions, it could not be produced until this current year, <margin>1625.</margin> as I said in the supplement. Therefore, in place of that *Chilias*, and in place of the common *Canon Hexacontaon* <note>Table of Sixties</note> which has 1800 areas, <margin>Page 125. Origin of the Heptacosiade.</margin> for each of the columns, here is the **Heptacosiade** <note>term: Heptacosiade — From the Greek for "seven hundred." It is Kepler’s table of 720 logarithms (representing 12 hours or 12 signs of 60 parts each).</note>. I gave it this name for the sake of brevity because it displays seven hundred and twenty logarithms, <margin>Reason for the name.</margin> corresponding to the same number of parts of one whole.

<note>This paragraph describes the columns of the Heptacosiade.</note>
The columns of the Heptacosiade consist <margin>Description of the Heptacosiade.</margin> <margin>The Sixtieth, Sexagesimal, and Twenty-Fourfold sub-columns.</margin> of two sub-columns each. Three of these are central; the twentieth of the Sixtieth, and the right-hand Twentieth, are unique to the columns. <gloss>their merits</gloss> Insofar as they are unique, I decided they should be named the **Sexagesimal** and the **Twenty-Fourfold** <note>original: "Quadrivicenaria"</note>. <gloss>so they are</gloss> The left one is inscribed as <gloss>Sixtieth</gloss> <gloss>Twenty-</gloss> the **Sixtieth**, and the right one as the **Twentieth**, <gloss>fourfold</gloss> <gloss>which</gloss> <gloss>sixtieth</gloss> which I thought should rather be called the Sexagesimal. This is sometimes called the **Sexagena** <note>sixty</note> and sometimes the **Twenty-Fourfold**, an application that does not apply to the Sixties.

<note>This paragraph explains specific numbers used in the system.</note>
If you ask what is denoted by 60' or by 24°, <margin>What kind of numbers are 60 and 24?</margin> it is noted generally as one whole, and <gloss>equal</gloss>...

# INSTRUCTIONS FOR THE TABLES

### THE PRECEPTS OF THE TABLES.

equal: specifically, however, 60' <note>60 minutes</note> denotes the total sine of an entire quadrant, while 24h denotes specifically an entire day, divided into 24 hours.

Therefore, these two small columns rise by constant increments: the first by 5 seconds (5''), and the "Twenty-Four" column by 2 minutes (2'); this is because the proportion of the divisions of one whole—the former into 60 and the latter into 24—is contained within these primary numbers, 5 and 2. Each part is one seven-hundred-and-twentieth (1/720th); 5'' of 60', and 2' of 24h.

<margin>What kind of columns of Logarithms? Why not round numbers?</margin>
As for the common logarithms of both these fractions of a whole, located in the middle column: they are all what the common crowd of mathematicians calls "irrational," and what I, in my *Chilias* <note>Kepler’s "Chilias Logarithmorum," a table of 1,000 logarithms published in 1624</note>, call "scrupulous" <note>original: "scrupulosi," meaning exact but difficult to handle, like small stones in a shoe</note>. Although I was free to establish a "rational" and "round" logarithm for the sixtieth part—for instance, a unit with pure zeros—I saw that there would be little gain and a fair amount of inconvenience. For if such rationality (or "roundness," as I call it) in a logarithm were pleasing, you would find no other round numbers besides this one; since none of the 720 parts fall upon the points of the mean proportionals between 1' and 60' which follow one another in a decimal progression. Therefore, the round logarithms 2000, 3000, 4000, etc., would not fit any of those parts.

However, if you desire to judge the logistic type of a number from the very "characteristic" beginning of the logarithm (something that could easily have been obtained through the logarithms of the Englishman <term>Briggs</term><note>Henry Briggs (1561–1630), who developed "common" or base-10 logarithms</note>: so that if 100,000 were assumed for the logarithm of one minute, then 200,000 would be the logarithm of one second, and 300,000 the logarithm of one third-second)—if, I say, you seek this: behold, the peaks of ancient logistics <note>original: "apices logistices antiquæ"</note> provide this far more conveniently. These logistic peaks even showed the way to these very logarithms for the worthy <term>Bürgi</term><note>Joost Bürgi (1552–1632), a Swiss clockmaker and mathematician who invented logarithms independently of Napier</note> many years before Napier's edition. Yet, being a hesitant man and a guardian of his own secrets, he abandoned his child at birth and did not raise it for public use.
<margin>The different form of BRIGGS' Logarithms.</margin>
<margin>On what occasion Joost BÜRGI discovered logarithms.</margin>

On the other hand, since that "Heptacosias" <note>The table of 720 parts</note> provides rational logistic numbers, it is much more fitting that their logarithms be irrational; so that by this distinction of irrationality, one may be more easily distinguished from the other.

<margin>What is the smallest element of the Logarithms?</margin>
Furthermore, I thought it better to retain the measure of logarithms supplied by the nature of the circle, rather than taking one by a freer choice. For in <term>Napier's</term> first edition of logarithms and in my own *Chilias*, although the proportion and its measure (the logarithm) extend much wider than the sine of a Quadrant of a circle; nevertheless, because there is room for choice in selecting the measure of proportions, we bind the logarithms more closely to the Quadrant of the circle itself because of their primary use there. To the sine which is closest in quantity to the radius (or "total sine") in the smallest division chosen, we assign as a logarithm the very "falling away" of that sine from the radius, which is the <term>versed sine</term> <note>original: "sagitta complementi Arcus," the "arrow of the complement of the arc"</note> of the arc. I say this measure of proportion is more agreeable than all others; and therefore, I did not think that measure should be exchanged for any other arbitrary one.

<column-break/>

Added to this is the comparison of the *Heptacosias* with the Canon of the Semicircle itself; for it is advantageous that the same arcs and sines in both places be marked and equipped with the same logarithms. One should not abuse the freedom of choice by picking one measure here and another there. A common service—the <term>chord</term> <note>original: "subtensio"</note> which the origin provides as master—best reconciles these rivals for dominance.

<margin>Why are the Logarithms constructed by the same method?</margin>
For these reasons, therefore, I have retained in this *Heptacosias* the same genus of logarithms that is in my *Chilias*. Thus, from those thousand differences or decreases of the *Chilias*, I have simply transferred the first seven hundred and twenty (of which the first is 69314.72 and the last 138.98) into the structure of the *Heptacosias*, from which I might build a series of as many logistic logarithms (following the instruction of Precept 5 in Chapter VIII of the Supplement).

<margin>On the length of the Logarithms.</margin>
As for the fact that you see the first and longest logarithms of the *Heptacosias* running out to eight figures, that was only done because of their origin: since the logarithms of the *Chilias* were calculated with great diligence, I did not want to violate the integrity of the differences between them by cutting off the last two places. However, so that these values in the *Heptacosias* would correspond in proper length to those inserted here and there in the planetary tables, I cut off the last two figures, placing a point between them. By this separation, the calculator is warned that the two final figures following the point are never to be copied out or used for these specific Tables. But I will say more about the meaning of this punctuation in Chapter XI.

And so far, I have discussed the inner three columns of the *Heptacosias*.

<margin>The Sexagesimal columns of "privatives."</margin>
<margin>Concerning the name "Sexagesima."</margin>
It follows that I should also speak of the outermost columns, and first the last one on the right. This column, as its title indicates, is of "sixtieths"—minutes and seconds—which exceed the number of sixty first-parts, or one whole; therefore, these minutes and seconds, exceeding a whole, are attached to the whole parts.
<margin>Not exact.</margin>
Most of them, however, which do not end in a round number, have an imperfect final Second. This is because these minutes relate to their lateral counterparts in the left-hand Sexagesimal column just as the <term>secant</term> of an arc relates to the sine of its complement—lines which are usually <term>incommensurable</term> <note>meaning they cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of whole numbers</note> to each other, and therefore can be perfectly expressed by no number.

Although for this reason these minutes decrease unequally in this column, I did not think their decreases needed to be inserted between them, because these "sixtieths of privatives" rarely come into use, especially where the number of wholes is large. For the same reason, I cared for them more loosely, and I do not sell them all as being entirely accurate; for perhaps one Second or another will be in excess or deficient, especially toward the beginning of the *Heptacosias*. However, their use is never extended that far in these Tables; so that column is made continuous through the whole Table from bottom to top, or up to 720 wholes, merely for the sake of decency and integrity.

<margin>On the name of the privative numbers.</margin>
That small column is titled the "Sixtieth of Privatives" <note>original: "Sexagesima privativorum." In Kepler’s system, "privative" refers to negative logarithms, used here for values greater than the whole or for specific inverse calculations</note>, because as often as these logarithms of the minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum"</note> are needed, the privative sign (—) must be prefixed to them in the calculation. Conversely, when a logarithm is presented with a prefixed privative sign (—), the minutes are not to be extracted from the left "Sixtieth" column, but from this right-hand column of privatives.

<margin>The Column of Arcs.</margin>
The other outermost column on the far left is the column of Arcs of a Quadrant <note>90 degrees</note>. For the purpose of these Tables, it is somewhat redundant, because I have placed each of their parts—amounting to 5,400 <note>90 degrees × 60 minutes = 5,400</note>—to the left of the logarithms that mostly take the place of this column. However, this column of arcs was also added, first, so that the sines in sexagesimal division <note>division by 60</note> could be joined to the parts of the Quadrant, and in the Canon of Logarithms of the half-ten <note>likely referring to a base-10 related sine table</note>. By a specific design, the sines of the decimal division were omitted by me, so that the defect of their logarithms in the tables—through the quadrant of the *Heptacosias* <note>the 720-part table</note>—would not appear. Secondly, it was included so that the *Heptacosias* might display its origin from the *Chilias* <note>Kepler’s 1624 table of 1,000 logarithms</note>, showing the certain added dimensions on both sides. By this method, the precepts of the *Chilias* (learned from the supplement through the elements) apply to most examples of this *Heptacosias*, even those that extend beyond the boundaries of these Tables. For the multiplications and divisions for which the *Heptacosias* was constructed, that column of Arcs does not contribute much by itself.

### THE METHOD OF EXTRACTING VALUES FROM THE Heptacosias.

<margin>Precept 2.</margin>
If a given Arc, minute, or temporary hour and minute—by which you seek a logarithm—is not found exactly in any of the lines of its column, take as their logarithm the middle value between the logarithms of the nearest lines. At the very least, do this for those figures where the logarithms begin to differ from the left, by one or two digits; then fill the remaining places up to the decimal point with zeros <note>original: "Cyphræ"</note>. Or, if the calculator does not mind the extra work, he may take the difference between the two logarithms of the *Heptacosias* Table (which is placed in small characters between them) and subtract a proportional part for the excess seconds from the larger logarithm, or add it to the next smaller one, where the (privative) logarithms increase along with their logistic numbers.

<margin>Precept 3.</margin>
In the sexagesimal column, the method for taking the proportional part is as follows: take the excess of one, two, three, or four seconds, double it, and multiply it by the difference placed between the two logarithms. From the result, cut off the last digit; the remainder will be the portion due to the excess seconds. When this is taken away from the larger logarithm, it leaves the desired value.

For example, if the logarithm for 59' 13'' must be extracted: these fall between 59' 10'' and 59' 15'' expressed in the sexagesimal column. The logarithm placed at the side of 59' 10'' is 1398 62 <note>on page 27</note>, with a difference of 140 75. Here it is sufficient to take 
<column-break/>
the intermediate value 1320 between the nearest found values of 1399 and 1258. But if you act accurately: because the proposed 59' 13'' exceeds [the table entry] by 3'', if you multiply the difference of the logarithms (1600) by 6 (which is double the 3''), the result will be 9600. By cutting off the last digit of the result, you produce 96. This, subtracted from 1399 (which stands next to 59' 10''), leaves 1303 as the correct logarithm for 59' 13''. <note>Kepler's example numbers here vary slightly from the text due to potential OCR or original typesetting errors, but the interpolation method of "double the difference and truncate" is clear.</note>

For the logarithm of 5° 12': here, in the third place from the left, the logarithms begin to differ. For the first two places are the same (24). Therefore, between the two succeeding values on either side—namely between 52 and 36—a value is chosen to fill the two places, resulting in 244500. Acting accurately, multiply the difference of the logarithms (1600) by 4 (the double of the excess minutes), and shorten the result; this gives 640. Subtract this from the first and larger logarithm, and 244572 will remain as the logarithm for 5° 12'.

For temporary minutes, whose constant difference is two: if the logarithm is extracted by the minutes, but they exceed the listed minutes, the calculation is performed as described.

Logarithms are extracted by Arcs with more difficulty; see Chapter IX, Precept IX in the supplement to the *Chilias*.
<margin>folio 203</margin>

<margin>Precept 4.</margin>
Through the right-hand sexagesimal column, privative logarithms are extracted toward the end of the *Heptacosias* (where they are used) by the same method and logic. But for their beginning: observe this carefully, that if a logarithm is not found exactly in the column, it should be treated as lying between the two. One must choose the value closer to one or the other in the columns, if the logarithm tends that way. For example, if the Logarithm 298000 is given: it will correspond to 5° 13' from the "Twenty-Four" column <note>original: "Quadrivicenaria"</note>. Here, 3' must be extracted. Thus, the labor is greatly reduced for the calculator.

If, however, one prefers the laws of the sexagesimal column in the free part of the logistic number, seeking a proportional part for any value, he may subtract the given logarithm and find the division between which the proposed value falls.
<margin>folio 204</margin>

<margin>Precept 5.</margin>
Therefore, the second is very much sought after from the logarithms of the arcs, which must be carefully foreseen.

### PRECEPTS FOR THE TABLES.
<note>original: "PHI PRÆCEPTA." In the Rudolphine Tables, "PHI" often refers to the specific logarithmic scale or physical instructions.</note>
A 3
<note>original: "A 3" is a signature mark for the book binder.</note>

...ten-thousandths, or even hundred-thousandths. As in the example: the Logarithm 298,000 finds the nearest smaller value 29,573 at the Logistic value 3' 0" <note>In this context, the prime symbol refers to minutes of a degree</note>; and the next smaller 296,833 at the Logistic value 3' 5". The difference between the given 298,000 and the smaller 29,573 leaves 1,573. If you divide the half of this <note>likely referring to a specific interpolation step</note>, which is 767, into 2,740, the result is 3". Add these to 3' 0", and you will have the exact 3' 3".

<margin>PRECEPT 6.</margin>
Here I will also teach the curious how they ought to extract the Logarithms of the smallest minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum minimorum," referring to seconds</note> where the differences are not proportional, and indeed for all Seconds below one Prime <note>one minute</note>.
*For example, if the Logarithm of 0' 17" is sought: Extract the Logarithm of the 17 sixty-fold, which is 126113.12, and add the Logarithm of one prime, which is 409434.46. Therefore, the Logarithm of 0' 17" is 535547.58.*
*Similarly, the Logarithm for 0' 1" will become double the Logarithm of 0' 1", namely 81,886.92.*
Through the "privative sixty-folds" <note>negative logarithmic values for the base-60 scale</note>, the same exception can be continued even above 1' 0" by subtracting them.
*As if the exact Logarithm for 1' 12" were sought: Take the sixty-fold of 1' 12" on the right of the search. Subtract that Logarithm (18,232.14) from the Logarithm of 1' (409,434.46); the Logarithm of 1' 12" will remain: 391,202.32.*

<margin>PRECEPT 7.</margin>
CONVERSELY, if a very large Logarithm is given, extract the accurate minutes with it thus: subtract from it the Logarithm of a minute, if it is smaller; with the remainder, extract the Primes and Seconds, but for those, write down the same number of Seconds and Thirds <note>moving down one level of precision</note>.
Or, subtract the given value from the Logarithm of a minute, if it is larger; with the remainder, extract from the right-hand Sexagesimal column the Wholes, Minutes, and Seconds; but for these, write down the same number of Primes, Seconds, and Thirds.
*For example, let the given Logarithm be 300,000.00. I subtract it from 409,434.46. With the remainder, 109,434.46, I extract 2' 59" 4"' as a privative. Therefore, to the given Logarithm, the minutes 2' 59" 4"' correspond.*

### CHAPTER IV.
### ON THE COSSIC ADDITIONS AND SUBTRACTIONS OF LOGARITHMS.
<note>The term "Cossic" (from the Italian 'cosa' or 'thing') was the early modern term for Algebra. "Cossic addition" refers to what we now call signed arithmetic—adding and subtracting positive and negative numbers.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'U' featuring swirling vines and floral patterns.</image-desc>
Until now, "privative" <note>negative</note> Logarithms had to be used with the prefixed sign (—); hence this part of Arithmetic, known from antiquity, is necessary. And although I have inscribed the precepts within the Tables themselves wherever I conveniently could, so that it would not be necessary for me to send calculators back here, this little part of Arithmetic is nevertheless extremely familiar to Merchants and Accountants. For a Logarithm, to which one is ordered to add or from which one is to subtract another Logarithm, is the same to us as the **CASH BOX** is to merchants; and a positive Logarithm behaves as ready **Money**

<column-break/>

and **Credit** does for them; whereas a privative <note>negative</note> one is like **Debt** or **Owed Money**. Adding is like the accounts of **Receipts**, and Subtracting is like the accounts of **Expenses**. The entire doctrine of Addition and Subtraction consists of two Rules.

## I. RULE
->Of Arithmetic.<-

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'C' with ornate, mirrored scrollwork.</image-desc>
When the signs of two given Logarithms are the same—either purely + positive or — privative—the operation <note>original: "species," meaning addition or subtraction</note> also remains the same as that which is commanded in the cossic <note>algebraic</note> style; except that a commanded subtraction, if it is truly cossic, is done with the terms inverted. Whenever the signs of the given numbers are different—for instance, one is — privative and the other is + positive—then cossic addition is performed through the usual subtraction of the Lesser from the Greater; conversely, cossic subtraction is completed through the usual addition of the given numbers into one Sum.

## II. RULE
->On the Sign of the Result.<-

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'M' with thick, leafy flourishes.</image-desc>
The sign of the result <note>original: "exeuntis," the 'going out' value</note> remains that of the Greater number, except where the number to be subtracted is larger; for then the result takes the opposite sign to the sign of the Greater. Inspect these patterns:

->Forms of Cossic Additions.<-
To be added: { + 6 | + 6 | — 6 | — 6
{ + 2 | — 2 | + 2 | — 2
Sums: + 8 | + 4 | — 4 | — 8

To be added: { — 6 | — 2
{ + 2 | — 6
Sums: — 4 | — 8

->Forms of Cossic Subtractions.<-
From which to subtract: + 2 | + 6 | + 2
To be subtracted: + 6 | + 2 | — 6
Remainders: — 4 | + 4 | + 8

From which to subtract: — 2 | — 6 | — 2
To be subtracted: + 6 | + 2 | — 6
Remainders: — 8 | — 8 | — 4 | + 4
<note>Note: The table layout in the original shows how signs flip when subtracting a negative or a larger positive.</note>

<margin>Precept 8.</margin>

### CHAPTER V.
### ON THE RULE OF THREE OR PROPORTIONS, TO BE EXERCISED IN LOGISTIC NUMBERS BY THE HELP OF THE HEPTACOSIAS, TO HUNT FOR THE PROPORTIONAL PART.

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'M' with an ornate floral background.</image-desc>
Cossic Multiplications and Divisions in Astronomical tables are used almost exclusively in the Rule of Three, in which, among other things, proportional parts are usually elicited. In this work, we usually proceed as far as Seconds, and rarely as far as Thirds. In these WORDS...
