# PRECEPTS OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES

...mostly, however, regarding the southern regions of the Horizon: in the parts of the quadrant tables, with the order of Degrees descending to the left, and the signs of the further Quadrants descending, with the order of degrees ascending to the right; just so that the Degrees of Right Ascension from the <term>Antiscia</term> <note>Points on the zodiac that are equidistant from the solstices or equinoxes, often used in traditional astrology and astronomy to find symmetry in planetary positions</note> may meet in the same line; one on the right, the other on the left margin <gloss>so they may be recognized</gloss>. In the joining of any of the signs, columns are arranged for the full Times of Right Ascensions, showing for both [quadrants] the common full Times of each semicircle; a column is placed at the side for the First and Second [minutes and seconds]. In the middle of both Quadrants, I have inserted two columns: one for the common Declinations of the Angles of the Ecliptic with the Meridian, and fifteen times ten declinations <gloss>of the Declinations</gloss>.
<margin><term>Antiscia</term></margin>
<margin>Of the Angles with the Meridian</margin>

<margin>The Foundations of the Tychonic Obliquity of the Ecliptic, etc.</margin>
But I have not yet touched the head of the matter. Namely, regarding the **Obliquity of the Ecliptic** <term>Obliquity of the Ecliptic: The angle of the Earth's axial tilt, roughly 23.5 degrees, which determines the limit of the sun's northern and southern movement</term> itself: whether it was larger, smaller, or equal in the past is not established by valid arguments from the observations of the ancients, and is undoubtedly plainly false. If, however, the **Obliquity** was once going to be larger than it is today, we would certainly have preceded that fact; therefore, we could not devise a rule, and we stand for all astronomical ages with the most exact modern Obliquity.

Regarding the measures of Obliquity known to modern Astronomers, that which was used by Tycho in his Tables of Directions. Indeed, regarding the Directions offered, he corrected it, so that I think there will be no one in his age who would wish to explain to me how I received this Tychonic declination into the precepts of the <term>Rudolphine Tables</term> <note>The star catalog and planetary tables published by Johannes Kepler in 1627</note>, which were once for lesser [men]; since it is well known that Tycho himself is the author of this name for the Tables. Nevertheless, I thought the students of the art should be warned, for the sake of avoiding perplexity: Tycho himself, in establishing the Obliquity of the Ecliptic, took into account an adjusted parallax, the quantity of which at the Horizon was 3 minutes. In the *Archives* and long ago in the *Commentaries on the Motion of the Star Mars*, and now in these Rudolphine Tables, the Parallax of the Sun from <term>Reinhold</term> <note>Erasmus Reinhold, an astronomer who produced the earlier Prutenic Tables</note> in Table P. 23. 28'. From <term>Copernicus</term>, offered as an error from Refractions, he corrected it, so that I think no one in his age [would disagree].
<margin>Where does the <term>Tychonic Parallax of the Sun</term> come from?</margin>

<margin>Why the <term>Tychonic Obliquity</term> was not corrected.</margin>
When the diligent students of the art have understood these warnings, they will judge that not only should this Tychonic Declination of the Ecliptic have been corrected, but also adapted to my solar parallax. But let them know that a single Minute in the altitude of the Sun [is found] by observations of such great subtlety... [there are] most certainly two acts of observing: one of the Sun itself, the other of the Ecliptic. Between these two minutes, neither of which Minutes agree, prejudices in favor of a slightly larger Obliquity prevailed with me, as did the fear lest an error greater than 1' Minute should be mine. Thus Tycho himself, in establishing the Obliquity of the Ecliptic, took into account an adjusted parallax, the quantity of which at the Horizon was 3 minutes <gloss>so they may be recognized</gloss>. In the *Archives* and long ago in the *Commentaries on the Motion of the Star Mars*, and now in these Rudolphine Tables, the Parallax of the Sun from Reinhold in Table P. 23. 28'. From Copernicus, offered as an error from Refractions, he corrected it, so that I think no one in his age [would disagree].

<margin><term>Precept</term> 32.</margin>
<margin><term>Proportional Part</term></margin>
There is therefore a certain Rule excerpted through the whole Degrees of Right Ascension, so that those who are the most certain Astronomers, like Tycho—who established or sought these not only from observations but from their own reasons—may use this compendium: for the Minutes, the whole Degrees must be traversed by ten-minute equal intervals from the differences between the two columns, which are shown in the increments and decrements <gloss>to be taken</gloss>.

<margin><term>Precept</term> 31.</margin>
If, for example, the Right Ascension is given from any of the three fronts or ends, entering with the degrees found and the sign found: from the right, upward to the right; from the left, downward to the left; and at the intersection of the line of the degree found with the column of the sign, you will find the full Times of Right Ascension. In the side column, however, you will find the Minutes of one [degree], with the addition of the Firsts and Seconds, so that the Right Ascension of the degrees of the Ecliptic occurs on that same line; the Reduction and the Angle between the columns are whole in the First and Second Parts.

<margin><term>Proportional Part</term></margin>
But if Minutes are attached to the whole Degrees of the Ecliptic, the differences between the two columns, which are shown in the increments and decrements, must be taken through those <gloss>to be taken</gloss>.

<margin><term>Increments in 10'</term></margin>
<margin>Number of Seconds. Example.</margin>
But for those who are accustomed to the old logistics and others, the columns in the difference of two neighboring Ascensions, Declinations, or Angles of the space between columns are distinguished by the upper title **Increments in 10'**. This difference of the inter-column space, multiplied by the Minutes attached to the whole degrees of the Ecliptic arcs, and with the last figure removed from the result, gives the number of Seconds (reduced to the first [minute] if they exceed [sixty]) which should be added.

<margin><term>Proportional Part</term></margin>
Thus, the difference of the inter-column space, multiplied by the Minutes attached to the whole degrees of the Ecliptic arcs, and with the last figure removed from the result, gives the number of Seconds (reduced to the first [minute] if they exceed [sixty]) which should be added.

## EXAMPLE.

Suppose we seek the **Right Ascension**, **Declination**, and the **Angle**, corresponding to the point of the **Ecliptic** <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> at 7 degrees and 12 seconds of Pisces. Therefore, since Pisces [♓] is the sign, we extract the whole degrees of Right Ascension as 332 from the column under which the sign of Pisces is placed—one of those in the ascending Semicircle. From the column of common minutes, 6 minutes and 17 seconds are extracted. From the space between the columns, we take the **Increment** of 572 seconds. If this is multiplied by the 7 minutes and 12 seconds <note>original: "Scrupula 7'. 12''" — scrupula refers to small divisions of a degree, usually minutes</note> attached to the whole degrees, the result is 4118. By dropping the last digit, it becomes 412 seconds, which is 6 minutes and 52 seconds: the **proportional part**. The same result is obtained more concisely this way: the Increment lacks 28 seconds to reach 600. Multiplying these [28] by 7 gives 201; by cutting off the last digit, we get 20 seconds. Subtract this from 7 minutes 12 seconds, and 6 minutes 52 seconds remains as the proportional part, just as before. Therefore, add that to 332° 6' 17'', and the sought **Right Ascension** becomes 332° 13' 9''.

<margin>Folio 24. Restore the titles transposed at the bottom.</margin>
With the same 0° of Pisces, the **Declination** is extracted as 11° 30' 43''. The **decrement** <note>A value used to adjust calculations when numbers are decreasing between entries</note> in the intercolumn space is 212 seconds. When multiplied by 7' 12'', this yields 1526; rejecting the last digit gives 153 seconds, or 2' 33'', which must be subtracted so the correct Declination is 11° 28' 10''. This is Southern, just like the sign. Similarly, the **Angle** at 0° Pisces is 69° 20' 36''. The decrement is 113, which, when multiplied by 7' 12'', gives 813. Cutting off the last digit gives 81 seconds, or 1' 21'', so the correct Angle is 69° 19' 15''. This is to the left, as it is formed by the following arc of the ascending Semicircle.

If the point of the Ecliptic had been the opposite sign, Virgo [♍], everything would remain the same, except the degrees of Right Ascension (or the "Times") would be 152 instead of 332, from the column where the sign of Virgo is placed at the bottom. The Declination would be understood as Northern, like the sign Virgo. Finally, the Angle would be to the right of the **Meridian**, as it is in the descending semicircle, formed by the preceding arc.

Thus, if the Right Ascension is given as 341° 20' 29'' and the assigned Declination must be extracted: at 341° 32' 43'', I find the assigned Declination to be 7° 50' 46'', with an Increment of Right Ascension of 561. The given Ascension is exceeded by 18' 3'', which, when multiplied by the decrement, produces 4090. Divide this by the Increment of Right Ascension, and the result is 7 minutes and a small fraction. Therefore, 7 minutes and that fraction must be added to 7° 50' 46'' in this place; thus the sought declination becomes 7° 58' 0'', which is sufficiently accurate. ## CHAPTER XIII.

### ON THE RISING AMPLITUDE: AND ON THE ASCENSIONAL DIFFERENCE, and the use of its Synoptic Table.

**I**n the spherical doctrine of the **Primary Motion** <note>The apparent daily rotation of the heavens</note>, the **Ascensional Difference** <note>The difference between the Right Ascension and the Oblique Ascension of a celestial body</note> is usually calculated by the declination of a given point of the Ecliptic or a star. When combined with the Right Ascension of that point, it constitutes the **Oblique Ascension**. However, Oblique Ascensions are typically described for each individual degree of the Altitude of the Pole <note>The observer's latitude</note>, so that when a given point of the Equator is rising, the corresponding rising point of the Ecliptic can be extracted.

<margin>The necessity of Oblique Ascension.</margin>
Even though this entire part of spherical doctrine is used in various ways—not only for the rising, setting, emergence, and occultation of the fixed stars, but also for the calculation of Solar Eclipses—neither the locations on Earth where any phase of an eclipse occurs, nor the **Parallaxes**, nor the calculation of the Rising Degree can be computed without Oblique Ascensions. Nevertheless, the direction tables of **Regiomontanus** <note>Johannes Müller, a 15th-century mathematician</note>, and those of **Reinhold** <note>Erasmus Reinhold, author of the Prutenic Tables</note> who continued them, were not to be transcribed into this work, since **Magini** <note>Giovanni Antonio Magini, an Italian astronomer</note> has long since repeated them in his *Primum Mobile*, and copies are commonly available for anyone to use in calculating eclipses according to the instructions of those tables.
<margin>Why the Tables are omitted here.</margin>

Therefore, since I have omitted the tables of Oblique Ascensions themselves for the stated reason, I have nevertheless compensated for this deficiency in some part. To ensure that our table of Right Ascensions—and especially the **Canon of Logarithms** of the Semicircle—might be adapted to many more uses as necessary parts of this work, it seemed fit to provide these precepts from which the omitted parts of the Tables of Primary Motion are calculated, at least as much as the use of the **RUDOLPHINE TABLES** requires.

<margin>Concerning Rising Amplitude <note>The angular distance from the East point of the horizon where a star rises</note>.</margin>
**GIVEN ANY POINT OF THE SPHERE**,
and its Declination from the Equator, to find its **Rising Amplitude**.

<margin>PRECEPT 33.</margin>
**F**rom the Logarithm of the Declination, subtract the Logarithm of the Altitude of the Equator [not the Pole].

<margin>Usage.</margin>
The law of the Height of the Pole <note>The observer's latitude</note> is the same as the common one; the remainder will be the Logarithm of the Rising Amplitude <note>term: <term>Rising Amplitude</term>; the angular distance of a celestial body from the true east at the moment it rises</note>. This is useful for determining various circumstances of Eclipses and, above all, has the widest application in Navigation. An example follows immediately.

But sometimes the value is smaller or the signs are private <note>original: "signa privata" — likely referring to specific mathematical notations used in the tables</note>, or perhaps the calculator was unaware of a missing value. <margin>See Rule 8.</margin> Let them inspect the Synopsis Table regarding the sign itself and the resulting sign. For example, if the Height of the Pole is 54°, which is smaller, and the Declination area is 21° 3', it shows an Ascensional Difference of 32° in the left margin. The Ascensional Difference increases with a greater Height of the Pole; therefore, the result must be something greater than 32°. Having realized this, the calculator will not easily err in addition, subtraction, or the resulting sign.

## GIVEN A POINT ON THE SPHERE
<margin>Of the Ascensional Difference.</margin>
With any point's Declination from the Equator, to investigate its Ascensional Difference under a given Height of the Pole <note>latitude</note>.

<margin>Rule 34.</margin>
The shortest way to compute only the Ascensional Difference is by the Mesologarithm <note>term: <term>Mesologarithm</term>; a specific middle-logarithm used in Kepler's trigonometric calculations</note>, which however is not part of this work, as we said above. From the Mesologarithm of the Declination, the coefficient Mesologarithm of the Equatorial height is subtracted (or the Mesologarithm of the Polar height is added); the remainder, as the Logarithm shows, reveals the sought Ascensional Difference. This way is indeed short, but complex due to the various cases and the mixture of Logarithms and Mesologarithms.

<margin>Rule 35.</margin>
Therefore, another way, longer indeed but convenient for other parts of the work, is this: Nine Logarithms of the Semicircle are to be processed, especially for the person who first seeks the Rising Amplitude; then, from its Antilogarithm, subtract the Antilogarithm of the Declination, which will leave the sought Ascensional Difference.

<margin>By Rule 33.</margin>
Lest the calculator, unaccustomed to the full Synopsis of Logarithms, should easily go astray—especially in the first method or where the entire surface is not used—it seemed best to add a short Synopsis of all variations of Ascensional Differences to the page where the table of Right Ascensions is found, and to interpose the Right Ascension and the Eastern Angle as their common link.

<margin>Description of the Synopsis of Ascensional Differences.</margin>
At the head of this Synopsis, therefore, are the Heights of the Pole <note>latitudes</note> jumping by six degrees. In the fields are the precise declinations, so measured that any value under that Height of the Pole (which it has written above it) exhibits the Ascensional Difference in whole degrees. These are first expressed individually up to 10; then by twos up to 20; then by fours up to 40; and finally by tens up to 90.

<margin>page 25.</margin>
<margin>Usage.</margin>
<margin>Rule 36.</margin>
When, therefore, the given Height of the Pole and the Declination are not found exactly—the former at the head, the latter in the area under the polar height—then the Ascensional Difference cannot be exactly copied from the left margin. Instead, one must find the middle ground <note>interpolate</note> between the extracted steps, fairly and reasonably. This is done for this use only: so that he who wishes to use logarithms may know approximately what the result should be. With this before his eyes, he may be guided in his calculation from the start; and when the result comes out, he may be free of doubt that the operation was performed correctly.

Although greater certainty should not be sought from this brief Synopsis, nor is it advised that anyone wear themselves out hunting for an exact calculation of proportional parts, it seems to me that the Synopsis also brings light to other uses in the study of the Sphere. But now I shall add something about the use of the Ascensional Difference, which is necessary for the practice of these Tables, especially because of the Catalog of Places.

<margin>More on the usage of the Synopsis.</margin>
## GIVEN THE HEIGHT OF THE POLE,
TO INVESTIGATE the semi-diurnal and semi-nocturnal time <note>the length of half the day and half the night</note> by the Ascensional Difference of the Sun's given position, and thus the length of the artificial day.

<margin>Rule 37.</margin>
Extract the Declination of the Sun's given position. With this, and with the given Height of the Pole <note>latitude</note> which we have, convert it into Hours and Minutes. When the signs are Northern, add what results to six hours; but when they are Southern, subtract it from six hours. Thus the semi-diurnal time <note>half-day length</note> will emerge in both cases. If this is then subtracted from 12 hours, the semi-nocturnal time will remain. Finally, these doubled become the quantity of that day and that night respectively in the given Pole <note>latitude</note> with the Sun moving in the given point.

Since both are positive and the latter is smaller, the subtraction is easy, proceeding directly.

From the length of the longest semi-diurnal time, subtract six hours; convert the remainder into Equatorial Times <note>degrees of the equator</note>, and the Ascensional Difference <note>term: <term>Ascensional Difference</term>; the variation in rising time due to latitude</note> will be revealed. This, combined with the Declination of the Sun <note>the Sun's angle north or south of the celestial equator</note>, will give the Altitude of the Pole <note>the observer's latitude</note>, either from the *Synopsis of Ascensional Differences* or by subtracting the Logarithm of the Ascensional Difference from the Middle-Logarithm <note>original: "Mesologarithmo"</note> of the Declination, so that the Middle-Logarithm of the altitude of the Equator remains—or, by changing the sign, the Altitude of the Pole.

For example, because the same *Baron Sigismund* <note>Sigismund von Herberstein (1486–1566), a diplomat whose writings provided early European accounts of Russia</note> reported that in the city of Moscow the longest day is held to be 17 hours, 45 minutes, it is asked what altitude of the Pole can be derived from this.

Therefore, the semi-diurnal time would be 8 hours, 52 minutes, 30 seconds. Subtracting 6 hours from this, the remaining 2 hours, 52 minutes, 30 seconds give 43° 7' 30'' in Equatorial Times for the Ascensional Difference.
<margin>Through precept 17.</margin>

->Therefore 43° 7' 30'' has a Logarithm of 38039.<-
->The Middle-Logarithm of the Sun's Declination is 83165.<-
->This yields an Equatorial Altitude of 32° 30' (Middle-Logarithm 45126).<-
->The Altitude of the Pole is 57° 30'.<-

In the *Synopsis*, an Ascensional Difference slightly smaller than this is found in the margin, namely 40°. The Declination slightly larger in its line is 25° 2', above which at the top stands the Altitude of the Pole, 54°. Above the slightly smaller Declination of 20° 22' stands an Altitude of the Pole of 60°. Conversely, an Ascensional Difference slightly larger than ours is found in the margin as 50°, in whose line Declinations occur: one larger than ours at 23° 52', and one smaller at 18° 50'. Above the former stands an Altitude of the Pole of 60°, and above the latter 66°. You see that the one we calculated, namely 57° 30', is between 54° and 60°. Thus, no error was made in adding or subtracting, or in exchanging Logarithms for Middle-Logarithms; for otherwise, the results would have been quite different.

Thus, these two traditions concerning *Moscow* do not agree with each other exactly. The BARON could have missed two degrees, having used a crude solar instrument and observation; it is also possible that the estimate of the longest day was extended beyond measure due to the great refractions of the Sun at its rising and setting, by which it is lifted up. Since neither cause is beyond suspicion, the discrepancy can probably be distributed between both, and the Altitude of the Pole set at 56° 30', with the length of the day being about 17 hours, 30 minutes.

Necessity of the Angle of the East.

This part of spherical doctrine is missing from the Direction Tables of Regiomontanus and Reinhold; yet it is extremely necessary to us for the 

<column-break/>

doctrine of parallaxes, as I handed it down in the section on optical Astronomy 21 years ago and strengthened it with demonstrations. *Copernicus* indeed displayed a brief rudiment of this Table in his work *On the Revolutions*; I am surprised it was not transcribed by *Reinhold* into his *Prussian Tables* and refined, as other things were. Therefore, a not insignificant part of the RUDOLPHINE TABLES is constituted by this table of angles, calculated for all degrees of the Northern Altitude of the Pole; it would have been three times larger if I had displayed the whole as I have it calculated in my papers. However, because of the slow change of this angle, it seemed sufficient to me to proceed by every three degrees of the Ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path across the sky</note>. Furthermore, to save paper and labor for the printers, in a table that is lengthy in its own right and not strictly part of *Theoretical* doctrine, I have not represented every single minute <note>original: "Scrupula"</note> attached to the degrees, but have expressed them at least by fives, using the notation of the parts of the *As* <note>term: <term>As</term>; a Roman unit of weight divided into 12 parts, here used to represent fractions of a degree</note>, a custom which *Ptolemy* mostly preserved in his demonstrations.

<margin>Notation and value of the parts of the As.</margin>
Thus, one or two minutes can always be understood as more or less. For example, if solitary degrees like 30° occur, they could also be 29° 58' or 29° 59'; likewise 30° 1' or 30° 2'. So the note **n**, although it is worth 25', remains uncertain whether it might not be 24' 23'', or perhaps 26' 27''. However, if the same note recurs frequently in a continuous order of lines or columns, then in the middle it will have the value ascribed here exactly; toward the neighboring notes, it will have a value closer to them by one or two minutes.

I have also added, for the sake of clarity, the distinctions of the Zones and their Astronomical properties; and I have noted the centers of the Climates at the head of the columns, and their Parallels at the foot, following the usage of *Ptolemy*, and that in the Temperate Zone.
<margin>Zones and Climates. / Parallels.</margin>

In the Northern half of the Torrid Zone, I have expressed at the foot the boundaries of the arcs which, when rising, cause the Nonagesimal <note>term: <term>Nonagesimal</term>; the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon, representing its highest point</note> to turn toward the North—or in whose preceding Nonagesimals the Sun is placed when it becomes vertical at noon; the starting boundary is turned downward, the final one upward. Conversely, in the Frigid Zone, the arcs that are perpetually above the Horizon are indicated by their boundaries inserted into the empty spaces on the left, with the letters of these words: **ARCS NEVER SETTING** <note>original: "ARCUS NUNQUAM OCCIDENTES"</note>. For each of these letters, in ascending order, the initial boundaries stand above, and the final boundaries stay far below. Opposite these are the letters of the words: **ARCS NEVER RISING** <note>original: "ARCUS NUNQUAM EXORIENTES"</note>, descending in reverse order and an inverted position in the rightward parts of the small areas. Each has its initial boundaries of the non-rising arcs written below, and the final ones written far above: though in Altitude of the Pole 67°, due to lack of space, this could not be entirely maintained. But even the angles that these precise boundaries make with the horizon are added in an interlinear position.
<margin>Concerning the transverse notes at the foot.</margin>
<margin>Concerning the empty areas of the Frigid Zone.</margin>

# [RUD]OLPHINE PRECEPTS.

& the Angles of the East <note>term: <term>Angle of the East</term>; also called the rising angle, this is the angle at which the Ecliptic (the Sun's path) intersects the horizon at the moment of sunrise</note>, for those joined together, are indeed much more harmonious: so that in this conjunction there is a certain conformity with the Table of Right Ascensions, of declination, and of the Angles of the Ecliptic with the Meridian: at the same time, the Ascensions of the counter-polar arcs joined together fill the circle. This conjunction could, if the Tables of First Motion are ever reprinted, be continued through all degrees of the Altitude of the Pole <note>latitude</note>; the Rising Amplitude could also be inserted in place of the Declinations: finally, the angles themselves in the areas could be expressed in the usual precise numbers <note>original: "scrupulosis"; referring to minutes and seconds</note>, just as I have them computed in my papers. In this work, this simplified form seemed sufficient, serving as a shorthand.

<margin>PRECEPT 39.</margin>
EXTRACTION is easy: the given rising point of the Ecliptic is sought in either of the margins, and the Altitude of the Pole is sought interchangeably either at the top or the bottom; from the area of their common intersection, the degrees are copied down with an appended Note. This note is converted into Minutes <note>original: "Scrupula"</note> using the small table placed on the preceding leaf, by observing which neighboring note the found note most closely approaches, so that the number of minutes is either increased or decreased by one or two according to that proximity.

<margin>PRECEPT 40.</margin>
BUT if it pleases you to test the accuracy of the Table and compute this angle precisely: first, from the Table of Right Ascensions, extract the Angle and the assigned Declination for the given rising point of the Ecliptic. Subtract the Antilogarithm <note>a mathematical function used in logarithmic calculations of the period</note> of this declination from the Logarithm of the Altitude of the Pole; the remainder will be the Logarithm of an angle, which is to be subtracted from the extracted angle so that the Angle of the East remains.

<margin>The Logarithms here are understood not to be from the "Seven-hundred" [Table], the Logistics, but from the Semicircular Canon.</margin>
*For example, because the Angle of the rising point at 0° 7' 12'' of Aries <note>original: "$\Upsilon$"</note> is 69° 15' 15'', and the Declination is 11° 28' 10''; let the Antilogarithm of this, 2017, be subtracted from the Logarithm of the Altitude of the Pole at 38°, which is 48506. The remainder is 46489. This is the Logarithm of an arc of 38° 55' 5'', which, when subtracted from the copied angle, leaves 30° 24' 10'' as the Angle of the East. The Table under the Altitude of the Pole 38 at Aries <note>original: "$\odot$" (Sun symbol, but context implies the start of the sign)</note> shows 30° with the Note N, which is worth 25'; therefore, a point just beyond 0° Aries will have less than 30° 25', because 1° Aries has 30° 0'.*

<margin>PRECEPT 41.</margin>
IF, however, the rising point of the Ecliptic itself is not given, but rather its Oblique Ascension <note>term: <term>Oblique Ascension</term>; the arc of the celestial equator that rises with a star or point on the ecliptic in a non-right sphere</note>, and you nevertheless seek the Angle of the East of the unknown point: in this case, use the given arc of the Equator as if it were an arc of the Ecliptic, converting it into signs and degrees. Having sought these in the margin of the Table of Right Ascensions, extract the Declination and Angle as before. To this angle, in the first and fourth arcs of the Equator, add the altitude of the Equator; in the second and third, subtract it. To the Logarithm of the resulting sum or remainder, add the Antilogarithm of the extracted Declination (or its equivalent), and the Antilogarithm of the Angle of the East will be produced.*

*For example, if under the Altitude of the Pole 38°, the Oblique Ascension 341° 20' 29'' is given: this, converted into signs as if it were an arc of the Ecliptic, gives 11 signs, 20° 29' of Aries <note>Note: 11 signs + 20° corresponds to a position in Pisces/Aries transition</note>. This, sought in the margin of the Table of Ascensions, has a declination of 7° 20' 11'' and an angle of 67° 34' 54''. Add to this the altitude of the equator, 52°, because we are in the fourth equatorial quadrant: the sum is 119° 34' 54''. To its Logarithm, 13967, add the Antilogarithm of the declination, 822; the sum is 14789. This, as an Antilogarithm, shows 30° 24' as the Angle of the East.*

<meta>catchword: Extraction <note>original: "Exceptio,"</note></meta>

<column-break/>

in the Frigid Zone <note>the Arctic or Antarctic circles</note>, which a curious calculator, by employing a Sphere, will easily discover by his own effort <note>original: "suo Marte"; literally "by his own Mars"</note>.

<margin>PRECEPT 42.</margin>
ANOTHER easier way: for the rising point of the Equator, take the Midheaven <note>term: <term>Midheaven</term>; the point of the ecliptic that is on the meridian</note>, or the Right Ascension of the Midheaven (MC), by subtracting 90° from the given Oblique Ascension: and find the distance intercepted by the Altitude of the Pole; or, having added the southern declination, add the Logarithm of the copied Angle to the Logarithm of the remainder or sum: this will result in the Antilogarithm of the sought Angle of the East.

*For example, because the Oblique Ascension 341° 20' 29'' was given, let the Right Ascension of the Midheaven be taken as 251° 20' 29'' (having removed 90°). To this Right Ascension, the assigned Angle in the Table is 82° 39' 43'' and the Declination is 22° 24' 52'' Southern, because the Right Ascension exceeds a semicircle. Therefore, having added the Altitude of the Pole, it becomes 60° 24' 52''. To its Logarithm 13971, the Logarithm of the Angle 822 is added, making 14793—the same Antilogarithm as before, namely for the arc of 30° 24'.*

<margin>Use of the Angle of the East.</margin>
Now, as pertains to the primary use of this Angle of the East in these Tables, I shall deal with that below in the doctrine of Parallaxes. Now let us see how it might supply the lack of the omitted Tables of Oblique Ascensions.

## GIVEN THE RISING POINT OF THE ECLIPTIC, TO FIND THE OBLIQUE ASCENSION THROUGH THE ANGLE IT MAKES WITH THE HORIZON.

<margin>PRECEPT 43.</margin>
Take the point which is the Nonagesimal <note>term: <term>Nonagesimal</term>; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon, representing its highest point</note> from the east—that is, distant by a quarter of a circle—and use it as if it were a point of the Equator, converting the signs into times <note>degrees</note>. Having sought these among the Right Ascensions of the Table, copy out the Declination and the Arc of the Ecliptic from the corresponding headers and margin. If the declination is northern, subtract it from the Angle of the East; if southern, add it. From the Logarithm of the resulting remainder or composite arc, subtract the Logarithm of the altitude of the Equator; there will remain the Logarithm of the arc of the Equator—the rising arc, if the Nonagesimal is in the Eastern Quadrant; the setting arc, if in the western. That rising arc, added to the extracted pseudo-Ecliptic arc (having first converted it back into Times), constitutes the Oblique Ascension. That setting arc, however, when subtracted, constitutes the Oblique Descension.

*For example, if the rising point 0 signs 7' 12'' of Aries <note>original: "$\Upsilon$"</note> is given and its Angle is 30° 24' under the Altitude of the Pole 38°, and the Oblique Ascension is to be sought: The Nonagesimal from the rising point will therefore be 0 signs 7' 12'' of Cancer <note>original: "$\sigma$"</note>. This, converted as if into Equatorial Times, becomes 240° 7' 12''. Having sought these among the right ascensions, there is extracted from the headers and margin 2 signs 13' 12'' of Aries; and this arc of the Ecliptic, extended again on the Equator, becomes 242° 13' 12''. The Declination is extracted through that same arc as 20° 40' 46'' Southern. To this, add the Angle of the East 30° 14' <note>Note: minor discrepancy in minutes from previous 24'</note>; the sum is 51° 4' 46''. From its Logarithm 25101, the Logarithm of the altitude of the Equator (52°), which is 23824, is subtracted, leaving 1277, the Logarithm of the arc of the Equator 80° 51' 48'' setting, because the Nonagesimal is in the Western quadrant, since it is in the descending semicircle. This, therefore, subtracted from the extracted 242° 13' 12'', leaves the Oblique Descension 161° 20' 24''; and with a semicircle added, the Oblique Ascension becomes 341° 20' 24''.*

# [RUD]OLPHINE TABLES.

<margin>PRECEPT 44.</margin>
**Another way.** Find the Declination <note>The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator</note> of the Ecliptic point of the East <note>The point where the ecliptic meets the eastern horizon</note> from the Table, and join to it the Angle of the East; add the Logarithm of this sum to the Logarithm of the declination: from the total, subtract the Logarithm of the altitude of the Equator <note>This is calculated as 90 degrees minus the latitude of the observer</note>. The result will be the Logarithm of the ascensional difference: which must be subtracted from the Right Ascension of a Northern point, or added to a Southern point, so that the required Oblique Ascension is established.

For example, if the point of the Ecliptic is 0° 7' 12'' of Pisces (♓), and the Altitude of the Pole <note>The latitude of the observer</note> is 38° 0'. Its declination is 11° 28' 10''. The Angle is 69° 19' 15'', but with the following arc to the left, therefore with the preceding 110° 40' 45''. The Angle of the East at 0° 7' 12'' Pisces is 30° 24' from the Table. The sum of both, 141° 4' 45'', has a Logarithm of 46482, to which add the Logarithm of the Declination 161522: the sum becomes 208004. From here, subtract the altitude of the equator 52°, Logarithm 23824; there remains 184180, the Logarithm of the arc 9° 7' 20''. This is therefore the ascensional difference to be added. Now, the Right Ascension of 0° Pisces is 332° 13' 9''. Therefore, the Oblique Ascension will be 341° 20' 29''.

### BUT THE RISING POINT OF THE ECLIPTIC ITSELF CAN ALSO BE INVESTIGATED THROUGH its given or assumed Angle with the Horizon, and through the given Oblique Ascension.

<margin>PRECEPT 45.</margin>
**For** a given Oblique Ascension, take the Right Ascension of the Midheaven <note>term: <term>Midheaven</term>; the point of the Ecliptic that is on the meridian of the observer</note>, and find the point of the Ecliptic which mediates the heavens with it, and its Declination; if this is northern, let it be added to the Altitude of the Equator: if southern, let it be subtracted. From the Logarithm of the remainder or the sum, subtract the Logarithm of the Angle of the East; there will remain the Logarithm of the Ecliptic arc: a rising one, if the point mediating the heavens was in the descending semicircle; a setting one, if in the ascending. Therefore, that added to the point mediating the heavens reaches the rising point; this subtracted, reaches the setting point. If subtraction cannot be done, the given Angle of the East does not correspond to the given Oblique Ascension.

For example, let the Oblique Ascension be 341° 20' 29'', then the Right Ascension of the Midheaven will be 251° 20' 29'', with which 12° 47' 49'' of Scorpio (♏) mediates the heavens from the descending semicircle; its southern Declination is 22° 24' 49''. This being subtracted from the Altitude of the Equator 52°, leaves 29° 37' 11''. From the Logarithm of this arc 70576, subtract the Logarithm 68115 of the given Angle of the East 30° 24' (provided all given values correspond to each other), and there will remain 2461, the Logarithm of the now-rising arc 77° 20' 26''. Therefore, add this to 12° 47' 49'' Scorpio, and the rising point of the Ecliptic comes out to 0° 8' 19'' Pisces quite precisely. For the Angle of the East 30° 24' 8'' now produces 0° 7' 12'' Pisces.

In this way, if you assume a known Angle of the East and work through it, if indeed the point having this angle is produced, the assumption was fortunate: if otherwise, the angle of the resulting point is assumed, and the operation is repeated: which method, although imperfect due to the brevity of the Table, will not be useless in this place.

<column-break/>

->*FINALLY, I WILL TEACH HOW TO COMPUTE, BY LOGARITHMS ALONE, WITHOUT ANY other Tables, both the Angle of the East and at the same time the rising point itself, from a given Oblique Ascension, universally and exactly.*<-

<margin>PRECEPT 46.</margin>
**First** observe the cases, which of the Equinoctial points <note>Aries or Libra</note> is above the Horizon, and in which quadrant of the heavens it is. For if it is in the eastern; the rising degree is to be sought, or the arc from the high Equinox all the way to the rising: but if in the western; the setting degree is sought, or the arc of the Ecliptic from the setting point all the way to the high Equinox. In either case, the corresponding arc of the Equator is used. For the Logarithm of this, added to the Logarithm of the altitude of the equator, constitutes the Logarithm of the altitude of that equinoctial point. And the Antilogarithm <note>The inverse of the logarithm</note> of this, subtracted from the Antilogarithm of the Equator, leaves the Logarithm of the angle between the Equator and the Vertical circle which is drawn through the equinox. To this angle, the Obliquity of the Ecliptic is added if Aries (♈) is at the rising, or Libra (♎) at the setting; it is subtracted if Libra is at the rising or Aries at the setting: thus the vertical angle with the Ecliptic will be established. The Logarithm of this, added to the Antilogarithm of the altitude of the Equinoctial point already elicited, gives the Antilogarithm of the Angle of the East; which, together with the Logarithm of the same, is useful for Parallaxes. Indeed, this Logarithm of the Angle of the East, subtracted from the Logarithm of the Altitude of the Equinoctial point, leaves the Logarithm of the required side of the Ecliptic, which together with the angle of the Ecliptic and the vertical previously used, either exceeds a Quadrant or falls short of it. It is useful, however, to become accustomed to certain forms, one of which I will provide in an example.

Suppose the Oblique Ascension is 346° 48'. Therefore Pisces (♓) is above the Horizon and at the setting; and the side of the Ecliptic from the setting point all the way into Aries (♈) must be sought. To this corresponds the side of the Equator 12° 12', which is the distance from 166° 48' Oblique Descension to 180° or to Libra (♎).

### GIVEN THE LONGITUDE AND LATITUDE OF A STAR, UNDER A GIVEN ELEVATION OF THE POLE, TO FIND THE POINT OF THE ECLIPTIC RISING WITH IT, BY MEANS OF THE ANGLE OF THE EAST.

<margin>PRECEPT 47.</margin>
**I**f the latitude is northern, some point preceding the position of longitude rises with it; if it is southern, some point following it. Therefore, extract one of the angles, either from those preceding or those following. The Logarithm of that angle, subtracted from the logarithm of the latitude, leaves the Logarithm of the arc of the Horizon. From the Antilogarithm of this arc, subtract the Antilogarithm of the Latitude; there will remain the Antilogarithm of the arc of the Ecliptic, which in the first case is subtracted from the position of Longitude, and in the second case added, giving the rising point, approximately. For with this, a truer angle is now extracted to repeat the process, so that a truer result may emerge again.

#### E X A M P L E.

Since Mars, with 2° 30' Aries rising, is still below the horizon, I will assume some angle from those that follow 3° Aries.

### CHAPTER XV.

## ON EQUALIZING TIME ON ACCOUNT OF THE INEQUALITY OF NATURAL DAYS, and the Tables serving this purpose.

<margin>Table f. 32.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative letter S showing an astronomer holding a book, surrounded by floral vines.</image-desc>
**T**HE sum of the astronomical art is reduced to this: that once the inequality of apparent motions and its causes have been brought to light, the laws of calculation may be compiled in such a way that whatever has appeared at any time may be demonstrated to have appeared so by the necessity of the suppositions; or whatever is to appear may be predicted from the same calculation. But the inequality of apparent motions cannot be perceived or estimated otherwise than by comparison with that which is equal. Furthermore, the equality of motions is defined by the multiplication and application of an equal measure; the measure of motions is time; the final element of time known to us earth-dwellers is the day; which is completed by the revolution of the Sun to the same Meridian of any place from which it had departed. The Greeks called this *nychthemeron* <note>original: $\nu\upsilon\chi\theta\acute{\eta}\mu\epsilon\rho o\nu$, meaning a 24-hour period of night and day</note>, because it consists of night and day; Latin Astronomers have been accustomed to call it the *Natural Day*, so that they might distinguish it from the other notion of the word, for that part only which has the Sun above the Horizon.

<margin>The measure of motions.</margin>
<margin>Day.</margin>
<margin>Natural Day.</margin>

Therefore, although from the time of refined science until Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the famous Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used</note>, this common Principle was held by all astronomers: that the course of the first movable sphere <note>Latin: *Primum Mobile*, the outermost celestial sphere that carries the stars</note> (whatever body might deserve that name) was most equal through all parts of its time, and therefore properly suited to express the modules of equal motions: nevertheless, because something was added to one revolution of the First Movable to count as one day—namely, the returning of the Sun to the same spot—it pertained to the skillful diligence of the Astronomer to examine whether any inequality of the composite thing which is the Day resulted from these additions of parts by the necessity of demonstrations; and if any were found, to smooth it out, lest the measure of unequal motions should itself be not perfectly equal.

<margin>The revolution in the elements of the Day.</margin>
<margin>And the Addition.</margin>

After the hidden recesses of the art were thoroughly examined under Tycho, and the motions of the Moon called to a more exact examination, that greatest Axiom of astronomers—concerning the equality of the motion of the First Movable—first began to waver a little, while Tycho himself was still living and approving. And it seemed that the body which represents the first motion, together with the departure of the Sun from the center of the Earth, lost something of the speed of its revolution, and was in turn accelerated by its approach; however, that was not distributed over the duration of one entire revolution according to this proportion of approach and departure, but at least in a small part of it: just as if the Sun, by its manifold proximity to the Earth throughout the whole circuit of the year, assisted that force which completes the first motion, by one hundred and eightieth part of the whole. And so Tycho, on the advice of Christian Severini Longomontanus <note>Tycho's primary assistant</note>, who then in this sphere...

# RUDOLPHINE TABLES.
<meta>catchword: conver-</meta>

<margin>Danish Astronomy, Theory I, page 42.</margin>
...was occupied, he ordered that one cause of the equation of time—introduced by his predecessors out of the necessity of demonstrations—should again prevail, as it did not cohere in any periods of the Moon, lest that astronomical cause be exactly balanced by that physical intensification and remission of motions <note>Kepler refers to the speeding up and slowing down of planets in their orbits</note>: in this matter, Longimontanus <note>Christian Sørensen Longomontanus, Tycho Brahe’s former assistant</note> follows my stated judgment in his *Danish Astronomy*, Theory I, without exception.

<margin>The occasion found for the Physical Equation of days. Their page... ignored.</margin>
However, since in the first volume of the *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe’s *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata*</note> (specifically in the lunar pages inserted later), the matter itself was proposed—namely, a different equation of time in the motions of the Moon than in the Sun—the cause was not explained, and was moreover hidden by that very diversity: {for if the cause is physical, it ought to be observed in the Sun as much as in the Moon}. From this it happened that astronomers everywhere voiced complaints about the perceived violation of the most certain demonstrations and appealed here to my judgment. Therefore, to gratify them, I dared to publicly propose in the *Epitome of Astronomy*, Book III and Book VI, and in the introductions to the *Ephemerides*, what I had long meditated on regarding this business, and to indicate what seemed to me to be the causes of the matter. And indeed, in the matter itself, I seemed to have succeeded; yet in this I hesitated not a little; for whereas for the 180th part of a Period, that is, for nearly 2 days <note>original: "diebus 2 ferè"</note>, which were to be ascribed to the Sun's assisting power so that the cause of the matter might be plain, there was offered to me instead 54 days <note>Kepler is likely discussing a cycle or period here</note>. This signified, namely, for 360 years <note>original: "Anni 360"</note>... the physical [equation] grew for me to 21 minutes and 40 seconds of one hour, not only balancing what Tycho had discarded concerning the astronomical and demonstrative equation of time, but even demanding more in the contrary direction.

<margin>Epitome page 283 and page 721. Number 30.</margin>
<margin>Physical.</margin>
And if I confess frankly, this measure of 54 days also failed me by an excess of about a fourth part elsewhere, where I deduced the Variation <note>A specific lunar inequality discovered by Tycho Brahe</note> from it. Thus, the most probable argument fights for the cause I have submitted, while simultaneously leaving the quantity in doubt. Perhaps a later day will finally reveal its agreement with the Tychonic quantity, something which has happened to me more than once before; and Longimontanus predicted the whole outcome above.

<margin>No equation of days agrees with experience.</margin>
Nevertheless, the more Eclipses of the Sun and Moon I examine from that time, the more I experience this: which method of calculation should be followed—the astronomical one of the ancients, the Tychonic one, or my physical and causal one—since there is none of these that is not confirmed by some eclipses and refuted by others, though the Tychonic least of all. Meanwhile, day by day, a multiple and imperceptible variety in the motions of the Sun, Moon, and the Prime Mover <note>The "Primum Mobile," the outermost sphere of the heavens</note> brings itself to light regarding certain tiny fractions, which provide the most certain evidence.

<margin>Because the first motion is not entirely uniform.</margin>
For those physical [causes] (to begin with the superfluous conjunctions of the Planets into one place), a plan arises for me from the facts themselves: that we should return to the merely astronomical and certain causes for equating time, so that, just as in the doctrine of some concerning the Sun and Moon, I teach how to calculate the quantities and appearances...

<margin>Yet the demonstrative ratio of equating must be embraced.</margin>

<column-break/>

...of those eclipses which are shaped by purely astronomical causes, and I discern <note>original: "necernoque," likely *discerno*</note> the physical and optical enlargements of the appearances—whether true ones, through the envelopes of the Earth's or Moon's atmosphere and the splendors of the ether around the body of the Sun, or deceptive ones, through those things which happen to human sight by reason of the sensory instrument <note>the eye</note>. So also in equating time, by astronomical laws that are purely astronomical, such an agreement appears that we can use it as a regular rule; moreover, something extra-astronomical has been detected here from physical causes. For if anything has been detected in these matters through long observation, or at least through better examples closely adapted, the calculator will be more correctly taught regarding it at the end, in the astronomical precepts.

However, this liberty had to be left to Astronomers, so that I, who build upon Tycho's foundation (or rather Tycho [via] Christian Severinus Longomontanus), do as the aforementioned Christian Severinus Longomontanus does; while in the rest, both the demonstrative method of the ancients and the astronomical and physical method reduced by me [are used]. According to the mode of each cause, which is constant, two Tables of the Equations of Time have necessarily been constructed. The first represents the Tychonic mode alone, adapted to the signs of the Zodiac, and serving the astronomical [method]. For the second element, there are twin columns: the left ones, which have larger characters, [show] the equations [and those with] smaller characters <note>original: "miuſculos," for *minusculos*</note> from their own species, deleting that of the ancient demonstrations and transforming the Tychonic empirical-physical one, with both modes adapted to the Anomaly of the Sun <note>The angular distance of a planet from its perihelion</note>.
<margin>Why are three modes of equating days proposed?</margin>

<margin>The first is the Tychonic Mode. PRECEPT 49. Table page 32.</margin>
Therefore, when you are about to equate time according to the opinion of Tycho Brahe, keep the true position of the Sun in the Zodiac and enter the table called the Tychonic Table. Look for the sign of the Sun at the top, and the degree in the margin and at the bottom—this in the right margin... and it will show, at the common intersection, the Equation of Days in Times and their parts. If, therefore, the apparent time <note>Solar time as shown by a sundial</note> is to be converted into equal time <note>Mean time, which flows uniformly</note>, these minute-equations of the hours must be handled, proceeding from either of the solstitial points toward the solstices... thus the apparent time will be produced. This is a general precept.

<margin>Special observation.</margin>
Specifically, if the question about apparent time is asked for no other reason than to obtain the rising Degree <note>The Ascendant</note> and its angle formed with the Horizon, for the sake of perceiving the differences in the Parallaxes of the Moon, then for the purpose of determining that rising point, there will be no need for conversion...

### [RUD]OLPHINE PRECEPTS. 35

<margin>
Why in the Tables of the equation of Time, Equatorial times are shown, rather than hourly minutes.
</margin>
...the conversion of **Equatorial Times** <note>Time measured in degrees of the celestial equator, where 15° equals one hour</note> of this equation into **hourly minutes**; instead, those very Times and **Scruples** <note>Small units of measure, usually 1/60th of a degree</note>, as they are drawn from their own Table, can be immediately added to the **right ascension** <note>The position of a star or planet along the celestial equator</note> of the **Midheaven** <note>The highest point of the ecliptic on the meridian</note>, or the **oblique ascension** of the **Horoscope** <note>The Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, which was established through equal time, or subtracted from it. Because this is almost the only use of this equation, I thought it better to present these quantities in Equatorial Times and Scruples rather than in hourly minutes.

<margin>
Tycho's method of equating time, even without his specific Table.
</margin>
That same Tychonic <note>Referring to Tycho Brahe, the great Danish observer</note> equation of days is also calculated in another way and without a special table, using only the Table of **Right Ascensions**; for it is nothing other than the difference between the longitude of the **true position of the Sun** from the Equinox and its Right Ascension. It will be helpful to keep this in memory when you move to the second astronomical method of equation, which is to be compared with this one.

<margin>
It is perpetual.
</margin>
This Precept is valid in any century, nor does it require any other application for a specific age to make it shorter, as the remaining equations do; surely because it encompasses a single, and indeed the simplest, cause for equating time.

<margin>
Why it is first in order.
</margin>
And I have given priority to this method, both because of this very simplicity and because the following second and "astronomical" method holds this one as a single element of its composition, and cannot be completed without it. Even if that were not the case, respect for the first author of these Tables <note>Tycho Brahe</note>, who embraced that method, would have secured this place for it. Finally, although this method of equating time is merely **empirical** <note>Based on observation rather than pure theory</note>, it has so far found more supporting evidence from the eclipses accurately observed in our age.

<margin>
Concerning the second or Astronomical method of equating days. Its two causes.
</margin>
I PASS to the second method of equating days; of which, as it is a composite, more must be said. And first, it must be repeated here from ancient Astronomy: there are two causes for equating natural days; one from the inequality of **Right Ascensions**, the other from the unequal motion of the Sun through the **Zodiac**. The former begins from the equinoctial or solstitial points; the latter from the **Apogee** <note>The point in the orbit furthest from Earth</note> or **Perigee** <note>The point closest to Earth</note> of the Sun. Therefore, we have only two years from all passed ages when the principles of both causes converged: in the year 3993 before our current Christian era, on April 24, when the Sun and the Sun's Apogee <term>☉</term> were at 0° **Aries** <term>♈︎</term>; and after Christ in the year 1466, on June 14, when that same Apogee and the Sun itself were at 0° **Cancer** <term>♋︎</term>.

<margin>
The third cause is neither certain nor necessary. The cause of inequality in the Precession of Equinoxes.
</margin>
There is indeed a third astronomical cause that might require time to be equated, namely the unequal **precession of the equinoctial points** arising from the change in the **Obliquity of the Ecliptic** <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis</note>; but this change is uncertain, either in fact or at least in its manner (as will be said in its proper place), and in so short a passage of centuries, even if it existed and were clearly known, it would nevertheless accumulate no sensible difference in times. Therefore, it is rightly either omitted, or if it exists, it is ignored.

For that other unequal occurrence of the Equinoxes—which arises from the transition of the Sun's equations from the solstitial points to the equinoctial points—is not a matter of the positions or points of the Ecliptic, but of the moments of time, which have thus far lengthened the **Tropical year** <note>The year measured from equinox to equinox</note> starting from the Vernal Equinox and shortened it from the Autumnal. No **trepidation** <note>A discarded theory that the equinoxes "vibrated" back and forth</note> of the beginning of the Zodiac arises from this, and no alteration of Right Ascensions through it, nor any further material for equating time.

<margin>
The method is the same as in the Prutenic Tables, but the precept is distinct. The times of the Prutenic Epochs are "apparent." Why the Epochs of these Tables are for "mean" Times?
</margin>
Secondly, this must be especially impressed upon students of Astronomy: although this second method agrees entirely in its causes with the one handed down by the **Prutenic Tables** <note>Astronomical tables published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551 based on Copernicus</note>, a different logic of use must necessarily be observed here than in the Prutenic ones. For those tables, since they employ no more than five **Epochs** <note>Reference dates for calculations</note>, reduced the times of all of them through the equation of days to **apparent time**, and accommodated the positions of the mean motions to those times so taken. But because in these [Rudolphine] Tables more Epochs are placed (for reasons to be explained in their place), all of them are understood to be distant by equal intervals of hundreds or thousands of years. For it would have been most troublesome to reduce each and every Epoch separately to its own apparent time, and to thrust as many Right Ascensions of the true Sun's motion upon the calculator as there are Epochs, solely for the sake of equating time—especially since the methods of equating are many, and the matter is subject to doubt.

<margin>
PRECEPT 50. How the positions of the stars assigned to the Epochs of these Tables should be corrected, so they agree with their Times when taken apparently.
</margin>
THEREFORE, if anyone wished to compute the position of the Moon at the very Time of one Epoch placed in these Tables—specifically, at its exactly completed year—it would be necessary first to apply the equation of days to that time. This is done if one either subtracts the motions collected through the minutes of the equation of days from the position of the Epoch (if the equation is subtractive), or adds them (if it is additive). Thus the positions will correspond to the completed **apparent year** of the Epoch. For no moment of time can be given that does not require the equation of days, as it is handed down in these Tables, except for those in which either the causes of equating time begin from one and the same Cardinal point, or one compensates for the other; which happens twice in any year.

<margin>
Second Method of equating Time.
1. PRECEPT 51.
</margin>
The second astronomical and demonstrative method of equating time is not, strictly speaking, drawn from a Table, but from a comparison of the **position of the Mean Sun** and the **Right Ascension** of the **True Sun's position**. For the difference of these—whether consisting of Equatorial Times or converted into hourly minutes as before—is the equation of time itself. It is subtracted from apparent time if the Mean Sun's position exceeds the True Sun's Right Ascension; it is added if it falls short of it, so that it becomes **equal [mean] time**. The opposite is done if Mean time is to be converted into Apparent, as before.

<margin>
2. PRECEPT 52. With Precept 49.
</margin>
But yet, because the necessity does not occur so frequently in these Tables of computing the Mean Sun's position (since we are relieved of that if we work through the subsidiary Tables of the Sun), we shall err very little if we proceed like this: First, let the Tychonic equation be sought, as before, in Equatorial Times with its title. Then with the **equated Anomaly of the Sun** <note>The angular distance of the Sun from its furthest point, adjusted for orbital eccentricity</note> reduced into signs (or its remainder to the whole circle)...

<margin>Table on folio 32.</margin>
...entry) should be made into the second Table of the Equation of Days. From its left-hand columns, which are titled "From Astronomy," one should extract the degrees and **scruples** <note>small units of measure, 1/60th of a degree</note> of the Equation of the Sun, along with its label <note>original: "titulo," referring to whether the value is to be added or subtracted</note>, from either the top or bottom of the table. Third, these two elements are combined into one, as the labels require. For if the labels are the same, they are added into one sum with that same label; if they are different, the smaller is taken from the larger, and the remainder keeps the label of the larger. Thus, this combined equation will be established in degrees and scruples, which are easily converted into hourly minutes. 
<margin>By Precept 16.</margin>
This equation is then added to or subtracted from the **apparent time** <note>time as shown by the Sun's position</note> as the final label dictates. But if **equal time** <note>mean or "clock" time</note> is being converted into apparent time, one must do the opposite of what the combined equation's label says, as noted above.

<margin>Third method. PRECEPT 53.</margin>
The THIRD method, which I have chosen to call **physical**, needs no special instruction: for it is carried out just like the second, with the help of the second Table, except that the left columns of the Table are ignored and the right columns are entered. These right-hand columns show the "excess" of the physical cause I have proposed over the astronomical equation (the Equation of the Sun); the labels are opposite to those of the second method throughout.

<margin>A particular method of equating days adapted to our century. Table on folio 32.</margin>
Since there are three methods of equating, of which only the first is simple—and therefore that one perpetual and universal Table was suitable for any time—it was appropriate that I follow the example of the **Prutenic Tables** <note>Astronomical tables by Erasmus Reinhold based on Copernicus</note> and build another Table. In it, I have placed two columns for the two latter methods of equating, adapted to the year 1616 AD, when I began writing the **Ephemerides** <note>tables of daily planetary positions</note>; however, these can serve without trouble for fifty years or more, both before and after that date. Their use is easier, for they already show the finished result that must be calculated in the latter two methods, <margin>PRECEPT 54.</margin> and are even reduced into hourly minutes. The reasoning and use of the labels are the same as shown in the previous Precepts.

### EXAMPLE OF THE TRIPLE MODE OF EQUATING TIME.

Let an apparent time be assigned for the year 747 BC <note>the start of the Era of Nabonassar, commonly used by ancient astronomers</note>, on the 25th of February: at 22 hours and 12 minutes after equal noon, when the **mean motion** <note>average position</note> of the Sun is 10 **Signs** <note>segments of 30 degrees</note>, 28° 4'. The **Apogee** <note>the point in orbit furthest from the center</note> is at 25° 34' 8". The **equated anomaly** <note>the angle of the planet from its apogee</note> is calculated, and the **true position** of the Sun is 0° 7' 12" in Pisces (♓); its **right ascension** <note>position along the celestial equator</note> is 332° 12', leaving 85° 26' (or 2 Signs, 25° 26') to complete the circle.

*First, therefore, the Tychonic Equation is extracted from the first column based on the Sun's true position: 2° 6'. These are 8 minutes and 24 seconds of an hour, with the label "Add"; but because equal time is now being converted into apparent time, they should be subtracted; the apparent time becomes 22 hours, 3 minutes, 39 seconds.*

*Secondly, the astronomical equation of time is sought, which I calculate without a Table as follows: The mean position of the Sun from the equinox is 328° 4'. But the right ascension of the Sun's position is 332° 13'. The difference is 4° 9' 28", which equals 16 minutes and 38 seconds. And because the mean position of the Sun is less, the equation would have to be added to apparent time to make it equal. Therefore, it must now be subtracted from the e-*

<column-break/>

*qual time, and there remains an apparent time of 21 hours, 55 minutes, 22 seconds by the astronomical and demonstrative method.*

*Let the same astronomical equation be sought through the second Table. From the first small table, the first element has already been found as 2° 6' (Add). And because the equated Anomaly of the Sun is 9 Signs, 4° 34', searching below in the left column of the second Table gives 2° 3' 29" to be added as the second element. Since both elements are to be added, make a sum, which is 4° 9' 29" (Add); the same as before.*

*Thirdly, the physical (or quasi-physical) equation of time is sought. Therefore, retaining the first element already found, let the other element—the excess of the physical method over the astronomical, which Tycho rejected—be extracted from the right-hand column using the same Anomaly of the Sun. This is 3° 21' to be subtracted from the apparent; here, therefore, it is added to the equal time, if it is first reduced to minutes, making 13' 24". Thus, the apparent time will be 22 hours, 25 minutes, 24 seconds.*

To Tycho empirically -------- 22 h. 3 m. 36 s. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; }
To Astronomers demonstratively -- 21 h. 55 m. 22 s. &nbsp;&nbsp; } Apparent
To me, interpreting Tycho physically 22 h. 25 m. 24 s. }

### EXAMPLE ON THE USE OF THE TEMPORARY TABLE.

*In the year 1598, on the 25th of February in the Julian calendar (or March 7th in the Gregorian), at equal noon at **Uraniborg** <note>Tycho Brahe's observatory in Denmark</note>, the equation of Time is sought. Since the Sun is at 16° 49' Pisces, that position from the first Table provides a Tychonic equation in Time of 1° 3' 30", which are 4 minutes and 14 seconds of an hour to be added to apparent time (and therefore subtracted here from equal time). The same position of the Sun from the Temporary Equation Table, adapted to the year 1616, shows in the left column 12 minutes to be added likewise for the astronomical equation, but in the right column it shows 8 minutes to be subtracted for the physical equation.*

## CHAPTER XVI.

### ON THE REDUCTION OF TIMES CALCULATED IN DIFFERENT PLACES TO THE MERIDIAN OF THESE TABLES: and on the Catalog of Places.

<margin>Table on folio 33 and following.</margin>
<margin>What choice of places?</margin>
**I**n order that the use of these Tables might be as wide and popular as possible, I have seen fit to insert a Catalog of five hundred places and more. In choosing them, I followed various reasons. Since the Tables are named after **RUDOLPH** the Emperor of the Austrian family, and since I myself am German by nation and Austrian by residence, I have indulged heavily in the kingdoms and provinces of Austria and the rest of Germany. Nor did the fame of its locations allow me to touch upon Italy only lightly. Therefore, having taken into account the division of provinces—mostly modern, though in some places ancient—I have selected from each the seats and courts of Princes, Academies, Bishoprics, as-

He also begins a new chapter introducing a catalog of geographical locations, emphasizing his ties to the Holy Roman Empire.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the technical calculations of time to the geographical data required for astronomical observations. It introduces the catalog of locations, explaining how Kepler determined the latitudes and longitudes of various cities to ensure the Rudolphine Tables could be used accurately across the known world.</meta>

->[RUD]OLPHINE PRECEPTS<-

...legal assemblies, trading centers, busy markets, famous fortifications, promontories, ports, and places made famous by historical events. I have also included the residences of mathematicians who have worked on observing the stars, even those who are otherwise of obscure name. If any places are omitted from this list that have a legal, fair, or superior claim to be there, let that be blamed on other neighboring locations that could not be left out. Perhaps you will also find certain places assigned not to their own provinces but to neighboring ones; I ask that this be forgiven as a failure of memory. Indeed, the legal rights of territories are not the focus here; rather, I am assisting the reader’s understanding of external locations.

<margin>Description of the Catalog of places.</margin>
<margin>Table on folio 36.</margin>
The greater concern for mathematicians lies in the numbers; a single piece of evidence regarding the difficulty of this business has been placed at the end of the Catalog to fill the space. There are two orders of numbers: the latter is the **Latitude** <note>original: "Altitudinum Poli," literally "heights of the Pole," referring to how high the North Star appears</note> in Degrees and **Scruples** <note>arc-minutes, or 1/60th of a degree</note>; the former is the difference of **Meridians** <note>longitude</note> in Hours and Minutes, with a label of "Addition" for Eastern places and "Subtraction" for Western places.

<margin>What reliability do the latitudes have?</margin>
<margin>See Precept 38.</margin>
As far as the latitudes are concerned, their entire certainty depends on celestial observations. However, since observations have been made in few places—and not always accurately—the authors of geographical maps often lack data for those spots from mathematicians. Instead, they adapt neighboring places within the same province based on travel distances and directions. Often, they even trust the *Geography* of **Ptolemy** <note>an influential 2nd-century Greco-Roman mathematician and geographer</note>, who followed almost nothing but the length of the longest summer day as he was able to gather it from the reports of others.

<margin>The latitude of Paris.</margin>
Today, mathematicians use maps already completed as if they were authentic, essentially reversing the proper order of things; few pay attention to how weak the foundations are upon which those maps rely. Because of this, some variation arises even regarding latitudes, which might surprise you. For **Paris** <note>original: "Lutetia Parisiorum"</note>, **Tycho Brahe** <note>the famous Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used</note> gives 48° 10' in the Catalog corrected by **Longomontanus** <note>Christian Severin, Tycho’s assistant</note>, while the mathematicians **Fernelius** and **Orontius** <note>Oronce Finé</note> put it at 48° 40'. **Vieta** <note>François Viète</note>, writing more recently, gives 48° 49'. Nevertheless, the geographical maps of **Mercator** and **Piscator** <note>the Latinized name of the mapmaker Visscher</note> stay closer to Orontius; following them, I have set it at 48° 39'.

<margin>On the Longitudes of places.</margin>
<margin>Ways of finding the differences of Meridians.</margin>
<margin>Precept 61.</margin>
Regarding the **Longitudes** <note>original: "Longitudines," the east-west position</note> of places, or the differences of Meridians, the matter becomes much more complex, as we stray further from direct observations. Various **schemes** <note>original: "Epichiremata," a Greek-derived term for methods or attempts</note> exist for finding these differences through observations, but as usually happens, most possess more ingenuity than practical convenience for the task at hand. This is not the place to discuss the other methods; I will speak below of the one that uses the observation of the Moon when it is at its **nonagesimal** <note>the highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon</note>.

For the construction of this Catalog, I made use of this single method of observation, which must be managed by different people working together: when certain phases of one and the same **Eclipse** are observed in different places. This type of observation is a very rare occurrence, but it was sought out with great zeal for the preparation of this Catalog. Even so, I could not always be certain of the reliability of observers in other places, except when different reports agreed with one another.

<margin>The utility of Solar Eclipses.</margin>
Regarding this method, it must be noted first that Solar Eclipses, especially large ones, are much more suitable than Lunar ones. For their beginnings or ends are recognized accurately, and the time-distance

<column-break/>

of different phases is given by calculation. This allows phases observed in different places to be compared with one another, and the method for removing **parallax** <note>the displacement in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight</note> is most certain and refined in these Tables. Additionally, a diligent observer can use a compass to explore the size of the phases as they increase and decrease on a small tablet upon which the Sun's ray falls.

<margin>An apology for the changes in this catalog.</margin>
When mathematicians discover that I have attempted something new and unusual in this Catalog, I would ask them first of all to examine the foundation of that geographical map whose evidence they think reveals the "strangeness" of my numbering. Second, I ask them to compare the various foundations of maps with one another and consider the disagreements among the authors from whom those maps sought their foundations. They should reflect that no map gains greater authority from long use than the authority of the original observation upon which it relied.

<margin>What reliability in regional maps?</margin>
Some credit should certainly be given to maps of individual provinces if they were made by diligent inhabitants. However, that only applies to the layout of places within that same province and its common borders with neighbors; it cannot be extended to joining together provinces that are far apart. If a geographer has correctly placed Paris, he will not place the remaining cities of France poorly; but if he began from Paris and erred by half a degree, that same error will overflow into all of France, even if the individual distances between cities remain correct.

<margin>Rome moved toward the west.</margin>
<margin>Table on folio 36.</margin>
Now, to come to the main points of my innovations: the first was proposed above, with **Rome** being related to the meridian of **Hven** <note>original: "Huennæ," the island where Tycho Brahe's observatory, Uraniborg, was located</note>, which all of Italy follows. I held to the foundation found at the end of the catalog: two eclipses of the Moon observed in Rome, **Tübingen**, and **Linz**. If you ask what happens to the borders of Germany and Italy? I say those borders are occupied by the Alps and the Apennines; therefore, I took part of the difference to be removed from the former and part from the latter.

<margin>The shores of the North Sea contracted.</margin>
**Snellius** <note>Willebrord Snell, a Dutch astronomer and mathematician</note> in his *Dutch Eratosthenes* notes that there is an extra degree between Belgium and **Hamburg**; he establishes similar findings between **Kassel** and **Goes**, and the map of Piscator agrees. I have therefore removed 4 minutes. For travel routes also agree: 27 miles between **Osnabrück** and Hamburg, and 40 miles between the same and **Antwerp**. The former makes 9 minutes, the latter 15. The total from Hamburg to Antwerp is 24, or a little less if the miles are small. From the eclipse of the <term>Moon</term> <note>symbol: ☾</note> in the year 1598, even more was to be removed: for 18 minutes were found between **Alkmaar** and **Wandsbek** <note>original: "Wandesburgum"</note>, the castle near Hamburg where Tycho was then staying; I have left 21.

From the eclipse of the year 1560, I find 47' between **Leuven** <note>original: "Lovanium"</note> and **Vienna** in Austria; I find almost the same from travel intervals and the latitude, using **Augsburg** <note>original: "Augusta"</note> as a midpoint, since 86 and 61 miles are counted. The observation of the eclipse in 1600, held in **Prague** and **London** in England, also agrees to contract the space. Likewise, the eclipse of the year 1621, observed in **Butzbach** in **Wetterau** <note>original: "Putzbachij in Wetteravia"</note>, and in **Danzig** and Linz, indicates a difference of 45'. This is consistent with the maps. For Piscator's Denmark and Mercator's Poland are connected by **Kaerius** <note>Pieter van den Keere, a Dutch engraver and mapmaker</note> through nearby places; between **Greifswald** and **Stargard** (the former seen on the map of Denmark, the latter on the map of Poland), he places 8 minutes; these two maps, I say, place Danzig...
