->RUDOLPHINE TABLES<-

<margin>Exception to the authority of Tycho.</margin>
...thus they connect them with Hamburg. Therefore, with several arguments converging, and relying on the good faith of those who supplied me with the foundations of these arguments, I agreed to this contraction; though I am not unaware that Tycho Brahe, in the second book of his *Progymnasmata*, makes Kassel 25 minutes further west than Hven. I considered, however, that I was not dealing with Tycho himself, but with those maps of more ancient locations which he had followed.

I confess indeed that I am not entirely satisfied. For I would prefer to place Prague under the Meridian of Linz, and thus move all the locations in Bohemia, Silesia, Poland, Hungary, Lower Austria, and Styria 4 minutes to the east: travel distances seem to require this, provided that for all these places 15 miles are computed for one Degree of a great circle. For from Nuremberg to Prague they count 36 Miles, from Augsburg to Graz 60, from Linz to Vienna 30, and to Prague 26—a conspicuous inequality, since Prague is further than Vienna, as a ship can reach the latter in 16 hours when the river is high. I would also wish, on the contrary, to pull the Meridian of Rostock half a degree to the east of the Uraniborg <note>Uraniborg was Tycho Brahe's observatory on the island of Hven</note> meridian according to Tycho's opinion, and to remove the Nuremberg meridian further to the west of it. <margin>Progymnasmata, Tome 1, p. 51.</margin> But whoever might do such things will find themselves in trouble either with recent maps or with those who observe eclipses. Therefore, as if in a tangled lawsuit regarding minor details, let the reader treat this Catalog as an **Interlocutory Decree** <note>original: "Interlocutoriæ," a temporary legal ruling made while a case is still ongoing</note>, and let them put their own hand to the work, starting from their own location and fitting the whole neighborhood together according to the following precepts.

I reserve for myself the same freedom to correct this catalog if experts in the Art, invited by this Catalog, share their observations of distances with me. I say this so that no one may prematurely misuse my authority in world geographical maps.

BUT having now dismissed the nearby places and the minor points that are in doubt, we shall wander further afield to remote Meridians. For it pertains to the reputation of these Tables that the reader understands how the Uraniborg Meridian, which is specific to these Tables, is connected with that of Alexandria and the others under which observations were made by the ancients.

<margin>Transfer of the Meridian of these Tables through Germany and Italy</margin>
Therefore, regarding the connection of Linz and Graz with Uraniborg on one hand, and Linz and Tubingen with Rome on the other, I seem to be certain enough; and I have successfully extended the Meridian from Uraniborg all the way to Rome. I know the student of Geography will wonder that by this reasoning Venice becomes somewhat west of Rome, and Ancona approaches Villach; but they will cease to wonder if they compare the maps of Hondius and Jansson <note>Famous Dutch cartographers</note>, who have already represented this proximity for the most part. And when I consider travel accounts, the logic of the land journey from Padua to Rome—two hundred miles—seems to correspond well.

<margin>Sicily and Africa</margin>
Now, I seem to be able to safely trust the geographical maps that Rome and Lilybaeum <note>A city in Sicily, modern Marsala</note> share the same meridian, since the crossing from the port of Ostia to Palermo is hindered by no obstacles, and ships go almost daily to Malta, for which they must sail around Lilybaeum. But indeed, the end of the Carthaginian

<column-break/>

<margin>The Meridian of Carthage.</margin>
territory in Africa—the eastern promontory which was called Hermæum <note>Cape Bon in modern Tunisia</note> by the ancients—is so close to Lilybaeum in Sicily that once a certain Lynceus <note>A mythological figure known for keen eyesight</note>, watching from the heights of Lilybaeum, supposedly reported the number of ships setting sail from that port. Therefore, the Meridian of Carthage is not much further west. Let Hermæum be 4 minutes, and Carthage 9.

<margin>The difference of the Meridians of Carthage and Alexandria: Strabo. According to Precept 53 and following. How many stadia in a degree. Pliny.</margin>
Furthermore, from Carthage to Alexandria in Egypt, Strabo, in the second book of his *Geography*, counts a total number of stadia <note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</note> greater than thirteen thousand; but in book IV, he gives 10 stadia to an Italian Mile; let him therefore compute 40 for a German Mile. Thus 600 stadia make one degree of a great circle: so that this sum of stadia produces 21 Degrees and 40 Minutes. When combined with the latitudes of the North Pole, this subtends an angle at the Pole of 25° 28'. Indeed, the *Geography* of Ptolemy has exactly 25° 40'. Thus there is no doubt that the Alexandrian geographer <note>Ptolemy</note>, in establishing the meridian of Carthage from that of Alexandria, used this very same tradition of travel distance. Nevertheless, elsewhere eight stadia make a Mile. In that case, the difference between the Meridians of Carthage and Alexandria would be gathered as about a fourth part larger, namely: 32 Degrees. It is useful, therefore, to consult other authors on this distance. Pliny, following Eratosthenes and Polybius, counts 1,629 miles: he himself, more accurately through individual stations, gathers 1,792. Yet because of the great bends of the two Syrtes <note>The Gulf of Sidra and Gulf of Gabès off the coast of Libya</note>, through which Pliny leads his count, about a sixth part must be thrown out; thus 1,500 Miles will remain.

<margin>The Antonine Itinerary</margin>
The *Antonine Itinerary* <note>An ancient Roman register of stations and distances along roads</note> also moderately confirms this sum: for it counts 1,541 Roman Miles from Carthage to Alexandria by way of Thenae and Leptis Magna. If you assign 60 Italian Miles to a degree, you gather 25 Degrees of a great circle, which subtend an angle of 29° 22' at the Pole; and this is worth 1 hour and 57 minutes of time. From which, subtracting the 9 minutes of Carthage, there remains 1 hour and 48 minutes between Rome and Alexandria.

<margin>Meridian difference of Rome and Alexandria. Who is the author of the *Geography* which bears Ptolemy's name?</margin>
In my *Commentaries on the Motion of Mars*, I used 2 hours between Hven and Alexandria, based on the trust of Jansson’s map. Here Ptolemy himself, in the application of a certain observation made by Menelaus at Rome, uses only 1 hour 20 minutes. Therefore, Werner <note>Johannes Werner, a mathematician</note> not undeservedly thinks that the author of the *Geography* was someone else.

<margin>Difference of the Meridians of Alexandria and Babylon.</margin>
I proceed further. Between Alexandria and Babylon, Ptolemy’s *Great Synthesis* <note>The *Almagest*</note> uses 50 minutes, but the *Geography* uses 1 hour 24 minutes. Behold another proof of the diversity of the authors of both works. To me, when computing the Babylonian observations, that larger difference did not poorly represent the observations. However, I decided that faith should rather be placed in Al-Battani <note>Albategnius, a 9th-century Arab astronomer</note>, who again reduced this interval; which he himself, an inhabitant of those places, could know better. Thus it happened that instead of 1 hour 14 minutes, I retained 1 hour 3 minutes. From this is composed a difference for Babylon from Rome and Uraniborg of 2 hours 51 minutes. It was a pleasure to find this sufficiently consistent with the ancient book of the *Tables of Arzachel* <note>The Toledan Tables by the Arab astronomer Al-Zarqali</note>, translated from Arabic into Latin by Gerard of Cremona, as I believe. For he has the Longitudes distributed thus: that between Rome and Alexandria there are 1 hour 40 minutes, between Rome and Baghdad 2 hours 18 minutes, New Babylon 2 hours 36 minutes, and Old Babylon 2 hours 50 minutes. And because for the latitude of the Pole, he assigns 35° 0' to Old Babylon...

### RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS.

At New 30° 30': is that therefore the New Babylon, which today is Basra? Certainly, it is 4½ degrees further south than Old Babylon.

<margin>— Which Antioch according to Al-Battani?</margin>
Regarding Antioch and Aracta, the records of Al-Battani <note>original: "Albategnius," the Latinized name of the 9th-century Arab astronomer Al-Battani</note> make everything doubtful. There is a multiple overlap of names from antiquity, trade routes have been interrupted for a long time, and the numbers differ from those of Ptolemy. Ptolemy's *Geography* shows seven Antiochs in as many provinces: in Caria, Pisidia, Pamphylia, Cilicia, Commagene, the Cassiotis province of Syria, and Mesopotamia. Even though a certain Araca is joined to Antioch of Commagene near the Taurus mountains, the numerical data warns us to be wary of being played by similar-sounding words. Therefore, it is more likely that this is the Great Antioch on the Orontes. Although the *Geography* places it 34 minutes beyond Alexandria and 7 minutes before Aracta, I follow Al-Battani; he has almost the same total for both, but distributes it differently, setting 25 minutes there and 15 minutes here.

<margin>Where is Aracta?</margin>
Determining which name from the *Geography* corresponds to Al-Battani's "Aracta" brings a new doubt. Regarding Araca of Commagene, we have discussed it; but the polar altitude <note>latitude</note> of 37° 40' conflicts with it, for Al-Battani gives 36° 0' to his Aracta. The Hebrew surname *Erech* <note>original: "Erech," a city mentioned in Genesis 10:10</note> favors Edessa in Mesopotamia, as found in Jerome; perhaps the Arabs pronounce this "Arach." However, both the polar altitude of 37° 30' and the 48-minute interval are inconsistent.

But at CHARRÆ, in Hebrew called Haran, the polar altitude is 36° 10', which agrees. Let those skilled in Arabic linguistics see how the Hebrew *Haran* becomes the Arabic *Arach*. Let the Arabic manuscript of Al-Battani also be inspected to see how faithfully the translator rendered it as "Aracta," and another as "Mohammed of Araca." For even the longitude of Charræ from the *Geography*, which is 51 minutes, corresponds reasonably well if it is shortened by the same proportion by which Al-Battani shortens the Babylonian measurements. For where Ptolemy has 74 minutes, Al-Battani retains 63. And so, for the 51 minutes of Charræ, we shall by the same logic set 40. For in this way we also set 25 minutes for the 34 minutes of Antioch.

<margin>On the different starting points of Longitudes for Ptolemy and the Arabs. *Introduction to the Canons*, page 259.</margin>
I have taken the interval for Tybenes in Persis from Toledo, Spain, as 72° longitude and 38° latitude, based on the trust of the mathematicians of Persis <note>modern-day Iran</note>, whom Jakob Christmann cites from Isaac the Monk, and Scaliger from George Chrysococcas. This is despite the fact that Scaliger, following a Tunisian astrologer and his Arabic commentator, translates the starting point of longitudes, *Gezaer chalidath*, word for word as the "Islands of the Blessed" and the "limit of the West"—the same starting point for counting that Ptolemy followed in his *Geography*. Indeed, he brings forward from Giovanni Battista Ramusio (preface to the second volume of *Navigations*) the Arabic geographer Abu'l-Fida Ismael, who warns that the Arabs, in their counting of longitudes, subtract 10 degrees from Ptolemy’s figures. Thus George Chrysococcas, and Isaac himself, apply that Arabic name to Gades <note>Cádiz, Spain</note>, whose longitude is almost the same as Toledo’s, specifically: "at the farthest and western sea" <note>original Greek: "τῇ ἐσχάτῃ καὶ δυτικῇ θαλάττῃ"</note> which begins at Cádiz. It is as if the Arabs confused the "limit of the West" with the "limit of the western sea." Fame certainly accrued to Cádiz from the eventual arrival and success of the Arabs there.

<margin>See Scaliger, *Emendation of Time*, Book VI, folio 584.</margin>
<margin>Why most make the Toledo Meridian the start of their counting.</margin>
Because of this, the Muslim Arabs of Spain, followed by the Jews and the Alphonsine tables, set the longitude of Toledo as 0°, making it the starting point of their calculations.

<column-break/>

<margin>What is Tybene?</margin>
To try to find this "Tybene" of the Khazaria province of Persis in Ptolemy's *Geography* is like a man on foot chasing birds. Scaliger warns about Sogdiana, but there is no likelihood in either the numbers or the name. The conjecture regarding Adiabene seems better; in Ptolemy’s *Geography*, this extends between Arrapachitis and the Garamæans [namesakes of Arphaxad and Aram] between 77° and 80° Longitude, and between 38° and 41° Latitude. Now, I have already said that 80° from the "Blessed Isles" are 70° from Toledo and Cádiz.

<margin>Europe contracted toward the West. See Snell's *Belgic Eratosthenes*.</margin>
In contracting the intervals of Europe toward the west, I have followed not only the opinion of Snell but also observations of eclipses, frequently consulting travel distances based on popular estimates and booklets published on this matter. Although both methods are slippery, the matter cannot be settled without a certain multitude and averaging of opinions. The reduction is indeed quite large, since Santritter, in his edition of the Alphonsine Tables, sets the time between Toledo and Nuremberg at 1 hour and 24 minutes, while I set it at 1 hour 0 minutes. Yet this reduction fits well for making the eclipse of the year 1560 total at Coimbra. Peter Apian in his *Cæsareum* does not differ much, placing Toulouse in France 41 minutes from Nuremberg; if I add to this what I have between Toulouse and Toledo (22 minutes), it totals 1 hour 3 minutes. He places Narbonne 35 minutes away; if I add the 24 minutes I have between Narbonne and Toledo, we total 59 minutes. I have looked for more Spanish eclipses in vain so far. I have distributed this reduction proportionally along the coasts, but especially in the Ligurian and Marseilles gulfs, because the measurement of journeys through the Alps and Pyrenees ending at this sea is usually very distorted.

<margin>To be extended toward the East.</margin>
Conversely, in the extension of Muscovy and Russia toward the East, as I lacked eclipse observations, I placed my trust in the travel dimensions found in Sigismund von Herberstein. Meanwhile, I have left the Crimean Peninsula <note>Taurica Chersonessus</note> and the Caspian Gates to Jansson, though with hesitant agreement. For Herberstein makes the Crimea east of Moscow, and Strabo seems to move the Caspian Gates closer to India; he is the only one among the inland authors who deserves as much trust as our sailors do for the coastlines. For who after Alexander—the source of Strabo’s material in this place—has both measured those lands and committed his expeditions to writing? Aside from the obscure descriptions of the private travels of Marco Polo the Venetian and Ludovico di Varthema, whose reliability regarding intervals is mostly uncertain. I believe the journeys of caravans through vast and inhospitable wildernesses are very inconsistent; and if they must be measured by the strength of camels, we Europeans generally remain ignorant of them.

<margin>The Meridian of Frombork observed by Copernicus. His Polar Altitude, page 22. *Progymnasmata*, Vol. 1, p. 34.</margin>
In establishing the meridian of Frombork <note>original: "Frueburgum," in Warmia, Poland</note>, where Copernicus observed, I also consulted travel distances in addition to the sources mentioned above. They count 80 miles from Lübeck to Danzig by the shortest route along the Baltic coast, which is 31 minutes. Lübeck is 8 minutes from Rostock according to the maps; thus 29 or 28 minutes remain for Danzig. From there to Frombork is 4 minutes according to the maps. I find in my papers elsewhere 15 minutes between Rostock and Stargard via eclipses; based on the principles stated here, I have made it 11 minutes.

### RUDOLPHINE TABLES

Chapter 11, in the meantime, while I deliberate further on the promotion of eastern places, of which I spoke shortly before.

But let there be a limit to this etiology <note>original: "αιτιολογιας," an explanation of causes or reasoning</note>; let us move on to the precepts.

<margin>PRECEPT 55.</margin>
The first and proper use of the Catalog is in the reduction of the time—at which some future Eclipse or a conjunction of the Sun and Moon with the stars is calculated—to the meridian of any given place. At that time, the titles of the meridian differences added to the catalog must be observed: namely, the Hours and Minutes to which the letter **A** is added must be *added* to the time found by calculation; those followed by the letter **S** must be *subtracted*; because those to the east count more time, and those to the west count less. By this reasoning, it will sometimes happen that the number of Hours, growing beyond 24 by addition, must be assigned to the following day after those 24 are subtracted; or if a larger number is ordered to be subtracted from a smaller number of Uraniburg <note>The meridian of Tycho Brahe’s observatory, Kepler's primary reference point</note> time, 24 hours of the preceding day must be adopted, and the phenomenon itself must be ascribed to a different day of the month in different places.

If, however, a certain time for any place is offered under which the Moon was observed, and you are commanded—either because of this observation or for another cause—to compute the position of the Moon or planets from these tables for that local Meridian: before you undertake that work, subtract or add the Hours and Minutes assigned to each place in the Catalog (contrary to what the titles "A" or "S" command) from the offered time, so that it may be reduced to the Uraniburg or Roman meridian. The precept is easy and well-worn, and needs no peculiar example.

But take heed, calculator, also of the method for correcting these differences of meridians, if they should have need of correction, or if the care of expanding the Catalog touches you.

<margin>What a Mile is and how many in one Degree.</margin>
A German mile is commonly estimated as the journey which any fit traveler completes in an interval of two hours. Fifteen of these Miles are contained in one degree of a great circle drawn across the surface of the earth. When, therefore, the interval between two places is offered in German miles—provided they are standard miles and the path <margin>PRECEPT 56.</margin> is the shortest, not winding with long detours—divide the number of miles by 15, so that they may be reduced into degrees and minutes <note>original: "scrupula," literally "scruples," used here for small parts of a degree</note> of a great circle. Then, obtain for yourself the difference in the polar altitudes <note>latitudes</note> of both places from somewhere. For if both places are in the same detailed map, this difference is easily sought out and without danger of error, even if the altitudes themselves have a flaw. But if the places are located further apart toward the east or west, there will be little harm even from some small error in this difference. Thus, you will be able to use the Polar Altitude of one place even taken from this Catalog, and the Polar Altitude of the other place, somewhat distant, excerpted from any map or tradition. Now, if the interval is not large, it is expedient to pursue a shortcut, however unscientific: subtract the Antilogarithm <margin>From the Table on page 23.</margin> of the difference of the Polar altitudes from the Antilogarithm of the interval reduced into degrees; the remainder, as an Antilogarithm, will show an arc, from whose Logarithm or Logistic <note>referring to Kepler’s sexagesimal logarithmic system</note> (sought in the Sexagesimal Heptacosfadis <note>Kepler's "Table of 700," a specialized logarithmic table</note>) or Canonical value, subtract the Antilogarithm of the greater Polar altitude; there will remain either a Logistic or Canonical value showing, either in the Sexagesimal Heptacosfadis or in the Canon,

<column-break/>

the degrees and minutes of the Equator, which when multiplied by 4 give the hourly Minutes of the difference between the places.

> *For example, because from Linz to Graz there are 30 miles, which divided by 15 gives 2° 0'; but between their Polar altitudes there is a difference of 1° 14'. The Antilogarithm of the former is 61, and of the latter 23. The difference, 38, shows an arc of 1° 46' of the parallel. Its Logistic Logarithm is -56900. Now the Polar altitude of Linz is the greater, 48° 16'; therefore, <margin>As in Precept 8.</margin> subtract its Antilogarithm 40697 from the code (which in this place is done by addition), and it becomes diminished to -97597, which gives from the Heptacosfadis an arc of 2° 39' of the Equator. Therefore, that being multiplied by 4, the Difference of Meridians becomes 10' 36''. Thus, since Graz is a more Easterly place, with the 10' A that are assigned to Linz in the Catalog being added, 20' 36'' should be assigned to Graz. But since the Catalog, for causes explained hitherto, shows only 16' A.*

<margin>PRECEPT 57.</margin>
If, however, the interval of the places is a little further; then it cannot be done otherwise than that the Spherical triangle of the given sides be solved by the legitimate Method, and the angle at the Pole be sought. The tenor of the precept is this. Let the imagination be transferred, for the sake of clarity, to the triangle between the places and the Pole; and instead of the Polar Altitudes, let the altitudes of the equator be written, or the distances of the places from the Pole.

Therefore, join the Logarithms of these Equator Altitudes [the Antilogarithms of the Pole] into one sum. Then, to the third side (which is obtained from the travel intervals), add the difference of those same arcs, and from the same subtract it, and make halves of the arcs, both of the composite and the remainder. Join the Logarithms of these halves also into one sum; from which subtract the prior sum; half of the remainder, as a Logarithm, shows in the Canon the half of the angle at the Pole, which gives the difference of Meridians in Hours and minutes, as before.

-> E X A M P L E . <-

*From Augsburg to Madrid in Spain, there are reckoned to be 200 German miles: let the faith of the estimation rest with the travelers. 200 divided by 15 makes 13° 20' parts of a great circle. Augsburg is at Polar Altitude 48° 22', Madrid at 40° 45'.*

-> Pattern of the Process. <-

<margin>Longitude of Madrid.</margin>
This, as a Logarithm, gives 7° 39', the half-angle at the Pole. Therefore the double, 15° 18', is the very thing sought; which multiplied by 4, gives 1 Hour and 1 Minute. And because Augsburg has 45' in the Catalog, 1° 5' roughly would belong to Madrid; for which the Catalog has 1° 1'. Say that those 200 miles are somewhat short, each being 1 2/3 hours. If I had computed by the first method, the Antilogarithm of the Difference 7° 37' (namely 886), subtracted from the Antilogarithm of the interval 13° 20' (namely 2732), would have left 1846, the Antilogarithm of the Arc 10° 58 1/2'.

# PRECEPTS OF RUDOLF.

58½. Its logistical Logarithm <note>Logarithms were a new mathematical tool at this time; Kepler used them extensively to simplify complex astronomical and geographical calculations.</note> sought in the Table of Twenty-Four is 78243; from which the Antilogarithm of the greater Altitude of the Pole, 40893, was subtracted, leaving 37350. When this is sought in the Table of Seven Hundred, it erroneously shows 16° 31' in the Table of Twenty-Four, and a meridian difference of 1° 6', which is too large.

### ANOTHER EXAMPLE.

Strabo, in Book 15 of his *Geography*, counts 4200 stadia from Susa to Persepolis. However, so that we may know how many stadia make a degree of a great circle in this location, it should be noted that the same author counts 14,400 stadia from the southernmost Promontory of Caramania—which forms the strait of the Persian Gulf—to the Caspian Gates. <margin>How many stadia in one Degree.</margin> The Altitude of the Pole <note>Latitude</note> there is 25° 30', and here it is 43° 30'. The difference is 18° under nearly the same meridian, because Strabo traces the length of Persia from North to South. If 18° span 14,400 stadia, then 800 stadia correspond to one degree. And if 800 stadia give one degree, 4200 will give 5° 15'. These are the degrees from Susa to Persepolis. The Altitude of the Equator <note>The complement of latitude (90 minus the latitude).</note> is indeed:

### WHAT if, however, a calculator seeks this utility from our Catalog: that he might demand from it an indication of the travel distance between places?

<margin>PRECEPT 58.</margin> Then both ways will be the opposite. The first way, for short distances or where the difference in the Altitude of the Pole is not great, is as follows. Combine the Logarithm of the lesser Altitude of the Equator with the logarithm of the angle at the Pole (which the Difference of Meridians divided by 4 indicates) into one sum. This sum, acting as a Logarithm, will show the perpendicular arc. Join the Antilogarithm of this to the Antilogarithm of the difference in the Altitudes of the Pole; the result will be the Antilogarithm of the arc of the distance, which, as before, will show the German Miles.

### EXAMPLE.

Nuremberg is at Altitude of the Pole 49° 26', with a meridian difference of 4'. Jaroslaw in Poland is at Altitude of the Pole 49° 45' with a difference of 42'. The difference in the Altitude of the Pole is 0° 19'; the difference of Meridians is 46', which makes 11° 30'. <note>Kepler is converting time/longitude units here.</note> Logarithm 161260. Add the Logarithm of 40° 15' (the lesser equatorial altitude), which is 43676; the sum 204936 gives a perpendicular arc of 7° 24'. Its Antilogarithm, 837, increased by the Antilogarithm of 0° 19' (which is 2), makes 839, the Antilogarithm of the arc 7° 25'. This, multiplied by 15, gives 111¼ common German Miles. They are actually counted as 130; therefore, I have long been thinking of increasing the addition for this place. Although some religious travelers, when asked, affirmed that they commonly complete seven of these miles each day in Poland, and in some places eight or nine.

<margin>PRECEPT 59.</margin> The second way, more accurate, proceeds by the same principle, seeking the perpendicular; but now the Antilogarithm of this must be taken away from the Antilogarithm of the lesser equatorial altitude; with the remainder acting as a Logarithm, the arc is extracted

<column-break/>

to be compared with the greater Equatorial Altitude. For the difference of both is now to be used in place of the difference of the two Altitudes of the Pole, and thus the above process is continued through it.

For instance, if the Antilogarithm of the perpendicular, 837, is taken away from the Antilogarithm of the lesser equatorial altitude, 27019, the remainder 26182, as an Antilogarithm, shows an arc of 30° 41'. This, subtracted from 40° 34' (the greater Equatorial Altitude), leaves 0° 53', the Antilogarithm of which is 12. Added, as above, to 837, it makes 849, the Antilogarithm of arc 7° 27', which is only two minutes larger.

### ON THE UNIVERSAL WORLD MAP. <margin>Folio 36.</margin>

I hope, meanwhile, as the printing works proceed, that a Geographical Chart of the world will be produced at the same time, which I have proposed to delineate by a new method using Hourly Meridians. <margin>The starting point for numbering the longitudes of places in these Tables.</margin> Indeed, amidst the great variety of ways to establish the starting point for the Longitude of places, I thought it better to use a numbering system in which the Meridian of the island of <term>HVEN</term> and its fortress <term>URANIBORG</term> <note>Tycho Brahe’s observatory on the island of Hven, which Kepler used as his primary reference point.</note> would be the primary one. Because these Tables were constructed for that location, all those distant to the West would have a known subtraction, and all to the East an addition.

<margin>Use of the Map.</margin> Because the Tables of the Moon's motion—for which the difference of Meridians is sought—primarily serve maritime affairs, I decided that I must especially look to this. And yet the shores of both Oceans, the promontories, islands, bays, ports, river mouths, sandbanks, and similar places, in such a great variety of languages, are better known by their own natural sequence than by their names. Therefore, instead of an alphabetical sequence, I thought the map of the world itself would be more suitable for those who intend to search for any place for their own needs.

Moreover, the copy of the map is transcribed from <margin>The foundation of Jansson’s Map.</margin> the Universal Map of the World published by Willem Jansson of Alkmaar in the year of Christ 1605, during the reign of Rudolf II, from whom these Tables take their name. It relies on no other authority except for the places expressed in the Catalog and those nearby.

In this map, therefore, the central Meridian is expressed by two (or rather three) straight lines; the first of which is drawn through the broadest continents of the whole world via the upper semicircle, and it is proper to these Tables, as I have said, distinguishing the western Hemisphere, through which the...

# RUDOLPHINE TABLES

...of the difference of the Meridians, from the east, by which things must be added; the other is a straight line, which terminates the semicircular lateral disks on the right and left. It is double in appearance, but single in its power, defining <margin>The Meridian of the Antipodes of Uraniborg.</margin> the lower Meridian of the Antipodes of Uraniborg <note>Uraniborg was Tycho Brahe's observatory in Denmark, which Kepler uses as his prime meridian.</note>. In this meridian, subtractions from the west and additions from the east commonly meet; thus, from 12 hours subtracted and 12 hours added, one full day is established, despite the differences in counting to that point and beyond. However, no confusion should arise. For in this way, almost all of America—both known and hidden—is considered "Western" by me; and only the most remote hemisphere of the East extends out, in which place there is little or no commerce of ours. Conversely, 
New Guinea (perhaps a part of the Southern Land), together with the Solomon Islands and Japan, are received within the limit of the Eastern Hemisphere. This extends almost to the island of Paxaros <note>Likely the Desventuradas Islands or similar remote Pacific outcrops.</note>, and generally as far as anything is known of the Southern Land. The inhabitants of the Continent in that region are certainly beyond the danger of confusion, as shown by the Tables and the Map thus far. From here, they pass back and forth across our Antipodes.

Those navigating the Southern Ocean <margin>A warning for the Argonauts <note>Kepler uses "Argonauts" as a poetic term for sailors and explorers.</note>.</margin> (called the "Sur" or Pacific Sea) should remember that the limits of numbering are completed here, which can cause confusion and interruptions. For what appears in these tables as the 20th day of the month in Japan or the Moluccas (using the increased Eastern numbering), will be seen by those coming from the American fleets from the east as the 19th day in their own diminished numbering, if they wish to continue that sequence. And conversely, if in Panama in America a full moon is predicted by these Tables and the Map for March 22nd, the Saturday before Easter, a ship arriving from the Philippines from the west will reckon (guided by this same Map of ours) the day of the full moon to be March 23rd, the first day of the week or Sunday, according to their numbering continued from the Philippines. Therefore, having dismissed the increased numbering of their homeland, they must transition into the diminished numbering of America. This is only fair, for the port does not travel out to meet the flying ship, but the ship is carried into the port, which remains immobile.

<margin>PRECEPT 60.</margin> The use of this whole work and these Tables is primarily this: Because the meridians are distinguished on the Map, it is well known that when an observer—having set out from the meridian of Uraniborg—observes an eclipse of the Moon or its distance from a known star, they do not assume the same time applies everywhere. One should observe at the nonagesimal degree <note>The point of the ecliptic that is 90 degrees from the horizon; observing here minimizes errors from parallax.</note> from the horizon, lacking longitude parallax. Or one might observe the conjunction of the Moon with a planet, as this does not require complex instruments. The same observation <margin>See regarding this method the *Theories of Danish Astronomy*, folio 196, and the appropriate instruments and fixed stars.</margin> which the observer finds by watching, he should also compute from these Tables to see at what hour it would appear at Uraniborg. If he recorded more hours than are computed for Uraniborg, he is that many hours to the east; if fewer, he is to the west. This number of 

<column-break/>

hours of difference, when sought on the Map, will show the meridian under which the observation was made. If the ship is then at a specific port already located on the maps, the reliability of the map regarding that location can be tested, and the map corrected where necessary; especially if several such observations agree. For although it cannot be denied that certain peculiarities intervene in lunar motions which seem to reject the rules by about a quarter of an hour, this usually happens rarely and stems from physical causes; thus, many observations here can prevail over one or two outliers without danger of error.

## CHAPTER XVII.
### ON THE REDUCTION OF YEARS, MONTHS, AND DAYS USED BY OTHER NATIONS TO THE YEARS BEFORE AND AFTER CHRIST, AND TO THE JULIAN DAYS, MONTHS, AND YEARS TO WHICH THESE TABLES ARE ACCOMMODATED.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial 'I'.</image-desc>For these uses, I first present a <margin>On the Synopsis of Eras.</margin> synopsis of eras. 2. A model of the <margin>Tables on folios 37, 38.</margin> Year of Confusion <note>The year 46 BC, when Julius Caesar reformed the calendar.</note> and the faulty intercalations performed, as well as the connection of fixed exotic solar years <margin>Table on folio 39.</margin> which correspond to the Julian form to some extent and are thus reduced to it with less effort. 4. The necessity of a Synopsis is known to all. For the first care of a Calculator must be the year of numbering, which either ancient or new history, or different provinces of the world provide; and how that year corresponds to the year of the Era I will follow in these tables. Ptolemy indeed deduced years from Nabonassar, because older observations do not exist; others have looked to other things; most to the turning points of kingdoms, or the honor of the Kings under whom they wrote. Thus Vettius Valens, the astrologer of Antioch, numbered from Augustus's triumph at Actium; thus the mathematicians of Persia numbered from the death of Yazdegerd <note>Kepler writes "Jelda-girdis," referring to the last Sassanid king.</note>, after which they fell under the power of the Arabs. Thus the Egyptians numbered from the death of Alexander and the rise of the Ptolemaic kingdom of the Lagidae; and the Chaldeans from the beginning of the Seleucids. Thus the Saracens from the HEGIRA, the withdrawal or flight of Muhammad, who was the author of their liberty. Thus even the Alphonsine tables established a new but customary Era for Alfonso.

But in these Tables, Tycho, the first author, <margin>No specific honor for Rudolph.</margin> although he named them after the Emperor Rudolph, thought there was no need for a new "Rudolphine Era" to be established in an inscription <note>Original: "τη Ελεγεια". Kepler uses the Greek for 'elegy' or 'inscription' to suggest a formal dedicatory era.</note>. He judged it sufficient to use the Era of Christ, accepted and used throughout the West and in the domains of Western Kings.

# PRECEPTS OF RUDOLPH

<margin>Counting from our era is twofold</margin>
Therefore, these tables count this era in two ways: first, in a backward order, from Christ toward the beginning of things and beyond, as far as one wishes; second, in a forward order from Christ down to our own time and further. These years are Leap Years <note>original: "Bisextiles"</note>; after Christ, they are all the even-numbered years; before Christ, however, they are the odd-numbered years—the first, and then every fourth year upward from there.

<margin>Why there is only one kind of numbering for motions in these Tables.</margin>
I have judged that multiplying eras with a variety of numbering systems—as the authors of the *Alphonsine Tables* <note>A 13th-century astronomical table</note> and the *Prutenic Tables* <note>16th-century tables by Erasmus Reinhold based on Copernicus</note> did—is not only unnecessary but even harmful. Furthermore, it is not fitting to present individual national eras in a universal work. One cannot satisfy all nations by favoring a few, and it is better to set rules for reducing their local times to the Julian years of Christ rather than leaving the rest in a state of necessity.

<margin>Concerning the various beginnings of the Years of Christ.</margin>
Moreover, while most Christians have agreed upon the Era of the Incarnation of the Word <note>The AD/CE dating system</note>, there has been great variety in observing the start of the year. I have placed all this variety before your eyes, as far as I could gather from reading, so that I might impress this observation upon calculators with a more distinct mark: <margin>Their beginning in these Tables.</margin> that the very Kalends of January <note>January 1st</note> are held in these Tables as the first day of the year. Thus, they may learn to be careful regarding the numbering of others who observe a different start to the year; for this reason, they sometimes differ from us by one unit in the numbering of years.

<margin>The author's commentary on the Eras. (Pages 37 to 40)</margin>
Concerning the intervals of these eras, and the names, order, and length of the months, I have written a specific commentary. In it, I demonstrate everything contained in these pages with historical monuments and suitable reasons. I also defend my work against the authorities of other chronologists—even <term>Joseph Scaliger</term> <note>A famous 16th-century scholar of chronology</note> himself—wherever they diverge from me. I will share this with readers on another occasion, if life remains to me; for this chronological material seemed likely to exceed the boundaries of this astronomical work.

<margin>The era of years observed in these Tables; in what sense they are called JULIAN.</margin>
The calculator must be diligently reminded that when "Julian Years" are named in these Tables, this name is not to be understood as the Era of Julius Caesar or the number of years deduced from it, but only as the *form* of the year and the arrangement or distribution of days into months. Meanwhile, the years also called Julian are the Years of Christ—being 45 years fewer after Christ, and just as many years greater before Christ, than if they had been counted from the time that this form of the year was established by Julius Caesar.

<margin>PRECEPT 62.</margin>
Now I will provide the way to use this Synopsis <note>Kepler refers to a summary table on another page</note>. If you are presented with a year from a numbering system starting before our Era of the Incarnation (years that do not count continuously backward, for I will deal with those separately), and you wish to know which year of the Incarnation it is for use in these Tables: if the proposed year does not exceed its own interval of numbering noted in the synopsis, subtract the completed years from the interval as it is placed there. The remainder will be the current Julian year [BC] in which the proposed current year of that era began. The Julian day and month from which it began is found added to the interval in the Synopsis.

But if the proposed number of years exceeds its own interval (for those that precede Christ), subtract the interval as it is placed from the given number of the current year. The remainder will be the current Julian year of the Incarnation after Christ, from whose day and month (annotated in the Synopsis) the proposed current year began.

->EXAMPLES.<- <insert>Rabbi Abraham bar Hiyya</insert> <note>A 12th-century Jewish mathematician and astronomer</note> says the Era of Contracts <note>The Seleucid Era, used widely in the ancient Near East</note> fell at the beginning of the Jewish year 3450. <gloss>To know which year of the Incarnation this is: look at the Jewish Era and its interval of 3761. Because the proposed number is smaller, subtract the completed 3449 from it; 312 remains as the current year before the Incarnation [BC]. Therefore, on the Nones of October of that year (which are annotated at 3761), the Era of Contracts is said to have begun.</gloss>

<margin>But for Ides, Nones, and Kalends, it is mostly understood to be attributed to either October or September, as below.</margin>
Conversely, <term>Arzachel</term> <note>The Arab astronomer Al-Zarqali</note> writes that the era of the Arabs began in the year 933 of Alexander. <gloss>Which year of Christ will this be? Look at the Era of Alexander; its interval is found to be 312. Since the proposed number is larger, subtract 312 from the current 933; 621 remains as the current year after Christ. Therefore, in October of this year (which you see attached to 312), the year 933 of Alexander began, and consequently ended in the following year 622 of Christ.</gloss>

Thus <term>SIGISMUND, BARON VON HERBERSTEIN</term> <note>A diplomat and historian of Russia</note> reports from the annals in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs* that Demetrius, grandson of Ivan Vasilyevich, was created Grand Duke of Moscow in the Year of the World 7006, in the month of February. <gloss>This is the era of the Greeks [Byzantine Era], and the number exceeds the interval [5508]: therefore, subtract this, and the current year of Christ 1497 remains, as the Baron himself also notes.</gloss>

<margin>Application of Olympiads.</margin>
Regarding the notation of time by Olympiads, there is a specific caution: you must quadruple the number of completed Olympiads and add the expressed current year; Scaliger calls this sum the "Years of Iphitus."

<margin>The eclipse while Christ was suffering.</margin>
For instance, <term>Phlegon of Tralles</term> <note>A Greek historian whose works are mostly lost</note>, as reported by <term>Eusebius</term> <note>An early Christian historian</note>, noted a very great eclipse of the sun at the 6th hour of the day in the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad. Eusebius understands this to be the eclipse that happened while the Savior was hanging on the cross at the feast of Passover. <gloss>The question is: what year of the Incarnation was that? Therefore, quadruple the 201 completed Olympiads and add the 4th expressed year; this makes 808 current years of Iphitus. Subtract the interval of 776 in the Synopsis; 32 [AD] remains as the year of the Incarnation. Therefore, the year Phlegon speaks of either began from the solstice of this year 32, or (what is more likely) from the preceding winter, encompassing the Passover of the year 32 of the Incarnation. But because the Passion of Christ certainly fell in the preceding year 31 of the Incarnation, we understand that an error occurred in Phlegon's text, and the numeral 3 <note>original: "elenij"</note> was changed into a 4 <note>original: "$\delta$"</note>.</gloss>

If, however, the offered numbering began after Christ, and the years do not count continuously backward (for those will be dealt with separately), add the completed (not current) interval from the Synopsis to those current years. In this way, the year of the Incarnation will come forth in which the offered year begins, starting from the month and day assigned to the interval in the Synopsis.

For example, <term>Theon</term> <note>Theon of Alexandria, a 4th-century mathematician</note> in his commentaries on <term>Ptolemy</term> reports an eclipse that happened in the year 81 of Diocletian. The question is: what year was this in these Tables? <gloss>The Synopsis shows the interval of the Diocletians as 284. Therefore, add the completed 283 to the current 81; 364 [AD] current of the Incarnation comes forth. Therefore, on the 29th day of August of this year (which is added in the Synopsis), the 81st year of Diocletian began.</gloss>

Likewise, from Lviv <note>original: "Leopoli"</note> in Russia, letters were written concerning the calendar of the Armenians to <term>Bartholomaeus Scultetus</term> of Görlitz, the consul, in the year 1044 of the Armenians. <gloss>To know which year of the Incarnation this is, look at the era of the Armenians; this has an interval of 552. Therefore, add the completed 551 from the synopsis; the year 1595 of the Incarnation is produced, in whose month of August that Armenian year 1044 began.</gloss>

# PRECEPTS OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES

<margin>PRECEPT 63.</margin>
Therefore, regarding these 48 years, the rule is as follows: If a year from Roman history is presented that falls within these stated limits, and you wish to know which day of the standard month matches the day of the later observation (which is also valid in these Tables, extended backward), look for the year in the lower part of the Diagram <note>The "Typus" or reference table provided in the book</note>. If you do not find it, take the next highest year and see on which day of the month the standard Calends <note>the first day of the month</note> fell. For if the Calends fell on the first days, then all days were conducted correctly from the position of the leap day until the following noted year. However, if they fell on the second days, one unit must be added to the expressed day number; if on the third, add two; if on the fourth, add three.

*Let this be an illustrious example regarding our subject:*
*In the year Caesar Octavius <note>the Emperor Augustus</note> occupied Egypt,*
*it was observed that the beginning of the Egyptian year fell*
*on the 3rd of the Calends of September <note>August 30th</note>: that is, on the 29th of Sextilis <note>the old name for August</note> of the Roman*
*year, as it was then conducted. The question is: what day*
*would this have been according to the corrected, subsequent form? The year is new in history; 15 years*
<margin>Table page 40.</margin>
*of the Julian form had passed, and the sixteenth was running; it was the thirtieth before the era of the Incarnation. Therefore, this very year, 30 before the era of the Incarnation, is found in the Diagram, and the number three is adjacent to the day on which the Calends of each month fell after the leap day in February. Since the Calends of September fell on the corrected 3rd of September, the 4th of the Calends fell on the last day of August: so that there was a difference of two days everywhere.*

<margin>A Caution.</margin>
But regarding the days of the year marked in the Diagram that precede the leap day, this caution applies: they should be counted with the preceding year. For instance, if a day is expressed in the 16th standard Julian year in the month of January, one should not take the 16th year, but the 15th. And because the year is not found there, take the next highest, 13, whose Calends from March [until the March of year 16] fall on the second days, so that there is a difference of only one day.

<margin>When the modern form of intercalation began.</margin>
The third form of the Julian year began with the year 50 of the Julian era, which was the fifth year of our counting from the Incarnation. It lasted until October 4th, 1582, and it still persists in many places and in these Tables; it requires no special precept.

<margin>Table page 39, at the top.</margin>
Gregory XIII, the Supreme Pontiff, introduced the fourth form of intercalation, for which the first Table of Reduction serves.

<margin>The very wide use of the Gregorian Calendar.</margin>
This GREGORIAN correction of the old Julian calendar has been accepted in almost the entire West, in the Holy Roman Empire, and in the Kingdom of Spain with its vast provinces stretching through the East and West. It has come into such common use that not even those who retain the old form can afford to be
<margin>Why the Epochs are adapted to the Julian Calendar.</margin>
ignorant of it. Yet, it was not for that reason to be adopted into the calculation of these Tables, nor should the solemn Epochs of motions be adapted to it. For Ephemerides <note>daily astronomical tables</note> are not written here for specific years, where the standard Gregorian observation would rightly hold sway; rather, universal Tables are built, not only for future times but also for the observations of time past. Now, regarding the "Astronomical Age," so to speak, the most

<column-break/>

significant part passed under the observation of the old Julian calendar. Indeed, it was accepted immediately upon its publication in all provinces of the Roman Empire, and the forms of provincial years gradually faded away because of it. Therefore, astronomers after Ptolemy, even from those nations that did not recognize the Roman Empire, adapted their Tables to this form of the old calendar. Nor was this done without cause: for after the Egyptian form, it is the most uniform, and it is more convenient for the motion of the Sun than the Egyptian form itself. Just as Ptolemy adapted his tables to the Egyptian year—undeterred by the custom introduced by the Roman masters of the world, who had already held the fixed Egyptian year for nearly two hundred years—and just as the Persian mathematicians inserted the ordinary form of the Persian year into their tables of celestial motions (which inserts those five days, called *Musteraka* <note>the epagomenal or "stolen" days</note>, at the end of the last Persian month, *Asphandar*), they did not look to the standard placement of those five days at the end of the month *Aban*, which they found in their own time. They did this because their own form of the year seemed more suited to calculation for both themselves and others. 

So too Tycho Brahe, the first proposer of these Tables, in the first volume of his *Progymnasmata* published in 1602, chose the old Julian form of the year over the Gregorian because of its simplicity and suitability in the handling of calculation. He saw clearly that if he derived the Epochs of motions from the beginning of the Gregorian year, he would nonetheless still need the old Julian year, by comparison with which alone one can understand how much must be subtracted from the old Julian intercalation in any given century. For even according to Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius, the primary mathematician behind the Gregorian reform</note>, the calculator of the Gregorian year, this very old Julian form is the moderator of the Gregorian intercalation and the index of intercalary days—the guardian or commentary of the intercalations performed, from which the number of days to be removed in any age must be drawn.

And although the Gregorian intercalation is superior in one respect—that it keeps the Equinoxes around the same days of the months—this is achieved by a certain leap and back-and-forth movement across the days. It is a thing more desired by astronomers, through the use of the old Julian calendar, to observe the amount of the regression of the equinoxes in any age. This is because Nature herself established the handle for observing this regression in the longer sidereal year, and because the length of the Julian year, by a beautiful chance, falls exactly in the middle between both Natural years—the retreating Tropical year and the Sidereal year that creeps forward into the following days of the Julian year. I will not demonstrate at greater length how much and how perplexed a labor it would be to multiply Epochs, to burden students with cautions, and to reduce the calendars of all other nations to the Gregorian form, which varies through different centuries. How much easier it is to make a summary of such work by adding a single precept concerning the reduction of either the motions computed in Julian times to Gregorian times, or Gregorian times to Julian times, which are better suited for calculation.

<margin>Because it is customary for astronomers.</margin>
<margin>Because the form is simple and uniform. Suited for calculation.</margin>
<margin>Because it is the rule of the Gregorian.</margin>
<margin>Because it marks the equinoxes of all times.</margin>
<margin>From the transitions of the stars in the Tropical year.</margin>
<margin>Because it is less laborious and intricate.</margin>

And indeed, the Table itself encompasses the precept to some extent. For when a day of the old Julian month is presented, for which the celestial motions are computed...

# PRECEPTS OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES

Rules: if it is asked which day of the <term>Gregorian</term><note>The "New Style" calendar introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 to correct the solar year.</note> year it will be; if the day follows the position of the <term>bissextile</term><note>A leap day, literally the "twice-sixth" day before the Kalends of March.</note> day, look for the proposed year in the table, or the one immediately preceding it; and you will find the number of days set down, which you shall add to the proposed <term>Julian</term><note>The "Old Style" calendar established by Julius Caesar.</note> number. Thus the Gregorian number of days for that year will emerge, either for the same month, or, if the quantity of days exceeds the length of the month, that surplus is rejected and it becomes the following month. If, however, the day of the offered year precedes the position of the leap day, treat January and the part of February as an appendix of the preceding year. There is no need for examples.

Conversely, if Gregorian times are to be computed, add the same amount; if the month and this clear name have a predecessor, there is no labor. But so that it is entirely in one form, I have written as many days for the <term>Epochs</term><note>A fixed point in time used as a reference for astronomical calculations.</note> as if he had written <term>Ephemerides</term><note>Tables predicting the positions of celestial objects.</note> for the Julian and Gregorian systems for the proposed century, and those who have them in their charts should either have a handle provided or the <term>Calculato-Popilianum</term><note>Likely a specific reference book or computational table named after a scholar named Popilius.</note> book.

<margin>Advice for writing Ephemerides.</margin>
But I submit this advice to the writers of Ephemerides: when days are to be removed from the Julian system, they should subtract the motions of the days from those which are accommodated to the Gregorian form. Although I did not think that the Julian and Gregorian Epochs, and the Epochs of the Julian Tables and the Popilian ones, should vary or provide a handle for confusion, or even burden the book.

<margin>Concerning years not expressed in the Table.</margin>
However, this precept is valid in which the years are expressed, up to the February immediately following in the small table. But for October of the year 1582, you are ordered to add the adjustments in which the correction was made. That, therefore, ought to be done in all, and in all following years: 1600, and even the beginning of the year 1700, the Julian Leap Year. For even in that year, or on the 6th day before the Kalends of March <note>original: "sextum calendas Martias," the traditional Roman way to mark the leap day</note>, 10 days are added as intercalary ones, so that the measure of the month of February was 34 days: from which 28 is taken away, leaving 6; it will therefore be the 6th of March in the Gregorian style. But since by the 24th of February of the year 1700 these were included; or if you are ordered to add not 10 but 11 days, add them to the 24th of the ordinary February, or the later 6th Kalends of March, and they become 35; with 28 taken away, 7 remain for February; it will therefore be the 7th of March in the Gregorian style.

<margin>Caution regarding the days of February.</margin>
You will note, therefore, that in this reduction table, according to the Roman custom, only 28 days are imputed to February in a leap year, just as in the weekly cycle, the letter A is placed twice; I mean that which the Christians added to the popular Code, which in a leap February counts to the 24th of February. For if the leap year were counted at the 24th of February up to 29 days, these words would have no place, but instead [A 1st of March].

<column-break/>

to be compared and connected according to the things above. For when the Romans had a period of 24 years, in which the Pontiffs—who were most just—were accustomed to intercalate twelve times, they themselves intercalated only eleven times in the intercalary month: this omission, therefore, disturbs everything. For there is no certainty among the Consuls <note>Roman years were named after the two presiding Consuls.</note> as to which had the intercalary month. And so, in the first years of the "Year of Confusion," for two old Roman years we struggle, and there is uncertainty about 23 days: even if the consulship of that 24-year period is useless and allows no freedom for speaking out of order, if it is usurped for oneself. Whatever, therefore, can be taught in this place about the years that preceded the "Year of Confusion" <note>46 BC, the year Julius Caesar corrected the calendar by making it 445 days long.</note> is entirely doubtful and slippery. And while we [calculate], we nevertheless reduce to two conditions the five years that immediately precede the Year of Confusion: either we place an intercalation, or we assume an intercalation was omitted somewhere.

Since this is the case, it would be superfluous to conceive the precept in solemn words: a single example, and a noble one at that, will serve in place of the precept.

<margin>PRECEPT 65.</margin>
In the Consulship of <term>Cicero</term> and <term>Lentulus</term>, which was in the year 63 before the beginning of the Christian Era, C. <term>Octavius</term> (afterwards called Augustus) was born in July, so it is said. He was born in September. As you see in the model of the Year of Confusion, it had 29 days in September and reaches the 22nd of September. Therefore, he was born on the ninth day before the Kalends of October. The question is: on what day of today's Julian year, extended backward through the time of the Consulship of Cicero, can a dreamer sent down establish his birth-chart <note>original: "genesin pangere," referring to a natal horoscope.</note>? Of the times of the Year of Confusion, which was when the <term>Popilian</term> September of the Julian Tables falls on the 22nd of July. Because backward between the 46th and 63rd years they intercalated, 24 days would have clearly passed, as much as would have been probable for the Popilian months.

In the Julian months within the proposal in which they were, in some intermediate year of the Year of Confusion, in which the years 52, 54, 56, 58, 60, and 62 were intercalary; therefore, two possibilities are offered to us: that it was omitted, or later omitted; therefore from the 22nd of September of the year 62, 16 old Roman years ran their course, which counted to the 24th of February.

### CONCERNING THE MODEL OF THE YEAR OF CONFUSION; AND AT THE SAME TIME, OF THE ANCIENT POPILIAN YEARS.

BEFORE I move away from our local calendar form, something must also be said about that form which immediately preceded it: which was indeed derived from the very ancient form of the Greek year. But since there do not exist sufficient documents in Roman histories from which the entire logic of this year can be elicited, and with the modern Julian [calendar]...

<column-break/>

there were 16 Julian years, and the days were to be placed at the 22nd of September in the Popilian style, let us ascend backward into the Popilian year. And because the ascent of the year 62 was doubled from the stated condition, it is known for certain in either 22 or 23 days. Of the 377 days of the Popilian year. Similarly, 377 days in a simple year happen at the 24th or 23rd of September, which offers us the 23rd or 24th. The intercalations of year 17 were omitted between the years 46 and 62, and the conditions are set out through 23 days, we revolve back to the 16th or 17th. Intercalations, provided that nothing in the meantime has disturbed the order...

# EXAMPLE OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES BEFORE CHRIST.

->High Priests, the arbiters of the seasons.<- Our Model will hardly be able to affirm anything more certain. Yet nothing more certain than this Model has been gathered so far from ancient monuments, as far as I know.

If anyone follows both my precepts and what I casually add here: for this is not foreign to the so-called Rudolphine Tables, as I explained in a booklet to several Emperors who requested it long ago. <margin>Birth of Augustus.</margin> Augustus is said to have been born a little before sunrise; born under the sign of the Archer <note>original: "Arquimenfe", a variant of Arcitenens, the Archer or Sagittarius</note>, as tradition confirms, though he claims the setting of Capricorn. For Octavius, his father, predicted before the birth that his wife’s child would be born in <term>Capricorn</term><note>The tenth sign of the zodiac; Augustus famously used the image of a Capricorn on his coins to signal his destiny.</note>. Besides this Catilinarian conspiracy, and the delay in the labor of Octavius’s wife, Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and astrologer</note> also predicted from the time of birth, having promised Julius [Caesar] that with the Sun rising in Capricorn, he... How then did those who thought him born under the same sign, which the Moon held at his birth? Among your 25 days, ask whether the Moon could be in Capricorn, and on which days; you will find July 1st and 2nd. Therefore, the <term>intercalary month</term><note>A month inserted into the calendar to keep it in sync with the solar year.</note> was not omitted in these 17 years; but the length of the year, clearly 355 days with the intercalary, could not have been preserved. For 6, 7, or 8 days are missing. Thus the judgment of the Priests [Pontifices] might have detracted from their own ordering, or authors of a later age might have poorly reported the length of the year.

## PRECEPT 66. ON THE CONVERSION OF EGYPTIAN TIMES into Julian.

Given a day of a given Egyptian month and year from the <term>Era of Nabonassar</term><note>A chronological era starting in 747 BCE, named after a Babylonian king and used by Ptolemy for astronomical records.</note>, you will learn to which day of which year before or after the Incarnation [BC/AD] it corresponds. In the <term>Table of Conversion</term><note>Refers to the reference tables printed on page 39 of the original volume.</note>, a series of Egyptian years from Nabonassar is found, with the day of the corresponding Julian year at the side. Therefore, seek the Egyptian number for the given year, and the next highest (if not equal) to the one proposed; subtract from it the proposed current year, and add the remainder to the corresponding line of the Incarnation before Christ, or subtract it after Christ; thus you have the year from the Incarnation, backward or forward, in which the proposed Egyptian year begins. Divide those same remaining years by 4; as many times as it goes (increased by one if there is a remainder), add that to the number of the Julian day found in that same line; thus the position of the first <term>Thoth</term><note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note> will come forth.

Thirdly, collect from the appropriate column the number of days from the start of that Julian year up to the found position of the 1st of Thoth; noting whether it is a common year or a <term>bissextile</term><note>A leap year.</note> year. Do the same for the proposed Egyptian year, using the column specific to Julian years—namely, collect the sum of days up to the proposed date. Combine both sums into one, which in turn, by the help of the Julian column, convert into Julian months. Thus the remainder will be the completed day of the following Julian month. If the sum of days exceeds the measure of a year, first subtract 365 days (or 366 in a leap year), and for those, decrease the Julian year count by one before Christ, or increase it after Christ; proceed with the remaining days as before.

<column-break/>

It is asked: in the 425th year of Nabonassar, to which day of which Julian year does the first day of Thoth correspond? <margin>In the Conversion Table of Egyptian years from Nabonassar.</margin> The number immediately larger than this in the Table of Egyptian and Persian Conversion, to the right under the title of "Nabonassar," is found to be 468; from which 425 is subtracted, leaving a remainder of 43. When these are added to the 281 years before the Incarnation found in the same line, they make 324 before Christ.

The same remainder divided by 4 gives 10, with a fraction. Therefore, for the same line, the day is November 1st. It becomes November 12th. Here, because this is not a completed Julian year 324, 4 will be given. <margin>From the Table of Conversion of Roman Months. From the Table of Conversion of Egyptian Months. In the Table of Julian Months.</margin> If however the question was about the 27th of <term>Mesori</term><note>The last month of the Egyptian calendar.</note> currently: the operation is simple: the Julian year 324 is complete. Therefore the completed month of October shows 304 days; add the 11 completed days of November. It makes 315. Thus take the year 324 and the 26 completed days of the current Mesori, totaling 645. From this sum, first subtract 304 (the time is after Christ, and before the Incarnation it is simple) since the year 324 is earlier, even 323 follows) the nearest smaller is 273 found in the same line, leaving 280 days: by this number... (for the simple is 304 days) which when taken away, the remaining 181 are the completed days of October, in the year 323 of the Incarnation. Thus the 27th day... falls on the 8th day of October.

## ON THE CONVERSION OF PERSIAN TIMES INTO JULIAN Tables and vice versa.

The wandering Egyptian year has ceased; the <term>Persian year</term><note>The Yazdegerdi calendar, which, unlike the Egyptian 'wandering' year, eventually incorporated leap years.</note> has succeeded it, taking into itself almost all the months of the former, as I advise at the bottom of the Table. I believe this Persian system is still in use today. Therefore, for the Egyptian, a temporary precept sufficed, supported by a Table extended to the quantity of one <term>Sothic year</term><note>original: "Cynici anni", referring to the 1,461-year cycle of the star Sirius (the Dog Star).</note>; for the Persian, I hand down a more general precept.

# RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS

<margin>PRECEPT 67.</margin>...having completed half-months, along with the days passed in the current month, reduce them to a total sum of days (extracting first by thousands of years if there are that many, then by hundreds, thirdly by tens, fourthly by individuals, and fifthly always subtract 199 from the total sum <note>The number 199 refers to the day-count difference between the start of the Persian Era and the Julian year epoch</note>). Conversely, reduce this into Julian years and months, <margin>Through the Table of the Egyptians and the Physicians, page 39.</margin> paying attention to the leap year; always add 632 full years to the resulting Julian years <note>The Era of Yazdegerd began in 632 AD</note>: you will then produce the total of Julian years and <margin>Through the Table of Centuries, Years, and Julian Months.</margin> months, and the current month with the remaining days of that month. Conversely, from the given years of the Incarnation <note>Anno Domini</note>, subtract 632 from the Julian years; of the remaining full years, after the exception of days is made, first by thousands of four-year cycles contained in the proposed Julian number, second by tens of the same, third by the four-year cycles themselves, and finally by individuals below four, reduce the complete extracted numbers of days, along with the number of days of the completed month and the days of the current month, into one sum: and add the sum of 199 days. Once increased this way, let it be reduced into <margin>Through the Table of the Julians.</margin> Persian Times, with the exception of years made in the margin, by the sum of days nearest to the smaller collected amount, or its remainders—excepting also the current days—so that the remaining days of the following current month may appear.

->EXAMPLES.<-

<margin>In the Table of Julian Years.</margin>In the year of <term>Isdagardis</term> <note>Yazdegerd III, the last Sassanid King of Persia; his era began in 632 AD</note> 814, on the 17th day of the month <term>Termà</term> <note>Tir</note>, what is the day of which Julian year and year of the Incarnation? 
The completed day of the Julian month and year of the Incarnation is 17 of the current month, <term>Termà</term>, which is [calculated against] the Julian month. 800 <term>Egyptian</term> or <term>Persian</term> years <note>These years are "vague," consisting of exactly 365 days without leap years</note> give 292,000 days, 10 years give 3,650, and the 3 remaining years give 1,095 days. With all days gathered into one sum and the modulus of 199 perpetually subtracted from it, the sum of days becomes 292,200. This results in Julian [years] 800 and 4,453 [days]. This sum is 12 Julian years smaller than the nearest; there remain 70 days, which, since they belong to the following 13th simple Julian year, after subtracting 59 days found with a simple February, there remains the 11th day of the current month of March. To the collected years, with 812 at the last current, add the perpetual number 632, and the current year of the Incarnation 1445 arises.

<margin>Through the Table of the Julians.</margin> Conversely, in the year of the Incarnation 1079, the 23rd day of February, what is the day of which year and month of Isdagardis? Subtracting 632 from the 1079 Julian years, 447 remain, with the last being current. But 400 Julian years give 146,100 days, and 40 completed give 14,610, and 4 completed give 1,461, and two additional completed give 730. Now there are 163,144 days; from which [add] the perpetual modulus. The sum forged from all days becomes 163,144: from which 146,000 make 400 Persian years, and the remainders are 17,144 days. Again, from these, 14,600 make 40 Persian years, and the remainders are 2,544 days. But even from these, 2,190 make 6 Persian years, and 354 days remain. Finally, the nearest smaller value, 335, is assigned to the month of <term>Pechman</term> or <term>Behem</term> <note>Bahman</note>; there remain 29 days of the current month <term>Asphandar</term> <note>Esfand</note>, which is the last day of the year 347.

<margin>Through the Egyptian Table.</margin> You will note that the names of the Persian months are rendered with very different letters, transcribed from one language to another. For first they were transcribed from the Persian language into Arabic, and afterwards from Arabic into Latin;

<column-break/>

thus they sound among the <term>Alphonsinos</term> <note>Followers of the Alphonsine Tables, commissioned by Alfonso X of Castile</note> in the edition of Santritter: *<term>Fordimech</term>, <term>Cardimech</term>, <term>Cardimech</term>,* *<term>Zirmedach</term>, <term>Mardary</term>, <term>Sarembemech</term>, <term>Mahramech</term>,* *<term>Ebenmeech</term>, <term>Dimeech</term>, <term>Behmamech</term>,* *<term>Azfirbamic</term>.* I shall omit my own manuscripts. I, however, have hoped to remain closer to the <term>Persian</term> idiom, and from the <term>Greek</term> authors, <term>Chrysococce</term> <note>George Chrysococces, a 14th-century Greek physician and astronomer</note> and <term>Isaac the Monk</term> <note>Isaac Argyrus</note>, I might transcribe them into the Latin language.

### ON THE CONVERSION OF ARABIC AND TURKISH TIMES OF THE *Hegira* INTO *Julian* TIMES.

<margin>PRECEPT 68</margin> The method is not unlike the previous one. Convert the <term>Arabic</term> years of the *<term>Hegira</term>* <note>The Islamic era, starting with Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 AD</note> into days, extracting first by ten times the collected years, if such a sum of years is offered, then by the remaining full <term>Triaconteridos</term> <note>A 30-year cycle used in the Islamic calendar to regulate leap years</note>, thirdly by completed years below 30, and fourthly by completed <term>Arabic</term> months. All four extracted numbers, together with the number of days of the current day in the current month, collect into one sum, which you increase by 561 days. Thus increased, convert it into the Julian years and months of the year of the Incarnation (which assigns the Arabic Epoch in the <term>Arabic</term> Calendar thus). From the proposed years of Christ, subtract 620 years perpetually; convert the two remainders into days, and likewise also the Julian months by the Julian or leap-year term. To all the extracted days, also subjoin the number of the day of the passing month; and make a sum of all, from which conversely always subtract 561 days: convert the sum thus reduced into Arabic times, extracting by the nearest smaller numbers either from the collected sum or its remainders, a number smaller than the quantity of the Hegira, and the number of the day of the current <term>Arabic</term> month, responding to the proposed day of the Julian month.

Therefore, the proposed 23rd of December in the year of the Incarnation 1576 is the 2nd day of the month of Shawwal in the year 984 of the Turkish Prophet <note>Kepler refers here to Muhammad and the Islamic calendar</note>. At that time, a truce of 8 years was made between Rudolf II, the Roman Emperor, and Murad <note>original: *Amurathem*</note>, King of the Turks. Thus, in the book of Martin Crusius, which Scaliger cites, it is likely that the *Character X* <note>The Roman numeral ten</note> was omitted. For the truce could not have been made on the Kalends <note>the 1st</note> of the beginning of the year 1576, when Rudolf was scarcely yet elected and his father Maximilian was still alive, but rather at the end of that year, namely on the 10th of the Kalends of January. Correct Scaliger on this point.

## ON THE APPLICATION OF DAYS IN THE EGYPTIAN AND ARMENIAN FIXED YEARS TO JULIAN DAYS.

<margin>Table page 40 above on the right. PRECEPT 69.</margin>
A specific Table serves this purpose, which is itself in place of a rule, provided only that you remember: in the Armenian year there is absolutely no difference from the Julian (for only the days of the completed Armenian month are added to the day of the assigned Julian month; and if the quantity of that month is exceeded, the remainder becomes the current day of the following month). However, in the Ethiopian <note>Coptic or Abyssinian</note> year, throughout that six-month period which precedes the Roman leap year <note>original: *intercalationem Romanam*</note>, there is a discrepancy of one day. Thus, the fixed Ethiopian feasts of that six-month period, in that year when the Roman leap year is imminent, fall one day later in the Julian calendar than they did in the three preceding years.
