## ON THE CHARACTERISTICS AND WEEKDAYS OF YEARS AND DAYS.

<margin>Tables on pages 37, 38.</margin>
This subject is more Chronological and should be relegated to calculations; a certain time must be proposed to the astronomer so that he may calculate motions for it. However, because some "characters" <note>identifying numbers for years</note> are derived from the motions of the moon, and some are even used by astronomers—especially the Hebrews—to track these more easily, I will also deal briefly with these Characters.

Three cycles are usually inserted into Calendars: the Indictions, the Solar Cycle, and the Lunar Cycle or Golden Number. The circle of Indictions <note>a 15-year tax cycle</note> begins with three eras, as you see in the Synopsis: with the era of the Greeks from the beginning of the world, with the Antiochian years, and with the year of Christ 312 or 313, depending on the different start of the Indictional year.

<margin>PRECEPT 70.</margin>
Therefore, we simply divide the Greek Years of the World and the Antiochian years by 15; the remainder is the year of the Indiction, or if nothing remains, the Indiction is numbered 15.

*As an example, if it is asked what Indiction it is in the Greek Year 5509: the division by 15 having been performed, 4 remains. Therefore, in September of the year 5509, Indiction 4 ends.*

<margin>PRECEPT 71.</margin>
But regarding the years of the Incarnation, there is a caution: to elicit the indiction, a three <note>the number 3</note> must be added to them, and then let the division by 15 be made. Thus, the start of our era <note>AD 1</note> falls in Indiction IV, by adding 3 to the 1st year of Christ.

### ON THE SOLAR CYCLE.

<margin>PRECEPT 72. Table page 40.</margin>
To find this, add 9 to the years of the Incarnation after Christ; from the sum, remove the numbers of years in whole cycles <note>multiples of 28</note> sought from the little side-table, which is to the right of the Weekly Table; the Solar Cycle will remain in this way, or if nothing remains, the Cycle will be 28.

But if your years are current *before* the Era of the Incarnation, then do not add 9 to these, but to the next largest number of years found in the side-table of Cycles, add not 9 but 10; from that sum, subtract the years current before Christ; and then from the remainder, as before, cast away the whole Cycles.

### ->EXAMPLES<-

*In the year of the Incarnation 1507, for the Solar Cycle add 9; from the sum 1516, first take away 1400 (namely 50 cycles) found in the side-table; 116 remains. From these, further take away 112, which you find in the same place (namely 4 cycles); 4 remains, which is the Solar Cycle of that year.*

*Conversely, in the year 3993 before the Incarnation, to have the Solar Cycle, look in the side-table for the next largest number; you will find (by adding two zeros) 5600, namely 200 cycles. Add 10, because the proposed sum is before the Incarnation; from the sum 5610 take away the proposed 3993; 1617 remains. Now from this remainder, as in the previous example, take away the next smallest number found in the side-table, 1400 (50 cycles, adding one zero); 217 remains; from this take away 196 (7 cycles); the Solar Cycle 21 remains.*

# RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS

<margin>
What the beginning of the Solar Cycle is in these Tables.
</margin>
The individual years of the Solar Cycle and the Julian months are interspersed. But note carefully, as you were also warned in the *Synopsis of Eras* and as the months themselves advise in the table areas: for the purpose of these Tables, we begin the Solar Cycle not from the Calends of January (January 1st), as in other calculations, but either from the 6th day before the Calends of March <note>original: "VI. Cal. Martiis", referring to February 24th, the traditional leap-day point</note> or from the Calends of March (March 1st). Thus, January and February are considered an "appendix" to the previous given year; furthermore, in the backwards counting before the Incarnation, the preceding year is increased by one unit.

With this in mind, look for the Solar Cycle of the proposed year (or, if the day is within the first two months, the Cycle of the preceding year) in the areas of the Weekday Table, and from the top of the Table, bring out the "ferial character" <note>a numerical value assigned to a weekday</note>. Do the same with the current month. Add both characters to the current days of the month; cast out all groups of seven from the sum. The remainder will be the Number of the Feria (the day of the week). The top of the table indicates how this day is named in Greek, or which Planet it belongs to according to the Chaldeans and Arabs.

For example, if one asks about January 13th in the year of the Incarnation 1507: the Solar Cycle previously found is 4. But because this example asks about one of the first months of the year, the Cycle of the prior year (3) is used. Finding this in the table areas, it shows VII at the top. And January (following the year 1506) shows V. Add 7 and 5 to 13, which totals 25. Having cast out all the 7s (25 divided by 7 leaves 4), the remainder is Feria IV (Wednesday).

<margin>
By Precept 60.
</margin>
Likewise, in the year 3993 before the Incarnation, on the 24th of July, what was the day of the week? Above, the Cycle was found to be 21, which shows II from the top of the Weekday Table; July shows III. When these are added to 24, they total 29, and with the sevens cast out, it is Feria I (Sunday). Thus, for the Jews, the second day <note>Monday</note> began from the following evening. Indeed, among the Western Antipodes <note>people on the opposite side of the world</note>, the night of Feria II (Monday) had already begun; among those nearby but to the west, the night of Feria I (Sunday) was beginning.

Likewise, in the year 38 before the Incarnation, on the 1st of January, what was the day of the week? It is exactly as if we were asking about the preceding year 39, which this January follows. Therefore, Solar Cycle 27 gives II from the top. The following January (after year 39) gives V. Add 2 and 5 to the 1st of January and subtract 7; Feria I (Sunday) is formed.

### TO REVEAL THE DAY OF THE WEEK

If the day of the week is sought for a date in the Gregorian year or others: first, let that date be reduced to the corresponding day of the Julian year; then the day of the week found for the Julian date will also be the day for the other. But there is a unique skill for the Arabic year <note>the Islamic Hegira calendar</note> that should not be omitted. The lower part of the Weekday Table serves it, along with the same common header and the small table of Periods. For what the short 28-year Solar Cycle provides for us in the Julian calendar, a longer cycle of 210 years provides for the Arabs. This cycle begins from the Arabic Era itself and consists of seven thirty-year cycles <note>term: "Triaconterteris", a 30-year cycle used to align lunar months with the solar year</note>. Therefore, inserted into the table areas are first the completed years of the individual thirty-year cycles, then the individual running years of one cycle, and finally the 12 Arabic months.

Because nothing is added to the number of Arabic years to find the thirty-year cycle, three entries must be made into the areas of the Weekday Table: 1st, by the completed thirty-year cycles (casting out

<column-break/>

whole Periods and using the remainder); 2nd, by the current year of the thirty-year cycle; and 3rd, by the current month. From the common header (which sits above the Julian months), extract as many characters. These are to be added to the proposed number of the day of the Arabic month, and once the sevens are cast out from the sum, the Feria (day of the week) remains.

(As was done above in the Great Cycle of Dionysius, which contains twenty-eight Lunar Cycles). Then, by dividing and casting out all the 19-year cycles, the year of the Cycle remains.

<margin>
The marking of time through movable feasts and the numbering of Sundays.

Notable diversity.

Ecclesiastical Computation; the use of Calendars in these Tables is superfluous and uncertain.

However, to determine the Christian Easter and other movable feasts and Sundays—which were numbered from Trinity Sunday in the ancient fashion throughout Germany and surrounding kingdoms, and were very frequently used by our ancestors to mark time, though now from Pentecost in the Roman fashion, which is beginning to be expressed in German calendars—one would need a transcription of the entire Calendar with the Golden Number. Therefore, both this ancient form of the Calendar and the part that succeeded it in the new Gregorian Calendar—the Cycle of Epacts <note>the age of the moon on Jan 1st</note>—must necessarily be relegated to Ecclesiastical Computation. This is true along with the most laborious Jewish calendar, and the lunar calendars of the Athenians, Macedonians, and Syrians; especially since these latter often leave us in uncertainty about one day or another. Thus, we come closer to the truth of the day through the very easy calculation of the moon's age from these Tables—which gives the name to each day among the mentioned nations—than by any Cycles. Furthermore, Ptolemy already referred the eclipses marked by the days of the Greek Calendar back to the Egyptians.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

### CONCERNING THE TABLES OF EPOCHS AND MEAN MOTIONS, AND HOW MEAN MOTIONS ARE TO BE GATHERED
### *from these Tables, and the mean positions of individual moving bodies assigned.*

<margin>So that Motion may be understood.</margin>
The whole method of this teaching consists in the description of the individual parts in the Tables. Therefore, let the calculator note at the beginning that Motions are one thing, and the Epochs of motions are another. For since every motion requires both a Place (or length of space) and a Time, and since there is never motion without time, it follows that the beginnings of both things are also joined; and that no perception of motions can even exist unless this coupling of the beginnings of both things is brought before one's eyes and placed in a clear light.

<margin>What an Epoch is.</margin>
Therefore, whatever point of the course or circular line the line of mean motion of any moving body has reached at any moment of time (whose distance from the present time is known): that point is customarily called in Greek the *Epocha* of that time or Moment, which in Latin sounds like "Place" [Locus]; because any of the moving lines, at an assigned moment of time, is said to occupy <note>original: "ἐπέχειν" (epechein), meaning to hold or stay at a position</note> that place on its circle.

Even though the circles of the moving bodies are different, and a circle has neither beginning nor end, astronomers nevertheless needed to establish some common starting point for all circles. So that the motions of all could be compared among themselves, all others had to be referred to one common circle for the sake of a common starting point and division. Furthermore, <margin>By the divisions of which circle Mean Motions should be counted.</margin> which other of the circles would they choose for this work but the Solar circle? This is in a way the leader and shaper of all motions; it is even marked by the wandering circle of the moon, such that the Moon, with its excursions to either side of it, surrounds this fixed circle of the Sun over a succession of 19 years. Finally, the circles of all the other Planets receive this circle of the Sun into their middle, so that they themselves are inclined to one another at much greater angles than they are to this middle [solar] circle.

<margin>The path of the Sun: by what marks it is recommended to us as the mean for all Planets.</margin>
And so that it may be clear by all evidence that Astronomers, in this choice, imitate that Supreme Moderator and Architect of all motions: behold, in the beginning of the motions (which is known to us from the divine oracles, from the prophet Moses through the succession of all ages to us, preserved in the Universal Church <note>original: "Ecclesia Catholica"</note>), in this beginning of motions, I say, the excursions of all five [planets] toward the North did not deflect to one side of the Solar circle, but were arranged in completely opposite parts of the circle: Saturn in Cancer, Jupiter in Libra, and Mercury in the opposite, Aries. It is necessary, therefore, by the counsel of the Creator himself, that to this ap-

<column-break/>

parent circle of the Sun was granted not some withdrawal to the side, but a complete mediation of position among the others, even in latitude.

<margin>What the starting point of the circles is in the numbering of mean motions.</margin>
Therefore, since the circles of all the Planets appearing under the fixed stars were to be referred to the apparent circle of the Sun under the fixed stars—which, drawn through the middle of the Signs <note>original: "ζωδίων" (zodiōn), referring to the zodiac signs</note>, obtained the name "Ecliptic" from its particular function—no other starting point for all the circles was to be established than that which would correspond to the beginning of the Ecliptic itself in each case. This would be established naturally, as it were, by the intertwining of the Primary motion [the daily rotation of the heavens] and the Secondary motions [the planets' own paths]—the former being common, the latter being proper to each; namely, the point of the Equinox.

<margin>What the starting point is for Copernicus and the Prutenics, who are the starting points or goals of the Mean Motions.</margin>
Although Copernicus, because of his conceived opinion of the unequal precession of the equinoxes, follows another starting point for the circles—namely, that which corresponds to the first star of Aries in any given circle—he thought it more convenient for us to observe a fixed starting point of the circle, from which (just as most motions go forward) the motion of the equinoctial points themselves would go backward. But the first author of these Tables, Tycho Brahe, when he discovered that such a great inequality of precession was either fictitious or at least uncertain, decided he should return <margin>Why is the Equinoctial point here the goal?</margin> to the Ptolemaic custom. He felt one should study the practical shortcut of calculation more than the contemplation of the Nature of motions; so that while we derive motions from this retrograde initial point of the Ecliptic (which holds the name of the Equinoctial point or the beginning of Aries), we may gather at one and the same time both the backward motion of the point and the forward motion of the planet, as if from a fixed point.

<margin>What is understood by the "beginning of Aries" in the orbit of each planet?</margin>
By the "beginning of Aries," therefore—the equinoctial point or equinox—when mean motions are gathered, we understand in every Planetary circle (imagined under the fixed stars) that point which is equally distant from the common intersection of these two [circles] in the same direction as the point of the Ecliptic so named. And from this point, thus standing next to the true Ecliptic beginning of Aries, the twelve Signs (or 360 degrees) are numbered in each of the planets' circles under the fixed stars, no less than in the Ecliptic itself.

<margin>What kind of Epochs these are.</margin>
Now, since one is free in establishing the very first Epochs, either to apply one and the same point (say, the beginning of Aries) as the prefix to all motions at distinct times when each individual mean motion falls upon it; or one and the same...

...to choose a beginning of time, and in it to assign distinct locations of the circle, specifically one to each Planet. Each of the Ancient astronomers chose the same starting time according to their own judgment. My first concern in all of Astronomy was to see if I could join the identity of a circular starting point with the identity of a point in time. However, when I saw that such a principle would range across the most immense spans of time, far beyond the age of the World, I set aside this useless concern. Instead, I followed the custom of the other practitioners, and most especially that of Tycho Brahe. Indeed, in these Tables, I ought to be seen as having done this by his right as the primary author. He presented the Epochs <note>Starting positions for calculation</note> of the Sun and Moon in his *Progymnasmata*, Volume I: first, in the Era of the Incarnation and in the old Julian form of the year; second, in blocks of four hundred years, and for individual years, and others in blocks of twenty; third, he fixed the Meridian for these at the island of Hven in the Danish Strait, and at his fortress of Uraniborg there; fourth, he established the meridian hour for them as the noon that follows the completion of the Epoch year on the approaching 1st of January. I have imitated all four of these points in these Tables.

But if calculating an earlier date, one must seek the interval between the "Century of 1600" and the target date by subtracting years of the Incarnation <note>AD years</note> less than 1600, or by adding years before the Incarnation <note>BC years</note> to 1600. Then, with the thousands, hundreds, and individual years below a hundred, the collected sum of the motion is taken away from the Epoch which the proposed Fixed Star has in the Catalog. Alternatively, it can be done this way: collect the location of the first Descending Node <note>original: ☋</note> as if it were one of the Planets, and to that location add the arc of distance of the proposed fixed star from the first Descending Node, which it has in the Catalog. In the case of the Fixed Stars and the Apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> of the Sun, the frequencies are immense and scattered, and the innermost values were admitted perhaps not quite advisedly; this has reduced us to a non-continuous numbering of Degrees. In the Apogees of the parts of the whole, excerpts were taken for a non-continuous numbering of Degrees; <margin>As in Chapter XIV.</margin> nor in the last thousands did he wish to write the seconds by marks instead of the characters of the sign, because this was not sufficiently carried out at the beginning. Secondly, except for the Node of the Moon. Because it is retrograde <note>Moving backward compared to the stars</note>, as is noted at the head of its motions: for its Epoch, write the complement to the circle <note>Subtract the value from 360 degrees</note>, and do the same by addition for the remaining sums. Or, what amounts to the same thing: the motion of the Moon’s node with the smaller hundreds elapsed from the Epoch, and also with the thousands and individual years below a hundred—throw these motions, I say, separately into one sum, which you then subtract from the numbers written out for the Epoch itself.

This is the reason for the operation.

### CHAPTER XIX.
## ON THE SEXAGENARY CANONS AND THE METHOD OF CALCULATING FROM THEM.

<margin>Table page 47 and page 88.</margin>
Even though it was not strictly necessary to establish Sexagenary Canons <note>Tables based on the number 60, common in ancient Babylonian and Greek astronomy</note> for the mean motions—since the Tables are already completed and their Epochs multiplied for every occasion—I nevertheless decided they should not be neglected regarding the motions of the Sun and Moon. I did this partly because the invention of the Arabs is skillful and of good repute; partly so that the Epochs and motions of these heavenly bodies could be verified through them and compared with the motions in other Tables; and finally, to serve the calculators of the Ecclesiastical Computus <note>The calculation of the date of Easter and other church feasts</note>, who are accustomed to extend their accounts over many tens of thousands of years.

<margin>On the Canon of days in the Julian year, Table page 102.</margin>
Therefore, whoever wishes to use these Canons should know that two things are needed: an Epoch and a reduction of the time elapsed from that Epoch into days, fractions of days, and sexagenas <note>groups of sixty</note>. This reduction is done through the Sexagenary Canon of Days in Julian years, which differs quite significantly from the usual method of counting years; this difference must nevertheless be carefully noted. For in common practice, we only count whole days in ordinary years,

...neglecting the hours and minutes, which we previously discussed by calculation from the first Table attached to the left in Chapter 41—specifically, that time which falls between a given date and the nearest Epoch <note>A reference date used as a starting point for astronomical calculations</note>. For the Law of the first Canon is that the sums of Julian years, whose Sixty-fold units, Days, and Scruples <note>original: "Scrupula"; small units of time or measurement, here referring to minutes or fractions of a day</note> are to be referred to the nearest preceding Epoch, should be noted in essential Sixty-fold units, as well as the Days and Scruples of days—specifically those which, belonging to this Canon, cannot be contained within sixty days. This could not be done except through the first Canon, or through the collected Sixty-fold units, Days, and Scruples of days, or through the addition of Sixty-year units, where 1`. 0`. 0`. is taken absolutely: such as the year 360, and its multiples and parts. For in this part of the Tables, the account of time is not held as strictly as is necessary in all these Tables to be so accurate. Therefore, since the year 360 and each of its multiples (namely a completed Sixty-fold unit) shows 1`. 0`. 0`., whenever any Julian year does not yield 360 days, nor shows whole Sixty-fold units in the number of years, the parts of that Sixty-fold unit are noted in the Tables next to the Sixty-fold sign. Thus, in the calculation of sixty-day units, the scruples of those collected days beyond 360 days (which are completed Sixty-fold units) are not placed in the margin, nor are they added to the calculation, because the perfect Sixty-fold units stand in their place.

<margin>RULE 77.</margin>
Furthermore, it is a law of the first Sixty-fold unit that the sums of years which do not essentially form a complete Sixty-fold unit in Julian years—that is, which do not yield 360 days and are not referred to the year 360—should have the parts of those years' Sixty-fold units noted in the tables next to the Sixty-fold sign. The remaining use of the Canon is easy, insofar as in the Sixty-fold units sought in the margin, they extract the Days of the Second and First Sixty-fold units and the Scruples of the Day. If the proposed sum of years is greater than sixty, a unit in the margin signifies 60 years, a two signifies 120, and so on. If they extract the Third, Second, and First Sixty-fold units, and no individual Days, the total addition is made by subordinating the same types of extracted numbers to each other. For the Law [of] Logistics <note>The arithmetic of base-60 (sexagesimal) calculations</note> which holds the days and Scruples.

<column-break/>

the first to the left is sought in the types of hours of the proposed number: that is, in the same descending line of numbers which the common indices of the column have (namely in both of the borders). One seeks in these categories the proposed number, which is the first member of that sum. In this way, the type of items to be extracted is selected. In the margin, however, the Sixty-fold units are noted, but for more [units], the category is selected: in the tables, however, those which have similar marks are noted. In this way, the category of things to be extracted is selected: in the tables, indeed, the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Sixty-fold units are noted, which have the Sixty-fold sign marked: nor is there any difference with the parts of these Sixty-fold units. For in these Sixty-fold units, the types of descending numbers are no individual ones. But subordinated into one Sixty-fold unit are 60 Sixty-fold units, and one higher sign, which is a Sixty-fold unit of 60 years, and so on. <margin>As in Rule 76.</margin> If the Epochs are determined from the equinox, the preceding motions collected separately from the Canons are subtracted from the Epoch.

<margin>RULE 78.</margin>
Conversely, if it is asked of some sum of days conceived in Sixty-fold units, how many Julian years it makes, including every fourth leap year: let it be multiplied by the Number nearest smaller in the Canon as the situation requires or for a similar [number], either by 60, or finally by 3600. Then, after subtracting that nearest smaller number from the proposed one, let the remainder be dealt with by that nearest smaller number in the Canon, which, since it is of lower types, will also show a margin of a type depressed by an equal degree. Thus from two or three sums, whatever remains is less than 6°. 5'. 0". to be resolved into the method of months from the beginning of the year, and the remaining days. When all the days are consumed.

<margin>Table 41 or also 91.</margin>

In the beginning, the Epoch is copied out, but the binary Signs are to be reduced into one Sixty-fold unit of degrees, and one higher Sign, numbered in 30° degrees. Then it should be noted.

## HOW THE MEAN ANOMALY
### OF EACH OF THE SEVEN PLANETS IS TO BE FORMED:

### CHAPTER XX.

## ON THE TABLES OF PROSTHAPHERESES, AND ON THE METHOD OF EXTRACTING FROM THEM THE MOTIONS OF ANOMALY, *and* ALSO THE EQUATIONS OF THE ECCENTRIC.

<image-desc>Large ornate initial 'U' with intricate scrollwork.</image-desc>

# RUDOLPHINE TABLES

...touches at A and P, of which the two foci are S and Q.
<margin>Refer to the diagram here.</margin> Regarding the mechanical method of description, twenty-one years ago in my *Optical Part of Astronomy* <note>Kepler refers to his 1604 work, *Ad Vitellionem paralipomena, quibus astronomiae pars optica traditur*.</note>, following Apollonius of Perga, I proposed this: with pins fixed at S and Q, a double thread is attached from A—specifically, a shorter one AQ and a longer one AS. Then, a third stylus is inserted between both threads at A and moved around with the thread kept taut; as the shorter part QA grows, the longer part AS decreases. For this third stylus, descending from A through points F, H, and L toward P, will describe the required ellipse. However, because this method of drawing possesses more elegance than practical convenience—being more suited for manual work than for calculation, as far as I know—I will now teach another method, which indeed
<margin>Demonstration.</margin> uses the inner circle described above. For having taken any arcs of the Eccentric <note>An "eccentric" is a circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth or Sun.</note> starting from A, such as AB, AG, and AK, let the endpoints of the arcs B, G, and K be connected to the center C. Then, from these endpoints as well as from the intersections of the drawn lines and the small circle (namely D, M, and N), let perpendiculars BE, GC, and KV be drawn to the diameter AP, as well as DI, MC, and NO. Therefore, to mark the points on the lines BE, GC, and KV through which the ellipse passes, take with a compass the interval PI, and moving one foot to S, draw an arc through BE (which is conjugate to DI) that will intersect it at F. Similarly, with the same center S and interval PC, an arc drawn will intersect GC (conjugate to MC) at H. And again, with center S and interval PO, an arc drawn will intersect KV (conjugate to NO) at L. Thus, F, H, and L are the points through which the ellipse passes.

This delineation is most suitable for calculation. For the
<margin>Instruction for Calculation.</margin> semidiameter of the circle CB is given as 100,000, and in this dimension, the Eccentricity CS or CD is also given, along with A, the aphelion <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note>. Having now taken the arc AB, the sine EC of its complement BG is given in the same dimension. As BC is to CE, so DC is to CI, because the triangles are similar; adding the semidiameter CP, one obtains PI, which is equal to SF. Again, by adding CS to EC, one obtains ES, the other side of the rectangle SEF; therefore, by a single operation, the angle ESF will also be revealed. Finally, because as GC is to CH, so is the area of the circle AGP to the area of the ellipse AHP; and as that same GC is to CH, so is BE to EF, and as these heights are to each other, so also is the area CBS to the area CFS. Therefore, just as the area of the circle is to the area of the ellipse, and the area of the circular sector ABC is to the area of the elliptical sector AFC, so too is the area CBS to the area CFS. Thus, the parts composed of these proportions, ABS and AFS, have the same ratio. Therefore, alternately, as the area of the circle AGP is to the area of the part ABS, so is the area of the ellipse AFP to the area of the part AFS. Thus, one will have the proportion of the area AFS to the total ellipse if one has the proportion of area ABS to the total circle. Yet this is easily compared: since ABS has two parts, ABC and CBS, the proportion of ABC to the circle's area is the same as that of the arc AB to the circumference; but the proportion of this CBS to the area of the circle is composed of the ratio of the height BE to the height GC, and from the ratio of the base CS to the circumference of the circle extended into a straight line. That is, the area of the largest triangle upon CS (let us say CGS) is to the area of the circle as the base CS is to the circumference, but to the area CBS as the height GC is to the height BE. Indeed, these are the three things entirely sought through calculation: the length SF,

<column-break/>

the angle FSA, and the proportion of the area CFS to the area of the ellipse in a measurement where the area of the total ellipse is equal to 360°.

The geometric foundations having been explained, let us
<margin>From where did the hypotheses of the ancients come?</margin> now apply the hypotheses of the authors. It was observed in ancient times that planets return to the same fixed stars after certain intervals of time. It seemed consistent with the nature of celestial bodies that this occurred through the description of a most perfect circle around the center of the world, and indeed with a most uniform motion, which would complete equal arcs of the circle in equal times. This philosophical hypothesis was soon partially overturned when it was discovered that planets in certain parts of the sky appeared both larger and faster than in the opposite parts. It was therefore necessary to establish that their circles had a different center—for example, if S were the center of the world, but C the center of the Eccentric. Then, with the help of geometry and based on the measure of apparent slowness, the length of the line CS was investigated, while retaining the idea that the planet's motion was itself most uniform, both at the apogee <note>The point furthest from the center of motion.</note> A and the perigee <note>The point closest to the center of motion.</note> P. All the fault for the slowing was attributed to the deception of sight and the distance of point A from S, and the acceleration to the proximity of point P. This hypothesis endured for saving the motions of the Sun among others until our own times. But for the planets, long ago even Ptolemy
<margin>Ptolemy’s Hypothesis.</margin> himself abandoned the uniformity of motion. For he noticed that if he established the length of the line CS from the apparent speed and slowness, the apparent sizes of the Epicycles <note>Small circular orbits whose centers move along the circumference of a larger circle (the deferent).</note> carried by the Eccentric did not correspond to their apprehended centers; for these accounted for only half of what the timing required. For example, if the Eccentricity SC were derived by consulting the apparent sizes of the Epicycles, the length of time they delayed in the upper semicircle compared to the brevity in the lower one resulted in an Eccentricity SQ that was clearly double. Faced with this conflict of motion, Ptolemy did indeed retain the centers of the Epicycles on a perfect Eccentric circle of simple eccentricity SC, but he said the motion of this entire Eccentric was regular not around its own center C, but around a different center Q, which stood at an equal distance from center C as the center of the world S, but in the opposite direction <note>This point Q is known as the "Equant."</note>. Thus, when the planet (or its Epicycle) moved through A, the entire Eccentric moved slowly in all its parts; when it descended into P, it again became fastest in all its parts.

But this seemed an unworthy deed to Copernicus: to cast such a disgrace upon the purest substance and upon the movers of the simplest nature. Therefore, when he had learned from Ptolemy that a Concentric with an Epicycle fixed to its circumference (with uniform and constant motions in opposite directions) could produce the same effect as a simple Eccentric, he then also
<margin>Copernicus’s Hypothesis for the equations of the Eccentric.</margin> dissolved this Ptolemaic Eccentric of inconsistent motion into one concentric and two epicycles, so that the larger might carry the smaller, just as the concentric carried both. The smaller was also twice as fast as the larger, with both in constant motion. Thus Copernicus removed that "disgrace" from the circles, but upon the planets themselves, if one may say so, he cast another disgrace. For while Ptolemy left the path of the center of the planetary Epicycle ordered in a circle, Copernicus distorted the path of the planet itself through so many circles into many twists and turns.

# RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS

<margin>
Tycho's [model] departs much more from observations.
</margin>
...the Ptolemaic effect is not achieved, and it departs much more from observations. Tycho, regarding these particular Hypotheses, remained in agreement with Copernicus while he was mapping the paths of the Moon; what he would have done regarding the other planets he left uncertain due to his untimely death. Indeed, concerning the simple Eccentric <note>An "eccentric" is a circular orbit whose center is not the center of the world.</note> of the Sun, when he saw that it was not supported by the observations of the other planets, <margin>
See the appendix to Volume I of the *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe’s *Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata* (1602).</note>.
</margin> he began to abandon it in his final years; he allowed it to be equal to the other planets, by whatever Hypothesis that matter was to be explained.

It is now apparent which circles and which orbs each astronomer introduced; their successors, the Arabs, and from them Gerard of Cremona, and from him Purbach <note>Georg von Peuerbach (1423–1461), a key figure in reviving Ptolemaic astronomy in the Renaissance.</note>, even "clothed" these models in physical matter, or nested them together, assigning to each its own "thickness," as they call it. I believe they were imitating those "Revolving Orbs" of Aristotle and his audacity in inventing physical spheres.

<margin>
Hypothesis of these Tables.
</margin>
IT REMAINS, therefore, that I discuss my own (particular) Hypotheses for these Tables. I retain the return of a planet to the same tracks, but I deny that this happens by being carried in any perfect circle. For just as the ancients rejected the concentricity of the orbit, and Ptolemy rejected the uniformity of motion, so I reject both of those and, most especially, the Ptolemaic circular figure of motion. For (to reveal those things demonstrated from observations made of the planet Mars), although the planet begins its journey from A and reaches P, it does not pass through the points B, G, and K; rather, it bends inward, descending through F, H, and L, the tracks of an Ellipse. The same occurs in the ascent through the other semicircle. Since, therefore, Ptolemy's perfect circle A G P has no place, Copernicus's "flexuous" <note>Kepler critiqued Copernicus for using complex combinations of circles that created a "wavy" or "swollen" path rather than a clean ellipse.</note> path will be tolerated even less; for it moves the planet outward from S beyond B G K, making its composite motion appear deformed and swollen. If you ask whether an elliptical planetary orbit could not also be constructed through <margin>
Transformation of the path into circles.
</margin> some composition of circles? I say: certainly, there was one who attempted this while he was alive, David Fabricius <note>A German astronomer and correspondent of Kepler.</note>, the Frisian Mathematician; he attained the matter to some extent using Ptolemaic apparatus—namely, by the regular motion of some small circle around a center other than its own (that is, in truth, an unequal motion). This was not a simple motion, but composed of two, which would balance the center of the Eccentric C on a transverse diameter that was parallel to G C itself. But I believe there is no need for these "baseless" <note>original: *ἀναιτιολογήτοις* (unaccountable/without physical cause)</note> maneuvers, which crucify the intellect and bring blindness to the eyes of reason. For the natural causes, by which an Ellipse is formed from the planet's orbit, have been brought into the open: the Sun, twisting the planet into a circuit according to the laws of the lever and the balance in proportion to the distance, by the rotation of its own body around its axis; and with it, the "species" of light diffused through the whole amplitude of the world; and the magnetic disposition in the body of the planet, by whose struggle (like the rowing of an oar) through the whole circuit, the distance between the Planet and the Sun is changed. But let it suffice to have pointed the finger; let the curious reader seek the rest from the *Commentaries on Mars* <note>Kepler's *Astronomia Nova* (1609).</note> and from the *Epitome of Astronomy*.

<margin>
To what extent circles are rejected or retained.
</margin>
Thus, I have rejected circles and solid orbs from the natural formation of the planetary Orbit; yet, to describe it in a table and to regulate the calculation, I employ a perfect

<column-break/>

Eccentric circle A B G K P. The planet is never actually found on its circumference, except at point A, the Aphelion <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun.</note> (farthest from the Sun S), and its opposite P, the Perihelion <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Sun.</note>. Likewise, I reject the Epicycle equivalent to the Eccentric; yet I describe a circle Q D M N S equal to it from the center of the Eccentric C. On its diameter, divided by perpendicular lines, I weigh the increases and decreases of the distance between the Planet and the Sun. Furthermore, I reject the Ptolemaic equatory point Q <note>The "Equant," a point used by Ptolemy to account for the observed speeding up and slowing down of planets.</note>, not only because there is no need for the "stretching and loosening" of the motion of whole circles or solid orbs, but also because point Q, held immobile as it is in Ptolemy, does not entirely produce the angles A S F consistent with observations. I reject, I say, the angles around Q which Ptolemy embraces; but I substitute the areas of the triangles C F S (or their proxies C B S), which encompass the power of the distances S F in the formation of said angles. I also substitute lines from Q and S, by which the true and genuine elliptical orbit of the planet can be described (specifically, by the true intervals of each time). What parts of the Equation Tables are derived from these proxy circles, their lines, angles, and areas, I shall now say further.

<margin>
Description of the Equation Tables.
Tab. pp. 44, 50, 56, 62, 68, 74.
Tab. pp. 80, 81.
</margin>
The Table of equations for each Planet is explained in six columns; for the six planets, two columns occupy each face of the paper; for the Moon, there are three. The columns are subdivided into three small columns, with one space inserted between the two leftmost ones. In the first of these are the arcs A B, A G, A K, with the areas of the triangles C B S; these are the two parts of the areas A B S, which encompass the power of the distances of arc A F and the Sun S. After crossing the inter-column space, the second small column follows, in which are the angles A S F, etc., corresponding to the arcs A B, etc. Finally, in the third ones to the right are stored the distances S F, etc., belonging to the same arcs. The methods for computing these things were already explained at the beginning; examples may be sought from the *Epitome of Astronomy*.

Both, when added together in the mind, constitute the Mean Anomaly. For the Mean Anomaly is not expressed in any other way in its entry than through these two component parts.

Now, to this Eccentric Anomaly and to this Mean Anomaly corresponds its "coequated" anomaly <note>The Coequated Anomaly is the planet's true position as seen from the Sun, adjusted for its elliptical orbit.</note> on the same line, but in the column for the Mean, which in the case of the Moon is the one on the far right.

Let the entry in the Table of Lunar Equations be an example. Here, 30° is the Eccentric Anomaly of the Moon: but 1° 14' 59" is the part of the physical equation, by which the Mean Anomaly (so-called) of that entry exceeds the 30° Eccentric Anomaly written above it: that is, the Mean Anomaly of this entry is 31° 14' 59". And to this Mean Anomaly, as well as to that Eccentric Anomaly, corresponds the coequated anomaly of 28° 46' 23" in the right-hand column of the same line.

<margin>
PRECEPT 82.
On extracting the Coequated Anomaly.
</margin>
Therefore, when a Mean Anomaly is proposed in degrees, minutes, and seconds (taking 30 degrees for any given sign), if it is less than a semicircle or 180°—which is always the case for the planets due to the preceding precept—look in the first columns for the Mean value that is closest but smaller. Always keep in mind the sum of the two numbers subordinate to each other in the same entry. Then, write down the coequated value corresponding to it from the second column. Subtract that "closest smaller value" from the Table from the value you were given. Multiply the excess by the degrees, minutes, and seconds found in the difference between columns (the intercolumnar value); add the result to the coequated value you wrote down. Thus the Coequated Anomaly is completed. For the sake of future use, attach the label "Add" in the first case of the preceding precept, and "Subtract" in the second.

If, however, a Mean Anomaly greater than a semicircle is proposed—which must be watched for in the Moon when its position is verified outside of conjunctions—subtract it from a full circle (360°). With the remainder, extract the Coequated Anomaly as before; then subtract this result in turn from 360°, which will leave the Coequated Anomaly greater than a semicircle that was sought. However, in the general precept for calculating the motions of the six planets, a coequated anomaly greater than a semicircle will not be necessary.

In this precept, although the calculator seems burdened by the subtraction of the Mean Anomaly in the Table from the proposed Mean Anomaly—a subtraction not needed in common tables—he is in turn relieved by the addition of the equation, which common tables require. The form of the Tables was not changed out of a desire for novelty, but because the form of the Physical Hypothesis demanded it.

## A SHORTCUT FOR TAKING the proportional part THROUGH LOGARITHMS.

<margin>
Frequent use of the Heptacosias <note>Kepler's "Heptacosias" is a specialized table of 700 logarithms he developed to simplify astronomical multiplication and division.</note>.
</margin>
To be relieved of the burden of logistical multiplication <note>Base-60 (sexagesimal) multiplication used in astronomy.</note>, ignore the intercolumnar difference and instead write down its superscripted Logarithm found in the same cell, with the label "Addition" if the difference is less than one degree, or "Subtraction" if it is greater. Then, taking the "excess" of your proposed Mean Anomaly over the closest smaller value in the table, enter the sexagesimal column of the Heptacosias and extract the Logarithm from that section. Place the Logarithm of the intercolumnar difference below it, and—as its label instructs—either add it to or subtract it from the Logarithm of the Excess. The result will be the Logarithm of the proportional part, to be found in the sexagesimal column of the Heptacosias, usually on the left.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Refers to precept 10, page 14.
</margin>
And here, let those unskilled or unaccustomed to Analysis or "Cossic" art <note>The "Cossic art" was an early term for algebra (from the Italian *cosa*, meaning "thing," referring to the unknown variable).</note> note: if the excess is greater than one degree, one must work with the minutes attached to the single degree; the entire intercolumnar difference itself must be added to the quotient. Thus the correct proportional part will be produced. It can also be done otherwise, but this method is the easiest.

<margin>
Cautions to avoid the necessity of precept 8.
</margin>
<margin>
According to Note I of precept 10.
</margin>
Conversely, regarding an intercolumnar difference greater than one degree, it may happen that its negative Logarithm is greater than the positive Logarithm of the Excess, so that it cannot be subtracted from it. This is an indication that the proportional part will be greater than one degree. In that case, the Logarithm of the Excess should instead be subtracted from the Logarithm of the intercolumnar difference; the remaining Logarithm will show the sought proportional part—which is greater than one degree—not in the left sexagesimal column, but in the right column of negatives.

<margin>
According to Note II of precept 10.
</margin>

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE MOON.
In the Table of the Anomaly of the Moon's equations, the Part of the Physical Equation <note>original: "Pars Æquationis Physicæ"</note>, or the lower and minute number of the left-hand cells with this its quantity, has its place only during the Conjunctions and Full Moons <note>original: "Interluniis & Pleniluniis"</note>: in the other phases, it increases successively through the months of the year, until in a full month it acquires a quantity exactly double that which is found in the Table: as will be indicated more fully below. Therefore, the use of the inter-column and the method of extracting the Coequated [Anomaly] outside of these joinings <note>original: "extra copulas," referring to the New/Full Moon alignment</note> either ceases or is not sufficient. Thus, only the Moon, to the left of the physical

<column-break/>

part of the equation, has outside the assigned cells the differences or Increments of this physical equation in the descent through the first upper quadrant; and decreases through the lower one. As in the next example, the Increment in the first 10 [units] is 22''.

# TO FIND THE ECCENTRIC ANOMALY OF ANY PLANET, either by the Mean Anomaly or by the known Coequated Anomaly.

->Especially for the calculation of the Position of the Moon outside the Syzygies.<-

<margin>PRECEPT 83.</margin>
If the Mean Anomaly proposed to you is found precisely in the sum of two numbers of one cell: then their upper value is also precisely the Eccentric Anomaly sought through the proposed mean. But if your Mean Anomaly is not found precisely in one of the cells; then from the mean proposed to you, subtract the next smaller one which the cell shows: the first minutes <note>original: "scrupula Prima," the 60ths of a degree</note> that remain, add those to the whole degrees of the Eccentric Anomaly found in that cell: thus the correct Eccentric Anomaly is produced approximately. For to descend to the Seconds <note>original: "Secundā"</note>, or even to worry about a single minute, is not worth the effort in this place.

> *As in the previous example of the Moon, the mean Anomaly was 37°. 4'. 7''. This was not found precisely; therefore, having subtracted the next smaller value from the Table of lunar equations, which was 36°. 26', 38 minutes remain. To the whole degrees of the Eccentric Anomaly, therefore, found in that cell which showed the Sum from both numbers as 36°. 26'. 0''—namely, to 35°—I add the 38' of excess. Therefore, the corrected Eccentric Anomaly will be 35°. 38' approximately.*

<margin>PRECEPT 84.</margin>
But if the Mean Anomaly is not known at the start, but rather the Coequated Anomaly itself was given: again through this, the Eccentric Anomaly is found from the Table of equations, almost as before. For look for the given coequated anomaly in the second small column: if it is found precisely, then from the corresponding cell of the left small column, the upper number will be the Eccentric Anomaly itself. If, however, the coequated anomaly is not found precisely in one of the lines of the second small column; then that which is found in the Table to be next smaller than it must be taken away from the coequated anomaly given to you; the first minutes which remain are to be added to the whole degrees written above in the corresponding left cell, so that the correct Eccentric Anomaly is produced approximately.

> *As in the previous example, if I am ordered to track down the Eccentric Anomaly through the coequated Anomaly 34°. 11': I look for it in the Column of the coequated anomaly: I find indeed the next smaller, 33°. 35' (ignoring for now the 29 seconds); which being taken away from 34°. 11', 36' remain; in the cell of the left column, however, corresponding to the smaller coequated anomaly, I find the upper number or Eccentric Anomaly to be 35°. Therefore, with the 36' added—that is, the remainder from before—the Eccentric Anomaly becomes 35°. 36', nearly as before.*

These rules hold true if the Anomalies established for the proposed time are less than a semicircle. But if they are greater, and their complements to the whole...

...data for a whole circle <note>original: "integrum circulum"</note>; with these, one must proceed as before. However, the value that is extracted in that case is likewise the complement of the Eccentric Anomaly; it must again be subtracted from 360° so that the Eccentric Anomaly itself may be obtained. For this has a singular use in the case of the Moon, outside of its syzygies <note>original: "extra copulas," referring to the Moon's positions other than conjunction or opposition with the Sun.</note>.

<margin>
*Use of the Eccentric Anomaly.*
<br/>
*Table page 84.*
</margin>
*For the sake of example, let the coequated anomaly already be 250°, which is greater than a semicircle. Its complement to the full circle is therefore given as 110°. When this 110° is sought under the column for the Coequated Anomaly in the Lunar Table, the nearest smaller value encountered is 109° 39' 46'', to which the Eccentric Anomaly of 112° corresponds on the left. Therefore, because 109° 40' subtracted from 110° 0' leaves 0° 20', I say that the Eccentric Anomaly of 112° 20' corresponds to the coequated value of 110° 0'. Because the previous 110° was the complement to the circle, then 112° 20' will also be the complement of the Eccentric Anomaly to the circle. And thus, by performing the subtraction of 112° 20' from 360° 0', the Eccentric Anomaly itself will be 247° 40'.*

# ON EXTRACTING THE ECCENTRIC 
# EQUATION AND 
->its parts.<-

<margin>
PRECEPT 85.
</margin>
Even though we do not require this for the calculation of planetary motion, if it is nonetheless sought—perhaps to compare it with the equations in other Tables—it is very easily extracted for the whole degrees of the Eccentric Anomaly. Subtract the Coequated [Anomaly] of any line from the Eccentric Anomaly; the optical part of the equation will remain. To this, add the physical part <note>Kepler distinguishes between the "optical" part (the effect of perspective from the Sun) and the "physical" part (related to the area-sweep of the orbit).</note> from its own cell in the same line, and the total equation is composed.

If, however, the anomalies for which equations are sought are not found precisely in their lines, one must find the equations for the two cells immediately surrounding the given value, from which the proper equation for the given Anomaly must be measured proportionally.

*In the diagram, assuming the Eccentric Anomaly AB, the optical part of the equation is the angle CFS; the physical part is the area CFS, which is not exactly equivalent to the angle CFQ, although it approaches it, being sometimes larger and sometimes smaller. Thus, the total equation is nearly the angle QFS.*

# ON EXTRACTING AND REFINING 
# BOTH THE DISTANCE, 
->and the Logarithm of the distance of a<-
->Planet.<-

<margin>
*As stated above in the chapter.*
</margin>
In the third columns of the Tables, two simple numbers appear in each cell. The upper one, in a larger typeface, expresses the interval or the distance <note>original: "intervallum vel distantiam"</note> itself of the five Planets from the center of the Sun, and for the sixth, the Sun from the Earth. In the seventh, the Moon, this column is missing, because the distance of the Moon from the earth is not a necessary finding except for parallaxes; and indeed the parallaxes of the Moon are obtained from its tables more simply and with less labor. The other number in each cell, the lower one expressed in a smaller typeface, is the Logarithm—that is, the proportion which that planet's distance has to the number 100,000, which indicates the mean interval or distance of the Sun from the Earth.

And this Logarithm of the distance is always negative <note>original: "privativus"</note> for the superior planets, marked with the sign --; for the inferior planets, it is positive, marked with -+-. For the Sun, when it moves in the upper semicircle, being more than 100,000 distant from the Earth, it is likewise negative; when in the lower, being less than 100,000 distant, it is positive. These signs are correctly found expressed at the heads of the columns; remember that they pertain not to the distance itself, but to its logarithm. Both of these numbers, the distance as well as its Logarithm, are adjusted to the Anomalies expressed in the same line.

<margin>
PRECEPT 86.
</margin>
Therefore, if one of the three Anomalies given for extracting the distance or its Logarithm is not expressly found in its cell, the number for the Distance will be the middle value between the two surrounding cells, and its Logarithm will be the middle value between the two expressed.

<margin>
*Refinement of the distance.*
</margin>
The adjustment and refinement <note>original: "limatio," literally a "filing down" or polishing.</note> of the distance itself, where it is indeed necessary, is quite laborious. For the Anomaly of the upper cell must be subtracted both from the given value and from the Anomaly of the lower cell; also, the smaller distance of the lower cell must be subtracted from the larger distance of the upper cell. With these three differences placed in the usual rule, called the Rule of Three <note>original: "Regula Detri," the Rule of Three or Rule of Proportions.</note>, and neglecting the appendages of seconds, the corresponding portion must be computed and subtracted from the upper distance. I have left this operation without further aid, both to avoid confusion and because the use of the distances themselves was to be of less primary importance in these Tables, and they can be ignored.

<margin>
*Refinement of the distance logarithm.*
<br/>
PRECEPT 87.
</margin>
Conversely, since the use of the Logarithm of these distances (which occupies the lower place in the cell) is very frequent and most convenient: in order that this Logarithm may be adjusted with easy labor to a Mean Anomaly not found exactly in the cell, small numbers have been placed at the side of the third column. These are the middle values between two Logarithms of the cells, expressing how much is owed for every ten first scruples <note>original: "Scrupulis Primis," meaning minutes of arc.</note> of the mean anomaly for the correction—not of the distance itself, by whose side they stand, but of its Logarithm, as it is also expressed in small numbers.

This lateral number, being small, is easily multiplied in the mind by the minutes of the difference between the given Mean Anomaly and the one next smallest in the Table. By cutting off the last digit from the result, the portion is established to be subtracted from the Logarithm of the cell for the superior Planets and the Sun, or added to it for the inferior Planets and the Sun, because the series of Logarithms decreases there in descent, and increases here. Thus, there will be no need for the differences of the cells themselves or for the full Rule of Three.

<header>RUDOLPHINE RULES.</header>

# EXAMPLE OF ONE OF THE SUPERIOR PLANETS, FROM THE RUDOLPHINE GENESIS <note>Kepler uses the term "Genesis" to refer to the calculated "birth" or specific worked example of a planetary position within his tables.</note>.

The *Mean Anomaly of Mars* is proposed as *116° 13' 18''.* First, the interval itself must be extracted through this value. Therefore, the value nearest to and smaller than this is found to be 115° 57' 20'', which differs from the given value by 15' 58''. It differs from the next lower value by 57' 58''. You will find the interval in the third column as 147292, followed by the next smaller value of 147063, the difference between them being 293. Therefore, if 58 gives 293, then 16 will give 81, which must be subtracted from the higher value: thus the corrected interval between the centers of the Sun and the Planet in its Orbit becomes 147211.

However, if the Logarithm is to be extracted, setting aside the interval itself: here it is found in the cell—38725 in a decreasing series. The lateral number is 27, which, when multiplied by 16, makes 432. Therefore, 43 is the portion which, when subtracted (as is done for a superior Planet), gives the corrected Logarithm — 38682. Relying on this, I can be certain of the interval itself.

In this same manner, with the *Mean Anomaly of Jupiter at 56° 46' 1/2*, the *Logarithm of the interval of Jupiter and the Sun* is found to be *— 167625*. And with the *Mean Anomaly of Saturn at 70° 38' 2/3*, the *Logarithm of the interval of Saturn and the Sun* is *— 227358*.

### EXAMPLE OF ONE OF THE INFERIOR PLANETS.

The *Mean Anomaly of Mercury* is given as *105° 23' 54''*. The nearest smaller value in the Table is 105° 0' 57'', followed by 106° 0' 11''. The interval is 38380, followed by 38238. The differences are 59' and 23', and 142. By the rule of three <note>original: "regulam Detri," a mathematical method to find a fourth value from three known ones</note>, the portion to be subtracted becomes 55. Thus, the corrected interval is 38325.

But if I prefer to use the Logarithm, it is found in cell 95763 in an increasing series, with a lateral number of 62. This, multiplied by 23, makes 1428. Therefore, the portion is 143 to be added, as is done for an inferior Planet; and the corrected Logarithm is + 95906. Likewise for Venus, with a *Mean Anomaly of 135° 45'*, the *Logarithm of the interval + 32771* is extracted. And for the Sun, with an *Anomaly of 31° 20'*, — 1534 is extracted, specifically with the negative sign placed in front (as with the superior Planets), because the Sun's interval of 101546 exceeds 100000; thus, on this occasion, the Sun is reckoned among the superior planets.

And so much for the tables of Equations: now for the use of the coequated Anomaly.

<margin>RULE 83.</margin>
# TO COMPUTE THE PLACE: INDEED THE TRUE PLACE OF THE SUN, AND THE ECCENTRIC PLACES OF THE FIVE PLANETS (AS WELL AS THE MOON FOR CONJUNCTIONS) WITHIN EACH ONE'S ORBIT.

<margin>By rule 81.</margin>
<margin>By rule 82.</margin>
Once the Mean Anomaly (or its complement to a semicircle) is found, and the coequated anomaly is labeled as "Add" (or its complement to a semicircle labeled "Subtract"), let the former be added to the place of the Apogee or Aphelion <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth or Sun, respectively.</note>, and let the latter be subtracted from it. In this way, the Eccentric place of the Orbit will be established, reckoned from the mean Equinox: which, in the case of the Sun, is its true 

<column-break/>

and absolute place. In the case of the Moon, when she is at the conjunctions themselves <note>original: "copulis," referring to the syzygies of the New or Full Moon.</note>, this is also her true place; however, away from the conjunctions, it is called the "fictitious" or "first-equated" place of the Moon.

As in the RUDOLPHINE Genesis, the *coequated Anomaly of the Sun 180° 27' 28''*, added to the place of the Apogee 3s 4° 54' 37'', establishes the *true place of the Sun as 5s 22' 5'' in Libra ♎︎*.

Thus, the eccentric places of the planets in their own orbits become: *Saturn 29° 34' 30'' in Aquarius ♒︎, Jupiter 13° 55' 36'' in Leo ♌︎, Mars 11° 51' 37'' in Taurus ♉︎, Venus 15° 22' 56'' in Gemini ♊︎, Mercury 2° 37' 40'' in Aquarius ♒︎*, with the lines of motion drawn from the Sun through the Planets. Finally, the fictitious place of the Moon’s Orbit, *as if at the conjunctions, is 2s 5° 15' in Cancer ♋︎*.

## CHAPTER XXI.
## ON THE LATITUDE TABLES.

### To form the argument of latitude.

<margin>RULE 89.</margin>
Seek the place of the Ascending Node from the Tables of Epochs; the Descending Node is positioned exactly opposite it at the same Degree and Minute in the diametrically opposite Sign.

Therefore, if the place of one of the five Planets or the Moon is sought, subtract the place of its nearer Node from the found Eccentric place of the Orbit, or conversely, subtract the latter from the former if it precedes it. The remainder will be the Argument of latitude: North, if the Eccentric place of the Planet was either after the ascending Node or before the descending Node; South, however, if it was after the descending or before the ascending Node. This caution is sufficient so that there is no need to extend this argument across the full width of the circle solely for the sake of distinguishing the direction.

*As in the RUDOLPHINE Genesis, the places were found thus:*
| | Saturn ♄ | Jupiter ♃ | Mars ♂ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Node ☊ | 9s 20° 2' 15'' | 3s 5° 23' 9'' | 1s 16° 12' 26'' |
| Eccentric | 10s 29° 34' 30'' | 4s 13° 55' 36'' | 1s 11° 51' 37'' |
| Arg. of lat. | 1s 39° 32' 15'' South | 38° 32' 27'' North | 4° 20' 49'' South |
| | Venus ♀ | Mercury ☿ | Moon ☽ |
| Node ☊ | 2s 12° 22' 47'' | 7s 11° 16' 32'' | 4s 19° 4' 36'' |
| Eccentric | 2s 15° 22' 56'' | 10s 2° 37' 40'' | 3s 2° 5' 15'' |
| Arg. of lat. | 3° 0' 9'' North | 81° 21' 8'' North | 46° 59' 21'' South |

For Saturn and Mercury, the descending node had to be used as it was nearer. For Mars and the Moon, the eccentric place of the orbit was subtracted from the nearby Node; in the others, the node was subtracted from the place: this variation determines the Labels of the Argument.

<margin>What Inclination is.</margin>
The calculation is directed toward finding the true place of the planet on the Ecliptic <note>The Ecliptic is the apparent path of the Sun across the sky; it serves as the reference plane for most astronomical measurements.</note> and its latitude; it is also for the purpose of "Reducing the Place in the Orbit" to the Ecliptic and learning the Ecliptic position. This is the angle formed at the center of the Sun by two lines: one to the planet’s position on the Ecliptic, and one to its position in its own Orbit. The Tables of Inclinations serve these uses; their origin and use are described more extensively in the left margin.

<margin>Latitude Tables of Inclinations.</margin>
From this, you have the first small column for the "argument of latitude" <note>The argument of latitude is the distance of a planet from its orbital node, used to calculate how far above or below the ecliptic it is.</note>; then the second, third, and fourth columns. In the preceding column for the argument of latitude, while the preceding number is smaller than the following one; the fifth, sixth, and seventh columns deal with the place in the Orbit which must be reduced to the Ecliptic; and finally the eighth, ninth, and tenth columns deal with the "interval" <note>the distance from the Sun to the planet</note> by which the planet must be reduced to the Ecliptic; and finally the eleventh column deals with the place of the planet on the Ecliptic where it is to be reduced; and the twelfth column deals with the interval by which the planet is reduced to the Ecliptic.

<margin>Reduction.</margin>
<note>The following text is partially obscured or very tightly packed, making it hard to read all words with certainty.</note>
Let it be reduced to the Ecliptic. These numbers are found in the tables of latitudes and inclinations. The eleventh column displays this in Degrees, Minutes, and Scruples <note>original: "scrupulis"; small astronomical fractions</note> of the First, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth orders.

<column-break/>

Regarding Curtation <note>Curtation is the mathematical shortening of the planet's distance from the Sun when that distance is projected onto the flat plane of the Ecliptic.</note>, and the discarding of the final digits, the remainder must be subtracted: and that is done if we have operated from a given number and through Logarithms, and then the remainder, which will be in the Logarithms, must be subtracted: and then the Curtation in Logarithms will be completed.
<note>This text appears to be discussing the general method of calculation with logarithms and curtation.</note>
As is demonstrated in Precept 87. Precepts 89, 90, and 91 deal with the "curtated interval," and with the shortening of the interval itself, if anyone wishes to combine them. This is so necessary in Astronomy and Geometry that without it, no one may perfectly approach Astronomy.
Finally, the curvature in these operations must be applied; for shortened Logarithms and whole Logarithms are so necessary in these Tables that without them no one may approach the Tables, nor operate perfectly from them.

This curtation in Saturn and Jupiter is of minimal effect; in others, the nodes often remain, as when they are opposed to the Sun, or when Venus and Mercury are joined to it below.

### TO REDUCE THE PLACE OF THE ORBIT TO THE ECLIPTIC. <margin>PRECEPT 92.</margin>

When you have learned to extract from the Table of Inclinations using the Argument of Latitude, you have found the Reduction to the Ecliptic in Minutes and Seconds. Subtract this from the planet's place on the Ecliptic, from the orbit to the Ecliptic, or from the Ecliptic to the Earth; add it in the present article if the place of the planet has been reduced to the Ecliptic. I shall deal with the Moon in its own place.

<column-break/>

->EXAMPLES.<-

In the Rudolphine Genesis, with the Arguments
<margin>Precept 89.</margin>of Latitude indicated above, the Reductions are:
<margin>Precept 90.</margin>Saturn 1' 38'', Jupiter 0' 28'', Mars 0' 7'', Venus
<margin>Precept 88.</margin>0' 19'', Mercury 3' 42''. The position of the Node relative to the planets, and the preceding rule, orders these to be subtracted from the eccentric places, as follows below, and the place of the planet is reduced from the orbit to the Ecliptic.

Mars: 11° 51' 44'' in Taurus

Mercury: 2° 33' 58'' in Aquarius

This reduction in other cases, and usually in Mars and Venus, can be neglected; since it is of minimal effect, except around the opposition of Mars with the Sun, or the inferior conjunction of Venus with the Sun.

### ON FORMING THE LOGARITHM OF THE SHORTENED INTERVAL and on shortening the interval itself, if anyone wishes to combine them.

<margin>PRECEPT 91.</margin>
The use of the discovered ratio is twofold: the first is very easy, in forming the Logarithm of the shortened interval; the second is more laborious, in shortening the interval itself. Therefore, he who prefers to work with the Logarithm of the interval rather than the interval itself (which requires no small labor, even if the Logarithm itself were formed with a rougher tool), should follow what its precepts teach: for the superior planets, add to the Logarithm of the interval; for the inferior planets, subtract from the Logarithm. Thus will be formed in both cases the correct Logarithm of the shortened interval, which did not have the same sign it had before. For the interval itself, to compute the place of the planet, whoever has need of it in the usual calculation of a rectilinear triangle, it will be computed much more easily.

<column-break/>

This reduction in other cases, and usually in Mars and Venus, can be neglected; since it is of minimal effect, except around the opposition of Mars with the Sun, or the inferior conjunction of Venus with the Sun.

# ## CHAPTER XXII
### ON THE **PROSTHAPHÆRESIS** <note>An adjustment or "correction" added to or subtracted from a mean calculation to find a true value.</note>
_OF THE ANNUAL ORBIT; BY WHICH THE PLANET'S location is finally determined._

_On the formation of the Angle of Commutation._

<margin>Rule 83 found. RULE 93.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial O</image-desc> Write the true location of the Sun, found in the Ecliptic, below the location of the Planet; then subtract either the former from the latter, or the latter from the former—always the preceding from the following—so that the Angle of Commutation remains as the Anomaly. This should be marked with an Additive title in the first case—that is, the Anomaly of Commutation itself—
<margin>Rule 92 restored.</margin>
and in the second case, its complement to a full circle, marked with a Subtractive title.

_As in the Rudolphine Example:_ <note>original: *Genesi Rudolphî*; referring to the sample calculation used throughout the book to demonstrate the tables.</note> _since the location of the Sun is found at 4 signs, 22°, 5', it is subtracted from the eccentric locations of those planets reduced to the Ecliptic; such as from Jupiter’s 4 signs, 13°, 5', 8" and from Mercury’s 10, 2, 33, 58. Conversely, the preceding eccentric locations of the planets are subtracted from this location of the Sun: Saturn 10, 29, 32, 52; Mars 1, 11, 51, 44; Venus 2, 15, 22, 37. The resulting Angles of Commutation are: Saturn 5 signs, 5°, 49', 13" (or 155° 49' 13") subtractive. Jupiter 8, 3, 3, 21 (or 83° 3' 21") additive. Mars 2, 23, 3, 3 subtractive. Venus 1, 19, 59, 28 (or 177° 59' 28") subtractive. Mercury 5, 27, 11, 53 (or 177° 11' 53") additive._

<margin>In what sense the Angle of Commutation is spoken of. page 57.</margin>
Authors have called this the Anomaly of Commutation to distinguish it from the Anomaly of the Eccentric (which until now had three names: Mean Anomaly, Anomaly of the Eccentric, and Equated Anomaly). This is because the latter refers to something inherent to the planet, while the former comes from the outside, causing the planet to <term>change position</term> <note>Greek: *parallassein* (written in OCR as τσαραλλόειν), meaning to deviate or shift; the root of the word "parallax."</note> or commute its eccentric place, not from an internal cause, but an external one.

However, since we do not compute any "mean" Anomaly of Commutation in these Tables, being satisfied with the Zodiac whose arc would exceed the mean Sun, I have also abstained from the word ANOMALY, substituting the word ANGLE. This is not the Commutation or Parallax of the eccentric place itself, but its cause and Argument.

->**THE PROPORTION OF THE FORM**<-
->**OF THE INTERVALS, OR**<-
<margin>RULE 94.</margin>
->**the distances of the Earth and the Planet from the Sun.**<-

<margin>Rule 86.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial Y</image-desc> YOU HAVE LEARNED above how to extract the Logarithms of the intervals of the Sun and the Planet, each with its own sign, and also how to conform the Logarithm of the Interval. If the signs of both these Logarithms—both for the Sun and for the Planet—are the same, subtract the Logarithm of the Sun from the Logarithm of the Planet's current Interval; if they are different, add them. Thus the true proportion of the intervals is established. Here, be careful not to confuse these; you were ordered to seek the arguments for whether the Commutation is to be Added or Subtracted from the signs of the individual Logarithms.
<margin>Rule 91.</margin>
<column-break/>
Here, the rules for subtracting or adding the Logarithm of the Sun are not drawn from the results or the signs themselves, but from a comparison of the two signs. Consider every rule, and you will observe this: the more unequal the intervals become, the greater their proportion and its Logarithm will be.

_As in the Rudolphine Example, the Sun’s Logarithm, which was —1534, is taken away from the Logarithms of the Superior planets <note>Planets further from the Sun than Earth: Mars, Jupiter, Saturn.</note>; but since at Aphelion <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note> its sign is —: so the Proportion of the interval becomes 225784 for Saturn, 166081 for Jupiter, and 37148 for Mars. That same Logarithm of the Sun, —1534, is added to the Logarithms of the Inferior planets <note>Planets closer to the Sun than Earth: Venus, Mercury.</note>, not because they have a — sign, but because it is similar to the signs of the superior Logarithms. Thus the proportion of the interval becomes 34306 for Venus and 98153 for Mercury._

->**TO DEFINE THAT ANGLE OF COMMUTATION,**<-
->_in which the Prosthaphæresis of the Orbit occurs,_<-
->_(or even in the Inferiors, the Elongation from the Sun)_<-
->_through any given maximum proportional of the intervals._<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial B</image-desc> BY using the proportion of intervals as a Logarithm, extract the Arc from the Table <note>original: *Canon*; a set of mathematical tables.</note> that can occur in the Table, or in this proportion of intervals, if a Quadrant <note>90 degrees.</note> were given for this purpose. Add a Quadrant to this; then, that is the Angle of Commutation which happens at the Maximum Prosthaphæresis of each of the five Planets, according to the maximum proportion of intervals.
<margin>RULE 95.</margin>

But the absolute Maximum Prosthaphæresis of the Great or annual Orbit is caused by the minimum Proportion of all that can exist for any Planet: if indeed, through the course of many centuries, it happens at a time when the Planet and the Sun are arranged in such a way, and the Apsides <note>The points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the Sun.</note> are also positioned to receive the appropriate Angle of Commutation.

_Thus the minimum Logarithm for Venus at its Aphelion is — + 31588, and the Sun's maximum at Perigee <note>The point where the Earth/Sun are closest.</note> is +1816. Therefore the Proportion 29772 is the smallest of all, which gives a Maximum Prosthaphæresis or Elongation of all of nearly 137° 56' 44", unless the Aphelion of Venus separates itself from the Perigee of the Sun, so that at that very moment both the Sun falls into its own Perigee and Venus into its very own Aphelion._

RUDOLPHINE TABLES

<margin>By Rule 26.</margin>
This can also be done with the help of the Table alone. The first method has already been proposed in Chapter 10. For, by using the given Commutation and Ratio—the latter at the top of the Table and the former in the margin—the sought arc is extracted, being close to the one required, and then refined through the Logarithms of the Table.

<margin>By Rule 25.</margin>
But if you find the Table of the Angle <note>original: "Tabulæ Anguli"; a specific reference table in the back of the book used for solving triangles.</note> tedious because of its length, let this be the second method: go to Chapter 10. For what was there called the "second arc" is here the Angle of Commutation; of its parts, what was there called the **MINOR** is here the Prosthaphæresis of the Orbit for all five planets, or even the Elongation from the Sun for the inferior planets <note>Mercury and Venus.</note>; what was there called the **MAJOR** is here, for the superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, their Elongation from the Sun. Finally, the sides named there are here the two intervals: the distance of the Sun from the Earth and from the Planet. Since that rule was general, this is its specific and indeed primary use.

<margin>By Rule 95.</margin>
Therefore, for shortcuts to that general rule, follow these specific ones. First, using the ratio of the intervals, extract the greatest possible prosthaphæresis in Degrees and Minutes, and define its Angle of Commutation. The closer your given Angle of Commutation is to this, the closer the Prosthaphæresis of the Orbit will be to the maximum just extracted. But the more it is either smaller or larger than that, the smaller the initial Prosthaphæresis must be set on either side. Next, for Saturn, Jupiter, and Mercury, always set something less than the complement of the Angle of Commutation. For Mars and Venus, however, when the angle of commutation is above 146° for the former and above 135° for the latter, always set a bit more than the complement of the given Commutation to a semicircle <note>i.e., the difference between the angle and 180°.</note>, as a measure of the excesses. By observing these things, you will arrive much more quickly and easily at the most exact determination of the required Prosthaphæresis, even without the table of the angle. You have the rest in the said Chapter 9.

<margin>By what names it is called by different authors.</margin>
Copernicus and the Prutenic Tables commonly call this the Parallax or the Prosthaphæresis of the Great Orbit; and for the sake of brevity, simply the Prosthaphæresis of the Orbit. Tycho Brahe sometimes called it the Prosthaphæresis of the eccentric center—not entirely properly, but in the sense that the center of some concentric circle, in which the eccentric is carried, and its line of Apsides <note>The line connecting the points of a planet's orbit closest to and farthest from the Sun.</note>, circling with the Sun itself in the annual orbit, causes this Prosthaphæresis.

<margin>on his leaf 16.</margin>
Maginus, in his *Supplement to the Ephemerides*, calls it the Equation of the Orbit or of the Planet's Argument, following the Alfonsine Tables. Ptolemy called it the Prosthaphæresis of the Epicycle.
