Ambiguity still lurks here; for this <term>Prosthaphæresis <note>The angle at the planet between the Earth and the Sun.</note></term> is also an angle (to the sight) and is measured by the same Zodiac; this is itself the Commutation of the eccentric place, which in Greek is called <note>original: "Græcè"</note> **Parallax**; its title is transferred to it more properly. But one must become accustomed to calling it "Prosthaphæresis" by common usage; that other term alone, in the Latin voice, is the "Angle of Commutation," or "Commutation," representing the path toward it, as mentioned above.
<margin>By Rule 93.</margin>

### TO DEFINE THE ELONGATION of a planet from the Sun, both the temporary elongation of any planet and the Maximum Elongation of the Inferior planets <note>Mercury and Venus</note>, for any proportion of their intervals.

<margin>RULE 97.</margin>
This is accomplished by the same operation that arises from the previous rule. Only the most diligent observation is needed: that the Elongation from the Sun (either toward the following or preceding signs) in the **Superior Planets** (Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) is the remaining part of the Angle of Commutation after the refined Prosthaphæresis of the Orbit has been subtracted. However, in the **Inferior Planets** (Venus and Mercury), it is not the remainder, but the Prosthaphæresis itself which is subtracted. Hold the same for the maximum Elongation of the Inferiors; for that is the same as their Prosthaphæresis, being the greatest possible at any given turn.

To this Elongation of whichever group of planets, the label which the Angle of Commutation previously acquired must be transcribed.
<margin>By Rule 93.</margin>

### TO INVESTIGATE THE INTERVAL between the Earth and any one of the five planets; and its Logarithm, if required.

The intervals of the Sun, and of each of the planets, and likewise of the Sun and the Earth, are arranged in the third columns of the Tables of Equations, as said above: but how far any of these five is removed from the Earth at any time must finally be investigated, for certain specific, albeit rare, uses.

<margin>RULE 98.</margin>
Therefore, either there is no Angle of Commutation, or it is 180 degrees; and likewise the Elongation of the planet from the Sun is zero, or (for the Superior planets) 180 degrees: then the two intervals of the Sun—both from the Earth and from the planet—are either combined into one in the first case; or the smaller is subtracted from the larger in the second; and the remainder will be the interval between the Planet and the Earth.

As for example, if the interval of Mars (♂) is 166465, and the Sun (☉) and Earth is 101800, with the Commutation being 0°, given these you will be distant

<column-break/>

from the Earth by 268265; and if Jupiter (♃) and the Sun (☉) are distant by 138234, and the Sun and Earth are 101800, but the Commutation is 180° (even if this can hardly happen within some tens of thousands of years), Jupiter will be distant from the Earth by 36432. Likewise, if Venus (♀) is distant from the Sun (☉) by 72163 and the Sun from the Earth by 101800, with the Commutation being 0°, Venus will be away from the Earth by 173963. But with an interval for Venus of 72847, and for the Earth 98200, and an angle of Commutation of 180°, Venus will be distant from the Earth by 25353, a little more than a seventh of the former distance. Such can be the change in the distances of Venus from the Earth.

Or thirdly, if there is some angle of Commutation and some angle of Elongation less than two right angles <note>180 degrees</note>, then let two logarithms be added to one another: one being the positive logarithm of the Commutation, the other the remainder of the interval of the Sun and Planet, according to the condition of its sign; from the resulting sum with its sign, similarly subtract (always positively) the Logarithm of the Elongation, taking care which is called the Elongation in whichever group of planets: what remains, provided with the sign it has acquired, will be the Logarithm of the Interval between the Earth and the Planet. For Saturn and Jupiter, this is always negative <note>original: "privativus"</note>, because these are always higher from the Earth than the Sun is; for Mars, Venus, and Mercury, it is interchangeably negative or positive, because these three sometimes turn out higher from the Earth than the Sun itself, and sometimes march lower and nearer to the Earth.
<margin>According to Rule 97.</margin>

| | | |
|:---|:---|:---|
| If the Commutation is | Mars 53°.19' | Venus 84°.31' |
| Its Logarithm | 20080 | 460 |
| And the Logarithm of the Interval is | — 50950 | + 32969 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The logarithmic sum will be | — 20870 | + 33429 |
| And let the Elongation from the Sun be | 33°.51' | 33°.55' |
| Its Logarithm | 58537 | 58364 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subtracted logarithmically it leaves | — 79407 | — 24935 |
| The Logarithm of the Interval between Earth and | Mars | Venus. |

Since, therefore, in the first cases the interval is given without a Logarithm, and in the third the Logarithm without an interval, it remains that we teach how to assign each its companion. The Tables of Equations (six held as one) will mostly serve us; specifically, whenever either the interval of any planet is found among the intervals of one of them, or the Logarithm with its sign is found among the Logarithms of one of them, written below the intervals in those same cells with the sign placed at the front. For once the interval of one planet is found in the Table of any other, its Logarithm written below is found at the same time: and vice versa; notwithstanding that the Table exhibiting this or that belongs to another planet, and that the intervals of the Tables are computed from the Sun, while here they are from the Earth.

Thus in the examples, the interval of Mars and Earth 36432, found in the Table of Equations for Mercury, shows the Logarithm + 100974.

But what if either the interval offered to us is found in none of the six Tables among the Intervals, nor the Logarithm among the Logarithms of the Tables?

In this case, therefore, it will sometimes suffice to know even this: that the planet is distant from the Earth further than an inferior planet is distant from the Sun at its furthest; but closer than the nearest superior is from the same Sun at its closest. But if this coarse knowledge does not suffice, and there is need for more exactness: here let the **Heptacosias** <note>Kepler’s own logarithmic table of 700,000 parts, from the Greek for "seven hundred."</note> help us: and if indeed in—

# RUDOLPHINE TABLES

...interval is offered first, let it be converted into Seconds, Minutes, and whole Parts or Degrees <note>original: "Secunda, Prima & Partes seu Gradus integros"</note>, by writing down as many degrees as the sixth figure to the left contains units. The remaining five figures are multiplied by 6, so that when the last 4 are cut off from the product, the Minutes and so on emerge. For these Degrees, and Minutes, and if desired, even Seconds, in place of the Number by which the interval was expressed, when sought in the Sexagesimal Table <note>original: "Sexagesimaria"</note> of Negatives <note>original: "Privativorum"; referring to negative logarithms</note>, will show the sought Logarithm in that region with a negative sign. But if the sum of the Minutes stays below 60, with the Interval having fewer than 5 figures, seeking it in the left-hand Sexagesimal Table will show the Logarithm with a positive sign.

If, however, a given Logarithm must be assigned its own Interval, let it be sought in its own column; and according to whether its sign is positive or negative, let the selection be made from either the right or left sexagesimal table—there for Minutes and Seconds, and here also for Degrees. These, when converted into an absolute number (which is easily done since 1 degree equals 100,000, 6 minutes equals 10,000, 36 seconds equals 1,000, and 3 seconds 36 thirds equals 100), will produce the number of the sought Interval, comparable to that which determines the mean Interval of the Sun and Earth, namely 100,000.

<margin>
Supplement to the Chiliads <note>Kepler’s *Chilias Logarithmorum*</note>, Chapter 8, page 164 and following, especially precept 4, page 180.
</margin>
If I had the leisure to discuss this in detail <note>original: "διεξέρειν" (diexerein)</note>, I could, not without pleasure, refer a calculator curious about small details to my *Chiliads*; I could much more advisedly refer them to Napier’s Canon, and especially to that of Ursinus <note>Benjamin Ursinus, a mathematician who published logarithmic tables</note> explained to ten seconds. But Cato <note>The Roman writer Cato the Elder</note> teaches such a way of country living that nothing is served to a guest that was bought elsewhere, which the farm itself did not produce.

We shall explain all this with the above examples. The Interval of Mars from the Earth is 268,265; since this is worth 2° 40' 57'', its Logarithm will be about –98,500. The distance of Venus from the Earth is 173,963; since this is worth roughly 1° 44' 24'', it will have a Logarithm of about –55,340. And the other distance <note>original: "discessio"; referring to the distance from the observer</note> of Venus from the Earth, 25,353, since it is worth a little less than 15' 13'', will obtain a Logarithm of +137,200.

Conversely, a Logarithm of the distance of Mars from the Earth of –79,407 offers from the Negative Sexagesimal Table roughly 2° 12' 40'', which is worth roughly 221,100 for the Interval of Mars and Earth. And a –24,935 Logarithm for the Interval of Venus and Earth offers from the Negative Sexagesimal Table roughly 1° 17' 1'', which is worth about 128,600. Thus, here Mars is a little less than twice as high as Venus, and higher than the Sun, whose height is worth 100,000.

### ->TO INVESTIGATE THE LATITUDE of a Planet.<-

<margin>
RULE 99.
Tables, page 22.
</margin>
IF the angles of Commutation and Elongation are moderate: to the Mesologarithm <note>A logarithmic value used in spherical trigonometry</note> of the Inclination, add the Logarithm of the Elongation, and from the sum subtract the Logarithm of the Commutation; thus there will remain a Mesologarithm which, from its own Table, will show the Latitude in the header and margin. This can often also be obtained through the areas of the latitude tables, if the Mesologarithm is found in the Table of any Planet.

If, however, there is either no angle of Commutation, or it extends to two right angles or 180°—so that the Elongation also vanishes in the former case for all, and in the latter case for the Superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, Saturn</note> it extends to 180°, and for the Inferior planets it vanishes—or if

<column-break/>

the angles even approach these limits, where Logarithms are less manageable due to the inequality of the increments: the complement of the Inclination to a Semicircle must be used instead of the Commutation, and through it, the Elongation from the Sun should be sought as if it were a search, so that once this is subtracted from the semicircle, the sought latitude remains.

But if anyone prefers to use the standard doctrine of Triangles without Logarithms: they must generally use the Sines of the angles of Commutation and Elongation; and the former, increased by 5 zeros, must be divided by the latter; the quotient is to be multiplied by the Tangent of the Complement of the Inclination so that, after discarding 5 zeros from the product, the Tangent of the Complement of the Latitude remains.

If, however, there is no angle of Commutation, or it is equal to two right angles, then the intervals of the Planet from the Sun and from the Earth must be used: and first, the Secant of the Complement of the Inclination multiplied by the interval of the Sun and Earth, must be divided by the Interval of the Sun and Planet; the quotient in the first case is to be added to the Tangent of the Complement of the Inclination, and in the second case subtracted; then this Sum or Remainder must divide the square of the radius, and the Tangent of the latitude itself is produced. Examples will follow immediately.

<margin>9.</margin>

However, for the Latitude, the same region or label remains which was <margin>By Precept 90.</margin> taken above with the Mesologarithm of Inclination.

Thus the latitude of both planets is found to be exactly the same. But in longitude at the 5th equal hour at Uraniborg <note>Tycho Brahe's famous observatory on Hven</note>, we found Venus to be ahead of Mars, and toward the 6th hour closer to it. For at Tübingen the difference of the meridian is 12 minutes, so that according to this calculation it altogether ought to have covered Mars, but later.

Nor is such a small discrepancy an indication of an erroneous calculation; rather, it seems to be confirmed by the observer. For he says that he noticed a difference in colors: ruddy in Mars and golden in Venus, and from this a conjecture could be taken that Mars was elevated further from the center of the Earth than Venus. Since the color of Venus almost entirely deleted the ruddy color of Mars, so that he could scarcely see a small part of it shining out from one side. Yet if the conjunction had been entirely central to the sight, no trace of the ruddy color could have remained from Mars; for the diameter of the body of Mars was altogether smaller (at this height almost twice as great as that of Venus, as you see in precept 98).

No account must be taken of parallax here. For Venus was distant from the center of the earth further than the Sun, and thus from the angle of Commutation, as was clear in the same precept 98. The Sun, however, changes its position on the horizon itself by nothing more than one minute of a degree.

To the calculation of the positions of the Sun and the two planets, only so many steps <note>original: "apicibus"; literally "peaks" or "points," referring to the amount of calculation required</note>—and not one more—are needed (even counting those for whose sake the calculations of other tables write innumerable figures on palimpsests <note>reused manuscripts</note>).

# INSTRUCTION ON SHORTENING THIS
# Calculation.

<margin>R</margin> The reduction of the planet's eccentric position and the "shortening" <note>original: *curtatio*; this refers to projecting the planet's distance onto the flat plane of the Earth's orbit</note> of the interval in steps 4, 5, and 6 are mostly omitted; the instruction is completed through the eccentric position of the orbit itself, and through the interval found in the Table and its Logarithm.

->Examples.<-

As in the previous examples, it should be understood that, as before, the *reduction and shortening would not be written out in the fourth step*, and in the fifth, the eccentric position of the orbit itself, 26° 2' 50'', would be subtracted to leave the angle of commutation <note>The angle between the Sun and the Earth as seen from the planet</note>. Likewise, in the sixth step, the Logarithm of the interval itself — 5950 — would be added to the Logarithm of the Sun's interval + 460, and this proportion is elicited for the calculation. The Prosthaphæresis <note>The correction added or subtracted to the mean motion to find the true position</note> of the orbit is not much different than before: 19° 27' 30''.

->In the same way, the eccentric position of Venus in its orbit, 24° 53' 56'' <unclear>Sun</unclear> subtracted from the true position of the Sun, leaves a commutation of 84° 27' 51''. And the Logarithm of the interval of Venus + 32508, neglecting the shortening, decreased by the Logarithm of the Sun's interval + 460, results in the proportion 32508. This, with the commutation of the orbit, establishes the approximate Prosthaphæresis as 33° 54' 46''.<-

Although it usually happens this way, in the case of Mars near its opposition with the Sun, and in the case of retrograde Venus near its conjunction with the Sun, the Reduction and Shortening must not be neglected.

### ANOTHER METHOD, WITHOUT LOG-
### ARITHMS, FOR COMPUTING
<margin>PRECEPT 101.</margin> the positions of the five planets from the same Tables: so that the ease of the previous instruction may be clear by a comparison of each individual part.

Then, while the other parts of the instruction remain, in the second part, the interval of the planet and the Sun is extracted (as inscribed above) in its own cell (omitting the Logarithm), and similarly the interval of the Sun and the <sig>4.</sig> Earth. In the fourth part, the extracted shortening is written below the interval of the planet and the Sun; and in place of the Mesologarithm of Inclination, the Inclination itself is extracted. With this, the Tangent of its complement is written out from the Table of Sines, to be saved for calculating the latitude. In the fifth part, half of the angle of commutation must be established, and its Tangent extracted. The sine of the whole angle of commutation (omitting the Logarithm) is to be written out and saved for the latitude. In the sixth part, the shortening is to be multiplied by the interval of the planet and the Sun, and the result, with the last five digits cut off, is to be subtracted from the interval. To this shortened
<column-break/>
interval, the interval of the Sun and Earth is to be placed beneath; first subtract it, then add the intervals into one sum. Since from the interval that product (extended by five zeros) is the quotient, the number is to be multiplied by the tangent of that half; once shortened by cutting off five digits, as with the tangent, the arc is to be extracted. In the upper orbit of the planet, this arc, added to half of the Commutation and taken from the Sun's position, or subtracted, establishes or leaves the Elongation of the planet from the Sun. Divide the sine of the commutation (extended by five zeros, omitting the Logarithm) by the sine of this Elongation. Let the quotient be placed under the Tangent of the complement of the orbit's Inclination. Then, in the middle interval of the planet and Sun, in the first part of the fifth member (if indeed the position of the Sun was subtracted), the longitude of the Sun's position must be added, and the sum of a whole circle rejected if it exceeds it. In the second case, the same Elongation must be subtracted from the longitude of the Sun's position, after first adding a circle if necessary: thus you will have the planet's true position from the equinox, or its place in the Ecliptic. In the ninth part, the Tangent of the complement of the Inclination is to be multiplied by the Quotient to save for the latitude: which, being added, gives the complement of the true latitude of the planet.

This method can also be completed using <term>Mesologarithms</term> <note>A specific type of logarithm Kepler used for trigonometric calculations</note>. However, I have not made the full table of these a part of these current Tables; their use creates complicated requirements for beginners <note>original: *Tyronibus*</note> and they are prone to lapses of memory.

<column-break/>

<margin>Instruction 95.</margin>
Whether a planet is moving out from the Sun's rays (emersion) or hiding beneath them (occultation) is learned as follows. Through what has been handed down so far, let the Angle of Commutation for one of the <term>Inferior Planets</term> <note>Mercury or Venus, whose orbits are inside Earth's</note> be formed, by which the Maximum Prosthaphæresis is made—which in the Inferior planets is also the maximum Elongation. If the Angle of Commutation for the given time (with the Sun preceding) is found to be smaller, the planet has not yet reached the maximum limit of its evening elongation, but is emerging more and more each evening from the Sun's rays, or is tending toward emersion. If the angle is larger, those conditions have already passed, and the Inferior planet is again approaching the Sun, soon to go under the Sun's rays in the evening. The opposite is true when the Sun follows. For then, if the temporary Angle of Commutation is larger than the Commutation of maximum Elongation, the Inferior planet proceeds to the furthest limits of these conditions, as if emerged in the morning, or emerging more and more from the Sun's rays; if it is smaller, it has passed them and returns to the Sun, to be hidden deeper in its morning disappearance.

Take Venus as an example. Its proportion of intervals in the nearby model was 32586. The arc for this is taken as 46° 13'. Add 90, and the angle 136° 13' is composed; through this, the Elongation would be 46° 13'. But because its angle of commutation at the proposed time is 84° 31', which is much smaller, and the Sun in Libra precedes Venus, the maximum Elongation has not yet been reached, and Venus is increasing its emergence from the Sun's rays.

<margin>
On the Elongations of the Superior planets from the Sun.
And on Occultations and Emersions.
Paradoxes in Mars.
</margin>
For the <term>Superior Planets</term> <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, whose orbits are outside Earth's</note>, the use of maximum Elongation is less obvious. They are hidden by the Sun overtaking them, just like the Fixed Stars—that is, only in the evening; and they emerge only in the morning, as the Sun moves further away from them. In this place, however, something marvelous happens to Mars: because of the slowness of its departure (since the planet follows the Sun with long strides), both might enter signs of different ascensions, and thus the planet, after emerging, may seem to hide itself again under the rays. But this happens to it from the accidental position of the Sphere; it is not a true occultation, since the planet then appears more clearly in the other Hemisphere of the Earth. It depends neither on the Prosthaphæresis nor on the maximum Elongation.

<margin>The Acronychal rising and setting of Superior planets.</margin>
The maximum Elongation of the Superior planets extends up to 180°, and at that time provides these planets with other types of risings and settings, namely <term>Acronychal</term> <note>Rising at sunset or setting at sunrise</note>—that is, an evening rising and a morning setting on the same night. This turns them from "Oriental" (rising during the night) to "Occidental" (setting during the night). For first the Superior planets are Oriental and visible before sunrise; later they are Acronychal for a single night, and then Occidental and visible after sunset. However, to track the exact moments of Emersions and Occultations, the latitude must also be applied; therefore, a specific instruction on those will follow below.

# RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS
<margin>Harmony of the World, Book 5, chapters 1 and 2, pages 187, 188. Epitome [of Copernican Astronomy], Book 6, page 901 and following.</margin>
...of my *Harmony of the World*: yet in Astronomy itself it is very necessary for the proper State of this science.

<margin>Difficulty of the Problem</margin>
At first glance, it seems to be one way, but the reality is somewhat different. Regarding the problem of motions: for example, if the daily motion of Mars were 59 minutes and 8 seconds. If each of these were similar to 60 minutes: then, by performing the subtraction of the Logarithms of the larger arc from the Logarithm of the smaller, 1454 from 64594, the work might seem finished. For 63140 is the proposed Logarithm; furthermore, in the eccentric orbit of the Sun, it would be equal to one degree in the eccentric orbit of Mars. However, because these mean motions must be compared to each other, and because they truly or properly vary at each point in the mean longitude of their eccentric orbit—being sometimes greater and sometimes smaller than the Mean Motion—and even the daily arcs of the eccentric orbit differ from the apparent daily arcs (specifically because these daily arcs are sometimes larger and sometimes smaller than they truly are), this whole business becomes quite intricate.

<margin>Elements of this Proportion</margin>
It must be known, therefore, that the Proportion of the arcs is composed of four elements. 1. From the proportion of the size of the Orbits or of whole degrees. 2. From the proportion of the numbers by which the mean daily motions are expressed. 3. & 4. From the proportions of the two arcs of time to their mean values. Truly, of these four elements, two are constant and are combined with little effort into one, serving for all days of the entire periods: so that the matter finally returns to three elements. For the proportion of the mean daily Numbers is the inverse proportion of the periods; because the degree is the maximum.

<margin>See Harmony of the World Book 5, chapter 5, and Epitome of Astronomy Book 4, page 501.</margin>
But this is the <term>sesquialterate proportion</term> <note>A 3:2 ratio, referring to Kepler’s Third Law where the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the distance</note> of the Orbits, or of the whole degrees, of which the degree is the maximum. Indeed, the proportion is of magnitude. To establish the true proportion, therefore, not only the numbers but also the proportion of the degrees in the composition must take two-thirds from the Proportion of the periods, as its inverse. Two-thirds, however, subtracted from three-thirds, leave one-third, or half of the proportion of the degrees in the different Eccentrics.

From these foundations, this Precept is born.

<margin>PRECEPT 103</margin>
FIRST, from the Table of Equations of the Planet whose daily eccentric arc is to be compared with the Solar daily arc, find the row for the <term>Eccentric Anomaly</term> <note>The angle used to define the position of a planet along its elliptical orbit</note> of 90°. From the column for the Mean Interval, take the Logarithm of the mean interval and divide it in half; for the half-sum thus established commonly indicates the proportion of the mean daily arcs of the Sun and the Planet.

Next, with the known Anomalies of the Planet and the Sun—and if they are in the [second] semicircle,
<column-break/>
greater than 180°, take their complements to the full circle—enter the Table of Equations. If the <term>equated anomaly</term> <note>The corrected position of the planet after accounting for its elliptical path</note> and the second equated anomaly are found in the first column of the Means, observe which two values most closely surround the known value: subtract the upper from the lower, and the Logarithm of the remainder will be taken from the <term>Heptacosias</term> <note>Kepler's specific table of 700 logarithms used for astronomical calculations</note>. This will express the proportion of the temporary arc to the mean arc.

In the Table of Equations, this difference of the cells of the equated Anomalies is placed between them.

I judge that this subtraction of one from the other and the extraction from the Heptacosias is necessary only for Mars and Mercury. For in the other four planets, and even in these two, if one does not seek the most subtle accuracy, the found cell will suffice, so that the Logarithm of the space between the columns will be the same as the Logarithm taken the first way, which is nearly the same as the Logarithm of the interval.

You now have three "halves" from which the correct sought proportion is composed. For if the Anomaly of the Planet being compared is found above the mean Longitude of the Eccentric, toward the upper <term>apsis</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion; the aphelion</note>, either in the first semicircle or the lower of the compared values, the half-sum should be added; but if it is in the other part, the halves must be subtracted from that common half-sum: thus the sought proportion of the arcs will remain.

Let whoever has enough intelligence use the whole values instead of halves, and having performed either the additions or subtractions, let the result finally be divided in half: the matter will return to the same result.

### EXAMPLE FOR ONE OF THE SUPERIOR PLANETS.

<note>The following is a calculation for the planet Mars</note>

Let the equated Anomaly of Mars (♂), or its complement to the circle, be 169° 32'. For the Sun, 53° 12'.
The proportion of the daily eccentric arcs is sought.
First, in the Table of Equations for Mars, at the row for the Eccentric Anomaly of 90° and the Mean 95° 18' 30", I find the Logarithm 421050, whose half is 21050.
Next, I find the equated 169° 32' in the Table of Mars between 169° 1' 52" and 170° 7' 37": these correspond to the mean values 170° 55' 20" and 171° 49' 51".
I subtract the former from the latter; there remains 54' 31", the Logarithm of which from the Heptacosias is 9584.
And because Mars is superior to the Sun, but its Anomaly was found to be 9584, I subtract 9584 from 21050; there remains [the value] below the Eccentric 90°.
Thirdly, I find the equated [anomaly] of the Sun between 53° 10' and 54° 9' 32".
To these correspond the mean values 54° 3' 0" and 55° 50' 41".
The difference of these is 60' 38", which has a <term>Logistic Logarithm</term> <note>A type of logarithm used specifically for calculations involving degrees, minutes, and seconds</note> of 1061.
The Sun, however, is here inferior to Mars, and its Eccentric Anomaly was found above 90°.

## ANOTHER EXAMPLE FOR ONE OF THE INFERIOR PLANETS.

Let the equated Anomaly of Mercury be 0° 0' 0'' 0'''. Therefore, in the Table of Equations for Mercury, across from the Eccentric Anomaly of 90°, or the Mean Anomaly of 102° 1' 57'', I find the Logarithm 94660, whose half is 47330. Next, the Anomaly of the Sun is 0° 0', which is found here in the first cell; it differs from the nearest Mean cell by 1° 12' 35'', the Logarithm of which from the *Heptacosias* <note>Kepler’s own table of 700 logarithms</note> is 19045. And because Mercury is one of the Inferior planets <note>planets closer to the Sun than Earth</note>, and its Anomaly is given as 0° 0' above the Eccentric Anomaly of 90 degrees, I therefore subtract 19045 from 47330, and 28285 remains. Thirdly, the mean Anomaly of the Sun at 0° 0' differs from the nearest cell by 1° 1' 5'', the Logarithm of which is 1792 (half of the Logarithm in the inner column would be 1785, and such is also the Logarithm of the Interval). But indeed, this is the "superior" one with respect to Mercury, and its Anomaly was found above the Eccentric Anomaly of 90°. Therefore, add this 1792 to 28285, and 30077 is produced; this is the sought proportion of the arcs.

## TO ASSIGN TO ANY ANOMALY OF A PLANET ITS ANGLES OF COMMUTATION AND THE PROSTHAPHAERESIS <term>Prosthaphaeresis: a correction factor added or subtracted to find the true position from the mean position</term> OF THE ORBIT, OR IN THE INFERIOR PLANETS, THE ELONGATION AT WHICH IT BECOMES STATIONARY.

In this problem, the geometer Apollonius of Perga once labored, and he said what geometers ought to do so that they might assist astronomers here: but he did not do himself what he ordered others to do, nor if he had done it and solved the problem, would he have satisfied astronomers by that deed. For he, out of the many causes that introduce variety into the limits of the Stations, assumed only a few; he left most untouched.

<margin>PRECEPT 104.</margin>
We, so that we may emulate the sharpness of Apollonius as much as is permitted, proceeding very closely to geometric exactness <note>original Greek: ἀκριβείας</note>, shall act as follows.

<margin>By precept 94.</margin>
In the beginning, the proportion of the Intervals or momentary distances must be established, both of the Sun from the Planet (the "curtate" or shortened interval) and from the Earth.

<margin>By precept 103.</margin>
Secondly, the proportion of the daily arcs of the Eccentric must also be established; indeed, the prescribed Anomaly carries with it the daily arc of the Eccentric of the planet; but for the Anomaly of the Sun, which represents its

<column-break/>

daily arc of the Eccentric, it is necessary to guess from afar roughly how much it will be in order to form the Angle of Commutation <note>the angle at the planet formed by the lines to the Sun and Earth</note>; concerning the assistance of this guess by the little Table, I shall speak later.

Thirdly, it is necessary to suppose that the rays from the Sun to the Planet and the Earth, along with the chords of their daily Eccentric Arcs, form angles outward greater than a right angle by the amount of their half-daily arcs; although this is not exactly true, except at the Apsides <note>the points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center</note>.

<margin>What a Station is</margin>
With these things prepared and assumed, since the astronomical definition of a Station is this: namely, when the line of Vision of the Planet, after exactly one day, falls upon the same point of the Zodiac in longitude as it had fallen upon the day before: whether that happens through the identity of a single line of sight, as with Tycho, or through the parallelism of two lines, as with Copernicus: therefore, that figure from Chapter 27 will be formed for us.

<margin>Precept, leaf 24.</margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing construction of angles for planetary stations. It depicts a central point S (Sun) with radiating lines to points O (Earth) and A (Planet). An arc represents the orbit. Points A, D, B, C, E, F are used to define segments and parallel lines for calculating commutation angles.</image-desc>

In this figure, S represents the Sun, O the Earth, and A one of the Superior planets—or conversely, A the Earth and O one of the Inferior planets. AD is the daily arc of the eccentric of the superior planet, and OP is the larger arc of the inferior; and they are intercepted between the parallel lines of sight OA and PC. Therefore, the proportion of AS to SO is given;

<margin>By precept 94 and Precept 101.</margin>
but the proportion of AD to OP was found to be smaller than the other. Therefore, having drawn from A the lines AE parallel to SO itself, and AB parallel to OP itself, as AS is to SO, so will CA be to AE (which is equal to OI itself), and thus their proportion is known. So also AB is equal to OP itself: therefore, the proportion of DA to AB is known. Finally, because triangles ASD and OSP are assumed to be isosceles, and the angle OSP is greater than ASD; therefore, the angle SOP is smaller than SAD; thus CAD is greater than IOP or EAB: and each is greater than a right angle by the quantity of the half-daily arcs.

Since, therefore, the Angle of Commutation is sought, through which the Planet becomes Stationary; its complement to two right angles is indeed the angle ASO, or CAE. Therefore, from the given data, let the angle CAE be sought, with a beginning made from the position of ACB itself as known: and by proceeding through the correction of the position, as you were taught above.

<margin>Precept 27.</margin>
We shall use examples of the preceding precept. In that example, the Eccentric Anomaly of Mars is given, and that of the Sun is finally sought; with these given, the proportions CA to AE and DA to AB will be known. Since, therefore, the Anomaly of the Sun was assumed to be 53° 12'; and there is no great error even through a large mistake in this assumption: therefore, let the same Anomaly of the Sun be valid here as well. The Logarithm of its Interval from the Earth is 1092, and the Logarithm of the curtate Interval of Mars is 32532; thus the momentary proportion of the Intervals is 31428. Since, therefore, in this Example Mars is conceived at A; this will be...

### HOW TO RECOGNIZE WHETHER A PLANET IS *direct, stationary, or retrograde?*

<margin>Precept 107.</margin> <margin>Through precept 93.</margin> <margin>Through precept 94.</margin> <margin>Through precept 103.</margin> <margin>Through precept 104.</margin> For any proposed time, find the Angle of Commutation of the planet and the proportion of the intervals of the Earth and Sun to those of the same planet and Sun (and thus, if not seen, the Table of Stations, and even their daily arcs). Then investigate the angle of Commutation corresponding to this proportion of intervals which would produce a Station. If, therefore, that temporary angle of Commutation is smaller than this stationary one, the planet is direct; if the planet is in its first conjunction from the opposite, or from the opposite to the conjunction; in the second case, if it is greater, the planet is retrograde. In the inferior planets, the distinction is the opposite: they are "Evening stars" when they reach their first station, and "Morning stars" when they reach their second.

### WHETHER THE PLANET'S LATITUDE WILL BE GREATER OR SMALLER THAN THE INCLINATION.

<margin>Precept 108.</margin> <margin>Precept 99 & 100.</margin> <margin>Formed by Precept 97.</margin> From the Guide for computing the positions and latitudes of the planets, these rules follow: In Saturn <note>original: ♄</note>, Jupiter <note>original: ♃</note>, and Mars <note>original: ♂</note>, whenever the Angle of Elongation <note>The angular separation between the Sun and the planet as seen from Earth.</note> is half of the Angle of Commutation; in others, the Angle of Elongation combined with the angle of Commutation fills two right angles [180 degrees], the Latitude is equal to the Inclination. Whenever this Elongation Angle is smaller, the Latitude is smaller than the inclination; whenever it is greater, the latitude is also greater. In Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> and Venus <note>original: ♀</note>, the Latitude is always smaller than the inclination.

### WHETHER A PLANET'S LATITUDE INCREASES, DECREASES, OR REMAINS STEADY?

<margin>Precept 109.</margin> LATITUDE remains the same when the distances of the Planet and Earth calculated for the following days are in an inverse proportion of the Inclinations—that is, when the Logarithm of the Inclination changes by the same amount that the "song" <note>Kepler often used musical terms like "Melos" (song) to describe the harmonic variations in planetary speeds or angles.</note> of commutation increases or decreases.
In Saturn, the peak of maximum Latitude coincides closely with its oppositions; it must sometimes recede further from the conjunctions of the Sun. And in Mercury, the consistency of Latitude is always at the limit of maximum Inclination.
In Mars and Venus, this matter has great variety. Indeed, the rule of the Superior planets applies itself here; but also that of the Inferior ones, specifically Mercury: the former because of the smallness of the Inclination and ease of Commutation; the latter because of the magnitude of the Inclination and a slightly shorter Commutation. However these things may be, in both planets nothing...

### EXAMPLE.

In the year 1625, on the 22nd of August at noon, the complement to the circle of the Anomaly of Mars is found to be 169º 32'. The Angle of Commutation of Mars is 169º 19'. The Logarithm of the shortened interval is -32475, and the Sun's Anomaly is 53º 8'. The Logarithm of the Sun's interval is -1054. Thus the proportion is established...

->RULES OF RUDOLPHUS<-

<margin>Rules 99 & 100.</margin>Nevertheless, concerning the Stations and Retrogradation <note>Retrogradation is the apparent backwards motion of a planet in the sky.</note>, their latitudes possess a great deal of variety: so much so that they cannot be prescribed by simple rules. The only exception is this: that the calculation of their motion should be deduced every two days, given by interpolating the members of the general rule—how the Logarithms are changed, and whether the Table of Angles can assist us in the formation of the latter **Prosthaphaeresis** <note>original: "Prosthaphaerefeos." A technical term for the correction added or subtracted to a planet's mean motion to find its true position.</note>. 
<margin>Tables, page 20</margin> Certainly, this variety is so great that while in Saturn and Jupiter the maximum latitude occurs near the day of opposition, it can actually differ by 20, 30, or 40 days before or after the true opposition.

### EXAMPLE.

In the year 1625, on August <gloss>18</gloss> at Noon, the position of the Sun was 5° 2' 20" in Scorpio, and the Longitude of the Interval was — 902. The position of Mars was 5° 9' in Virgo, Retrograde. The **Logarithm** <note>Kepler's logarithms were a specific mathematical tool he developed to simplify the complex multiplications required for orbital mechanics.</note> of the adjusted interval was — 33599. Thus, the proportion of the intervals was 31697. And the latitude of Mars was 5° 27½' South, at a distance of 63° 18' from the Node <note>The "Node" is the point where a planet's orbit crosses the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note> in Aries. And because Mars is approaching the Node, the Inclination therefore decreases, and its **Mesologarithm** <note>A secondary logarithmic value used in Kepler's calculations of planetary positions.</note> increases: the measure of increase in one degree of Eccentric motion toward the Node at 3° 1' is 875. But the daily motion of Mars is not one degree, but 31' 27", and in the Mean Anomaly of 168° 12', the index of the columns in the Table of Angles corresponds to approximately 3° 37½', which provides a measure of 875 for the increase of the Mesologarithm. The Logarithm of the Angle of Commutation <note>The angle between the Sun and the planet as seen from Earth.</note> is more than 193000, and by the proportion of 30000 in the Table of Angles, it corresponds to 4 degrees 4'—roughly a double decrease in the Prosthaphaeresis. Indeed, the Commutation was 171° 39' with a Logarithm of 120900; the Prosthaphaeresis truly was 20° 43', and with a Logarithm of 72190, the difference between them is 650. Yet earlier, on the 28th and 29th of August, the maximum Southern latitude occurred, even though there was no opposition with the Sun (as had been described), nor was the Planet properly at its limit, being in its Eccentric motion at 13° 42' Leo, 27 degrees beyond the Southern limit. However, Mars was near its Station; therefore, in the Table of Angles, between the angles of the Latitude Table and the Elongation, it is 1° 39'. Thus, the latitude is so large—namely 5° 27½'—because of its proximity to the Earth, even though the Inclination is only 1° 39'.

### TO INVESTIGATE THE APPARENT SEMIDIAMETERS OF THE PLANETS.

<margin>Rule 110.</margin><insert>T</insert>his is a slippery matter. For to natural sight, these bright bodies always appear with an optical dilation of light; however, when a dioptric instrument <note>A refracting telescope.</note> is employed, they are recognized (by applying reasoning) to be many times smaller. Saturn is never larger than approximately 30" seconds. I will therefore teach how to compute what appears
<column-break/>
through the **Telescope** <note>original: "Telescopium." Kepler was one of the first to provide a mathematical foundation for how telescopes work.</note>. For that optical enlargement follows no set rule.

From the Logarithm of the distance of the Planet (not from the Sun, but) from the Earth, subtract the coefficient from the Logarithm of the Sun’s furthest distance, which
<margin>Found in Rule 90.</margin>is left as the sought Logarithm; this shows, in the sexagesimal [base-60] scale, the minutes, which if they are reduced to a third sexagesimal part, will form the sought apparent Semidiameter of the planet.

### EXAMPLES.

<insert>L</insert>et the Elongation of Venus from the Sun be 180°, and that be 30° 45'. With an Interval of — 72847, and it being in Perigee <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note>, the Logarithm of the Interval of Venus is — 137200.
<margin>Tables, page 68</margin> This is for Venus at its Aphelion <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Sun.</note>.
<insert>L</insert>et the distance of the Sun and Venus be + 10529 from the right sexagesimal from the third part; subtract the Interval of Venus and Earth — 126671. This shows 3° 33' in the right sexagesimal. Therefore, the apparent Semidiameter of Venus is in appearance: since Venus, facing Earth, is seen with the full face of the Moon.

So, under the Interval of Mars at Aphelion, or 
<margin>Tables, page 62</margin> situated at Anomaly 0° 0', the Logarithm is placed as — 50962; from its third part — 16987, subtract the Logarithm of the Interval of Mars and Earth, — 117917. Again, by the coefficient proportion from the right sexagesimal, it is 3° 3' 15". Therefore, the Semidiameter of Mars is in a ninth proportion to the Earth, as much as the Logarithm or ratio would show in the quantity of a sexagesimal part, namely 3" 15".

Moreover, I place in the foundations of this rule the physical structure <note>original: "Anatomiam." Kepler uses "anatomy" here to mean the structural or physical makeup.</note> of all the planets: that their bodies 
<margin>Book IV, page 48.</margin>are in proportion to their distances from the Sun; therefore, the diameters are in a sub-triple judgment, which shows a more probable proportion.

# TABLES OF RUDOLPHUS

between the extremes, having no account for the latitudes of the Planets; and since that Table was adapted to only a single Climate <note>In historical astronomy, a "climate" refers to a specific belt of latitude on Earth.</note>, and only to the very beginnings of the Zodiac signs (which **Reinhold** <note>Erasmus Reinhold (1511–1553), whose *Prutenic Tables* were the standard before Kepler's.</note> does not deny, and indeed he promised he would soon publish more extensive Tables), I did not judge that I should publish that table myself, nor multiply it into many tables. <margin>For the sake of variety.</margin> For to what good would I do so? Since these Ptolemaic limits <note>original: "metae Ptolemaïcae." These are the specific distances from the Sun required for a planet to become visible.</note> cannot be the same across all Climates? For the higher the Pole is <note>meaning the further north one is in latitude</note>, the greater the rising amplitude becomes, and the further apart the Sun and the emerging or disappearing Planet stand from each other along the Horizon. But the further a Planet moves to the side from the point of the Horizon illuminated by the Sun's brightness, the more easily it comes into view by its own light. This same objection holds true for the fixed stars of various declinations, even under the same Climate.

Especially in the Inferior planets, **Venus** and **Mercury**, a far smaller depth of the Sun below the horizon is required for them to be hidden in the evening or appear in the morning: because at those times they occupy parts of their Orbs closer to the Earth, and they appear larger than if they were hidden in the morning or emerged in the evening. Thus, Venus frequently shines out even during the day, when the Sun is not submerged deep below the Horizon, but is elevated above it.

However, setting aside these Objections and assuming **Ptolemy's** tradition to be true, I have now compensated for these omitted Tables by using the Table <margin>Tables, fol. 37 and following.</margin> of the Angle of the Orient, the use of which is necessary in the present instruction. <margin>INSTRUCTION III.</margin> First, through the position of the Longitude and Latitude of the Star or Planet, <margin>By instruction 47.</margin> seek the point of the Ecliptic rising with it. Or, if the question concerns the disappearance of the slower planets or the emergence of the faster ones, seek the co-rising point through the opposite longitude and opposite latitude; the point opposite to this will be the point where the Star sets with the Sun. Next, take from the Tables of each constellation the solar depth corresponding to the appearance or disappearance of each Planet: <margin>By instruction 48.</margin> by which you shall compute the arc of the Ecliptic between the Sun and the Horizon. Add this arc to the point of the Ecliptic that rises with the star to find its morning appearance or disappearance; subtract it from the co-setting point for its evening disappearance or appearance. Thus the "limit" of the Sun will be established; if the Sun occupies that position, the star either begins or ceases to appear. But if the Sun is outside these limits, to discern whether the condition has passed or is yet to come, one must return to the daily motions of the Sun and the planet. For if the daily motion of the Sun toward the following signs is greater (as in comparison to the Fixed Stars, which lack daily motion, and always for the Superior Planets; but for the Inferiors, from their first maximum elongation through the whole time of retrogradation until the second), then this rule applies: When the Sun is before the limit of emergence or disappearance, the morning emergence of a hidden body, or the evening disappearance of a visible one, will eventually follow. When it is past the limit, the star has already emerged in the morning which had been hidden, or has already been concealed in the evening under the Sun's rays which was previously seen before sunset. But if the daily motion of the Planet is greater than the Solar motion (which always happens with the Moon, and in Venus and Mercury from the second maximum elongation

<column-break/>

until the first), then when the Sun is before the limit, the star has already emerged in the evening which was previously hidden, or is already concealed in the morning which previously appeared. But if the Sun is beyond the limit, the star is still hidden and will finally emerge in the evening, or if still appearing in the morning, it will be concealed in the following days; it will surely push its limits forward so that they eventually overtake the Sun.

## CHAPTER XXV.

->CONCERNING THE MOON SEPARATELY,<-
->AND FIRST CONCERNING THE<-
->UNBOUND ANOMALY.<-

I stated above that the Moon—with respect to those places on its Eccentric <note>An "eccentric" is an off-center circular path used to model orbits.</note> which it usually occupies during Syzygies, that is, in Conjunctions and Oppositions with the Sun—is entirely similar to the other Planets. So that this may be more clearly evident, and so that the rest of the teaching on the motions of the Moon may be more clearly explained, the Calculator must be warned at the outset that two types of Anomalies <note>An "anomaly" is a technical term for the angle used to track a planet's position along its path.</note> are found in the Moon, not unlike those in the five planets; however, they are not distinguished from one another by the same names as in the others. The reason is this: in the five planets, only the first Anomaly truly belongs to the motions of each through the Eccentric; the second comes to them entirely from the outside. That is, it is a mere accident of perspective according to **Copernicus**; or, according to **Tycho Brahe**, the entire Eccentric is moved from its position by the external motion of the Sun, which is perhaps common among all five. <margin>Dissimilarity between the motions of the Moon and the others.</margin> In the Moon, however, both types of Anomalies truly belong to the Moon's own motions, so that they are distinguished not by the subject, but only by their causes. Therefore, in the books published so far, especially in the <margin>Book VI, part IV, page 778, corrected.</margin> *Epitome of Astronomy*, I have seen fit to derive the names of these Anomalies from their relation to the Sun. Thus, what in other Planets is the Anomaly of the Eccentric motion, in the Moon shall be called the **UNBOUND** ANOMALY <note>original: "anomalia SOLUTA." Kepler means it is "freed" from a direct relationship with the Sun's position.</note>, meaning unbound from respect to the Sun; the remaining Anomaly, with its Equations, shall be called **MONTHLY** <note>original: "MENSTRUÆ."</note>, that is, tied to the Sun, which creates the month (that is, the phases of the Moon) by its illumination. The *Prutenic Tables* call the former "Periodic" and the latter "Synodic." Let these things be said in general; hereafter I shall deal with each individually.

### CONCERNING THE UNBOUND ANOMALY.

distance from the center of the Earth by a moderate interval. Therefore, D will be the first Mean Longitude, and G the second, or that in the posterior semicircle. Moreover, the Moon moves around the Earth (just as the other five planets move around the Sun in Tycho's system) by causes that are equally natural, producing a circle that is not indeed perfectly flat, but very nearly <margin>Epitome, folio 800.</margin> perfect. For the arguments that can be brought to the contrary from the *Epitome of Astronomy* are of no significance. Indeed, the Longitude from the beginning of the Zodiac is not corrupted by more than 17 seconds through that diversity; the interval between the Moon and the Earth, although it is not truly the same as that computed from a perfect circle, nowhere contributes to forming the diversity of the apparent motion, as happens in the five Planets. Therefore, I have drawn the path of the center of the Moon’s body in the form of a perfect circle, even if, strictly speaking, it is an **Ellipse**, deflecting inward a little from a circle, as in the others; and for that reason, the Table of Equations was also computed from an Ellipse.

Regarding what pertains to the motion of the Moon’s **Apogee** <note>The point in the Moon's orbit furthest from the Earth; original: *Apogæi*.</note> [for we consider an Apogee in the Moon, as in the Sun, which in the other five planets is called the **Aphelion** <note>The point furthest from the Sun; original: *Aphelium*.</note>], it is quite swift if we consider the slowness of the **Apsides** <note>The points of greatest or least distance in an orbit.</note> in the others; for it returns to the same place in the Zodiac after 8 ¾ years from whenever it departed. Therefore, while the **Eccentricity** <note>The measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note> TC remains, a small circle is described by the center C around the center of the Earth, more than double the size of the Earth’s greatest circle, and this follows the order of the Signs, from the right upwards to the left, in the order which you see in Diagrams I. VIII. VII. VI. V. IV. III. II. I. Indeed, the centers of the eccentrics of the remaining Planets will also describe small circles of this kind around the Sun, if they are given an adequate space of time.

<margin>Tables fol. 78. in 81. 82. 88. Precept fol. 58.</margin> And here is the entire apparatus of the real Hypothesis of the Moon. According to this, its Tables of Epochs, Motions, and Equations also had the same explanation above, the same use, and the same modes of comparison: except for the motion of the **Node** <note>The point where the Moon's orbit crosses the path of the Sun (the ecliptic).</note>, which is retrograde in the Moon but direct in the others. <margin>Tables fol. 86 above.</margin> The Latitude of the Moon itself is extracted by considering the Moon as if in "couplings" <note>original: *copulis*; referring to syzygies or conjunctions/oppositions.</note>, as Inclination is considered in the others; for in the Moon, Latitude and Inclination coincide, and the "coupling reduction" has also been added with titles, having a similar use. Indeed, there was no need for "shortening" <note>original: *curtatione*; a geometric correction for planetary distances.</note> because there was no need to shorten the intervals <margin>Description of the Table of Lunar Latitude. PRECEPT 112. On forming the Argument of Latitude in the Moon, and those things to be extracted for the Latitude and Reduction of the Couplings.</margin> in the Tables of Equations. Therefore, in place of this omission, I have added the right-hand edge of the second Quadrant, so that the extraction of Latitude might be a little easier than the Inclination was in the Planets. For in the Moon, one of the Nodes, whichever is closer, is always subtracted from the true Longitude of the Moon, and never the longitude from the node as in others: thus the remaining **Argument of Latitude** is sought in the left-hand margins for degrees below 90°, and in the right-hand margins for those above 90°. And because the Latitude of the Moon is great, and its use frequent: interlinear differences have also been added for every ten "First Scruples" <note>Minutes of arc.</note> of the argument—increases in the descent and the first Quadrant, decreases in the second and the ascent: the handling of which is similar to that in several other Tables explained so far.

As for what the Title of that Table holds—that this Latitude and this Reduction are valid when the Node is in the Quadratures <note>90 degrees from the Sun; original: *Quadris*.</note>—that is to be taken 

<column-break/>

broadly. These Latitudes of that Table, I say, are valid through the entire circuit of the Moon from Node to Node, if it happens that the Node exists in the Quadratures in that month, and insofar as this is true. But besides this case, they are also valid in every coupling of the Moon with the Sun, and thus twice in every single month, even if the Node is not then in the Quadratures.

If anyone prefers to collect the Argument of Latitude in the manner of the **Prutenic Tables** <note>Astronomical tables published by Erasmus Reinhold in 1551 based on Copernicus's system.</note> and equate it: he will find a **Sexagesimal Canon** <note>A table based on the number 60, used for proportional calculations.</note> of the mean Argument of Latitude <margin>Tables fol. 88.</margin>; he will be able to use it according to the instructions of the Prutenic Tables.

This place reminds me to apply to the motions of the Moon what I said above regarding all the Planets: that I have cast aside circles and orbs, and the regularity of motions around certain centers of constant position and interval, leaving to the Planets <margin>Why there are new Hypotheses in the Moon regarding the first inequality.</note> an **elliptical orbit**. Since I have computed the Tables of the Moon's Equations and the **Freed Anomaly** <note>original: *Anomaliæ Solutæ*; Kepler's term for the first inequality of motion which is independent of the Sun.</note> through an elliptical path and the areas of triangles, as in the other Planets, it is asked: what compelled me to recede from the circular circuit of the Moon, if, as I just said, that inward deflection of the center of the globe from the perfection of a circle is not felt in it? I offer two causes; the first is because the other Monthly inequality, which must be dealt with later, is entirely produced by natural causes without its own circles: thus there was a great presumption regarding this **FREED** Anomaly as well. The other cause is because the motions of the remaining Planets also provided an example for the Moon: and because their physical causes are so arranged that it is not likely that, if those causes rule in the motions of the rest, they would not likewise rule in those of the Moon: especially since the equivalence of various Lunar Hypotheses in saving the appearances of this first inequality stands within all subtlety of sense and observation. <margin>Various Hypotheses of the first inequality.</margin> **Ptolemy** indeed placed an Epicycle on a Concentric circle, testifying that it performed the same as a simple Eccentric whose eccentricity was equal to the radius of the Epicycle: such an Eccentric as he had also placed in the Sun. **Copernicus** retained the same Epicycle as far as this first Anomaly of the Moon is concerned. But when **Tycho Brahe** saw that this eccentricity was too great, and the diameter of the Epicycle too great, and could not be reconciled with parallaxes and the variations of the shadow's diameters: he took a plan such as Ptolemy had in the Eccentrics of the other Planets. But because Ptolemy had placed there another center of double eccentricity around which the progress of the Planet was regular—and thus the whole Eccentric, as said above, was perceived to have an unequal motion through different times around its own center—and Copernicus had escaped this inconvenience in the Planets by the duplication of his Epicycle, which he had embraced in place of an Eccentric: here Tycho, more devoted to Copernicus, also doubled the Epicycle of this first and Freed inequality in the Moon; an aim to which Copernicus had not yet aspired for the Moon. After Tycho, I, determining that the causes were to be referred not to Epicycles but to the natural ratios of the **lever and balance** <note>original: *vectis & libræ*; Kepler's physical analogy for how magnetic or solar forces drive planets at different speeds.</note>, by which the elliptical journey of the Planet is produced, established the same for the Moon.

A fifth Hypothesis also arises, from **Father Albert Curtz**, S.J., my astronomical <note>original: *Uranici*.</note> friend, one of a most beautiful wit; which, since it leaves the Balance to me, for the purpose of...

Though he orders the elliptical path, he nonetheless snatches away the "lever" <note>Kepler’s "lever" refers to a physical theory where a planet is moved along its path by a force originating from the sun, proportional to the distance.</note>; that is, he transfers the area of the triangle to the Ptolemaic equant point—the second focus of the ellipse—around which the Mean Anomaly is arranged in equal angles. However, in the effect of Longitude, which we are looking at here, this coincides almost exactly with the Ptolemaic Equant. Here, then, is a model of all these approaches, and in the equations of its areas for the Moon, there is an unbelievable closeness of the numbers.

<margin>Ease of calculation.</margin>
Tycho, following Copernicus’s method for the planets, wandered furthest from Ptolemy and Copernicus regarding the Moon, by as much as 7 and 9 minutes <note>original: Scr., short for scrupula, an old term for minutes of arc.</note>. I hold a middle ground, though closer to Tycho; Ptolemy’s planetary model applied to the Moon, my own model, and Curtius are in the middle. Between these, since observations of the Moon’s longitude cannot offer a final judgment (being a matter of only 2 minutes), logic will hear my case even for the Moon: why the natural causes of the "lever"—which the other planets require—should not be approved here, following the ease of the calculation. Although I have a dispute regarding equality with the aforementioned Curtius on this point, as far as the tables are concerned, once they are finished, it no longer matters to the user with what ease they were computed. Thus, enough has been said of the first Equality of the Moon, called the "Unbound" <note>original: Soluta; referring to the first inequality of the Moon which does not depend on its position relative to the Sun.</note>.

## CHAPTER XXVI.
# ON THE MONTHLY ANOMALY OF THE MOON AND ITS EQUATIONS.

<margin>Ptolemy's monthly Hypothesis.</margin>
Let us pass to the other kind of Anomaly: the Monthly one, which is tied to the Conjunctions and Quadratures of the Sun <note>The Moon's phases: New/Full moons and Quarter moons.</note>. For this reason, the Moon had to be treated separately in these precepts. In this Anomaly, it will be much more evident that the causes of motions are physical. Therefore, it was no injustice for me to bid farewell to the circles, celestial spheres, and centers that measure out angles equally over time. Ptolemy, to whom only one of the monthly inequalities was known, saw that the Moon's equations (which we have discussed so far) turned out larger in the Quarters <note>Quadratures</note> than in the Conjunctions. To mirror this in his own positions and conform his calculation to this observation, he taught that the Moon's Epicycle—which he had introduced for the sake of the first "Unbound" inequality—descended toward the Earth by a true and real motion twice a month, namely, in each Quarter.

<margin>Refuted by Regiomontanus.</margin>
This was believed by astronomers until Regiomontanus, who realized that if the equations of the Epicycle became larger due to this approach, the diameter of the Moon’s body would also appear more than half as large again in the Quarters as it does in the Conjunctions <note>Regiomontanus noted that if the Moon actually moved closer to Earth to explain the speed change, it would look much larger, which doesn't happen.</note>.

<column-break/>

<margin>Transformed by Copernicus into a second Epicycle.</margin>
Since observations refuted this, the dogma of such a great approach appeared false. Copernicus, having overturned this explanation of the phenomenon, substituted another—likewise real—using two epicycles instead of Ptolemy's one: a larger one that carried the center of a smaller one, and the smaller one carrying the Moon itself, making it appear furthest from the center of the larger one during the Quarters.

<margin>By Tycho into a Hypocycle.</margin>
What was Tycho to do, being then entirely devoted to the "perfection" of motions in perfect circles? It was difficult to imitate Copernicus even in the positions of the monthly inequality; for he had already accepted two epicycles for the "Unbound" Anomaly discussed in the previous chapter. Why should he now add a third, which Copernicus gave for the monthly Anomaly? Indeed, deceived by the Moon's sphere, he applied it to the Earth, placing its center on a line parallel to the line of the Epicycle's Apogee. In the circumference of this—not an Epicycle but a Hypocycle—the center of the Moon's sphere (carrying the two previous epicycles) was ordered to move so that in Conjunctions it reached the very center of the Earth, and in the Quarters it receded as far as possible. Yet Tycho still detected another "Variation" <note>A specific lunar inequality discovered by Tycho Brahe.</note>, unobserved by the ancients; he did not dare to introduce the mechanical devices for this into the system of the Moon's spheres, so he assigned them to the Zodiac itself. This last inequality finally opened his eyes, so that he began to see that these inequalities are produced not by real circles, but by other natural causes. What did I do after Tycho died? I will say it in a word: it was of no use to untie the Gordian Knot; I cut it. For after long contemplations and more than one transformation, it finally appeared: for the sake of the monthly Anomaly, nothing needs to be changed in the shape of the Moon’s orbit, nor in its distances. For all of it follows the logic of illumination; to which the natural speedings and slowings of its motions are accommodated, either by the power of its own light or by the animal-like service of the Sun <note>Kepler often used "animal" or "vital" force to describe the active, non-mechanical power he believed the Sun exerted on planets.</note>. It would take too long to explain the demonstrations themselves here; let anyone who desires them seek them in the *Epitome of Astronomy*. It is more in keeping with the purpose of the present work to build the foundations of the calculation through an explanation of the Diagrams. If these are ignored, the labor of the calculation—tedious enough by itself—would become vain due to the wonderful variety of cautions produced by this hypothesis, which is not newly invented, but offered voluntarily by Nature.

<margin>By me into natural causes and illumination.</margin>

Therefore, with the other letters remaining as I explained them previously—those pertaining to the **Free Anomaly** <note>original: Anomalia Soluta; the primary variation in a planet's speed due to its elliptical path</note>—in the eight diagrams, **I M** is now the extended diameter of the circle of illumination. To this, at right angles, is the line **S T U**, the **Line of Syzygies** <note>original: linea Copularum; the line connecting the Sun, Earth, and Moon during conjunction (New Moon) or opposition (Full Moon)</note>. **T S** points toward the Sun, and **T U** toward the place of the Earth’s shadow, opposite the Sun. This is also indicated by the halves of the Earth’s globe: the upper part is illuminated by the Sun, and the lower part is turned into the shadow of its own opacity. For the sake of this chart, the Sun and Earth are conceived as immobile, so that in all eight diagrams, the Sun illuminates the Earth from the upper position. Since the necessity of the chart requires this, it follows that we must conceive of the center of the Eccentric **C** as being separated from the Sun in this chart by a motion contrary to the upper one—namely, from left to right downwards—in the order given by the numbers of the diagrams: I, II, III, IV, V, VI, VII, VIII. This motion is now quasi-annual and a little longer; for it is not the motion of the Apogee itself among the fixed stars (which we said above is completed in 8½ years), but rather the motion of the Sun, which returns to this lunar apogee after 13½ months, even though with respect to the chart, the Sun always stays in one place. And thus, because it is left behind by the faster Sun, the **Moon’s Apogee** is imagined to move from the Sun and back to the Sun with a retrograde motion.

<margin>
Natural hypothesis of the Monthly Anomaly.
</margin>
<margin>
Distinction of the equation into three parts, by their causes.
</margin>
Therefore, the Moon's **Eccentric** circle **A B** has a double displacement: one of the center, from the center of the Earth, which is the **Eccentricity C T**; the other of the entire half **F S B**, from the continued plane of the circle of illumination **I T N M**, which is the **Eccentricity C N** or **T O**, which changes throughout the year. Each has its own effect in shaping the Moon's motions around the Earth. Thus, two causes of the Moon's **Equations** <note>An "equation" in historical astronomy is a correction added to a mean position to find the actual position.</note> emerge: 1. **Eccentricity**, and 2. the Moon's circular **Elongation** from the Sun. For each of these acting alone produces a single equation; the former explains the first equation of the "Free Anomaly" discussed so far; the latter explains the third equation detected by Tycho [Brahe], to be explained later in the third place. But when joined, both produce the **monthly equation** known to Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD) was the first to document this second major lunar variation, now called evection.</note>. The first has until now used the perpetual eccentricity **C T**; the third is completed without eccentricity; the second has a variable eccentricity **C O**, which vanishes every seven months: this I will now explain.

<margin>
The first monthly equation.
</margin>
Therefore, the Line of Syzygies **S T V** takes the place of a certain **Line of Apsides** <note>The line connecting the points where the Moon is closest to and furthest from Earth.</note>. For a line drawn through the center of the Eccentric **B F**, parallel to the diameter of illumination **I M**, cuts it at point **O**; this point takes the place of the center of a new Eccentric, so that **T O** is the new eccentricity. Just as the prior and genuine eccentricity **C T** caused the ordinary equation of the Free Anomaly (consisting of two parts, the optical and the physical), so also this new eccentricity **O T** causes—not indeed both parts of that prior one—but certainly the one that comes from the **area of the triangle**. For here also there is a certain "Apogee" and an opposite "Perigee." By dividing the Moon’s Eccentric through the Earth's circle of illumination **I M** into two parts, **I S M** and **I V M**, whichever of these contains the "Free Apogee" **A**—that is, whichever part is larger and further from **I M**—that part also contains the line of the **monthly apogee**, and the opposite part contains the **perigee**. Therefore, in Diagrams I, II, and VIII, the line **T S** and the 

<column-break/>

<margin>
Empty Month.
</margin>
<margin>
Full Month.
</margin>
subsolar point of the Eccentric **S** take the force of a monthly apogee. This is because in the first diagram, the Free Apogee **A** coincides with it; in the second, it precedes it closely; and in the eighth, it follows it in the same quadrant **S T M**. On the other hand, in Diagrams IV, V, and VI, the monthly apogee is represented by the line **T V** and point **V** of the Eccentric, located in the Earth's shadow. This is because in the fifth, the Free Apogee **A** coincides with it; in the fourth, it precedes it by an acute angle **V T A**; and in the sixth, it follows it. But in Diagrams III and VII, there is no monthly apogee or perigee. This is because the plane of the circle of illumination (by which this eccentricity is judged) cuts the Moon's eccentric orbit into equal parts, extending into opposite regions at equal intervals; therefore, lines **C N** and **T O** collapse into points, and the monthly eccentricity is zero. Thus, Diagrams III and VII show the type of an **EMPTY MONTH** <note>original: mensis VACUI</note> regarding the second equation; whereas the first and fifth show the type of a **FULL MONTH** <note>original: mensis PLENI</note>, because in these the monthly eccentricity **T O** becomes maximal and total.

<margin>
What is a Technical [Month]?
</margin>
By "month," understand here a **Technical Month**: that is, a collection of all positions of the Moon, gathered from any natural months, in which one and the same arrangement of the Eccentric center toward the Sun is found. Since this arrangement varies incessantly (as the Sun carries the Moon's apogee along by more than one degree every day), a Technical Month never remains in the same state for several consecutive days, except insofar as the variation of this position, creeping in secretly, escapes our limited senses.

<margin>
This monthly [equation] is not perpetual.
</margin>
When, therefore, there is no monthly eccentricity—because points **T** and **O** coincide, which happens when the Free Apogee falls on the "Quadras" <note>The 90-degree points or "quadratures."</note>, as in Diagrams III and VII—then there is no monthly equation (of the kind we are dealing with here) for the entire Technical Month, no matter where in the whole Eccentric the Moon is found. But as soon as the Free Apogee has left the Quadras and given rise to the monthly eccentricity **O T**, the occasion for this Equation arises simultaneously.

<margin>
The measure of the monthly Equation is the Triangle.
</margin>
Otherwise, its logic is the same as that of a single element in the first Free [Equation]. For the arcs beginning from the line that takes the place of the Apogee, stretching into either region, are completed more slowly by the Moon—specifically because of this monthly equation. In the same way, then, as in the Free [Equation], the **area of the Triangle** standing upon the monthly eccentricity **O T**, which has the body of the Moon at its vertex—this area, I say, measures the delay that has accrued to the Moon through that arc because of the longer distance of the whole arc from the circle of illumination.

<margin>
No monthly equation of the Moon in Syzygies.
</margin>
Thus, in Diagram VIII, when the Moon is at **s**, such that no arc lies between the Moon and the monthly apogee, the monthly equation is zero, even though the monthly eccentricity is **O T**. This is because **S**, **O**, and **T** lie in a single straight line and do not form any area. Here, therefore, the angle **A T S** of the equated anomaly (the "Free" one) finds its **Mean Anomaly** <note>The position the Moon would have if its motion were perfectly uniform.</note> from the area **A S T** alone.

<margin>
What is the reason for it, when the Apogee is with the Sun or opposite the Sun?
</margin>
But in Diagram I, if the Moon is at **D**, the equated anomaly **A T D** and the arc of the orbit **A D** require a time composed of the entire area **T A D** and the part of it that is area **D O T**; that is, from the Sector **A D C** taken once, and the area **T C D** or **N O F** taken twice. Similarly, with the Moon at **σ**, where the arc of the eccentric **σ A** appears under the angle of the equated [anomaly] **σ T A**, the time for this arc and angle—or the Mean Anomaly—would be measured by...
