# PRECEPTS OF RUDOLPH.

<columns>
...only the area **TσA**, if there were no monthly equation: where the small area **TCσ** increases the area of the sector **σCA**. But because it now happens to this month that there is some monthly equation—and indeed a full or total one [because the monthly eccentricity **O T** coincides with **CT**, the essential eccentricity, so to speak, and equals it]—therefore the same small area **TCσ**, being also established upon the monthly eccentricity **O T**, increases the time (or the **Mean Anomaly** <note>The mathematical value used to track a planet's progress in its orbit</note>) of this angle and arc a second time; and thus it contributes twice on this occasion to establishing the equation.

The same reasoning applies to Diagram 5: because when the Apogee of the **Free Anomaly** <note>original: "Anomalia Soluta"; the Moon's primary motion independent of the Sun's influence</note> **A** passed, the monthly Apogee also passed into **V**, the place opposite the Sun.

In the other diagrams, while the Apogee of the Free Anomaly moves through intermediate places between the four monthly points **S, M, V, I**, more difficulties arise due to the composition of the arcs. And first in Diagram VIII: while the Moon <margin>What is the ratio of the monthly Moon in Apogee?</margin> is moving in the Apogee of the Free Anomaly, the ratio is still simple. Here, although the equation of the Free Anomaly is zero (because **T, C, A** lie in one straight line), nevertheless the angle **STA**, or the distance of the place **A** (first equated from the Sun **S**), requires a monthly equation. For the Moon lingers in it so much longer than the ratio of the Free Anomaly and the area **SAT** would suggest, by as much as the small area **AOT** measures; because here the Sun **S** takes on the power of a monthly Apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth</note>, due to the proximity of **A** itself, the Apogee of the Free Anomaly.

<margin>Or in Perigee?</margin>
Likewise in Diagram IV, with the Moon situated in **P**, the **Perigee** <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Earth</note> of the Free Anomaly; where it lacks the first equation: yet because **V** is now the monthly Apogee (since angle **VTA** is less than a right angle, and thus **A**, the Apogee of the Free Anomaly, is closer to **V**), the Moon therefore lingers longer in arc **PV** and shorter in **SP** than the first equation (at points **V, S**) suggests, by the quantity of the small area **PTO**. For the measure of the delay in arc **PV** is composed of the areas **PVT** and **POT**; or, what comes to the same thing, the area **ACPSA** (which is worth 180° of Mean Anomaly), due to the Moon's departure **P** from **S**, the monthly Perigee, the small area **PTO** must be subtracted, because it comes from **S** to **P** so much faster; but it must be added to area **ACPVA**, because it comes from **P** to **V**, the monthly Apogee, so much slower. For the equations of the Free Anomaly are not valid, nor are the Anomalies (whether 0 or 180), except only if the Moon is in the **syzygies** <note>original: "copulis"; points of alignment like New or Full Moon</note> **S** or **V**; and therefore, if outside these points, they must be corrected.

<margin>What in other places?</margin>
BUT IF the Moon is in neither of its **apsides** <note>The highest or lowest points of the orbit: Apogee and Perigee</note>: even if the arcs started from both Apogees can be discerned (as in Diagram VIII, with the Moon placed at **F**, the arc **BF** acquires two parts, **SA** and **AF**), the mind should not be occupied with the consideration of both parts at once. For that place of Apogee **A** which we gather from the Tables of Mean Motions is always valid. This is not changed by any equation of the Anomaly, whether Free or monthly. Therefore, it is sufficient to consider one part **AF**, whose equated angle **ATF**, added to the place of Apogee **A**, gives the place of the Moon as first equated, to which corresponds the Mean Anomaly according to the measure of both area **AFT** (on account of the Free Anomaly) and **FOT** (on account of the monthly). In the same way, one must think about all the points of the **Eccentric** <note>The off-center circle used to model the orbit</note>, even in the ascending semicircle. For example, if <margin>And in the Ascending Semicircle</margin> the Moon is at **B**: then the angle **STB**, by which the place of the Moon first equated is elongated from the Sun, already has its Mean Anomaly from the Free Anomaly, as part of angle **ATB**; and thus through its first equation it would already be established and connected with the said Mean Anomaly if the Sun were joined to it at **B**, or the Sun's...

<column-break/>

...opposite: but because the Sun is not in **B** but in **S**, from which point in this Diagram the monthly Anomaly begins (as from a monthly Apogee), the place **B** additionally requires the equation of area **OBT**. Thus, the equated angle **ATB** will correspond to a Mean Anomaly composed of areas **ABT** and **OBT**: or what comes to the same thing; the arc of the Eccentric **AVB** will have a Mean Anomaly collected from areas **APD** and **PBT**, from which, however, the small area **OBT** has been removed.

So in Diagram IV, if one asks about the delay of the planet in arc **Sσ**: here there is no point in answering for them jointly; rather let it be answered separately for **S**, as above, and separately also for **σ**. For since **V** is the monthly Perigee here, from the time when the Moon by its mean motion could have been in **A**, the Apogee of the Free Anomaly, until that time in which it is truly seen in line **Tσ** [via the first two equations], a delay or motion of Mean Anomaly passes as great as area **AσT** measures, and additionally the small area **σOT**.

<margin>What between two Apogees?</margin>
There is indeed another more difficult observation, if the Moon is positioned between two Apogees—for example, in the same Diagram IV, at **G**: what then would be the Mean Anomaly? Since the Moon is moving toward **A**, the Apogee of the Free Anomaly, the area **TGA** will correspond to arc **GA** as the Mean Anomaly from the Free motion. But since it simultaneously departs from the monthly apogee **V** with a slower motion (due to the monthly variation), however much delay it adds to arc **VG** from the measure of area **GOT**, it will subtract the same amount from area **TGA** pertaining to the establishment of the mean anomaly.

Likewise, if the Moon is at **ε**, between both Perigees **S** and **P**; the Mean Anomaly corresponds to arc **AP**, of which area **AεT** becomes the measure; from which, however, the small area **εOT** is removed—the measure of acceleration through arc **S**, starting here from **S**, the monthly perigee.

<margin>Foundation of the Calculation.</margin>
It is clear enough what the use is of the triangles standing upon **TO**. The question now is: how were the irregular movements calculated—those that are always longer in that monthly quadrant in which the Apogee of the Free Anomaly is located than in the collateral quadrant; and always shorter in that quadrant which contains the Perigee of the Free Anomaly than in the other from which it is separated by the line of Syzygies?

The answer is that they must first be reduced to some regularity. Through the center **C**, a line **RE** is drawn parallel to **STV**, bisecting the Eccentric, which will also cut **IM** at **N**; then the triangles constructed upon **NC**, if their vertices are equally distant from point **R**, will be equal; as in [Diagrams] II, IV, and VIII, **CBN** and **CFN** are equal when **RB** and **RF** are equal. So also in IV, **CEN** and **CσN**, if **Rε** and **Rσ** are equal. Since any one of these triangles is easily calculated from the base **NC** and the height (which is the sine of the arc of the Eccentric between **R** and the vertex of the triangle), the small area of triangle **NCT** or **CTO** is then sought. <margin>In Diagram IV.</margin> This area, when added to **NσC** and subtracted from **NεC**, produces areas equal to **TσO** and **TεO**. The same small area **NTC** or **TCO**, added in Diagram VIII to **NFC**, constitutes **TFO**, and subtracted from **NBC**, leaves **TBO**. You have the demonstration of this matter in the **Epitome** <note>Referring to Kepler’s "Epitome of Copernican Astronomy"</note>, <margin>page 804 of it.</margin>

In Diagram VIII, with the Moon placed at **S**, at the moment of conjunction, the small area **CTN** subtracted from the equal **CSN** leaves **OST** as nothing. Conversely, with the Moon placed at **E** or **G**—180° of the Eccentric counted from **R**, where **CEN** is nothing—the small area **OCT** alone equals the monthly equation **OET**.

And here it sometimes happens that this small area exceeds one or the other of the triangles upon **NC**.

# THE TABLES OF RUDOLPH

<column-break/>

An example is in Diagram IV, with the Moon placed at point **g** between **V** and **E**. Here, the area **NCG** is not large enough for the area **NTC** or **TCO** to be taken away from it. Therefore, the area **NGC** is instead subtracted from **TCO**, and so in this place—where **TGO** currently stands—it measures the small monthly equation. But whenever these contrary parts must be added, **TGO** will be measured from **STV** (a line parallel to the previous one), rather than **NGC** from **RCE** (likewise parallel); this creates its own specific caution within the rules of calculation.

<margin>The cause of the precision.</margin> And here are the two elements from which the one monthly equation of the Moon is composed. These are by no means an arbitrary choice of mine, but are born from the very nature of the computational calculus of the eccentric and the illumination. Even though the little area **NTC** is of the smallest quantity—since the eccentricity was intentionally chosen as empty/minimal—and might therefore seem negligible in practice, it cannot be omitted from the rules of calculation without great difficulty. Whereas our predecessors were forced, for the sake of this monthly equation alone, <margin>The hypothesis of this equation is legitimate.</margin> to introduce real eccentrics and real motions of the entire lunar sphere all over again; here, I only propose this: that the equation arises from the accidental concurrence of illumination. And while the ancients were free, once they had chosen a model, to propose it under whatever conditions they liked, they bound themselves to their own externally imposed laws; thus, there was no freedom to fashion them after the pattern of the intended effect. But if I explain the cause of the matter through the collateral, accidental concurrence of illumination—explaining the whole mode in such a way that it agrees in five ways with the eccentrics of the ancients—who could object?

We used to wonder at the causes underlying this: why Tycho made this monthly equation precisely half of the equation of the **Solved Anomaly** <note>The "Solved Anomaly" refers to the Moon's primary motion once the major solar perturbations are accounted for.</note>. For Tycho did not give this in imitation of Ptolemy: <margin>How authors differ in the quantity of the monthly equation.</margin> for Ptolemy, from the observations of Hipparchus and his own, established the equation as 2° 39' at a mean anomaly of 90° (a sine of 8694, or 5° 1' 13" out of 60'). Nor did Tycho give this to Copernicus or the Prutenic Tables; for these establish the first equation at only 4° 55' 14" in the Anomaly, as derived from the Alphonsine Tables [at an excellent 3° 49' 42"]. But Tycho, having assumed the radius of Ptolemy’s epicycle from the round number 8700, turned it into a tangent so that the equation itself would come out smaller at 4° 58' 20". Then, having divided this into 2900 and 5800 for his two epicycles (as in the other planets), he precisely gave the half-value of 4348 to the diameter of the eccentricity of this circle, so that the radius would be 2174. We wondered at this, I say, as the cause was not apparent. But behold the cause from this physical hypothesis, which is quite elegant: <margin>Why the monthly equation is precisely half of the Solved Anomaly.</margin> the eccentric of the Moon, when placed higher, cannot be moved further by the aspect of the rays in the plane of the circle of illumination than its real eccentricity allows. Therefore, the triangle whose area measures the monthly equation cannot acquire a longer base 

<column-break/>

than that first one which measured the physical part of the Solved Equation. And that physical part is exactly half of the total Solved Equation. 

Why the Moon’s departure from the Center of the Earth should do as much as its departure from the circle of illumination is a matter of deeper investigation. And so much for the first monthly equation, which was known to Ptolemy.

<margin>VARIATION. See Danish Astronomy, Theory of Longitude, page 173.</margin> It remains for me to explain this other equation of **Variation**, which its discoverer Tycho called the VARIATION. This is because the former equation was natural to the different months of the year, while this one is of a quantity that <margin>his page 561.</margin> I have discussed with subtle arguments regarding its origin and causes in the *Epitome of Astronomy*. <margin>"Outside the Lunar Hypothesis," says Longomontanus, Danish Theory, page 116.</margin> Tycho therefore resumes the calculation for the Moon proportionally in the progressing place of the Moon, so that by the contrary revolution of a smaller circle (as described in Longomontanus's *Astronomy*, taking the diameter of the larger orbit), the whole Moon—just as in Copernicus’s reciprocal points—is moved. This hypothesis is well-suited for calculation. 

Tycho, and also in this equation, <margin>The natural hypothesis of the Variation.</margin> labels it as such, assuming natural causes that agree with Tycho's own conjectures, as well as with the plane of the little circle which the center of the eccentric describes around the Earth. <margin>Cause.</margin> For the cause of the lunar motion’s "incitation" <note>Kepler’s term for the acceleration or speeding up of the Moon's orbital speed.</note> around the center of the Earth is in proportion to the sines of the elongation of the Moon's place, proportionally shown in Diagrams I, III, IV, and VI. If the Moon is at **g**, and in VIII, if the Moon's place is near the Center of the Earth at **g**. 

Now, to collect this concisely, let us again take the area of the little circle as useful for all these lines: <margin>Measure, area.</margin> just as the equation of the Quadrant relates to the sum of the sines, so the area **CyN** relates to the arc **Cy**. <margin>His page 813.</margin> The demonstration of these things is in the *Arithmetical Astronomy*, Book VI. But it is computed from Ptolemy's triangle **ymN**, to the readings **CyT**. 

We return therefore to the computation of the two prior equations: which are clear, namely as the <margin>Rectangles of the Quadrant.</margin> Rectangles of the quadrant: and the area **yN** is equivalent to the height of these, of the incitation through **Cy** by ratio. That the ratio of computing more exactly prevails over the diameter of Tychonic libration, <margin>His page 813.</margin> you have demonstrated in the said place of the *Epitome of Astronomy*. But this little circle is such that its area can be matched to this effect of Variation; it formed this equation for us, not by a tiny amount, but scarcely a twelfth part of the present one. Yet it suffices for us to establish the maximum quantity of the smaller ones among themselves: the truest maximum quantity can be assigned from Tycho’s experience, <margin>From the Epitome of Astronomy, Book IV, page 565.</margin> at 4' 30", or even from the speculation of causes as being a little larger.

Thus, the triangles formed in the little circle described through **C** serve two offices: one <gloss>designated by the collateral triangles CFT, CBT</gloss> explained for the monthly equation, where they determine the genuine quantity; the other...

## DESCRIPTION OF THE TABLE

### OF MONTHLY SCRUPLES AND 
### Variation, etc.

<margin>Tables on folios 82, 83.</margin>
First, therefore, a Table of Monthly Scruples <note>In this context, "scruples" refers to small fractions of a degree, specifically minutes of arc.</note> has been assigned to these monthly equations; it occupies sixty lines on one side of the paper and the remaining thirty on the other. <margin>Left Parts.</margin> It is divided by width into three parts: the leftmost is enclosed by four borders, the right by two. The numbers in the borders, written in capital letters, show the entry point into the Table. The left borders have the title "Monthly Argument" written at the top and bottom; however, the numbers in them are common, as you will find noted down at the margin. <margin>Right.</margin> Thus, the outer border of the right part contains the "Annual Argument" increased by a quadrant, while the inner border contains it decreased by a quadrant: this is noted at the top of the former and the bottom of the latter. <margin>Middle.</margin> The middle part of the entire width contains the "Monthly Scruples" for the usual calculation, and their Logarithms for the new <term>Napierian method</term> <note>Referring to John Napier, the inventor of logarithms. Kepler was one of the first major astronomers to adopt this revolutionary shortcut for complex multiplication and division.</note>, which I primarily present in this work and recommend to everyone. 

Regarding this middle part, which provides common entries for the borders of both side parts: the numbers in the borders of the left part are the whole degrees of the "Monthly Argument." That is, they are the arcs of the Moon's Eccentric starting from point **R** (in Diagrams I, II, VIII) or from point **E** (in Diagrams I, V, VI), and ending at the Moon's position which it occupies in the Eccentric by reason of the first equation, with the Variation currently ignored. <margin>The Monthly Argument differs from Elongation.</margin> From this description, it is clear how the "Monthly Argument" differs from the <term>Elongation</term> <note>The angular distance between the Moon and the Sun as seen from Earth.</note> of the Moon from the Sun, even though they share a great familiarity. I say it differs in its starting point, which it takes alternately now from the Sun, now from its opposite; nor does it start from the very points of the Eccentric located on the connecting line **STV**, but from the corresponding points on its parallel **RCE**. It differs in its subject: for Elongation is an angle to the sight, measured from the Zodiac; this argument is an arc of the Eccentric Orbit of the Moon. It also frequently differs in the quantity of its numbering for both reasons. Furthermore, each border carries its own Title, which it eventually transmits to the appropriate part of the equation once it has been completed.

<margin>What are Monthly Scruples?</margin>
Corresponding to this Monthly Argument in the same line and middle part are the "Monthly Scruples." These are two-fifths of the area of the triangle built upon **CN**, which is the greatest of all in a "full month" <note>A month where the eccentricity is at its maximum.</note>, as seen in Diagrams I and V. For example, if the Moon is at **K**, and **RK** is 30°, then **RFEBK** 330° will be found in the outer right border of the left part, over which is placed the Title "Add." Therefore, the 30' scruples in the middle part, with their Logarithm 69320, signify the area of Triangle **CNK**. Even if the month is not one of the "Full" ones—as in Diagrams II and VII, where **CN** is not at its maximum and equal to **CT**—this triangle (or its 2/5) is nevertheless shown as if it were in a full month.

<margin>What are the Annual Areas?</margin>
The "Annual Argument" is the angle of the Sun's digression from the Moon's apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from Earth.</note> (either **STA** in Diagrams II and VIII, or **VTA** in Diagrams IV and VI). In Diagram VIII, **ATS**, and in Diagram IV, **ATV**, are Quadrants of increased numbering; because the remainders of these angles arranged to 4 right angles are in the right-hand border of the right part. Conversely, in Diagram II, **ATS**, and in Diagram VI, **ATV**, are Quadrants of decreased numbering (being below 90), which are themselves arranged in the left border of that same right part. The small areas placed within the borders of this right part are to be extracted using only these borders of the Annual Argument, <margin>What is the "Exfort Part"?</margin> under the title <term>Exfort Part</term> <note>Kepler's term (*Particula Exfortis*) for a specific correction factor related to the 'out-force' or eccentricity effects caused by the Sun.</note>; these are the areas of Triangle **CTN**. 

The titles or pairs of letters placed above or below at the bottom are extracted from the individual borders from which the entry to the letters lies open. The choice of one or the other depends on the semicircles of the monthly anomaly: the first semicircle chooses the first letter, the second chooses the latter. Finally, whichever letter remains for the "Exfort," that letter refers not to the Moon's position itself, but to the monthly equation to be corrected by the Exfort. Besides this Exfort part, this Annual Argument also extracts from the common middle part the <margin>Proportional Scruples.</margin> Scruples or their Logarithm; these are then truly "Proportional Scruples." For they take a proportional part of the eccentricity for any month that is not "full" from Triangle **CKN** (as if calculated from full eccentricity). They are to 60' just as, for example, in Diagram IV, **CN** is to **CN** in Diagram I, assuming the same arc **R$\sigma$** in both. <margin>The Competent Part.</margin> I call this the "Competent Part": and this "Competent **CN**," corrected by the "Exfort **CTN**," finally becomes the sought-after **TO**.

<margin>The Tychonic Variation.</margin>
But also, in the two borders on each side of the left part, the "Tychonic Variation" <note>The Variation discovered by Tycho Brahe, a major lunar inequality occurring twice a month.</note> is inserted in capital letters. It is to be extracted using only the borders of this left part, with its title placed above or below; the title indicates which border it belongs to by its proximity. However, in that case, the numbers of the borders (as said above) are no longer the arcs of the Eccentric, but are the "angle to the sight," or the arc of the Zodiac, numbered from the true position of the Sun all the way to the position of the Moon, which has now been rendered "near-true" by two equations.

<margin>Demonstrations: *Epitome of Astronomy*, Book IV, page 565.</margin>
<margin>Table, folio 83.</margin>
Because the Tychonic Variation does not have the same fixed quantity from all observations (leaving room for judgment here), and because conversely, there is a great likelihood of a slightly larger Variation deduced from archetypal causes, I have seen fit to show the same in a small Table in small type. It is separate from the Tychonic table so that there is less confusion. I have placed it at the bottom of the Monthly Table in the vacant space of the paper, divided into three parts of fifteen lines each. The logic of its borders is the same as that found in the inscriptions at the top and bottom...

These Tables are so overgrown with the riches of technical skill and use, and so rough to the touch—but such is the nature of all Hypotheses supplied by the nature of light, which had to be followed down to every minute detail. ### To form the Annual Argument of the Moon's longitude.

<margin>PRECEPT 113.</margin>
Subtract the position of the Moon's Apogee <note>The point in the Moon's orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> from the true position of the Sun, in Signs, Degrees, and Scruples; for Seconds can be neglected. Add 12 Signs to the position of the Sun to ensure the subtraction can be performed if necessary. Retain the remainder: if it is either more than 270° (that is, 9 Signs) or less than 90° (that is, 3 Signs), or 6 Signs. Keep that remainder; but if it is more than 90° but less than 270°, then either add or subtract a Semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>. Thus the Annual Argument will be established, either of the Quadrant or Increased (from 270° to 360°) or Diminished (from 0° to 90°).
<margin>See page 61.
See page 55.</margin>
*As in the Rudolphine Calculation <note>original: "Geneſi RUDOLPHI"; likely referring to a specific example calculation for Emperor Rudolph’s birth chart or a standard reference example</note>; the position of the Sun was 1 Sign, 27° 54' and the Moon's Apogee was 1 Sign, 27° 5' 4". The remainder was 0° 49'. Likewise 2, 7, 28, and 13, 5, 37. This is the Annual Argument: specifically of the Quadrant from these; about which one must be carefully warned from the Monthly [tables]. 
Note that in the physical hypothesis, everything here is annual, which in Tycho Brahe and his predecessors seemed to be monthly; but the effect, as far as this diversity is concerned, is entirely the same. This observation finally revealed the natural causes.*

### To form the Monthly Argument of the Moon's longitude.

<margin>PRECEPT 114.</margin>
<margin>Precepts 83, 84.</margin>
You have learned above how to investigate the Anomaly of the Moon's Eccentric <note>The displacement of the Moon's circular path from the center of the Earth.</note> in the common way as for all Planets. Whether this be smaller or larger, or larger than the complement to the full Circle, subtract the annual Argument of longitude from it. If necessary [add a circle] so that the subtraction can be performed: the remainder will be the monthly Argument of longitude. *As in the Rudolphine Calculation, the Annual Argument of the Moon's Eccentric was 3° 37'. Subtract from this the Annual Argument 67° 28'. That is, subtract 1 Sign 5° 37' (or having added 12, the Argument from 1 Sign 5° 37'); there remained 10 Signs 28° 9'. This is the Monthly Argument.*

### How to form the relevant portion of the monthly Equation from the two Arguments of the Moon's longitude.

<margin>PRECEPT 115.</margin>
<margin>Tables on folios 82, 83 above.</margin>
With the Annual Argument, extract the Logarithm and the
<column-break/>
outlying Part <note>original: "Particulam exfortem"; referring to a specific adjustment factor in the table</note> from the Table of Monthly [Equations] 56. This will require care, and that skill which is clear for the Annual [Argument], carefully noted at the bottom for "Increased" and at the top for "Diminished." If the other Annual Argument was from the first semicircle, refer back to the first set of Logarithms; if from the second, the second set, discarding the rest. Then seek the monthly Argument from which of those two; with the value found, extract the Logarithm from the middle of the Table, which we write below through its four borders; then add and apply the title written on the border in which you found the Monthly [Argument].

<margin>1.</margin> Thirdly, make a sum from the two extracted Logarithms, and refer that back to the series of Logarithms, so that from it may be extracted the writing in both Seconds and halves; the sum of the two Logarithms from the aforementioned example will be the relevant example. First, the calculator must be warned about several things.

<margin>2.</margin> <margin>Logarithms are not exact.</margin> First, the Logarithms placed in the Table are not perfectly accurate, but, setting aside extreme precision, are rounded at least to whole Degrees: so that the labor of addition itself may be performed with an easier hand, because little error is committed in the final result. However, he who wishes to use more accurate values, or to extract them with precise minutes of the Arguments without the trouble of finding proportional parts, should go to the Logistic Canon of the Semicircle: and there he will have the Antilogarithms for that, and the Logarithms for the monthly [Argument]. Let him seek the Antilogarithm there, and the Logarithm with the monthly [Argument]. Conversely, when the sum of both Logarithms must be extracted most accurately, compare it with the *Heptacosia* <note>Kepler’s table of 700 parts, used for sexagesimal calculations</note>, extracting the Scruples from the Sexagesimal table.

<margin>3.</margin> <margin>Logistics are readier for these.</margin> Next, what I have sought by bringing Logarithms into this Table—namely, that the preceding book [might be used] without the necessity of going to the *Heptacosia* and the Canon of Logarithms of the Semicircle—the use of moderate Logistic calculation can provide the same. For then, instead of two Logarithms, we will extract a pair, and we will multiply each by its own Argument; instead of multiplication, there will remain the halving and the addition of the double to the half. In this way also the relevant part of this Equation will come forth, to be fermented <note>Kepler uses "fermenting" (fermentanda) to mean adjusting or processing a value further</note> as above.
For this relevant portion, now extracted for the fourth time, is either to be added or subtracted according to its title, which in the upper parts is either: "Subtract" or "Add." The arrangement is not uniform; it is fermented as being of more or equal value; the stronger part [is that which] was suppressed when it was extracted with the Monthly [Argument]: namely, Subtraction in the first Monthly [Argument], and Addition in the Second, between 180° and 360°. Regarding this non-uniform arrangement of the title, I will deal with it at greater length in what follows.

<margin>4.</margin> *But concerning the "outlier" <note>exfortem</note> there is one exception, and that is very rare, nor of any importance except for quibbling if it is neglected: namely, if by the command of the Title, it must be subtracted from the Relevant [portion], but it is larger than it. In that case, the Relevant [portion] is subtracted from the Outlier, as the larger value: and then the remainder, which will be of a clearly minimal quantity, must be taken.*

# RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS

### PRECEPT 116

The **Title** <note>In these tables, a "Title" refers to a label or heading indicating whether a value should be added or subtracted.</note> opposite to that which was found in the border of the **Monthly Table** must be used.

*As in the next example, when the **Elongation** <note>The angular distance between the Sun and Moon as seen from Earth.</note> is 67° 28', the Logarithm 96000 is extracted; the Title is **Exfors** <term>Exfors</term><note>A technical term used by Kepler to describe a specific component of the lunar equation that acts "outside the force" of the primary orbital motion.</note> 2' 25". When the Title from the bottom of the same table, with a Monthly value of 328° 9', is brought in from below, the Title of the **Exfors** is deleted, while the **S.** <note>Likely "Subtractory" or "South."</note> of the former is retained. Then, the Logarithm 63700 is extracted, along with the **Scruples** <note>Minutes of arc.</note>, to which the Title is attached from the top or bottom of that border.*

*Finally, the **fermentation** <note>Kepler uses "fermentation" to describe the process of compounding or adjusting different parts of an equation.</note> occurs: Logarithm 24' 16" through the Monthly Logarithm 13' 10". Then the fermentation of Logarithm 28' 8" results in the value 95914 extracted from the Canon; these are given from the top of that border. Then, with 328° 9', the value is 63923; the sum is 12' 8" in the **Heptacosias** <note>Kepler's specific logarithmic system based on the number 700,000.</note>. Double this (24' 16") with its half (6' 4") makes the sum 30' 20" for the **Logistic Complement**. The chosen Title commands the "firmament" added from the **Exfors**; thus the fermented value becomes 32' 45", to which the Title **Ar.** <note>Likely "Additory."</note> previously attached to the Logarithm is owed. This, according to the simplicity of the Hypothesis, is entirely the first absolute Monthly equation. Regarding the later title, I shall advise further.*

->**To learn the Variation of the lunar motion.**<-

### PRECEPT 117

By Tycho’s own method, the **Variation** <note>The "Variation" is a lunar inequality that causes the Moon to move faster at new and full moon, and slower at the quarters.</note> is extracted thus: subtract the position of the Sun (or the point opposite the Sun, if that is closer) from the position of the Moon, to establish the **Elongation**. To this, the monthly equation is either added or subtracted, as the Title directs. 

<margin>Tables fol. 83</margin>When the Elongation has been thus equated, the **Variation**—either the Tychonic version (diminished) or the demonstrative version (augmented)—is extracted from the Monthly Table. The Tychonic version is found in the Monthly Table; the demonstrative version is found in the table at the bottom of the Monthly section. You may use whichever you desire, whether to follow the author or to test the reliability of either by comparing observations. The Table of Variation for the border in which the Elongation was found will show the demonstration; by the agreement of entry from the border of Elongation to the titles of either the bottom or the top, it will show: namely, **Additory** in the first quadrant of Elongation, and **Subtractory** in the second.

This, I say, is the Tychonic way. But it could be asked here what the "mean" is—that is, how much the Elongation from the Sun (or its opposite) pulls back or adds, so that the absolute position of the Moon is produced. But there, it establishes a whole degree of Elongation, without even a single second being gained. Therefore, the sixteenth parts remain, or

<column-break/>

the Elongation of the Moon (☽) from the Sun (☉), the North Node (☊), or the South Node (☋) is 22 ½°: where the maximum difference of the extractions does not exceed 30".

### PRECEPT 118

Having determined the positions of the Sun and the Moon’s Apogee, and having assumed the true position of the Moon through all Equations in the vicinity of that same time: to track the corresponding **Mean Anomaly**.

SUBTRACT the position of the Apogee from the position of the Moon, so that the **Equated Anomaly** (or its complement to the full circle) remains. Also subtract the position of the Sun from the position of the Moon, so that the **True Elongation** remains. From this, extract the **Variation** with its Title. Then form 

<margin>As in Precept 117, 84, 113, 114, 115.</margin> 
both Arguments, and through them, the monthly equation with its Title. Thirdly, extract the **Mean Anomaly** either with the **Anomaly of the Eccentric** or with the **Equated Mean Anomaly**. And by the complement to the circle, [keep them] always equal; and if through the precepts you likewise restore the Mean Anomaly, and correct it both by the Variation and the monthly Equation, it will respond correctly by way of the title.

<margin>By using the contrary inter-column space, as in Precept 82, by dividing itself.</margin>
For the sake of clarity, I will deduce this precept from the Tables to **Diagram VI**, so that it may appear how it is done geometrically.

<margin>In Diagram VI.</margin>
Let the line of the Apogee be **T A**, the line of the Sun's position **T S**, its opposite **T V**, and the line of the true position of the Moon (through the Earth ♁ and all equations) be **T G**. Let the measure of the Mean Anomaly be the amount of time the Moon has consumed in the arc **F G A**, assuming that at **A** is the fixed position of the Sun or its opposite. First, the Angle **A T V** (between the opposite Sun ☉ and the Moon's Apogee ☽), or **C T O** and **G T**, is given. Therefore, the Area and Angle **C T N** are easily obtained, namely by multiplying the height **T N** into half the base **N C**. This area is the **Exfors** particle. Next, the Angle **A T G** and the complement of the Equated Anomaly are given. Therefore, the Arc **A G** of the **Eccentric Anomaly** is calculated without difficulty; in the counting, the Sector **A C G** is equal to it. Therefore, by multiplying the sine **A G** into half the eccentricity **T O**, the area of the triangle **T G C** is obtained, which, when seen broadly and added to the Sector **A G**, constitutes the **Released or Periodical Mean Anomaly** of the arc **A G**. This, together with **A T V** and **A G E**, has the measure of the angle **E A**; **E G**, and its complement to the semicircle **G R**. Therefore, by multiplying the sine of area **G R** into half of **C N** (the monthly eccentricity), the area of triangle **T G C** is created, representing the competent part of the **Monthly Equation**. This, together with the **Exfors** **N T C** and **T G O**, creates the competent **fermentation**, which signifies the time or delay during which the Moon [lingers], due to the Moon's excess and the distance from the Apogee here at **V**. Thus, the complement of the Mean Anomaly **T G O** [and] **T A G** are to be subtracted from the Mean Anomaly itself.

## [Page 86]

Thirdly, the angle $S T M$ is given, which is the angle of the **Elongation** <note>The angular distance between the Sun and the Moon as seen from Earth.</note> of the Moon from the Sun. Therefore, the proportion of the area of the Triangle $T \zeta \sigma$ to the maximum of a quadrant—which is valued at 45' 30"—is also given. This, then, is the third equation, called the **Variation**, but in this method, it is once again employed as a measure of time. This value is therefore subtracted from the **Mean Anomaly** <note>The average position of the Moon in its orbit, calculated as if it moved at a constant speed.</note>, because the Moon is before the position of the **Quadrature** <note>The point where the Moon is 90 degrees from the Sun, such as a Half Moon.</note> at point $M$, moving toward the Sun at $S$. It travels through $S G$ more swiftly—that is, in a shorter time—which it compensates for by its slowness through $G M$. Thus, the Mean Anomaly corresponding to the arc $GA$ is composed of three areas: $GAT$, $GOT$, and $\zeta \sigma T$, following the value of the five-twelfths proportion. Just so much time would remain for the Moon from $G$ until it reaches $A$, the **apogee** <note>The point in the Moon's orbit furthest from the Earth.</note>, if it were to undergo no monthly equation at that point.

<margin>PRECEPT 119.</margin>
## HOW THE POSITION OF THE MOON AT ANY PROPOSED TIME IS TO BE CALCULATED BY THE INDIRECT PATH, ACCORDING TO THE NATURE OF THE Physical Hypothesis.

<margin>
By Precept 76.
By Precepts 81, 77, 79.
Tables, folio 88.
Precepts 82, 88.
By Precept 118.
</margin>
FIRST, from the Tables of mean motions, the positions of the Moon and the Apogee are collected from the equinox, and from these, the **Mean Anomaly** is formed. Or, if the time were converted into **Sexagesimals** <note>Base-60 units of time or measurement.</note> and **Scruples** <note>Small fractions of a degree or day; minutes.</note> of days, the Mean Anomaly could be collected immediately from its own **Canon** <note>A table of pre-calculated values.</note>. With this, the "equated" value is extracted, and through this, a "fictitious" position of the Moon is formed, as if it were at a **Copula** <note>original: "Copula"; a term Kepler uses for a specific alignment or meeting point in his tables.</note>. Then, by applying the position of the Sun, if the time is found to be outside of a Copula, one proceeds to the Mean Anomaly for this fictitious position, to be corrected as if it were the true one. And because the correction never reaches three degrees, it will be useful in that place—and is always permitted for one who disregards tiny and imperceptible details—to subtract that very correction from the fictitious position of the Moon if it increased the Anomaly, or to add it if it decreased it. But if an accurate position is sought, the process should be repeated, assuming another position for the Moon that is one, two, or even three whole degrees (as the case requires) either further ahead than the fictitious position if the Mean Anomaly was decreased, or further back if it was increased. Thus, having corrected the Mean Anomaly a second time, one will also have the difference of both corrections corresponding to the whole degrees of the Sun's positions, and therefore the portion corresponding to a single degree. Then, from the Mean Anomaly collected with the time, subtract the nearest smaller corrected value; let the remainder (so that we do not act too scrupulously even now) be added to that position of the Moon which had been assumed for that correction. In this way, the desired position of the Moon will finally be determined with sufficient exactness. However, the curious may first divide the small portion to be added by the value corresponding to one degree, using the **Heptacosias** <note>Kepler’s table of logarithms based on the number 700,000.</note> if they wish, and then add the quotient for that small portion.

Because this process is not the primary one, I shall refrain from burdening the book with examples; I proceed to the other method, in which the accurate will find less to desire, and those slower of wit will find more to complain about.

<column-break/>

### To reduce the portion of the Equation belonging to the area into the form of an angle.

<margin>PRECEPT 120.</margin>
THUS FAR, as the **Hypothesis** <note>Kepler’s physical theory of planetary motion.</note> required, the value was the area of a triangle and an alteration of the Mean Anomaly rather than the Moon's position, which it left untouched. Therefore, so that it may accommodate itself to **Old Astronomy** <note>The traditional method of calculating positions as angles on a circle rather than areas of an ellipse.</note>, and so that it might "equate" the fictitious position instead—while leaving the Mean Anomaly given for the proposed time untouched (as the titles of the tables command)—it must first be reduced to an angle. This reduction is done through the **Intercolumn** <note>The difference between values in adjacent columns of a table.</note> of the Anomaly. For either with the "fermented" **Competent** <note>A technical term for a specific adjusted value in Kepler’s calculations.</note>, take the Logarithm from the **Heptacosias**, and add the Logarithm of the Intercolumn to it if it is less than one degree, or subtract it if it is greater; with the sum or remainder, extract the **scruples** from the Heptacosias, and the Equation will now have been converted into the value of an angle. Or, without Logarithms, multiply the Intercolumn itself by the fermented Competent, which will be less tedious for those practiced in **Logistics** <note>The art of calculation or arithmetic.</note>. For here, in the handling of Logarithms, the matter sometimes falls back to the cautions in Chapter V. Thus, this equation will finally be capable of its title.

*As in our Example, since the Mean Anomaly is 37° 4', the Intercolumn is 55' 50", which is less than one degree; therefore, the Logarithm 7184 is added to the Logistic Logarithm 60544 of the value 32' 45". The sum, 67728, gives 30' 28" as the **Reduced** value. Or multiply 55' 50" by 32' 45", and you will find the same amount.*

<margin>Reason for the Reduction.</margin>
It is asked here: if the area of the triangle in the arcs near the Apogee is additive by the nature of the Hypothesis, why then is it made subtractive here and in the Tables, in the manner of Old Astronomy? And what is the cause of this reduction of an Area to an Angle, or what is the foundation of this matter? I answer from the first Diagram. If, as often as the form of the Month changes, the Table of the Moon’s equations had to be changed because of the growing monthly equation in the areas of triangles $O \sigma N$ and $O B N$—specifically, the Mean Anomalies of the cells had to be increased—there would be almost no shortcut for calculation from the Tables. Therefore, the Mean Anomaly of the Table is left to itself, consisting of parts $A C \sigma$ and $T C \sigma$. But if it were to be increased, a smaller angle is assigned to it rather than $A T \sigma$, the angle of the equated position in the Table. For if the angle of the equated position is established in a longer time than the time of each cell, which corresponds to the cell directly: therefore, by equivalence, if we suppose the correct time to be expressed by two numbers of the cell subordinate to each other, even outside of copulas: the arc or angle of the equated Anomaly will be made smaller than that which corresponds to the cell for the Copulas in the Table. <margin>The Hypothesis does not support an exact parallel.</margin> Therefore, having drawn $C k$ roughly parallel to $T \sigma$, since $K C \sigma$ and $C T \sigma$ become equal, the arc of the **Eccentric** <note>An off-center circle used in older astronomy to explain varying orbital speeds.</note> completed outside the copulas, $S K$, will now be assigned to the Mean Anomaly $A T \sigma$ found in the Table. And that will be seen in the angle of the equated Anomaly $S T K$, not $S T \sigma$ (which is in the Table), serving the Sun's copulas. Thus, from the area $C \sigma N$, which was to be added to the Mean Anomaly or the triangular area $A \sigma T$, there is made an angle $\sigma T K$, to be taken away from the equated value of the Table $S T \sigma$.

<header>RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS</header>

<margin>What the Reduction does.</margin>
However, let this not be done without the **reduction** <note>A mathematical adjustment to account for the difference between the Moon's actual path and the plane of the Earth's orbit.</note>, because the area of the triangle Sun-Moon-Earth (☉ σ N) is long toward the **Apogee** <note>The point in the orbit farthest from Earth.</note>, and its angle ☉ σ N is conversely acute. Toward the **Perigee** <note>The point in the orbit closest to Earth.</note>, however (that is, at an equal distance from it), the area is small and its angle is large. Therefore, from the areas themselves, that angle does not have its exact measure. The Reduction performs this task: that from any area of the Triangle Sun-Moon-Earth (☉ σ T), the genuine angle representing it may be extracted; namely, so that a large area provides an acute angle, and a small area a more obtuse one, and thus both are accommodated to the purpose.
<margin>See the Letter on pages 808, 809.</margin>

### To present the monthly Equation as simultaneously competent, fermented, and reduced.
<margin>PRECEPT 121.</margin>

Combine three **Logarithms** <note>Kepler was an early adopter of logarithms to simplify complex astronomical multiplications into additions.</note>—of the Annual Argument, the Monthly Argument, and the Intercolumn—into one sum, if the latter is less than one degree. If, however, the Intercolumn is greater than one degree, subtract its Logarithm from the sum of the other two. The Logarithm formed in this way, taken from the column of <term>Scrupula</term> <note>Latin: *scrupula*. Here referring to small units of measurement, specifically minutes and seconds of arc.</note> in the Monthly Table (or more correctly from the *Heptacos* <note>Kepler’s "Heptacosiform" table of logarithms.</note>), shows the minutes, the double and half of which will compose the **Competent** and **Reduced** values, but which must then finally be **fermented** <note>Kepler uses "fermentation" as a metaphor for a complex mathematical blending or correction of astronomical variables.</note> according to the laws already dictated. In this way, we shall nowhere err by more than 17 seconds.

> As in the Example: the sum of the three Logarithms 95914, 63923, and 7184 (since the Intercolumn is not greater than 60') becomes 167021, which gives 11' 17''. The double of this is 22' 34'', the half is 5' 39'', and the sum is 28' 13''. Ferment this by the <term>Exfortis</term> <note>A specific correction factor in Kepler's lunar theory, likely meaning "outward force" or an external adjustment.</note> value of 2' 25''; it becomes 30' 38'', which is only 10 seconds greater than the correct value.

### To form the Equation of Light, or the composite monthly equation.
<margin>PRECEPT 122.</margin>

<margin>By Precept 115.</margin>
1. **F**irst, let the **Competent** part of the monthly Equation be sought out as a single element, and let its own title be assigned to it, both fermented and reduced to the value of the angle.
2. Second, by subtracting the position of the Sun (or the opposite of the Sun) from the assumed position of the Moon, let its **Elongation** <note>The angular distance between the Sun and the Moon.</note> be established, to which the monthly Equation is either added or subtracted, as its title requires.
3. Third, with the Elongation thus equated so that it is nearly true, extract from the monthly Tables (which are located on the edges of the left side) the **Variation**—either the diminished Tychonic version or the increased demonstrative version, as one prefers, either following the author or testing the reliability of either by comparison of observations. This will be the second element. Assign to it the title placed above or below the Variation (not the edge). The Tychonic column will show this title by its proximity to the edges; the demonstrative Table will show it by the opening of the entry from the edges to the titles—for instance, *Additive* in the first quadrant of Elongation, *Subtractive* in the second.
<margin>By Precept 116.</margin>
4. Fourth, if the titles of the elements are similar, combine them into one sum, adding the common title; if they are dissimilar, subtract the smaller from the larger and 

<column-break/>

place the remainder, assigning the title of the larger. Thus the composite **Equation of Light** <note>In this context, the "Equation of Light" refers to a correction in the calculation of time and position, not the speed of light as understood in modern physics.</note> will be formed.

> As in our Example: the reduced Competent value was 30' 28''. But the assumed position of the Moon at 2° 5' Gemini was distant from the opposite of the Sun at 5° 22' Libra by 146° 43'. Therefore, add 30' 30'', making the nearly-true Elongation 147° 13' 30'', which gives a Tychonic Variation of 36' 53'' with the title *Subtract*, as it nears the bottom of the ascending edge where the Elongation occurs. The *Demonstrative* Variation separately is 46' 40'', also with the title *Subtractive*, because access to this title is open from the edge of the Elongation at the foot of the Table. But (omitting that now) because 30' 28'' is to be added and 36' 53'' is to be subtracted, there will remain 6' 25'' to be subtracted for the Equation of Light.

## DESCRIPTION OF THE TABLE OF THE EQUATION OF LIGHT or the composite equation.

<margin>Laborious.</margin>
<margin>Hebrew examples.</margin>
<margin>Origanus.</margin>
<margin>Magini.</margin>
<margin>Why narrow?</margin>
**S**ince this monthly Equation, though originating quite simply, created so much trouble in calculation, it seemed right to assist the less leisurely calculators by computing a peculiar Table that would perform all this variety and show that little bit we seek with a single entry. You have in it, therefore, a no small part of twenty years of cares: so many times has it been made and reshaped through writings, drawings, machines, and multiform calculation, until it both encompassed the full force of the Hypothesis and rendered it with as much brevity as possible. In this part, I have followed the **Hebrew Astronomers** <note>Kepler likely refers to medieval Jewish astronomers whose tables were known for their efficiency.</note>, whose tables I have seen in Hebrew characters, proceeding by sixes of the Moon's Anomaly and individual degrees of the Moon's Elongation from the Sun. I followed **Origanus** <note>David Origanus (1558–1628), a German astronomer.</note> to an extent, who cast both equations—of the Absolute and the Monthly Anomaly—into one sum, and made its entire series additive by subtracting a suitable quantity from the **Epochs** <note>The reference points in time used for astronomical calculations.</note> of mean motions. But these men as yet knew nothing of the **Variation** and had not woven it in. Therefore, I profess a more accurate guide for this deed to be **Magini** <note>Giovanni Paolo Magini (1555–1617), an Italian astronomer.</note>, who in his *Supplement to the Ephemerides* consumed 52 full pages in the texture of such a table; yet even he was not yet bound by those laws that would make the entire semicircles dissimilar through the intervention of the *Exfortis* particle. By that logic, his number of pages would have been doubled to 104. He proceeded by threes of the Anomaly and individual degrees of the Moon's Elongation from the Sun. To me, this multitude of pages also seemed something to be avoided, since I have experienced that from the turning of so many pages and the searching of arguments through them, there is born a labor and weariness—and even damage to the eyes—not lightly to be ignored. Thus I have acted: the 26 page-openings of Magini (or even 52, if he were commanded to express a natural Hypothesis) I have contracted into a single one, transferring to the mind a part of the trouble that the eyes would have undergone from the page; so that the mind might gather a proportional part here and there, since the headers of the Tables jump by only five degrees and the margins by three.

Therefore, in the header and the foot are placed five-degree increments, not of the annual Argument—there is no need for that—but simply of the distance of the Sun, or of its opposite

opposite the Moon’s Apogee <note>The point in the Moon's orbit farthest from Earth.</note>; in the margins, both right and left, are three-degree increments—not of the monthly Argument (as that was not necessary), but simply of the Elongation <note>The angular distance</note> of the fictitious or "first-equated" position of the Moon from the Sun itself; for these run all the way to 360 degrees. ### How the composite Equation of LIGHT is to be extracted from its Table?

<margin>
Tables, pages 84, 85.
PRECEPT 123.
</margin>

For this task, two subtractions are required: specifically, that of the position of the Moon's Apogee from the true position of the Sun, and that of the Sun from the fictitious or first-equated position of the Moon—two operations we have frequently used until now. If the distance of the Sun from the Moon's Apogee is less than a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>, then with both distances found through these subtractions, however large the latter may be, the entry into the Table will be clear.

<margin>
It differs therefore at times from the Annual Argument.
</margin>

But if the distance of the Sun from the Moon's Apogee exceeds a semicircle: first, both distances must be transposed into opposite semicircles, which is done by either the addition or subtraction of 180 degrees (or 6 signs).

Then the distance of the Sun from the Moon's Apogee (either the original value or, if required, the changed one) is sought at the **Front** <note>Top</note> of the Table; while the distance of the Moon from the Sun (again, either the original in the first case or the changed one in the second) is sought in one of the inner margins, into which the entry from the Front is open and not blocked by lines.

<margin>
Let the calculator make the scale more evident where it is less clearly marked, following the traces of the letters, especially the descending lines.
</margin>

If the area common to both falls on that part of the Table—divided by the transverse scale—in whose margin the distance of the Moon from the Sun was found, then the extraction can be done correctly. If, however, the middle Scale stands between the intersection area and the margin where the Moon-Sun distance was found, then the Front must be abandoned; one must then look for the same Sun-Apogee distance at the **Heel** <note>Bottom</note> of the table, and the Moon-Sun distance in one of the outer margins, into which the entry from the Heel is not blocked. In this way, the common area will stand (in respect to the scale) on the same side that showed the Moon's distance. And then that which is found in this meeting point or common area will be the **Equation of LIGHT** in Degrees and first Minutes; to which the chosen edges apply the title commonly assigned to them: for example, the Front with the inner margins is the *Subtractor*, and the Heel with the outer margins is the *Adder*.

#### EXAMPLE OF THE FIRST CASE.

Suppose the two distances found by subtraction are: Sun from Apogee, 150°; Moon from Sun, 230°. Since the first is less than a semicircle (180°), it is sought at the Front; and the distance of the Moon from the Sun, though exceeding a semicircle, is likewise sought in the margins connected to the Front. It is 

<column-break/>

found in the right-hand margin, since it is greater than a semicircle. The intersection also occurs on the right side of the Scale, and thus on the side of the margin being used. Therefore, the area is suitable for extraction. And since the margin for 231° gives 0° 56', and the margin for 228° gives 0° 51', the proposed margin of 230° will give approximately 0° 55'. To this Equation of Light, the title from the intersection of the front and the right inner margin is applied: *Subtr.* <note>Subtract</note>.

#### EXAMPLE OF THE REMAINING CASES.

Suppose the distances found by subtraction are: Sun from Apogee, 230°; Moon from Sun, 190°. Since the first distance (of the Sun) exceeds a Semicircle, a Semicircle (180°) must be cast off from both, leaving 50° for the Sun and 10° for the Moon. The required Sun distance of 50° being sought at the Front, the Moon's distance of 10° falls in the left inner margin, as it is less than a semicircle; and the intersection occurs on the left side of the Scale. Therefore, the area is fit for extracting the Equation of LIGHT, which is shown as 0° 2' *Subtr.*

Using that same distance of the Sun from the Apogee (230°), let the distance of the Moon from the Sun be 171°. After casting off the semicircle, we have the Moon at 351° in the right inner margin; but the intersection occurs to the left of the scale, showing 2' *Subtr.* as before, but erroneously, because the scale stands between the intersection and the chosen margin. Therefore, leaving the Front, let the Sun's distance of 50° be sought at the Heel, and the Moon's distance of 351° in the outer margins, which are connected to the Heel. This distance, being greater than a semicircle, will be found on the right; the intersection will also be toward the right from the scale. Thus, 0° 3' is correctly extracted from this area with the title *Add*.

Likewise in the *Genethlialogy of RUDOLPH* <note>original: "Genesi RUDOLPHI" — likely referring to the calculation for a specific birth chart or example case</note>, when the Sun's position at 5° 22' Libra is subtracted from the Moon's fictitious position of 2° 5' Cancer, the Elongation remains 326° 43'. Subtracting the position of the Apogee at 27° 54' Taurus from the Sun's position, the Elongation of the Sun from this Apogee remains 67° 28'. Seeking the latter between 65° and 70° at the front of the Table, and the former in the right inner margin, they show an area in the intersection sloping from the scale toward the margin where the Moon-Sun Elongation was sought. Therefore, despite its long distance from this margin, it remains valid. It shows an Equation of Light between 3' and 10', that is, 6½', with the title of the common corner being *Subtr.*

## HOW THE MOON'S POSITION IN ITS ORBIT IS TO BE CALCULATED FROM THESE TABLES BY THE DIRECT PATH, MORE ACCOMMODATED TO ANCIENT ASTRONOMY?

<margin>
PRECEPT 124.
</margin>

<margin>
By precept 88, or more briefly below through the subsidiary tables.
</margin>

FIRST, let the fictitious position of the Moon be calculated, namely through the first equation of the Resolved Anomaly. If it happens that at that same moment the Moon is exactly joined with or opposite to the Sun <note>A Syzygy: New or Full Moon</note>, that fictitious position will simultaneously be the true position.

<margin>
Why is it called a fictitious position?
</margin>

Even if the "Copula" <note>The conjunction or opposition</note> does not coincide, this fictitious position will still be useful, both for investigating the nearby Copula, and simultaneously for the further equation (in respect to which this position is called "fictitious")...

<header>PRECEPTS OF RUDOLPH</header>
<meta>catchword: True</meta>

...for calculating the true position, by means of the Equation of Light. <note>In 17th-century astronomy, an "equation" is not a formula with an equals sign, but a "correction" added or subtracted to move from an average (mean) position to an actual (true) one.</note>

If, however, the position of the Moon is to be sought outside of the Syzygies <note>original: "Copulas" — the points of New and Full Moon</note>, and not because of the Syzygies, one can proceed by a double path.

<margin>By precepts 119, 118, 117, 115, 114, 113.</margin> I. Either by setting the fictitious position as the true one, and by a correction of the mean Anomaly <note>The angular distance from the Moon's farthest point from Earth</note>, as above. Here it often happens that the position of the Moon seems to be what is sought, but it is more advisable, once that is set as if already known, to seek and correct the mean Anomaly itself. For example, if you are commanded to find the position of the Moon at the hour of an observed Sun and Moon, it is better (once the position of Venus <note>The text likely refers to the "venero" or "venerable" position, but in context it may be a typo for a "set" position</note> is established as the true position of the Moon) to seek the mean Anomaly, and thus the time, and compare that with the given time; for this is easier.

<margin>By precepts 122, 121, 120, 116, 115, 114, 113.</margin> II. Or we proceed with the fictitious position by finding the Equation of Light. Then the labor is least through the Table, as he intended by his precept; we either add to or subtract from the fictitious position, and the position of the Moon in its orbit will be found. But because the Equation of Light is not obscured, but rather exactingly refined for the taste of the curious: let them, therefore, take upon themselves the labor—hardly a small annoyance, truly—of selecting the "monthly minutes" <note>small fractional corrections</note> from the Table, and by them forming this equation; and let them use it in the same way.

Thus, in the Rudolphine *Genesis* <note>original: "Genesi" — here referring to the "birth" or foundational calculation example in the back of the book</note>, when the fictitious position of the Moon is 2° 5' 15'' of Aries. The Equation of Light is 6', or more exactly 6' 25''. By subtracting, the more absolute position of the Moon in its orbit will therefore be 1° 58' 50'' of Aries.

Here, because the two elements of the Equation of Light become angles, and thus three equations, they associate as many lines of the Moon's motion—fictitious, near-true, and true—with the line of mean motion: it is expedient to represent this variation to some extent. 

<margin>Application of the Precept to Diagram 8.</margin> Therefore, if the first equality of the Moon were to be at **B**, and the line of the fictitious position **T B**, but through the appropriate monthly adjustment (from its area **T Q**, converted into the angle **B T Q**), it is moved to **Q**, so that it becomes the line of the near-true position **T Q**, cutting the small circle at **π**, then showing the arc of Variation **ϱ π T**, which, converted into an angle, equals **Q T X**: the line of the Moon's absolute position will therefore be **T X**. Thus, from the monthly addition **B T Q** being added, and from the Variation **Q T X** being subtracted, the final Equation of Light **X T B** is produced as an additive, and the Moon—on account of the first equation—is at **B**; on account of the second, at **Q**; and on account of the third, at **X**, which is the truest position.

But again I warn that no one should think those three lines (in Diagram 8) emerging from the Center of the Earth represent anything less than a single position for the Moon; in reality, those three are entirely the same as the equations.

And now all parts of the calculation have been summoned to the laws of Geometry; so that no case can easily exist which cannot be reduced to one of these eight Diagrams and explained by these little Commentaries. I hope, however, that students of the art, having overcome the difficulty of the short time it takes to learn this novelty of positions, will thereafter find it a most pleasant wrestling-ground for exercising Geometry. For the rest, for those who withdraw from this exercise, rushing toward the end of the calculation, provision has been made regarding the Table of the Equation of Light, or

<column-break/>

composite table, which will relieve them of all this labor and the anxiety of such precautions.

### CHAPTER XVII.
## CONCERNING THE MONTHLY LATITUDE OF THE MOON,
and its Tables.

<margin>Precept 118</margin> Regarding the retrograde circuit of the Nodes <note>The points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path</note>, the double monthly latitude, and the simple latitude of the Moon which it has in the Eccentric—yet never pure, except in the Syzygies—either of the Moon itself (according to Tycho) or of the Node with the Sun, and its monthly ratio, the whole is from the discovery of Tycho [Brahe] himself; although traces might perhaps exist elsewhere in some observations of the ancients.

<margin>Variation of latitude</margin> <margin>Monthly form in doubt</margin> However, the matter is not yet clear in every part. For Tycho, since he has the orbit of the Moon originate in the Syzygies; he also sends the Moon out from the Syzygies at a small monthly angle, when the Nodes of the Moon exist. But I have found that to be very much against the observations of Eclipses; as they are entirely distant by as great an angle as the latitude of the Moon becomes in the Quadratures <note>The quarter-moons</note>: let that whole month, in which the Sun was walking through the locations of the Nodes, remain for this Eccentric relative to the Ecliptic. And the Moon would then not only end up in a great latitude of 5° 18' in the Quadratures, but would also begin to deviate from the Sun at an angle equal to it. And yet, if the magnitude of this angle were always constant through the Moon's whole journey from the Sun to its quadrature, the Moon could not—when it finds the Nodes in the Octants <note>The 45-degree points between Syzygy and Quadrature</note>—nevertheless have a very small latitude, which Tycho nonetheless confirmed by observations.

<margin>To what extent this Table and Tycho's will produce the same effect.</margin> <margin>See the Prologue to the Ephemerides.</margin> Because of this perplexity, I was engaged for quite a long time in great errors; while with one hand I brought a remedy for the Eclipse, with the other I withdrew it again, falling back into Tychonic equivalence; as will appear immediately: if, however, I warn of this one thing now, while I was providing for it through these hypotheses of the *Progymnasmata* <note>Referring to Tycho Brahe's book "Astronomiae Instauratae Progymnasmata"</note>: if these are the things in which they are applied. In which, whatever diversity there may be between the two, it is worthwhile to observe diligently in the frequent precept. I more conveniently advise here that I have moved the position of the Node for our times to 2' 5''.

Therefore, whatever diversity in latitude results from this advancement must first be subtracted from the difference between the Tychonic calculation and mine: only then can a sound judgment be made concerning the equivalence of the Hypotheses. Therefore, to the work.

### To Seek the True Tychonic Latitude.

I say **"True,"** but with a necessary qualification: you must understand that according to Tycho’s <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the Danish astronomer whose data Kepler used to derive his laws.</note> opinion, we are seeking the "true" latitude here, yet it is not *absolutely* true, as the study of Eclipses requires further correction to his theory.

To find this Tychonic latitude, I provide two paths. These are equivalent to each other and to the method Tycho taught in Volume I of his *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho's "Introductory Exercises" to the new astronomy</note>, at least as far as his principles allow. For as I taught in the Prologue to the Ephemerides: Tycho assumed the maximum <term>simple latitude</term> <note>The Moon's basic distance from the ecliptic without secondary perturbations.</note> to be 4° 58' 30" (which is equal to his <term>equation of longitude</term>), with an "Excess" of 19' 0", making a total of 5° 17' 30". I, however, assume that simple latitude to be 5° 0' 0", which is likewise equal to my own equation of longitude and fits Tycho’s observations. I set the "Augmentation" at 18', for a total of 5° 18' 0", which is nearly the same as Tycho’s.

The first path is as follows: first, have ready the distance of the Moon ($\mathbb{C}$) from the <term>Node</term> ($\Omega$) <note>The Node is the point where the Moon's orbit crosses the Earth's orbital plane.</note>, as instructed in the previous precept. Second, subtract the position of the Node ($\Omega$ or $\mho$) from the true position of the Sun ($\odot$), so that the distance of the Sun from the Node remains.

</margin>

Also look up the annual <term>Prosthapharæsis</term> <note>An "equation" or correction factor used to adjust mean motion to true motion.</note> of the Node ($\Omega$), titled according to the Tychonic equivalent, using the labels at the top or bottom of the table depending on whether you entered through the left side (descending) or right side (ascending). These titles refer to the position of the Node itself. Fourth, using this Prosthapharæsis, now correct the distance of the Moon from the Node (the "equable" distance found previously) by doing the *opposite* of what the titles suggest. Let the calculator, trained in Tycho’s *Progymnasmata*, not be hindered here by seeing me command the opposite of what Tycho ordered. It is not truly contradictory; rather, the different form of our equations requires it—Tycho’s is monthly, mine is annual—yet they reach a wonderful and unexpected equivalence.

### How do we find the true latitude, even for the necessity of Eclipses?

<margin>Tables, page 98, at the bottom.</margin>
Regarding the eclipses themselves, a shortcut will be provided in the third part of this work. However, to ensure that the same Hypothesis covers all latitudes and connects them in agreement, one must consider that Eclipses do not occur *only* when the Sun is exactly joined to the Nodes, but also when it is some distance from them, as far as the "Eclipse Limits" allow. If, therefore, this great inclination of the limit at the <term>conjunctions</term> <note>Latin: *copulis*. When the Sun and Moon meet.</note> is diminished as the Sun departs from the nodes, a yearly "libration" <note>A slow oscillation or swaying motion.</note> of the Nodes arises from this form of diminution, matching the monthly form of Tycho Brahe described in his *Progymnasmata*. Therefore, whatever value the magnitude of my angle gave to the Ecliptic latitudes, the yearly <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>A technical term for the 'correction' or 'equation' added or subtracted to a mean motion to find the true position.</note> of the Nodes will take away again.

This happened to me in my *Epitome of Astronomy* when I established the libration of the monthly limit upon an axis tied to the line of conjunctions. Meanwhile, in my *Ephemerides* <note>Kepler's published daily tables of planetary positions.</note>, I followed the logic of the limit's libration based on an axis independent of the Sun—specifically, on the line connecting the Nodes and the center of the Earth. By that logic, if no yearly correction is made to the Nodes, the latitude of the Moon is eliminated when it is in the Nodes or the <term>Octants</term> <note>Points 45 degrees away from the conjunction or opposition.</note>, which contradicts Tycho’s observations. For these reasons, I was forced to walk a middle path, introducing a doubled yearly (or

<margin>As in precepts 125 and 126.</margin>
<margin>In that work, pages 794, 818, and 821.</margin>
<margin>As in precept 126, which consequently hides the Node.</margin>
<margin>As in precept 125.</margin>
<margin>Therefore, this very precept restores it.</margin>

<column-break/>

quarterly) correction of the Node, as if from a new and separate principle. This was done so that when the Node is with the Sun, the correction is negligible, but in the Octants, it is total and equal to Tycho's monthly value. There is a perfect equivalence with Tycho’s system when the Node ($\Omega$ or $\mho$) is 45 degrees away from the Sun, either before or after; but when the Node is near the Sun, they are not perfectly the same. Thus, as the Sun departs from the Node, the minutes grow slowly, taking a part from the prior correction, and as the Sun approaches the Nodes ($\Omega$ $\mho$), they are slowly filled again. These are not from a semi-diametrical libration, but a diametrical one, just as the Hypothesis of the increase itself and its natural causes might have some kinship with the business of the **Variation** <note>A specific irregularity in the Moon's motion discovered by Tycho Brahe.</note>.

Thus, the latitude is 2' 27" Southern—one minute less than Tycho's in this example.

In the **RUDOLPHINE GENESIS** <note>Likely referring to the foundational calculation for the era of the tables.</note>, when the position of the Node by mean motion was 19° 5' Leo ($\Omega$) and the Moon was at 1° 59' Cancer ($\mathbb{C}$): the Moon precedes the Node by 47° 6', from which a simple latitude of 3° 39' 38" South is extracted, with a Reduction of 6' 32". Add this, because the Moon is approaching the node.

<margin>Precept page 55.</margin>
<margin>Precept 118.</margin>
This would be the case if there were a Conjunction; because there is not, I subtract the position of the Node (19° 5' Aquarius $\mho$) from the Sun's position (5° 22' Libra $\odot$), leaving 166° 17'. These give, from the Monthly Table, an Augmentation of the "Free Angle" of 17' 0", a Monthly Inclination of the limit of 17' 30", a Tychonic correction of 45' 38", and an Ecliptic correction of 9' 38"—both to be subtracted. I would add these corrections if the Moon followed the Node, doing the opposite of the labels; but because I have an arc of precedence (47° 6'), I subtract them from there: the true distance of the Moon from the Node remains—for Tycho 46° 20', and for me 46° 56'. The former gives a simple latitude of 3° 36' 52"; the latter gives me 3° 38' 40". The fifth parts are 43' 22" and 43' 44", which, multiplied by the 17' saved earlier, make 12' 17" and 12' 25". Add the former to 3° 36' 52", and the latter to 3° 38' 40"; the true Tychonic latitude is completed as 3° 49' 9" by the first path, and for me 3° 51' 5".

By the second path for Tycho: I subtract the Sun's position from the Moon's position; with the remainder of 326° 37', I extract 33' 3" minutes from the Monthly Table. I multiply these into the inclination of the limit (17' 30"), resulting in 9' 39", with a **Southern** label (because the Node is at 19 Leo, therefore the Southern limit in Aquarius is before the Sun, just as the Moon is relative to the Sun). I add this to 3° 39' 38" South, so it becomes the true latitude 3° 49' 17", which is the same as by the first path.

<margin>Tables, page 82</margin>
Furthermore, the distance of the Sun from the Node (346° 17') at the top of the Monthly Portion Table, and the distance of the Moon from the Sun (326° 37') in the right margin, show the same monthly portion, between 10' 0" and 9' 27", with the label of the shared corner being **Southern**.

<margin>Tables, page 86</margin>
Whoever honors or deserves the Nodes—that is, the sacred **Head of the Dragon** ($\Omega$) and the destructive **Tail** ($\mho$)—let them deal with the correction of the Nodes as the Label commands. For their motion here is also made unequal; but by the year, not by the month as it was for Tycho. This is the only difference in effect, but in which star? And how is it to be observed?
