<meta>This page continues the technical mathematical instructions for calculating the Moon's position. Having previously discussed the "monthly portion" of latitude, Kepler now moves toward the "Reduction to the Ecliptic"—the process of mapping the Moon's position from its own tilted orbital path onto the flat plane of the Earth's orbit (the ecliptic)—and begins the study of Parallax.</meta>

# RUDOLPHINE TABLES

### To reduce the position of the Moon in its orbit to the Ecliptic.

<margin>PRECEPT 129.</margin>
This is the **GENERAL** method. From the Table of Logarithms <note>original: "Canon Logarithmorum"</note> of the Semicircle, using the Degrees and Minutes <term>Minutes</term> <note>original: "Scrupulis." In early astronomy, minutes were often called "scruples," meaning small parts.</note> of the Moon's true distance from the location of the Node, find the difference between the <term>Antilogarithms</term> <note>The inverse of a logarithm, used here to find the actual value from a logarithmic scale.</note> corresponding to ten minutes. Using the true latitude, find the Antilogarithm itself; divide this by ten times that difference. The result will be the "Seconds of the Second Reduction," which are easily converted back into primary minutes by dividing by 60. This reduction should be subtracted from the position of a Moon that is moving away from the nearest Node, and added to one that is approaching it.

<margin>PRECEPT 130.</margin>
The **SPECIAL** methods of Reduction and certain specific cases are as follows: the first is when the Node is in <term>Quadrature</term> <note>A 90-degree angle relative to the Sun.</note> with the Sun. In that case, the Reduction is taken from the Table of Latitude, using the distance of the Moon’s true position from the Node. This column of the Table is useful for as many months as the Sun travels around the nodes. Furthermore, this Reduction is valid in every <term>conjunction and opposition</term> <note>New moons and full moons.</note> with the Sun, even if the Node is not in Quadrature; for then the latitude is similar to the Tychonic model <note>Refers to Tycho Brahe’s system of observation.</note> and does not differ by even one minute. It is said that this reduction is quite accurate; therefore, anyone may use it without exception and without significant loss of precision.
<margin>Tables, page 86.</margin>

<margin>See precept 112 and the note on page 77, line 5, at the end: "according to Tycho."</margin>
The second case occurs when the angle of the <term>Eccentric</term> <note>The off-center circular path used to model the orbit.</note> with the planet is larger; this is extracted from its own specific Table on page 98.
<margin>Tables, page 98.</margin>

->## CHAPTER XXVIII.<-
->### ON THE PARALLAXES OF THE MOON.<-

<margin>PRECEPT 131.</margin>
To find the Moon’s maximum Horizontal <term>Parallax</term> <note>The shift in a celestial body's apparent position when viewed from different points on Earth. This is crucial for pinpointing the Moon's exact location.</note>, as well as its apparent diameter, in the Table of Equations.

<margin>Tables, pages 80, 81. Note: watch the inter-column spaces.</margin>
In the columns for the <term>equated Anomaly</term> <note>The adjusted angular distance of the Moon from its furthest orbital point.</note>, let the difference between two adjacent lines be increased by its sixtieth part; this will result in the Horizontal Parallax. If that same sixtieth part is added to half of the Parallax, the result will be the Diameter.

<column-break/>

<margin>For example, if the Moon is at an Anomaly of 0° 0' or 180° 0', the equated difference here is 0° 57' 26". Add its sixtieth part (0' 57") to get a vertical parallax of 0° 58' 23". Here it is 1° 3' 44". The halves of these are 30' 8" and 31' 52"; if you add the previous sixtieth parts of 57" and 1' 3", the diameters of the Moon are 32' 5" and 33' 55".</margin>
<margin>Below, in the Third Part, you will be taught this method of extraction more accurately. For even the ancient hypotheses regarding the Moon's diameter are valid. Christian Severinus **Longomontanus** <note>Tycho Brahe's former assistant and a contemporary rival of Kepler.</note> attempted to encompass the same variety of physical and optical causes with the tools of the same calculus; but he did so in vain, for his effort used inconsistent angles and numbers, or was based on flawed judgment. *176.* See *Epistle to the Abbot, page 870. Also, Optics in Astronomy. And the Prologue to the Ephemerides of Danish Astronomy, Theory page 175.*</margin>
<margin>Indeed, when the Moon is near the <term>Zenith</term> <note>The point directly overhead.</note>, it shows a diameter larger by half a minute than when it is cast down toward the Horizon.</margin>

->## To investigate the Moon’s parallax of altitude.<-

<margin>PRECEPT 132.</margin>
Add the Optical Logarithm of the total parallax at the Horizon (in a cosine-like manner) to the first Logarithm of the Moon's altitude—which is the same as the Antilogarithm of the Moon's distance from the Zenith—which, when sought in the *Heptacosia* <note>Kepler’s book of 700 logarithms.</note>, provides the Parallax of altitude from its sixtieth parts.

<margin>Precept 146</margin>
In the "Optical Part of Astronomy," I provided a Table of Parallaxes for every single minute up to 66 at the top and bottom, distributed for every degree of distance from the zenith in the margin. Its use can follow Logarithms or other computations via triangles, if anyone dislikes this unusual or inconvenient method.
<margin>Precept 146. Tables, page 220 or 424. Vision.</margin>
<margin>The use of Parallax of Altitude.</margin>
When the sky is turbulent and only the Moon can be observed with instruments, so that the time may be derived from its altitude, the addition of the Parallax of altitude must first be arranged, so that the true altitude may be made from the visible one. Or, if observations are collected, this Parallax of altitude is subtracted from them, so that the true value remains.

Example of the general method from the *Origins of the Rudolphine Tables* <note>original: "Genesi RUDOLPHI"</note>. The true distance from the Sun was 46° 20'. If you look this up in the Table, the difference of the Antilogarithms for 10 primary minutes is 5. Dividing the ten-fold value of the Antilogarithm 222 (for a latitude of 3° 49' 4")—which is 2220—by this, gives a quotient of 444", which is 7' 24". The simple Table of Latitude had given 6' 32". Since the Moon is moving toward the Sun, add this Reduction of 6' 32" to its position of 1° 58' 50". If it is 1° 58' 50", the Ecliptic position of the Moon is 2° 6' 14".
<margin>Tables, page 98.</margin>

Furthermore, the calculation of Eclipses does not require the Parallax of altitude here, as is the case in other Tables.

If you have at hand the **Tables of Directions** by Regiomontanus (continued by Reinhold) or the **Tables of the Prime Mover** by Magini: having selected the altitude of the Pole <note>The observer's latitude.</note> for the intended location, add 90 degrees to the Right Ascension of the Midheaven. This forms the **Oblique Ascension of the Horoscope** <term>Horoscope</term> <note>In this context, the "Horoscope" refers to the Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>; find the degree rising there. This degree, when entered into its proper table and sought in the margins under the line for the given altitude of the Pole (at the top or bottom), will reveal the **Angle of the Orient** <note>The angle between the ecliptic and the horizon in the east.</note>.

However, he who lacks these books should return with his data to Chapter XIV of this work; there he will find several ways to track the Angle of the Orient through the data provided here.

One of these methods is as follows: subtract the declination of the culminating point <note>The Midheaven.</note> from the altitude of the Pole if it is northern; add it if it is southern. This gives you the distance of the culminating point from the **Zenith** <note>The point directly overhead.</note>. Then, by joining the **Logarithms** of this value and the extracted Angle, the sum—as an **Antilogarithm**—will show the Angle of the Orient. From this, one must then find the rising point itself, or the **Nonagesimal** <term>Nonagesimal</term> <note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the ascendant; it is the point highest above the horizon.</note> degree from it. This can be sought in our Table of the Angle of the Orient under the line of the correct altitude of the Pole, extracting this rising point of the Ecliptic from the right or left margin as the situation requires. Or, for more accuracy: take the Logarithm of the Angle of the Orient and subtract it from the Antilogarithm of the distance of the culminating point from the zenith; the remainder is the Antilogarithm of the arc between the Nonagesimal and the Meridian. This arc turns from the Meridian toward the parts opposite the nearby equinoctial point.

<margin>Precept 45</margin>
A second method uses the position of the angle of the orient as a known value, and the altitude of the culminating point, which is the complement of its distance from the zenith to a Quadrant (90 degrees).

<margin>Precept 46</margin>
There is also a third method in the said Chapter XIV.

Once the Nonagesimal is known, either directly or from the rising degree by counting back 90 degrees (or 3 signs) in our Hemisphere: compare the Moon's true place in the Ecliptic with it. For if the Moon is more to the east <note>original: "orientalior"</note> than that point, the parallax will tend toward the rising; if more to the west <note>original: "occidentalior"</note>, toward the setting. Therefore, having subtracted one from the other, write the Logarithm of the distance of the Moon (☽) from that point under the Logarithm of the Angle of the Orient for the **Parallax of Longitude**. For the **Parallax of Latitude**, write the Antilogarithm of the Angle of the Orient. Finally, place the Logarithm of the total horizontal parallax (either the logistic one with its sign or the canonical one) under both. Thus, for Longitude, reduce the three Logarithms into one sum; for latitude, reduce two. These two sums, sought among those Logarithms from which the Logarithm of Parallax was taken, show the Parallaxes: the former for Longitude, the latter for Latitude. If the Moon is east of the Nonagesimal, add the longitude parallax to the Moon's place; if west, subtract it. For Latitude, add the parallax to a true Southern latitude and subtract it from a Northern one to determine the visible place of the Moon in longitude and latitude. Unless, perhaps, the Moon's Northern latitude is smaller than the latitude parallax itself; in that case, the former must be subtracted from

<column-break/>

the latter, and the remainder will be the visible Southern Latitude, in place of the true Northern one.

These steps, then, are for the visible place of the **Center of the Moon**.

<margin>Extracting by precept 131.</margin>
But if the visible place of the **limbs** <note>The edges of the Moon's disk.</note> is needed: its apparent semi-diameter, added to the longitude and latitude of the Center, establishes the place of the limb—the Eastern one for longitude, and for latitude, that of its own region. If subtracted from the longitude and greater latitude of the Center, it establishes the place of the Western limb and the opposite region from that of the visible center. However, if the visible latitude of the center is smaller than the Moon's semi-diameter, the center's latitude is subtracted from the semi-diameter to find the latitude of the limb, which extends into the region opposite the center's latitude, but remains in its own proper region.

If the Southern Pole is elevated <note>i.e., if the observer is in the Southern Hemisphere.</note>, the use of the Tables of ninety Oblique Ascensions and our Table of the Angle of the Orient is the same, except you enter with an Ascension either increased or decreased by 180 degrees. For the rising degree you then extract, you must write the opposite degree in its place, while retaining the Angle. In that case, parallax increases Northern Latitude and decreases Southern. The rest is as above.

### E X A M P L E.

<margin>Observation of Venus (♀) and the Moon (☽)</margin>
*In the year of Christ 1625, on the 30th day of January (or February 9th), in the evening, at Erbach, Ulm, Tübingen, and throughout Swabia, Venus was seen as if in the embrace of the crescent Moon, or as others say, as if sticking to the left horn of the Moon. From that moment, it seemed gradually to go around the lower bright bulge of the Moon. From this it is understood that between the setting of the Sun and Venus, there was a central conjunction of the Moon and Venus in visible longitude, though the Moon was further North. Since the Sun set that day at Erbach at 4:53 PM, and Venus at 6:47 PM—as she was at 24° 42' of Aquarius (♒) with a Southern Latitude of 0° 53'—the time of Venus's setting was 6:47 PM. By the Tychonic equation of time, this was 6:57 PM equal time; and at Hven (Uraniburg) 7:09 PM. Her assigned place in the Ecliptic is found to be 24° 55' Aquarius, with a Southern Latitude of 0° 3' in Scorpio (♏); the total horizontal parallax is 63'.*

*The Moon's (☽) place was 21° 26' Aquarius, and its Right Ascension 323° 50'. Here we are given the apparent time at the very beginning as 6:47 PM; returning to this, we add it (converted into equatorial time as 101° 45') to the Right Ascension of the Sun (☉). Thus the Right Ascension of the Midheaven becomes 65° 35'. In this instance, we have no further need for the equation of time. The Midheaven culminates at 7° 24' Gemini (♊), with a Declination of 21° 37' and an Angle with the Meridian of 80° 30'. Since the Altitude of the Pole is 48° 30', subtracting the Declination gives the distance of the culminating point from the Zenith as 26° 53'. The Logarithm 79368 added to the Logarithm of the Angle 1381 makes 80749, the Antilogarithm of the Angle of the Orient 63° 31', for the Latitude Parallax. The Logarithm of this is 21086, which will later produce the Longitude Parallax. Now, subtracted from the Antilogarithm of 26° 53' (which is 11437), it leaves 351, the Antilogarithm of an arc of 4° 48'. This is the distance of the Nonagesimal from the meridian, or 7° 24' Gemini in the following signs, because the Sun in Aries (♈) is in the preceding signs. Thus the Nonagesimal is determined to be 12° 12' Gemini.*

*And because we have reached the knowledge of the Nonagesimal, before we pass to the parallaxes, we shall also process the example through other methods. For there was a second method, which uses one of the Angles of the Orient, which...*

The same result could also be achieved through the Logarithm of the Parallax from the Table of Sines 404000. For it produces the sums 413760 and 480700, which, when sought in the same table, give the former less than 55' and the latter more than 28'.

Because the Moon was further west than the nonagesimal <term>nonagesimal</term> <note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon; the highest point of the zodiac.</note>, the **parallax of longitude** of 54' 44'' must be subtracted from its position reduced to the Ecliptic, 25° 0' 49'' Pisces (♓). <margin>But applying the Monthly Equation of Time through Precept 171, in approximately 24° 50', there are 5' minutes of the Sun beyond Venus.</margin> Thus, the **parallax of latitude** of 28' 5'' is to be added to the true Southern latitude of 0° 3' 33'', and the apparent latitude is collected as 0° 31' 38'' South. The semi-diameter of the Moon (☽) was 16' 10''. And this, added to the latitude 31' 38'' South, makes the latitude of the southern margin 47' 48'' South. Therefore, Venus herself, at the hour of her setting, was five minutes further South than the lower margin of the Moon; but then the center of the moon had overtaken the position of Venus by visible motion by a little less than 19 minutes. Thus, about half an hour before the setting of Venus, the centers were joined according to longitude, at which time the Southern margin of the Moon had a latitude one or two minutes smaller, so that Venus could not have been covered by the passing margin. <margin>Or 18½ minutes of the Sun before setting, if the time before setting is taken monthly.</margin> For at the hour of Sunset, which was 4:53, the position <margin>Or 19 minutes after sunset, when the time is equated monthly.</margin> of the visible Center of the Moon, computed by the same method, is found in 24° 21' Pisces (♓), and Venus in 24° 42' Pisces (♓); and thus Venus was 21 minutes beyond the Moon and the tips of the horns, with 5' minutes of the Sun beyond the dark margin; and the Southern margin of the Moon, and thus also its outer horn, had an apparent southern latitude of 0° 47', while Venus had a latitude of 53', six minutes greater.

Therefore, during the entire time between the settings of both stars, the Southern margin of the Moon was higher than Venus and passed over it. The fact that she seemed to graze the very horn of the Moon was due to the **dilatation of light** <note>original: "dilatatione luminis"; an optical effect where bright objects appear larger than they are, creating a glow or "glare" around them.</note> of the Moon in the eyes of the spectators. The proof is that to others with more "humid" vision <note>Kepler suggests that people with watery eyes or different eyesight perceived the glare differently.</note>, she seemed as if immersed in the very embrace of the Moon’s light. This account cannot be used as an argument for either a larger latitude for the Moon or a smaller one for Venus. For if the Moon's horn at the hour of sunset had been further south than Venus herself, and if this had been the cause that offered the appearance of Venus in the embrace of the Moon, there would be no way Venus could have escaped a total occultation <term>occultation</term> <note>When one celestial body passes in front of another, hiding it from view.</note> under the Moon’s margin after half an hour. Yet others observed diligently that it was not a straight path, but after she came as if to a contact with the glowing horn, she afterwards moved around the curvature of its margin, which remained always visible.

Moreover, this appearance of "going around," which suggests a curved line of motion, has the same cause—not an astronomical one, but an optical one. For the more daylight remained, the less the splendor of the Moon was dilated; but the deeper one went into the night, the more it was amplified; so that the Moon's horn seemed to still touch Venus as if by contact, even though she had already moved further away.

# IN THE THIRD PART OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES: INSTRUCTIONS.
## CHAPTER XXIX.
### CONCERNING THE ECLIPSES OF THE SUN AND MOON

->TO BE PREDICTED.<-

*How to find the astronomical Golden Number <note>The Golden Number is a value in a 19-year cycle used to track the phases of the moon and determine the date of Easter.</note> proper to these Tables in any given year; and to designate the days of New Moons and Full Moons by it from afar.*

<margin>INSTRUCTION 134.</margin>
<margin>Tables, leaf 89.</margin>
If the current proposed year was counted backward from the birth of Christ: subtract the number of its completed years from the Heads of the Great Period, which is joined to the Type of the Golden Number; but if thereafter, or after Christ: add to it at least the Heads before Christ, or if it is so long that it exceeds, subtract from it that of that Head, or by one or another cast off [from the] Great Period, then the entire nineteen-year Cycles <note>The Metonic cycle of 19 years, after which the moon's phases recur on the same days of the year.</note>, or years 19, 38, 57, 76. What remains shall be diminished [by] the current Golden Cycle of civil years: or, if nothing remains, 19.

It falls, moreover, in the first year of the Calippic Period <note>A 76-year period used to refine the 19-year Metonic cycle.</note> of 76 years [or 84 for the Jews] before or after the noon of the 23rd day of March, the mean New Moon by as many hours as are found noted at the preceding subtracted Period. But for the following years, the Golden [number] after the moon is obtained from the mean New Moons; they take 36 hours on either side.

->E X A M P L E S.<-

*The Golden Number is sought for the year 3993 backward before Christ. Between the Type and the Great Cycle is inserted the Head with the number 3992 completed, the next largest being 6904; subtract the completed 3992, 2912 remain. From here subtract the smaller in the Great Cycle, 2860, and 12 remain. Subtract the course 3 and from here they are 9, 38 years until this Golden Number. But because this is 36 years before, that is Hour 4 and 11 minutes before the middle hours, subtract 36, 32 remain; but also for most mean moons they fall between two moments, of which one precedes the day by 40 hours, the other follows by 32 hours.*

*Thus in the year 1598 after Christ, since it is counted in order, being less than the Head of the Period after Christ 3297, add the minimum Head 1702, from which subtract 1696 found in the Great Period; then at 18 hours and 20 minutes after Noon, 6 remains: which since it does not exceed 19, it is therefore itself [the Golden Number]. The chief convenience of the Golden Number consists in this, that it indicates the locations of the New Moons through all—*
<column-break/>
—all the months of the year; the following in order, in the following year: and this through 100 years without notable variation, always returning from XIX to Unity.

*To designate Full Moons by the Golden Number.*

To <gloss>To</gloss> the Golden Number add both XV and IV (casting off XIX where the sum exceeds). In this way, two indicators of Full Moons will be formed approximately. For the Full Moon is either in the middle, or on the day which the latter signifies for the most part.

*To precisely bring forth the mean New Moon or Full Moon of any Roman Year and Month, whether before or after Christ.*

<margin>Chapter XVIII, leaf 51.</margin>

Observe the assigned order, whether the proposed current year be after Christ or before. For if it were after Christ: with the year in the margin, which was next smaller than the proposed current year, transcribe from the leftmost column the Epacts, days, and minutes; the remainder to the left is established at the noon of Uraniborg <note>The observatory of Tycho Brahe in Denmark, which Kepler used as his prime meridian.</note> on January 1st of the following year. Then subtract the ending years of the transcribed Epoch, as if they were completed, from the completed years of the proposed time, so that the interval of completed years that lie between is clear. Then with the thousands and with the hundreds of the interval, if it were only that much, transcribe similarly the Epact of the New Moon; the same below a hundred, the same with the Month, seeking from its own Table the one next preceding the proposed current one: to the transcribed original; which if the hours [exceed 24], cast off 24, and for those [add] unity to the number. # RUDOLPHINE TABLES
## [PART THREE: INSTRUCTIONS]

...of the proposed completed month, some New Moon precedes it. Therefore, if you subtract this interval of time from the sum of days immediately greater [than it], extracted from the Table of Syzygies <note>A 'syzygy' refers to the alignment of three celestial bodies—in this case, the Sun, Moon, and Earth—which results in a New or Full Moon.</note>, the remaining days, hours, and minutes will be of the current proposed month, which, once completed, the mean New Moon occurs.

<margin>On the same page, folio 99.</margin>
Note here that if, after the subtraction is made, there remains something less than the January Epact <note>The 'Epact' is the age of the moon in days on January 1st, used to synchronize solar and lunar years.</note>, the same sum must also be subtracted from the next larger value in the Table of Syzygies, so that it may appear whether something less than the length of the current month remains. For then, two New Moons will occur in that month: one at the beginning of the month, the other at the end.

Conversely, if the New Moon of February is sought, but by the use of the January Epact there remains something greater than the length of February (namely 28 or 29 days), that will belong to the beginning of March; and February will lack a New Moon. And therefore, through the February Epact, that same New Moon should be assigned to the beginning of March.

And since February shares a common Epact with January, and March in turn has two: it should be known that if the New Moon of April is to be collected, whichever of the two March values you use, the same New Moon will be produced.

<margin>For the Full Moon.</margin>
To the completed days and hours of the month in which the New Moon occurs, if you add half of the length of a lunation—14 days, 18 hours, 22 minutes, 2 seconds—you will have the completed times of the Full Moon, either of the same month or (if the numbers exceed the month's length) of the following month, after subtracting its total days.

<margin>For years before Christ.</margin>
If, however, the year was before the era of Christ: the number of that current year is subtracted from the immediately greater Epoch, but decreased by one unit, so that there remains an interval of completed years, and additionally the completed initial months of the proposed current year; which are to be used as before.

For example, let the current year be 622 <note>This refers to 622 AD, the year of the Hegira, the starting point of the Islamic calendar.</note> (simple), and let the mean New Moon for the current month of June be sought. In the Epochs of New Moons, the number immediately smaller (because it is after Christ) is 600, whose Epact is 21 days, 5 hours, 18 minutes, 48 seconds. There remain 21 completed years; and the Epact for the 21 ending years is 21 days, 13 hours, 50 minutes, 16 seconds. The Epact for the end of a simple June is 3 days, 19 hours, 35 minutes, 41 seconds. The sum of the three is 46 days, 14 hours, 44 minutes, 45 seconds. Subtracting this from the nearest larger value in the Table, 59 days, 1 hour, 28 minutes, 6 seconds, leaves 12 days, 10 hours, 43 minutes, 21 seconds. Therefore, the mean New Moon was on the 13th day of July, at 10 hours etc. after mean noon at Uraniborg <note>Uraniborg was the observatory of Tycho Brahe on the island of Hven, which Kepler used as his prime meridian.</note>; but in the East, at the hour of midnight. And indeed the Arabs, along with the Jews, began the day from the evening of that day, Friday <note>original: ♀ (Venus)</note> the 14th of July, when the mean New Moon was not yet completed. Therefore, the following evening, beginning for them the day of Thursday <note>original: ♃ (Jupiter). Kepler's weekday symbols here appear to denote the astronomical rulers of the days rather than the standard order, or reflect specific chronological debates.</note>, 15 July, as the first after the passed New Moon, is considered by some of them (whom the Alfonsines <note>Followers of the Alfonsine Tables, the standard astronomical tables of the late Middle Ages.</note> followed) as the beginning of the month of Muharram, the first <margin>See Tables folio 38 and Instruction 74.</margin> of the months in which they fix the start of the years of the Hegira. But others hold the modern custom of the Turkish reckoning, beginning from the following evening, which began for them the day of Friday, when the Moon could already be seen in the evening emerging from the Sun's rays.

Conversely, let the current year be 330 BC (simple); for from that year the Calippic Periods <note>A 76-year cycle used in ancient Greek astronomy to synchronize the lunar and solar years.</note> begin from the Solstice; which was the corrected beginning of the Attic year, or of the <term>Anticipation <note>original: "τῆς <unclear>Προλαυίσεως</unclear>" (tēs Prolauiseōs) — Likely referring to the 'Prolepsis' or the starting point of the calendar calculation.</note></term>. The calculation of the year was adapted to the Moon. The day and hour of the New Moon closest to the sol-

<column-break/>

stice is sought. Now, the solstice at that time occurred around June 28. Therefore:

<margin>By Instruction 14 below.</margin>
| | | |
|:---|:---:|:---|
| Nearest larger Epoch | 401 | 5 Days, 14 hours, 6 minutes, 26 seconds |
| Subtracting 330 from 400, remains: | 70 | 23 Days, 0 hours, 54 minutes, 9 seconds |
| Of simple May | | 3 Days, 8 hours, 19 minutes, 44 seconds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sum** | | **31 Days, 23 hours, 20 minutes, 18 seconds** |
| Sum prox. maj. from the Table | | 59 Days, 1 hour, 28 minutes, 6 seconds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Remaining** | | **27 Days, 2 hours, 7 minutes, 48 seconds.** |

Therefore, the mean New Moon was on the 28th day of June, at so many hours after mean noon at Uraniborg.

<margin>The cause for this beginning of the Calippic periods.</margin>
The 3rd year of the 112th Olympiad was running: and the third Dionysian years, namely the Triennial festival, were usually celebrated at Athens. The mean place of the conjunction was 23° 6' of Cancer. And because the apogee <note>The point in the Moon's orbit where it is farthest from Earth.</note> of the Moon was around 2° Gemini, the equation to be subtracted was about one degree. Thus the Sun was not a full half-degree beyond the solstice; so that the shadow of the Metonic Obelisk <note>A sundial or monumental pillar used by the Greek astronomer Meton to observe the solstices.</note> was the shortest of the whole year on that very noon. The New Moon itself is also found to be quite near noon, and the Moon, moreover, is near perigee <note>The point where the Moon is closest to Earth.</note>, with a small equation. Therefore, it is likely that Calippus, since the locations of the Lunar apsides <note>The extreme points (apogee and perigee) of an orbit.</note> were not yet exactly known, believed this conjunction of the Moon's mean place with the true Sun fell exactly at noon. These reasons for the beginning of the Calippic Periods, sought from this New Moon, appear from Astronomy itself. The victory of Alexander the Great over Darius, which happened in the preceding month of Boedromion, and the subsequent capture of Babylon, were added by chance. Free Calippus did not look to that, nor did Athens, a Republic hostile to Alexander. But these things belong to Chronology.

<margin>INSTRUCTION 136.</margin>
The Table of Epacts itself provides particular observations for accurately deducing conjunctions, one from another. To the number of completed days of the month, and hours etc., of any New Moon or Full Moon, add any number of Times of Syzygies from the Table; there arises the number for another sought New Moon, from which (if it has increased by that much) the days of the current month in which the previous New Moon was located are cast off, or even by the sum of days in a simple or leap year, the remainder will be the sum of days from the beginning of the following year or month, in which the later sought conjunction occurs.

<margin>Eight-year cycle <note>original: Octäeteris.</note></margin>
But after 8 years, there is added to the time of a known conjunction: 1 day, 12 hours, 41 minutes, 16 seconds, so that the time of the hundredth conjunction from then arises, returning in the same Julian month, or at the beginning of the one immediately following.

<margin>Calippic Period.</margin>
After 76 years, 5 hours, 50 minutes, 10 seconds are subtracted for the 941st following New Moon.

<margin>Period of 464 Years.</margin>
After 464 years: 1 hour, 40 minutes, 14 seconds are added.

<margin>Description of the Great Period of 3400 Julian Years. Tables folio 89.</margin>
Finally, after 3400 years, no more than 1 minute and 19 seconds of one hour are added: which is a most exact Period, bringing New Moons back, not indeed to the exactly same place of the Zodiac, but to the same day and hour of the Julian year and month. For this reason, I have distinguished this Period with small lines into its sections, so that the smaller periods composing it might appear. For it has two major parts, similar to each other, of 1468 years each: after which follows one minor period out of order, of 464 years. This minor one, indeed, is contained three times in each of the major ones, followed by one extra-order Calippic period of 76 years. Again, in each of 464 years, there are 6 Calippic periods, followed by one extra-order eight-year cycle (<term>Octäeteris</term>).

# ON THE CYCLE OF ENCOUNTERS
## Regarding the Sun ☉, the Ascending Node ☊, and the Descending Node ☋: the method of investigating from this cycle the day in the Julian year of the Conjunction of the mean place of the Sun and the Ascending Node of the Moon.

<margin>PRECEPT 137: A different method than that used in the Cycle of the Golden Number.</margin>
If the year proposed is Before Christ, subtract its current number from one of the Epochs <note>An 'Epoch' is a fixed point in time used as a reference for astronomical calculations.</note> placed on the right side of the Cycle, above the line marked for Christ. If the year is After Christ, subtract the number of the closest smaller Epoch below the line of Christ from the current year; or if you cannot, add it to the completed years of the nearest Epoch above the line of Christ. In both cases, you will thus have the current year of the Period. Then, seek the closest smaller number in the header lines and subtract it from the current Period; however, keep the days placed above that line to the right. Enter the left margin of the Cycle with the remaining years; at the intersection of that line and the column from the header from which you took the subtraction, you will find the day of the Month on the right. If you increase this by the number of days you kept aside, you will have the day of this encounter, approximately.

For the conjunction of the Sun with the other, descending node <note>The 'Descending Node' ☋ is the point where the Moon crosses the ecliptic moving from north to south; the 'Ascending Node' ☊ is the opposite.</note>, the numbers of the day of the month are placed to the right for the associated month, either following or preceding. Add to these the number of the day on which the Sun ☉ meets the Ascending Node ☊ to obtain the day of the meeting of the Sun ☉ and Descending Node ☋ in the specified associated month. If the number of days exceeds the length of that month, discard the excess, and the remaining days will belong to the following month.

For example, let the current year 3993 Before Christ be proposed <note>Many astronomers of this era used these calculations to attempt to date the biblical Creation.</note>; it is asked when the Sun ☉ and Ascending Node ☊ meet in that year. Subtract 3993 from 4597; 604 remains. The closest smaller number to this is found in the second line of the header, namely 595, above which 2 Days are placed on the right side in the same line. Having subtracted 595 from 604, seek the remaining 9 in the left margin; its line intersects with column 595 at 21, and the line ends in July. Add the 2 days kept aside; it becomes approximately the current 23rd of July. For the Epoch used suffers from a deficiency of 9 1/2 Hours <gloss>as you see noted</gloss>. Therefore, a truer calculation shows this mean meeting of the Sun ☉ and Node ☊ at noon on the 24th of July.

Similarly, if the year 1552 After Christ is sought: subtract the Epoch of 1060 from 1552; 492 remains. Subtract 483 from the header; 9 remains. The intersection occurs on July 29th; add 2 days from line 483, and you arrive at July 31st for the Sun ☉ and Ascending Node ☊. If you add these 31 days to the coupled January 8th, it becomes January 39th, which is February 8th of the preceding year, for the Sun ☉ and Descending Node ☋. But December 20th is also coupled. Add 31, and it becomes December 51st, which is January 20th of the following year, for the other meeting of the Node ☊, Sun ☉, and Descending Node ☋.

To investigate in any proposed year the two months in which Eclipses of the Sun and Moon can happen, the approximate days of those Months, and the Climate <note>A 'Climate' in ancient geography and astronomy refers to a latitudinal zone of the Earth.</note> that falls under suspicion of a Solar Eclipse.

<margin>PRECEPT 138. By Precept 137.</margin>
First, seek on which day of which Month the Sun by its mean motion arrives at the Ascending Node, and likewise at the Descending Node. For the Ecliptic Months are either those very ones in the proposed year, or those adjacent to them.

<column-break/>

<margin>By Precept 136.</margin>
Next, seek the Golden Number <note>The 'Golden Number' is the year's position in the 19-year Metonic cycle, used to determine lunar phases.</note> of that Year, specific to these Tables; having transferred it to the Diagram of the Golden Number, note in the Ecliptic month previously found at which day it is placed. For if the Golden Number precedes and follows the day of the Encounter with equal intervals, it makes both days suspect for a Solar Eclipse; but if with very unequal intervals, only the closer one. However, the fifteenth day from that, counted toward the more remote side, is suspect for a Lunar Eclipse; this will be closer to a total eclipse the more equal the distances of the Golden Number are from the day of the Encounter. But if the Golden Number of the Year marks the day of the Encounter itself, the suspicion of the nearest Ecliptic full moons is dissolved.
<margin>Tables, folio 89.</margin>

In that case, northern locations will not see the Solar Eclipse; rather, they see it only when the Golden Number marks a day that follows the Sun ☉ and Ascending Node ☊, or which precedes the Sun ☉ and Descending Node ☋. Hold the opposite to be true for southern locations and climates.

Thus, in the *previous example* for the current year 3993 Before Christ, the day of Encounter was found to be July 23rd, and the day connected to it was the preceding January 31st. The Golden Number of that year was 14 (XIV), which is applied to the nearest July 24th. There was, therefore, a great Solar Eclipse around July 24th. Truly, with the Sun ☉ and Ascending Node ☊ joined in the mean at noon of that day at the very solstitial point of 0° Cancer ♋, and the Sun and Moon, according to their true motions <note>original: "secundum veros motus"</note>, joined in 28° Gemini ♊, the latitude of the Moon )) was about 11' South. Thus, in this moment of Creation—as I believe it to be—there was a total Eclipse of the Sun in Ethiopia, in the middle place between the Tropic of Cancer ♋ and the Equator. Yet there was no Lunar Eclipse, nor could one have preceded in that month, nor followed in the following August.
<margin>Therefore (as Aijro infers), the Ethiopians are black.</margin>

Similarly, the Golden Number is placed at January 29th, two days preceding the encounter of the Sun ☉ and Descending Node ☋. Therefore, a Solar Eclipse would also be marked around this time; and around the following February 12th, one might probably ask whether a very small Lunar Eclipse ☽ might have occurred—if the stars had existed then.

The apogee <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center of attraction; original: "apogæum"</note> was located at 28° 52' 46" Gemini; 1° 7' 14" remains until the beginning of Cancer. Therefore, 66 years are added to these, and they also add 1 Day, 3 Hours, 22 minutes, and 3 seconds. Thus, in the year 1266, on June 14 at 5:18:08 AM, the Sun is at its apogee at 0° 34' Cancer.

These, when divided by the Sun's daily motion (57' 21") or the hourly motion (2' 23")—which must be extracted together by means of Logarithms (which are written to the side of the daily motions) or by common logistics—yield 15 hours, 4 minutes, and 12 seconds for the first, and 2 hours, 12 minutes, 30 seconds for the second. To make the intervals of time: the 31 Days, 15 Hours, 4 minutes, and 12 seconds must be subtracted from the time of the apogee (130 Days, 18 Hours, 48 minutes, 4 seconds); the 152 Days, 2 Hours, 12 minutes, and 30 seconds must be added. # RULES OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES

<margin>
Motion of the Apogee. But the apogee degrees at the bottom of page 97 of the Tables must be corrected.
</margin>
Here, it is useful to preserve the motion of the apogee <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth; original: "Apogæum"</note> extracted for two intervals of 9 hours and 23 minutes for other uses—namely, 1° 6' 34".

<margin>
PRECEPT 144. On daily motions.
</margin>
The same table implicitly shows the fictitious daily <note>original: "diurnos"</note> motions, just as it explicitly shows the hourly ones. These are calculated for any day and hour starting after the Moon is at apogee, by subtracting the arc of the preceding day from the arc of the following day at the appropriate hour line. However, on the very day the Moon reaches apogee, if the daily motion begins before the apogee, two arcs must be joined: one with the given hours, and the remaining part with the rest of the time up to 24 hours. In this way, all daily motions can be obtained up to the point which, at its furthest limit, is 14 full days distant from the apogee. For the remaining motions, which approach the perigee <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth; original: "Perigæum"</note> more uniformly with their limits, caution is needed due to the minutes attached to the hours in the half-cycle of restoration <note>A term for the completion of an orbital cycle; original: "restitutio"</note>.

## CHAPTER XXXI.

### ON THE REQUIREMENTS FOR THE CALCULATION OF ECLIPSES,

### On the Table of the Moon's Latitude in Eclipses.

<margin>
Chapter XXVII, precept 121.
Top of Tables page 98. Foundations of the calculation. Why the decrease of the angle was neglected. Why the Equation of the Node. Precept 128.
</margin>
I stated above what I granted for the reconciliation of Tycho Brahe's observations in the Octants; here I attend to the care of Eclipses. I present the Table of Latitude in Eclipses, which I have used most frequently, in its original form, based on the uniform motion of the Node and a constant maximum angle of 5° 18'. For although this angle—in the time it takes for the Sun to move 17° 20' from the Node—is reduced by 50 seconds according to the necessity of my hypothesis, only 15 seconds are actually added to the reduction of the absolute maximum latitude in this Table. Similarly, even if the Node, at a distance of 17° 20' from the ascending node <note>Symbol: ☊</note>, still loses 18 minutes—which would cut a portion of 1' 36" from the latitude in this Table and contract the extreme limits of all eclipses—even such a tiny difference in latitude is not distributed proportionally across the remaining distances of the Sun from the Node. For at the extreme limits of lunar eclipses, scarcely a quarter of it (24 seconds) remains, and in larger eclipses, it vanishes entirely. This is to say nothing of the fact that if the Moon's diameter, for physical reasons, expands slightly more than we have assumed, it would compensate for this entire discrepancy.

Receive, therefore, this Table of Ecliptic Latitudes, well-earned and well-deserved, preserved just as it has been until now, and from it, accustom yourself to:

### Extracting the Arc between Centers at maximum obscuration, as well as the latitude itself.

<margin>
PRECEPT 145.
</margin>
Subtract the uniform position of the nearest node from the position of the Sun or its opposite, at the very middle of each eclipse <note>original: "deliquii"</note>; or, if the Sun precedes, subtract its position from the node. With the remaining Degrees sought in the margin and the Minutes sought at the top, the required arc, perpendicular to the Moon's orbit, is found at the intersection.

This arc differs from the Latitude by a very small amount, just as the moment of exact conjunction <note>original: "Copulationis"</note> according to longitude on the Ecliptic differs from the moment of maximum obscuration.

<column-break/>

Therefore, if you use the position of the Moon instead of the Sun, while keeping everything else the same, you will elicit the genuine latitude, or the arc perpendicular to the Ecliptic.

### Reducing the position of the Lunar Orbit to the Ecliptic, and conversely, the position of the Sun (or its opposite) to the Lunar Orbit: that is, determining the point on the Orbit where maximum obscuration occurs.

<margin>
PRECEPT 146.
</margin>
When the Reduction <note>The correction needed to convert measurements from the slanted lunar orbit to the flat plane of the Earth's orbit (the Ecliptic)</note> is extracted using the arc between the Moon and the Node, it is valid for conjunctions, just like the latitude mentioned just now, and is used as described above.
<margin>
Precept 136.
</margin>
However, when the Reduction is extracted using the arc between the Sun and the Node, it must be subtracted from the position of the Sun (not the Moon) if the node precedes; or added if the node follows. Thus, you will have the position on the Moon's Orbit required for maximum obscuration and the middle of the eclipse.

### On the Table of Parallaxes, Hourly Motion, and the Semidiameter of the Moon.

<margin>
Middle of Tables page 98.
</margin>
I taught in Precept 131 how to compute Parallaxes and the diameter of the Moon <note>Symbol: ☽</note> from extracted data, and that only approximately. Eclipses required more frequent use and a more ready method. This is done either with the time elapsed since the Moon was in apogee, or the time remaining until it reaches apogee; or even with the equated Anomaly on the right side of the three small tables. This is the arc extracted along with this time of the Restoration of the Anomaly, but decreased by the motion of the apogee extracted for that same time from its own table.
<margin>
PRECEPT 147. Bottom of Tables pages 98 and 97.
</margin>

The Parallaxes and Semidiameters (no longer just the Diameters) are generally valid even outside of conjunctions; however, the Hourly Motions only serve for conjunctions. For the "Variation" <note>A specific irregularity in the Moon's speed discovered in the late 16th century</note> contributes to their composition. Longomontanus <note>Christian Severin Longomontanus, Tycho Brahe’s assistant</note> reports in his *Danish Astronomy*, Book 1, that the effect of Variation in accelerating the New and Full Moon was first noticed and calculated from the duration of the Moon’s stay in the Earth's shadow. For this reason, Tycho’s own value for Variation had to be retained when forming this hourly table, which, through demonstration, would be increased by 10 seconds at apogee and 14 seconds at perigee.
<margin>
The occasion of the discovery of Variation. His page 173, where he also corrects Tycho’s diameters, which he himself took from observations.
</margin>

Furthermore, this very brief Table encompasses many other powers usually taken from other tables for the calculation of eclipses; and it helps to:

### Define the Semidiameter of the Earth's shadow.

<margin>
PRECEPT 145. [Note: Margin likely intended 148].
</margin>
Combine into one sum the horizontal Parallaxes of the Sun and the Moon. From this sum, subtract the apparent Semidiameter of the Sun; what remains is the Semidiameter of the Earth’s shadow for that time.

This theoretical Semidiameter of the shadow is frequently found to be larger than the one Tycho presents in his *Progymnasmata*, which was shaped from observations of lunar eclipses; but those observations are deceptive due to the combination of physical causes that are inconsistent.
<margin>
Precept 141 discovered.
</margin>

Therefore, the width of the shadow which Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe, the primary observer whose data Kepler used.</note> reports—if his diagrams and numbers are dragged into a demonstration against their own nature—completely overturns those most beautiful Theorems of Hipparchus <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek astronomer who first estimated the distances to the Sun and Moon.</note>, which are of immense value (insofar as they cast the shadow into the heavens as a set of measuring scales). Longomontanus <note>Christian Sørensen Longomontanus, Tycho’s assistant.</note>, Tycho’s assistant in this practical matter, frankly admits this; he says this method is rendered void and that the ancients were in vain. I say, however, that these criticisms should have been leveled at the craftsmen more sparingly. For I too have spent much time and effort considering eclipses, and although I experienced some interference from physical causes, these were not so great across all eclipses that they would overturn the whole of astronomy. Therefore, since the archetypal <note>Kepler believed the universe was built on geometric archetypes or patterns.</note> ratios of the arrangement of the three bodies <note>The Sun, Earth, and Moon.</note> alluded very closely to the most significant and certain eclipses—especially regarding their beginnings and endings (for the moments of total immersion and emergence are more deceptive)—I did not hesitate to shape the Shadow from Parallaxes <note>The apparent change in position of an object when viewed from different points.</note> and Diameters, both archetypal and observed, setting aside abnormal appearances and attributing the fault to the inconsistency of physical causes.

### To form the Semidiameter of the Earth's Disc.

<margin>PRECEPT 149.</margin>
If you subtract one and a half times the Sun's horizontal parallax from the Moon's horizontal parallax, the remainder is this Semidiameter of the Disc.

### To determine the Semidiameter of the Penumbra and the Shadow (not the Earth’s, but the Moon’s own) where it touches the Earth; or if there is no shadow, the width of the circle remaining from the Sun's Disc.

<margin>PRECEPT 150.</margin>
If you combine into one sum the apparent semidiameters of the Sun and Moon, along with approximately half of the Sun's horizontal parallax, the semidiameter of the Penumbra <note>The partial shadow between the full light and the total shadow (umbra).</note> will be accumulated.

However, if the Sun's semidiameter is subtracted from the Moon's apparent semidiameter, the Semidiameter of the Lunar Umbra <note>The dark central part of the shadow.</note> remains. But if this cannot be done <note>i.e., if the Sun's diameter is larger, resulting in an annular eclipse.</note>; and if the Moon's diameter is subtracted from the Sun's because it is larger, the width of the circle remaining from the Sun's disc will remain. Finally, if the Semidiameters are equal, the very tip of the shadow <note>original: "mucro umbræ"</note> is proven to graze the Earth.

### To collect the Time of Delay and half-Duration, as well as Incidence and Emersion.

<margin>PRECEPT 151.</margin>
<margin>Great use of Antilogarithms. Tables folio 23 & precept 29.</margin>
Subtract the Antilogarithm of the arc between the centers at the moment of deepest Obscuration from the Antilogarithms of both the sum of the semidiameters and their difference: the remaining Antilogarithms belong to the Minutes <note>original: "Scrupulorum"; these are fractions of a degree or time used in calculation.</note> of the half-Duration in the first case, and the half-Delay in Darkness in the second.

Then, having subtracted the Sun's hourly motion from the Moon's true hourly motion in the Conjunctions <note>original: "Copulis"; refers to the meeting of the two bodies.</note>, let the remaining true hourly motion of the Moon from the Sun divide both sets of Minutes; the quotient will be the Hours and Minutes of the half-Duration and half-Delay, and by subtracting these from each other, the time will remain

<column-break/>

for Incidence <note>The start of the eclipse.</note> or Emersion <note>The end of the eclipse.</note> interchangeably: for they are equal, because we work through the moment of maximum obscuration. In place of division, if you prefer, Logarithms and Chapter 10 may be used.

### To provide the minutes of the defect, whether maximum or not.

<margin>PRECEPT 152.</margin>
From the sum of the semidiameters of the obscuring and obscured bodies, always subtract the arc between the centers (the latitude distance at the moment of maximum obscuration); the remainders will be the Minutes of the defect <note>The extent to which the body is covered.</note> at any given moment.

### To convert either the minutes of the defect or other diameters of the luminary into digits—that is, twelfth parts of the deficient diameter—and vice versa.

<margin>PRECEPT 153.</margin>
From the logistic Logarithm of the Minutes, subtract the Logarithm of the whole diameter of the luminary; the remainder, as the Logarithm shows in the "Quadrivic" table <note>A specific logarithmic table in Kepler's work.</note>, is double the digits.

If the diameter is precisely 30 minutes: the searched-for Minutes of the defect have the digits placed opposite them in the "Quadrivic."

Conversely, by adding the Logarithm of the whole Diameter in the Sexagesimal table and the double of the digits in the Quadrivicenal table, the Logarithm of the Minutes of the defect in the Sexagesimal table is composed.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

# THE METHOD OF COMPUTING ECLIPSES.

## How a preliminary judgment is made as to whether a Conjunction designated by the above method is truly Ecliptic: and if a Solar Eclipse occurs, in which Climate?

<margin>PRECEPT 154.</margin>
<margin>By Precept 138. Through precepts 141, 143.</margin>
<margin>Tables folio 98.</margin>
For the Noon of the day of Opposition <note>Full moon.</note> or Conjunction <note>New moon.</note> already found, seek the locations: the true Sun, the fictitious Moon, and the mean Node <note>The point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note>. Then compare the location of the Sun and the node with each other, performing subtraction of the preceding from the following: considering whether that distance or Remainder will be larger or smaller in the very moment of the true conjunction. And if the Remainder is to be larger, increase it; if smaller, decrease it, by such a portion of the Sun's daily motion for the amount of time by which the true Conjunction appears to be distant from noon. Compare the Remainder thus corrected with the Ecliptic limits <note>The maximum distance from a node at which an eclipse can occur.</note>. For if these limits—the smallest ones for Lunar eclipses at Full Moon, and for Solar ones at New Moon—are greater than that Remainder, there will definitely be some Eclipse, of the Moon in the former case and the Sun in the latter, in some part of the Earth. But if the maximum limits are smaller than that corrected Remainder, the luminaries will be free from obscuration across the entire Earth. If, however, the remainder, or the distance of the Sun and the nearby Node thus corrected, falls in the middle between the smallest Ecliptic limits

->Therefore, the daily motion is 13° 54' 10".<-

From this, having subtracted the daily motion of the Sun (57' 31"), there remains a daily motion of the Moon relative to the Sun of 12° 56' 39". Dividing the remainder of 4° 16' 21" by this (using Logarithms if you like) yields an interval of 7 hours, 55 minutes, and 24 seconds after noon.

With the position of the Sun, as it is more certainly known, reduced to the Hour of the Syzygy by its hourly motion so that it is 14° 54' 8" in Leo ♌, the fictitious position of the Moon (and in this case, the true Syzygy) is calculated for this hour as 14° 52' 39" in Aquarius ♒.

Since the Moon is still 1' 29" away, I subtract the true hourly motion of the Sun (2' 24") from the fictitious hourly motion of the Moon (34' 36"); the remainder is 32' 8", the fictitious hourly motion of the Moon relative to the Sun. Dividing the interval of 1' 29" by this gives a time of 2 minutes and 42 seconds. Therefore, the corrected time of the Syzygy will be 7 hours, 58 minutes, and 6 seconds in equal time, after Noon at <term>Uraniborg</term> <note>original: "Uranib."; Tycho Brahe's famous observatory in Denmark, used as the prime meridian for these tables.</note>.

There remains here an as-yet undiscussed question: what should be considered the "true" syzygy of the luminaries? Is it the one that occurs in the circle of latitude drawn through the center of the Sun? Or that which is in the circle perpendicular to the Moon's orbit through the center of the Moon? Or finally, that which has both luminaries equally distant from the Node, which we indeed achieve by this method, which employs no <term>reduction</term> <note>Correction for the difference between the ecliptic and the lunar orbit.</note>; for we have given instructions generally for all Syzygies.

## GUIDE ON HOW LUNAR ECLIPSES ARE TO BE COMPUTED FROM THE PREVIOUS RULES.

<margin>RULE 157.</margin>
<margin>By Rule 154</margin>
After it has been determined for some Full Moon that an eclipse will occur—specifically by calculating the positions of the Moon and the <term>Node</term> <note>The point where the Moon's orbit crosses the path of the Sun.</note> for the nearest noon—and after the hour of the <term>syzygy</term> <note>original: "copulæ"; refers here to the exact moment of the Full Moon alignment.</note> itself and the position of the Sun at that hour have been established; now, by the distance between the Sun and the Node, let the position of the Sun be reduced to the Moon's orbit. This we have called the "Required Position," namely, the position the Moon must occupy to produce the maximum obscuration. Compare this Required Position with the fictional position of the Moon, found either at noon or, better, at the hour of the syzygy. Take the difference found: if it is somewhat large, divide by the daily motion; if small, divide by the hourly motion of the Moon from the Sun (the "fictional" rate) to produce the Interval. This interval should be added to or subtracted from the time of the found position—whether it was noon or closer to the syzygy—depending on whether the Moon preceded or followed the Required Position. Thus, you will have the <term>equal time</term> <note>Uniform time used for calculation, distinct from solar time which varies slightly throughout the year.</note> of both the maximum obscuration and the true midpoint of the entire eclipse.

<margin>By Rule 155</margin>
<margin>By Rule 146</margin>
<margin>Required Position.</margin>

<margin>By Rule 145</margin>
Then, with the corrected interval of the conjunction, let the arc between the centers be extracted. Using the time from the apogee of each heavenly body (if calculated by subsidiary tables) or the equated <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angle used to find a planet's position in its elliptical orbit.</note> (if by ordinary tables), extract the <term>Parallaxes</term> <note>The apparent shift in position of a celestial body when viewed from different locations.</note>, Semi-diameters, and true hourly motions of both at the alignment. From these, form the semi-diameter of the shadow; and from this, together with the Moon's semi-diameter and the arc between the centers, calculate the <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "scrupula"; astronomical minutes or fractions of a degree.</note> of the eclipse, and convert them into <term>digits</term> <note>A traditional measurement of eclipse magnitude, where 12 digits equal the full diameter of the body.</note>. If these scruples are fewer than the scruples of the Moon’s full diameter, it will be a partial eclipse; if equal, a total eclipse without duration; if more, total with duration. Also calculate the scruples of the half-duration and half-stay, and convert these into time. When these times are subtracted from the moment of maximum eclipse, and also added to it, the beginnings and ends of the eclipse and the stay in darkness (if total) will appear. The difference of each beginning, called the "Time of Incidence," is also the same as the "Time of Emersion," because for all practical purposes they are equal in precision. All these are in the Meridian of <term>Uraniborg</term> <note>Tycho Brahe's observatory in Denmark, the reference point for these tables.</note> in equal time.

<margin>247, 131.</margin>
<margin>148, 145, 252, 153.</margin>
<margin>251.</margin>

It is also possible, with minimal loss of accuracy, to neglect the search for the syzygy, and instead immediately reduce the Sun’s meridian position to the orbit, and find the moment of maximum obscuration through this reduction. Then, once the Sun’s position is corrected, the reduction to the orbit is repeated, and the time of maximum obscuration will be amended if necessary.

### FULL EXAMPLE OF THIS AND SEVERAL PRECEDING RULES CONCURRING AT PRESENT, CONCERNING A PARTIAL ECLIPSE.

Let the Ecliptic Full Moon be sought and calculated for the 4th year before the current Christian era; for the historian Josephus marked the death of Herod with such a Full Moon just before Passover. First, I seek this Full Moon and on what day of which month it occurred. I therefore subtract 4 from 1769 (the nearest <term>Epoch</term> <note>A reference date in chronology.</note> before Christ) in the Table of Sun-Node Encounters. From the remainder, 1765, I subtract 1748, found in the fifth line of the Table of Encounters; 17 years remain. I add the 8 days standing to the right of this fifth line to the day found at the intersection of column 1748 and margin number 17, namely to February 27; the day of the Sun's conjunction becomes March 7. Then, looking at the <term>Golden Number</term> <note>A number in the 19-year lunar cycle used to determine the dates of new and full moons.</note> table among the Period Heads, I find 104 to be the nearest greater number to the 4th year before Christ. Subtracting the 3 full cycles here leaves 101, and subtracting all cycles of 19 from this leaves VI as the Golden Number. This indicates the next day of encounter in the Golden Type as February 26 for the New Moon, and March 13 for the Full Moon. Calculating the positions of the Luminaries and the Node for noon on March 13 from the subsidiary tables: the Sun is found at 21° 39' 28'' Pisces, with a daily motion of 58' 42'', hourly 2' 27'', and semi-diameter 15' 12''. The fictional Moon is at 26° 8' 20'' Virgo, the Node at 17° 0' 9'' Pisces. Time from the Apogee is 4 days, 1 hour, 15 minutes, 58 seconds; fictional hourly motion is 31' 12''.

## ANOTHER EXAMPLE OF A TOTAL LUNAR ECLIPSE.

In the year 1616, in the month of August, there was an Eclipse which some observers asserted was total, while others claimed it was partial.

At noon on August 15/25, the position of the Sun is gathered as 3° 19' 35'' of Virgo; its daily motion is 58' 2'', hourly 2' 25'', and Semidiameter 15' 7''. Thus the fictional position of the Moon is 24° 39' 26'' of Aquarius. The Node is at 9° 40' 30'' of the Node. The time since the Moon was at Apogee is 13 days, 17 hours, 22 minutes, 38 seconds. The fictional daily motion of the Moon from the Sun is 13° 24' 11''. And because the Moon is 8° 40' 9'' from the Sun, these divided by that daily motion <margin>by Logarithms, it is before the Sun</margin> give 15 hours, 32 minutes, and a corresponding solar motion of 37' 33'', so that it is at the hour of conjunction 3° 57' 8'' of Virgo, at a distance of 5° 41' 19'' from the Node, which was then at 9° 38' 27'' of Virgo. Therefore, a reduction of 1' 24'' is to be added to the Sun's position, so that the Required position of the Moon for maximum obscuration is 3° 58' 37'' of Virgo. The gathered position of the Moon at this hour, however, exceeds this by only 16'', which is completed in half a minute.

Having confirmed the position of the Moon at the very moment of maximum Obscuration, the rest follows.

one Sum of the Semidiameters of both lights <note>the Sun and the Moon</note> and the Parallax of the Moon; then from this Sum, let the Parallax of the Sun be subtracted; for by this method, the Sum of the Semidiameters of the Disk and the Penumbra <note>the partial shadow</note> is composed. From this and the arc between the centers, in the same way as before, the <term>scruples</term><note>Small units of measurement, here referring to minutes of an arc.</note> of half the Duration are elicited for an all-encompassing eclipse over the entire Earth. By subtracting these times from the time of maximum Obscuration, the beginnings become clear—both for the all-encompassing eclipse and for the stay of the Shadow on the Disk, which covers the whole Sun in its path; by addition, however, the ends are found. All these are numbered from Noon at <term>Uraniborg</term><note>Tycho Brahe's famous observatory on the island of Hven, used as the prime meridian for these tables.</note>.

This precision can suffice for the task at hand; however, it does not yet achieve the certainty of a full demonstration unless this further caution is taken: that the arc between the centers (before it is used to investigate the scruples of Duration and Stay) and the true hourly motion of the Moon from the Sun (before the scruples of Duration and Stay are converted into Hours and Minutes by it) should each be divided separately by the Parallax of the Moon, diminished by the Parallax of the Sun, and the quotients added to their totals.

### E X A M P L E.

There exists a passage in Plutarch, in his book *On the Face in the Moon* <note>original: "De facie Lunae"</note>, written around the year 100 AD, more or less. In it, one of the speakers reminds the others of that eclipse which had recently occurred, which uncovered many stars in various parts of the sky, having begun precisely at midday. Having examined many years around the hundredth year of Christ according to the doctrine of Chapter 29, no year seems more likely than 113 AD. On June 1st of that year at Uraniborg, at 10 hours and 16 minutes before Noon, the Sun is found at 8° 30' 17'' of Gemini (through uniform precession) with a Semidiameter of 15' 0''; and the Moon at 8° 32' 14'' of Gemini, with the <term>Node</term><note>the point where the Moon's path crosses the ecliptic</note> at 14° 31' Gemini. The distance between the centers was 0° 33' 8'' North, and by enlargement 33' 49''. The distance from <term>Apogee</term><note>the point in the orbit farthest from Earth</note> was 8 days, 15 hours. Therefore, the Parallax of the Moon was 61' 50'', the Semidiameter 15' 54'', and the true hourly motion 35' 10''. When the Sun's true motion is subtracted from this, it leaves the true motion of the Moon from the Sun at 32' 47'', enlarged to 33' 18''. The Sum of the Parallax of the Moon and the Semidiameters is 1° 32' 44''. Subtracting the Parallax of the Sun leaves the sum of the Semidiameters of the Disk and Penumbra at 1° 31' 45''. The <term>Antilogarithm</term><note>Kepler used specialized logarithmic tables to speed up these complex astronomical divisions and multiplications.</note> is 35.619. The difference of the Semidiameters of the Sun and Moon was 8. 70' 54'': such was the Semidiameter of the Shadow. Subtracting one and a half times the Parallax of the Sun (1' 39'' from the Parallax of the Moon), there remains the semidiameter of the Earth's Disk as 60' 21'', Antilogarithm 015.411. Subtract from both Antilogarithms the arc between the centers 33' 18'' (to act more simply than accurately); the Antilogarithm is 4.692. There remain the Antilogarithms of the scruples by which the Moon's shadow lingers on the Earth's disk, 50' 20'', and the arc of the total duration 1° 25' 26''. These, through the true hourly motion from the Sun of 32' 47'', give a half-stay of 1 hour 32 minutes, and a half-duration of any kind of 2 hours 38 minutes. Therefore, the Moon's shadow remained on the Earth's surface for over three hours, and the Sun was seen to be partially failing even longer—for more than one hour before and one hour after. And since it was 7:37 AM at Uraniborg (mean time), the Sun began to partially fail somewhere; at 8:43 AM it began to fail totally somewhere; at 11:47 AM the shadow left the Earth, and at 12:53 PM in the afternoon, even the 

<column-break/>

Penumbra left the lands—that is, every particle of the Moon's body withdrew itself from all lines that could connect any particles of the Sun and Earth. These things are tracked in this way because no specific place is expressed where those speakers saw the Sun totally covered.

<margin>RULE 159.</margin>
### To convert the Scruples of the Earth's Disk, numbered from the center of the Disk, into an Arc of the Great Circle of the Earth, starting from the place on Earth that is perpendicularly below the Sun.

From the Logistic <term>Logarithm</term><note>A mathematical tool developed to simplify calculations involving degrees and minutes.</note> of the Scruples that start from the center of the Disk (such as scruples of latitude, etc.), either take away the Logarithm of the semidiameter of the Disk if it is less than 60 scruples, or add it if it is greater. That which is accomplished by this method, when sought among the Logarithms of the *Heptacosïadis* <note>A specific table of 700 logarithms compiled by Kepler.</note>, shows the arc of the Great Circle under the column of arcs; or also among the Logarithms of the Semicircle.

Therefore, the arc of the Earth's great circle is 34° 4'.

<margin>RULE 160.</margin>
### How much space of the Earth, extended in width, the Moon's shadow involves.

Take the SCRUPLES of latitude, or those between the centers; subtract them from the Semidiameter of the Shadow (if there is any) and then add them. Convert that difference and this Sum into two arcs of the Earth's great circle; <margin>By Rule 159</margin> the difference between these will reveal the desired amount. For every degree of it is worth 15 <term>German Miles</term><note>A historical unit of distance; one German mile was approximately 7.5 kilometers or 4.6 miles.</note>.

Their difference of 2° 5' gives 31 miles.

If the air above our heads, for a width of 31 miles, is deprived of the Sun's light so that it creates no brightness, then the stars can certainly be seen. For if any splendor remains in the air that extends beyond these 31 miles, it either lies hidden behind mountains, or, if the air is very high, it recedes far around the region of the sky in which the Sun is observed.

# RULES OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES
<header>RULES OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES</header>

### INVESTIGATION OF THE ALTITUDE 
### OF THE NINETIETH DEGREE OF THE 
### ECLIPTIC FROM THE 
### EAST.

<margin>RULE 161.</margin>
## I. In a place where the Sun fails centrally in
## the Ninetieth degree itself.

<margin>By Rule 159</margin>
Let the arc between the centers of the Disk <note>the Earth's disk as seen from the Sun</note> and the Penumbra <note>the partial shadow</note>, at the middle of the Duration, be converted into an arc of a Quadrant <note>a 90-degree arc</note>. Therefore, the complement of that arc to the Quadrant is the altitude of the <term>Nonagesimus</term><note>The Nonagesimus is the 90th degree of the ecliptic from the horizon, representing the highest point of the ecliptic at a given moment.</note> at the middle of the Duration. If the altitude is Northern, the Nonagesimus verges toward the South; but if it is Southern, it declines toward the North. And in a place that admits such an altitude of the Sun—with the Sun being in the ninetieth degree from the eastern degree of the Ecliptic, and verging from the zenith toward the side opposite the Moon's latitude—the Sun fails centrally.

*As in the Example, the latitudinal <term>scruples</term><note>Small units of measure, usually minutes of an arc.</note> in the Disk gave an Earth arc of 34' 4". Therefore, the altitude of the Nonagesimus in the place where the Sun fails totally in the Nonagesimus was 55° 56'. And because the latitude was Northern, the Nonagesimus therefore verges from the zenith of the place toward the South.*

<margin>RULE 162.</margin>
## II. In a place where the Sun, in the Nonagesimus 
## itself, is grazed at the topmost or bottommost 
## margin, or fails by any number of digits 
## from that margin.

If the Sun is to be grazed from that side which names the latitude of the Moon; add the Semidiameter of the Penumbra to the latitude, and the sum will be of that same side. But if the Sun is to be grazed from the opposite side, then either subtract the Semidiameter of the Penumbra (if it is smaller) from the latitude of the Moon, and there will remain the scruples of latitude, similarly of the same side as the total latitude; or subtract the latitude (if it is smaller) from the Semidiameter of the Penumbra; the remains will be the scruples of the side opposite to what the Moon's latitude itself was.

Finally, for however many <term>digits</term><note>A standard astronomical unit for measuring the magnitude of an eclipse; 12 digits equal the full diameter of the Sun.</note> you wish to be covered from any side instead of mere contact, subtract that many twelfth parts of the Semidiameter of the Penumbra from the sum of the latitude and the Penumbra, or from the excess of the Penumbra; but add it to the excess of the latitude. If the scruples thus formed exceed the Semidiameter of the Disk and the Earth, there will be no place on Earth for the chosen phase, but it will run out beyond the boundaries of the Earth's globe to the North or South. But if the scruples are fewer than the scruples in the Semidiameter of the Earth's Disk, reduce them into an arc of the Great Circle of the Earth. Then again, the complement of this arc to the Quadrant is the altitude of the Nonagesimus, to which must be assigned the side opposite to that which the scruples of latitude had claimed.
<margin>By Rule 159</margin>

<margin>RULE 163.</margin>
## III. In a place where the Sun fails centrally 
## at the very Rising or Setting, namely, at the 
## beginning and end of the total failure 
## across the entire Earth.

<margin>By Rule 161</margin>
First, let the altitude of the Nonagesimus be sought in the shadowed place at the middle of the Duration, to which the appropriate title, Northern or

<column-break/>

Southern, should be attached. Then consider whether the Moon approaches either of the Nodes or departs from it. If it approaches, subtract 5° 18' from the found altitude for the beginning, and add the same amount for the end; but if the Moon departs from the Node, add for the beginning and subtract for the end. Thus is obtained the altitude of the Nonagesimus appropriate to the places where the Sun fails totally, rising at the beginning of the total Duration, or setting at its end.

But if the altitude first sought was greater than 84° 42'; after the addition is performed, for that which is collected beyond a Quadrant, the complement to the Quadrant must be taken, and the title or denomination of the altitude first established must be changed to the opposite.

*As in the Example, I desire to learn the track which the Shadow of the Moon observed across the surface of the Earth, especially from the beginning up to the central obscuration. And because the Altitude of the Nonagesimus in the maximum obscuration itself, or the middle of the duration, was found to be 55° 56' to the South, and the Moon is approaching the Node: I subtract 5° 18', and there will remain 50° 38', the altitude of the Nonagesimus in the place which the Moon, rising with the Sun, strikes with its shadow as it invades the earth.*

<margin>RULE 164.</margin>
## IV. In a place where the Sun, rising, begins 
## to fail from the upper and western margin, 
## or setting, ceases to fail from the upper 
## eastern part: of which the former is about 
## to see the failure from beginning to end, 
## and the latter has just seen it.

In this case, from the <term>Logistic Logarithm</term><note>A type of logarithm used by Kepler to handle sexagesimal (base-60) calculations for time and angles.</note> of the scruples of half the duration of every kind (but those which have been increased by as great a portion of themselves as the part of the Sun's Parallax is to the Moon's Parallax) subtract the Logistic Logarithm of the sum of the Semidiameters of the Disk and the Penumbra. There remains a Logarithm which—either in the column of Arcs of the <term>Heptacosias</term><note>original: "Heptacoſiadis". This refers to Kepler's 'Table of 700' logarithms.</note> or in the Canon of Logarithms of the Semicircle—shows the angle opposite to the scruples of Duration in the Disk of the Earth. And now, from this angle, either subtract or add 5° 18' according to the rules stated before: thus will come the altitude of the Nonagesimus appropriate to places where the Sun either rises beginning to be eclipsed, or sets ending it.

Furthermore, regarding the title or denomination of the Nonagesimus: in this case it is usually (and always when the Eclipse can be total somewhere) opposite to the denomination of the latitude. But when an Eclipse of minimum quantity can only be seen in the extreme parts toward the North or South, it sometimes happens that the angle opposite to the scruples of Duration comes out so small that 5° 18' cannot be subtracted. Then, therefore, in turn, that angle subtracted from 5° 18' will leave the altitude of the Nonagesimus of the same side as the latitude, not the opposite.
