# RULES OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES
<header>RULES OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES</header>

V. In a place where the Sun, either rising, is defined to begin failing <note>to be eclipsed</note> from the lower and eastern margin, or setting, begins from the lower and western margin; such that the former is more western than all places on Earth that have seen at least some small part of the increasing defect <note>the partial eclipse</note> at sunrise; while the latter is more eastern than all those for whom the Sun sets before the end of the defect.

<margin>RULE 165.</margin>
This first case pertains only to those Eclipses in the middle of which the arc of latitude is less than the difference of the Semidiameters of the Disk <note>the Earth's disk</note> and the Penumbra <note>the partial shadow</note>; or when the defect can happen both totally and from opposite parts of the Earth, with contrary characteristics—Southern from the North, and simultaneously Northern from the South.

Therefore, from the <term>Logistic Logarithm</term><note>A type of logarithm used by Kepler for astronomical calculations involving sexagesimal (base-60) divisions.</note> of the minutes of the half-Duration of the Penumbra in the Disk, subtract the <term>Logific Logarithm</term> of the difference of the Semidiameters of the Disk and the Penumbra. The remainder is the Logarithm of the Angle, corresponding to the minutes of the Duration, to be extracted either from the column of Arcs in the <term>Heptacosias</term><note>Kepler’s "Table of 700," a specific logarithmic table he developed.</note> or from the Table of Logarithms of a Semicircle. Then, by subtracting or adding 5° 18' to this Angle, the altitude of the <term>Nonagesimus</term><note>The 90th degree of the ecliptic from the horizon, representing its highest point.</note> is formed in places at the east and west, the furthest of all those that see at least some small part of such an eclipse. And in this case, the Nonagesimus always occupies the region opposite to the Moon's latitude.

->CONCERNING THE LOCATIONS ON EARTH<-
->TO WHICH THE PRINCIPAL PHASES<-
->OF A SOLAR ECLIPSE OCCUR.<-

->How the latitude of a place may be sought,<-
<margin>RULE 166.</margin> ->which represents the proposed altitude<-
->of any degree of the Ninetieth.<-

FIRST, from a given Phase, in this universal consideration of a Solar Eclipse, the rising degree is easily obtained. For in the middle of the universal duration, the degree of the Sun itself is the Ninetieth back from the rising; in the threefold beginning of the apparent Eclipse, the degree of the Sun itself rises.

Therefore, for the beginnings, use the location of the Eclipse itself; for the middle, use the location of its following square degree <note>the degree 90° ahead in the zodiac</note>; for the ends, use the opposite location of the Eclipse. Enter the Table of the Angle of the East, seeking the sign and
<margin>Tables p. 26.</margin> degree in the left or right margin; and having run through the whole line and the threads <note>columns</note> of all the altitudes of the North Pole, in whichever thread or column you find the altitude of the Nonagesimus (found through the preceding rules, with its proper designation), that altitude of the Pole placed at the top or bottom is the sought latitude of the Northern Location.

<column-break/>

If, however, this altitude of the Nonagesimus, with its proposed designation, is not found in the whole line through all the pages of the Table: this is 
<margin>p. 26 to 31.</margin> evidence that the Antarctic <note>South</note> Pole is elevated. Its altitude must then be sought through the degree opposite to the rising degree, and through the same altitude of the Nonagesimus in quantity, but now of the opposite designation.

In our Example, the latitude of the Place is to be sought, in which the location of the Eclipse itself at 8 ½ Gemini [♊] is the Nonagesimus from the rising point, having an altitude of 55° 56'. Therefore, 8 ½ Sagittarius [♐] rises. And the altitude of the Nonagesimus 55° 56', sought in the line for 9 Sagittarius [♐], is finally found nearest under the North Pole altitude of 55°. Therefore, the
<margin>Tables p. 29</margin> latitude of the place giving this Altitude of the Nonagesimus is 55°.

Again, it is asked what is the latitude of the place in which, as the Sun rises, the Nonagesimus (that is, 8 ½ Pisces [♓]) is elevated by 50° 38', which was the found altitude 
<margin>Rule 163</margin> of this Nonagesimus, corresponding to total obscuration. Therefore, the altitude of the Nonagesimus 50° 38', sought in the line for 8 ½ Gemini [♊], is finally found under the North Pole altitude of 28°.

Therefore, the latitude of the place where the Sun rises entirely covered by the Moon (or centrally) is 28 degrees.

->By what method the longitude of a place on<-
->Earth may be sought, in which each phase occurs,<-
->from a Solar Eclipse universally<-
<margin>RULE 167.</margin> ->considered—that is, initial, middle, or<-
->final: for considering the path<-
->through which the Moon's shadow<-
->proceeds.<-

IF the Arctic Pole is elevated: under the found altitude of the Pole 
<margin>By rule 166. By Ch. XIV. Rules 43, 44.</margin> in which each phase occurs, I seek the oblique ascension of the rising degree, from which, after subtracting 90 degrees, the <term>Right Ascension</term><note>The coordinate along the celestial equator, similar to longitude on Earth.</note> of the Midheaven <note>Medium Coeli</note> will remain in the place whose longitude is being sought.

But if the Antarctic Pole is elevated: seek under its found altitude the oblique ascension of the setting degree as if it were rising, and do not subtract from it, but add 90 degrees. By this method, the Right Ascension of the Midheaven is again produced in the place whose longitude is to be sought.

But if some Phase is now sought in the middle of the duration across the whole Earth: assign to that Phase the Right Ascension of the Midheaven which belongs to it at the <term>Meridian of Uraniborg</term><note>The observatory of Tycho Brahe in Denmark, used as the prime meridian for these tables.</note>. If, however, it concerns those places that see the central eclipse at rising and the beginning, or at setting and the end, use the Right Ascension of Uraniborg as it was at the beginning of the universal duration of the total Eclipse, or at its end. Again, if it is asked about those places where the rising Sun is touched, to be seen during the whole time of the defect, or where the setting Sun is touched after the whole defect has been watched: use the Right Ascension of Uraniborg as it was there at the beginning of the universal duration of every kind, or here at its end.

# RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS
<header>RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS</header>

Finally, if the extremities of the places are being tracked—those which see even the smallest bit of the Eclipse after the Sun rises or before it sets—one must record the Right Ascension of the Midheaven <note>The Midheaven, or *Medium Coeli*, is the point of the sky that is at its highest on the local meridian.</note> at Uraniborg, whether it occurred at the beginning of the Duration of the Penumbra <note>original: *Morae Penumbrae*; the "partial shadow" as opposed to the total shadow.</note> (not the full shadow) on the Disk <note>The Earth's disk as viewed from the Moon.</note>, or at its end.

By this method of subordinate Right Ascensions, subtract the preceding from the following, adding 360 degrees if necessary: thus the difference of Longitude between Uraniborg and the sought-after place will remain; extended toward the east if the Uraniborg value preceded it, but toward the west if it followed.

Therefore, convert this difference into hours; if you search for these on a Map of the World, the Meridian of the investigated place will be shown.

*As in the Example, to find the longitude of the place in which the Sun is covered centrally at the Nonagesimal <note>The 90th degree of the ecliptic from the horizon, representing the highest point of the sun's path at that moment.</note>: because the time at which the central conjunction of the Luminaries occurs (causing the maximum darkening) is reckoned at the Uraniborg Meridian as 22 hours, 15 minutes, 24 seconds of equal time (though apparent time should have been used, if such precision were worth the effort) and the Right Ascension of the Sun is 66° 45' 20": add this to the time converted into Equatorial Time, 333° 51': the Right Ascension of the Midheaven at Uraniborg becomes 40° 36' 20". But indeed, under a Polar altitude <note>Latitude</note> of 55°, with 8½ degrees of Virgo rising, the Oblique Ascension is 147° 57', and after subtracting 90° (because the North Pole is elevated), the Right Ascension of the Midheaven is 57° 57'. The difference from the Uraniborg value is therefore 17° 20' 40", which equals 1 hour, 9 minutes, and 9 seconds: this is how much further east the place where the Sun failed centrally at the Nonagesimal was from Uraniborg.*

*Again, for the location on Earth which the Moon’s Shadow first struck at Sunrise, because this is concluded to have happened at the Uraniborg hour of 20h 46', that is, 311° 30' in Equatorial Time: add the Right Ascension of the Sun 66° 42': the Right Ascension of the Midheaven at Uraniborg is totaled at 18° 12'. But under the North Polar altitude of 28°, which was previously found for this phase, with 8½ degrees of Gemini rising, the Oblique Ascension is 54° 42': therefore, the Right Ascension of the Midheaven in that same place is 324° 42': the former precedes this one, distant from it by 53° 30', which is 3 hours and 34 minutes. Thus, the place was that far to the West of Uraniborg.*

<margin>The Path of the Shadow.</margin>
Once the boundaries have been investigated, the line connecting those boundaries also comes into view—the Shadow, I mean, of the Moon, which is the cause of the total hiding of the Sun. Starting from the Atlantic Ocean, it crossed central Europe, and having traversed Germany, it extinguished the light of the Sun, positioned at the Nonagesimal, in Lithuania.

As for Plutarch, whether he was in Chaeronea, or in Athens, as it seems, or elsewhere in Greece, he could not have seen the whole Sun covered, according to the evidence of this calculation; but he might have well seen it if the Moon had come to the Sun a little sooner, with a smaller angle of the east. Or say, rather, that the Eclipse of which Plutarch made mention must be sought either before the year of Christ 93, or after the year 120, if indeed the author is to be understood as speaking of a total failure of the Sun.

Nevertheless, even those partial Eclipses of the Sun in which the Moon is seen a little higher than the Sun have this quality above others in which the Moon

<column-break/>

is lower: because when the Moon’s shadow is poured into the vast
<gloss>The cause of darkness. Solar Eclipse.</gloss>
fields of air and ether that are nearest above the zenith, their secondary light
<gloss>Solar eclipse.</gloss>
is extinguished, so that they cannot send down their brightness to the earth; while in turn, that thin horn of the Sun which projects lower down illuminates only the lower parts of the air.

->In what order the places on the Earth's surface follow one another, to which individual phases appear.<-

**F**irst, therefore, they feel some minimal decreasing Eclipse of the rising Sun, such that the Sun rises at the same time it ceases to fail; these are the westernmost of all places on Earth. These are followed to the east by those who see the Sun rise centrally covered. More eastern than these again are those for whom the rising Sun begins to be eclipsed, to be seen until the end of the defect. Much further east than these are those to whom the Sun appears covered at the Nonagesimal itself. And at almost the same interval further east are those where the Sun is observed failing from the beginning to the end, such that it sets at the very end. By a smaller interval, those follow toward the east who see the Sun set centrally covered; but the easternmost of all places on Earth are those who see the very minimum of the beginning of the Sun's defect at sunset, such that it begins to fail and sets at the same moment.

By this reasoning, the specific areas of the earth, throughout the long duration of the entire event, are distant from one another toward the east and west much less than the areas of the earth during a medium time of total duration; and again, the places specified by a short time of the Duration of the Penumbra on the Disk are further apart from each other: so that the longer any end is absent from its own beginning, the shorter the distance between the places.

But in those Eclipses in which the Penumbra exceeds the bounds of the Earth’s Globe, the definition of those two extreme places of the earth has great variety: for they run out under the Arctic or Antarctic circle of the earth. And if a Northern Eclipse occurs in Northern signs, or a Southern one in Southern signs, the entire Arctic or Antarctic Circle, and all places subject to it, can enjoy the sight of some small Eclipse.

If indeed the Eclipse and the sign of the Zodiac have their regions swapped, these two places under the polar circle will be at a minimum distance from each other. In both cases, a permutation of certain phases will occur, as well as in the order of places under the Pole, because of longitude. Therefore, the definition of those two is useless and unpleasant.

However, it is useful to know that if a place has been found in which the Sun is centrally covered at the very rising, then further to the west under the same parallel, some partial decreasing defect is seen, such that a place may be found in it where the Sun rises and ceases to fail at the same time.

But this does not occur at any of the principal moments of time, but rather at an intermediate one, between the entry of the center of the Penumbra <note>The lighter, outer part of a shadow; a partial eclipse.</note> and total Immersion. In the same way, if a place is found in which the Sun is covered centrally at its very setting: then under the same parallel further to the East some small portion of the increasing defect <note>The "defect" refers to the portion of the Sun's disk obscured by the Moon.</note> will be seen before sunset: thus some place will be found under it, in which the Sun simultaneously begins to fail and simultaneously sets; and that, at some intermediate moment between the beginning of Emersion <note>When the Moon begins to move off the Sun's disk.</note> and the exit of the center of the Penumbra.

## ON THE CALCULATION OF A SOLAR ECLIPSE FOR A CERTAIN SPECIFIC PLACE.

<margin>PRECEPT 168.</margin>
*Given two visible distances of the Moon from the Sun in the Ecliptic, close to each other, one preceding and the other passing the Sun, and the visible latitude of both, to find the distance of the position of both.*

<margin>By precept 29.</margin>
**I**f the latitudes are on different sides <note>i.e., one North and one South of the ecliptic line.</note>, make a Sum; but if in the same region, the difference; and add the Antilogarithm <note>Kepler’s "Antilogarithms" refer to a specific logarithmic system he developed to simplify multiplication into addition for astronomical work.</note> of the former or the latter to the Antilogarithm of the Sum of the distances from the Sun in the Ecliptic, which is increased by the appropriate hourly motion of the Sun; the result is the Antilogarithm of the sought distance, in a circle oblique to the Ecliptic. This Precept is necessary for calculating some solar eclipses with precision.

<margin>PRECEPT 169.</margin>
*Given two Ecliptic distances of the Moon from the Center of the Sun, one before and the other after, and the latitude of the Moon in both places, to find the Scruples <note>term: <term>Scruples</term> — An archaic term for minutes of arc or time, representing 1/60th of a degree or hour.</note> of the distance of the Moon from the point in which the maximum obscuration occurs, and at that point the distance of the Centers.*

<margin>Epitome of Astronomy leaf 887.</margin>
**S**OLAR eclipses are usually calculated in the Ephemerides <note>Astronomical almanacs or tables of positions.</note> according to the Precepts of the Prutenic Tables <note>Published in 1551, these were the standard tables before Kepler's Rudolphine Tables.</note>, supported by that lack of skill <note>original: "ἀτεχνίᾳ"</note> which Ptolemy handed down; which posits that the angle of the Moon's Orbit with the Ecliptic remains constant, even in its visible path. But I demonstrated in the *Optical part of Astronomy*, and repeated in the *Epitome*, that there is a great variety in this angle arising from the parallaxes of latitude.

<margin>Tables leaf 23</margin>
Therefore, whenever it happens that the magnitude is significant—either of the sum of the visible latitudes of the Moon (if the regions are different in the two positions of the Moon) or their difference (if in the same region)—one must by all means solve the rectilinear Triangle. This, indeed, will be done with the lightest labor possible, with the help of our Table of Antilogarithms.

<margin>By precept 29 or 152.</margin>
From the data, seek both distances of the Centers of the Sun and Moon, namely in each position of the

<column-break/>

Moon, and increase them by the proportional parts of the intermediate hourly motion of the Sun. Also seek the distance of both visible positions of the Moon. Thus a rectilinear Triangle will be established <margin>By precept 168</margin> between the two positions of the Moon's Center, and between the midpoint of the two positions of the Sun's center. Now if from this point a perpendicular is drawn to the distance of the two visible positions of the Moon (which <margin>Proper use of precept 30.</margin> must be investigated along with the parts of that distance which it creates), then this perpendicular will be the distance of the centers at the time of Maximum Obscuration: but that part of the distance which corresponds to the Antecession <note>The Moon's approach or position before it reaches the Sun.</note> of the Moon will have the scruples by which the preceding position of the Moon is distant from the point of Maximum Obscuration, and that which corresponds to the Passing <note>original: "Superationi"; the Moon's position after it has passed the center of the Sun.</note> will have the scruples by which the following position is distant.

Let the true position of the Moon be found at the equal meridian hour of Uraniborg <note>The observatory of Tycho Brahe, used by Kepler as his prime meridian.</note> as 16° 48' 27'' Gemini [♊], the visible Moon reduced to the Ecliptic as 17° 7' 58'' Gemini, the interval or Passing of the Moon as 19' 31''. But two hours before, the Sun in the meantime having moved forward by 5', let the visible position of the Moon be found as 16° 14' 39'' Gemini: the interval or Antecession of the Moon 28' 48''. Let the latitude there, at the later time, be seen as 15' 57'' North; here, at the earlier time, 1' 11'' also North.

The process will be easier after these first attempts.

### The Beginning, End, Magnitude, etc. of a Solar Eclipse: How they are to be computed for a certain specific place.

<margin>By precepts 155. 141. 143.</margin>
1. **F**IRST, either the Hour of the Eclipse is not known, or it is known only approximately. If the hour is unknown, then nothing should be done before calculating the exact time of the Conjunction <note>original: "Copulæ"; the moment the Sun and Moon meet in the same longitudinal degree.</note>, along with the positions of the Sun (☉), Moon (☽), and the Node (☊) in the Ecliptic <note>The path the Sun appears to follow in the sky.</note>, and the Parallaxes <note>The apparent shift in position of a celestial body when viewed from different points on Earth.</note> of the Sun and Moon should be taken, along with their true Semidiameters and Hourly motions. If, however,
<margin>By precepts 143. 156. By precepts 141. 143. 141. 143.</margin>
the Hour is known approximately, then at that time a "fictitious" position of the Moon should be computed and reduced to the true position; the positions of the Sun and the Node should also be calculated for the same moment. For a perfectly exact knowledge of the true Conjunction itself is not simply required, and one can save effort on this, as the work is laborious enough in other respects. In this case also, let the parallaxes and Semidiameters be taken as before.

<margin>2. 145</margin>
Secondly, with the distance not of the Sun, but of the Moon itself from the Node, let the Reduction be selected from the Table of Ecliptic Latitude. In this calculation for a specific place on Earth, that reduction should not be extended from the position of the Sun, as was done before when dealing with the general eclipse across the Earth, but from the position of the Moon toward the
<margin>By precept 146</margin>
Node, so that the position of the Moon reduced to the Ecliptic may be obtained.

<margin>3. 145</margin>
Thirdly, using the same entry in the Table, let the latitude also be selected, along with its direction <note>Whether North or South of the Ecliptic.</note>.

<margin>4. By precepts 49 or 51. 52. 54. or 53. 54. By precept 55. By precept 133.</margin>
Fourthly, let the equal Uraniborg time <note>Time calculated for Tycho Brahe's observatory at Hven, used as a reference point.</note> of the moment for which the positions were computed be converted into apparent time, and reduced to the Meridian of the place; then for this moment, let the Parallaxes of Longitude and Latitude be sought. I mean, however, the parallaxes not of the Moon alone, as in Chapter 28, but diminished by the parallax of the Sun, which are called the Parallaxes of the Moon from the Sun. And with these parallaxes, let the true position of the Moon (reduced to the Ecliptic) and its true Latitude be converted into visible positions. And by subtracting the position of the Sun from the visible position of the Moon (if the Moon has passed it), or the Moon's position (if it is still approaching) from the Sun's, let the intervals of Longitude and Latitude be preserved, with labels of either the Preceding or Passing motion of the Moon.

<margin>5.</margin>
Fifthly. If there should be no difference in Longitudes, you already almost have the moment of the maximum Obscuration, and the calculation has reached the point where you can proceed to the inquiry of the magnitude of the Eclipse; but some work still remains for gathering the beginning and the end. For the calculation must be repeated for both the preceding and the following Hour. Unless perhaps, when the equinoctial points or nearby degrees are rising, the angle of the Rising Point changes very little over two hours; then at

<column-break/>

least one or the other repetition will be necessary. But if there was any visible difference in the longitudes of the Sun and Moon, if indeed the Moon was preceding, add at most two hours to the apparent time, and to the true position in the Ecliptic add two true hourly motions of the Moon from the Sun; but if the Moon has passed, subtract these. To the distance of the Moon from the previous Node, add or subtract, as the case may be, two entire true hourly motions of the Moon, and take the latitude anew. For the time thus changed, repeat the process of the parallaxes of the Moon from the Sun, and again through them reduce the true longitude of the Moon (with respect to the Sun, which is meanwhile assumed to be stationary) and the latitude to visible ones, and seek the difference from the position of the Sun compared at the beginning, as before.

<margin>6.</margin>
Sixthly, having now joined the two visible distances of the Luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon.</note>, if only one is of the Moon’s Preceding and the other of its Passing (for if it were otherwise, subtraction would have to be used), thus there emerges the visible motion of the Moon from the Sun for one or two Hours. After also adding the visible latitudes, if they were of different directions, or subtracting the smaller from the larger if of the same direction, the change in visible latitude for one or two Hours is obtained. If the change in latitude should be zero, as can happen, or very small: through the visible hourly motion of the Moon from the Sun, and the visible precession of the Moon, the interval of time is easily found <margin>Time.</margin> by which the maximum obscuration will happen later than that moment for which the visible precession of the Moon was found: and through the visible latitude, being the same on both sides, the Magnitude of the maximum Obscuration is also computed; or if they are somewhat unequal, then by the intermediate latitude, either increased or decreased proportionally to the <margin>Magnitude of the defect.</margin> time of the Preceding motion. Finally, the exact position of the Sun in the Ecliptic <margin>Place of the Eclipse.</margin> will be determined by its hourly motion into the reliable time, and the resulting quotient added to the position of the Sun first computed.

But if there should be any significant Sum or Difference between the unequal visible latitudes; then, lest we pass over this quite notable variation—which is of no small importance in diminishing the light of the day in great Eclipses—we must investigate both the distance of the two positions and its remaining part or Scruples <margin>By precept 168</margin> up to the place of maximum Obscuration, and the distance of the centers therein. Therefore, again with the <margin>By precept 169</margin> distance of the two positions of the Moon (as if with the visible motion of the Moon itself for one or two hours, not the Moon from the Sun) and with that part of it which corresponds to the Moon's Preceding motion, the interval of <margin>Time.</margin> time will be tracked, from that moment at which the Moon was found to precede, until the maximum obscuration. <margin>Magnitude of the defect.</margin>

The Magnitude of the defect <note>The amount of the Sun's disk covered.</note> will be found through the Semidiameters of the Luminaries and this visible distance <margin>According to precept 152. 152.</margin> of the centers.

And through the Sum of the Semidiameters of the Sun and Moon, the minutes <note>original: "Scrupula"; refers to small units of measurement, here minutes of arc.</note> of the half-duration are sought. # EXAMPLE OF A SOLAR ECLIPSE
# to be computed for a specific Place.

ERASMUS REINHOLD, <note>A famous 16th-century astronomer known for the Prutenic Tables.</note> in the preface to the *Theories of Purbach*, <note>Georg von Peuerbach, a 15th-century astronomer.</note> mentions an eclipse of the Sun from a Polish writer on Bohemian disturbances in the year 1415, on the 6th day of June, at the 18th hour. At that time, stars were seen as if at night, and birds, terrified by the sudden darkness, fell everywhere from the sky to the ground.

<margin>1.</margin> Since the historian records the time of the day, the positions are found from the auxiliary tables by calculating for the 18th hour, equal to Uraniburg <note>Tycho Brahe's famous observatory.</note> afternoon time, as follows: Sun (☉) at 23° 50' 28'' Gemini (♊). Moon (☽) at 22° 54' 28'' Gemini (♊). Ascending Node (☊) at 1° 9' 0'' Cancer (♋). Parallax of the Sun: 0' 59''. Semidiameter: 15' 0''.

Therefore, because the Moon is not a full degree away from the Sun (specifically, 56 minutes), I will proceed directly to its visible position, setting aside the moment of the true Conjunction. <note>The exact moment the centers align in longitude.</note> For the distance of the Moon from its Apogee at 12 hours 1 minute gives a Parallax of 63' 26'', a Semidiameter of 16' 18'', and an Hourly Motion of 37' 55''. And because this position of the Moon is only a placeholder, since it is still outside the Conjunctions, I will reduce it to the true position, which will be 22° 50' 59'' Gemini. The position of the Node (☊) is 1° 9' 6'' Cancer. 
<margin>Through Precept 156.</margin>
<margin>2.</margin> The distance of 8° 18' 7'' gives a Northern latitude of 0° 45' 51''. 
<margin>3.</margin> A reduction of 2' 8'' is to be added to the Moon's position, as it moves toward the following Node; thus the position of the Moon reduced to the Ecliptic becomes 22° 53' 7'' Gemini.

<margin>4.</margin> When we have computed for the 18th equal hour, the Sun in 24° Gemini gives a Tychonic equation of time of 2' 12'' to be subtracted from the apparent time; therefore, it is to be added to the equal time, so that it becomes 18 hours 2 minutes 12 seconds. And on account of the reduction to the Prague Meridian, 5 minutes are added, because the place is further East. Thus, the time reduced to the Meridian is 18 hours 7 minutes 12 seconds.

For this time, therefore, the precise parallaxes of the Moon from the Sun, through an Oblique Ascension of 85° 2', are found to be: Longitude 37' 38'', Latitude 45' 18''. Thus the visible Northern latitude remains at 0' 33'', and the Longitude at 23° 30' 45'' Gemini in the Ecliptic, so that the Moon visibly precedes the Sun by 19' 43''.

<margin>5.</margin> Therefore, in the second computation, I will add 2 hours to the time and two true hourly motions of the Moon from the Sun to the Moon's true Ecliptic position (that is, 1° 11' 4''), so that the position of the Moon is 24° 4' 11'' Gemini, relative to the prior position of the Sun, as if it had remained in the same place in the meantime. Regarding the distance from the Node (8° 18' 7''), I subtract two true hourly motions from the equinox (that is, 1° 15' 50''), because at this later time, the Moon is closer to the node: the distance from the Node will be 7° 2' 17'', giving a true latitude of 0° 38' 53''.

Since previously the Oblique Ascension of the rising degree was 85° 2' 15'', after two hours it was 115° 2'; and the

<column-break/>

Parallax of latitude is computed as 37' 12'' and Longitude 32' 34'', and the visible position of the Moon is 24° 36' 45'' Gemini, provided the Sun had stayed in its place during that time.
<margin>6.</margin> Therefore, the movement past the Sun is 46' 17''; which, joined to the prior Approach, gives a visible motion for the two-hour period of 66'.

<margin>Middle of the Obscuration.</margin>
The visible Latitude becomes 1' 42'' North, nearly the same; thus the moment of maximum obscuration is easily obtained. For if a visible hourly motion of 33' 0'' gives one hour, the Approach of 19' 45'' will give 35' 51''.

<margin>Place of the Eclipse.</margin>
The middle was therefore at 18 hours 43 minutes 3 seconds apparent time in Prague, and the hourly motion of the Sun (2' 23''), multiplied by the time of 36 minutes, gives 0' 56''. Thus the exact position of the eclipse is 23° 51' 25'' Gemini. 
<margin>Quantity of the defect.</margin>
Again, if the visible latitude changes by 1' 9'' in 2 hours, and by 35'' in one hour, then 21'' are owed for 36 minutes. In the middle of the eclipse, therefore, the visible latitude is 0' 54'', which when subtracted from the Sum of the Semidiameters (31' 18''), leaves the minutes of the defect at 30' 24'', while the Diameter of the Sun was only 30'. The eclipse was therefore total in Prague: and the darkness was all the greater because the Center of the Moon was seen to pass a little higher than the center of the Sun, completely extinguishing the clarity of the air or the Aether poured over Germany (the diameter of the Shadow occupying an altitude and latitude of many thousands of miles).

The sum of the semidiameters (31' 18'') and the distance of the Centers in the Middle (0' 54'') produce 31' 17'' for the minutes of half-duration. 
<margin>Beginning and End.</margin>
When these are divided by the 33' visible hourly motion, the half-duration becomes 56' 54''. Thus, although the eclipse was total, because it was far from the Nonagesimal <note>The 90th degree of the ecliptic from the horizon, where parallax effects are specialized.</note> where Parallax does not greatly retard the visible motion, and because the Moon was swift, the eclipse could not last two hours. It began in Prague at 17 hours 46 minutes after the preceding Noon and ended at 19 hours 40 minutes apparent time.

Let him who has leisure compute for these three moments, and having deducted the parallaxes, let him establish the visible positions and seek out the distances of the centers, so that the times and magnitude may be corrected if necessary.

## ANOTHER EXAMPLE.

In the year of Christ 1598, on the day (either March 7 or) February 25, an eclipse of the Sun was observed in Graz in Styria, at Uraniburg, and in the borderlands of the Kingdom of Denmark. These observations were reported by me 21 years ago in the Optical part of my *Astronomy*. 
<margin>See his page 385, 390 etc.</margin>
Therefore, we compute for equal Noon at Uraniburg: Sun (☉) at 16° 48' 27'' Pisces (♓). Moon (☽) at 17° 32' 26'' Pisces. Node (☊) at 6° 58' Pisces.
<margin>1.</margin>
Hourly motions: Sun 2' 30'', Moon (Placeholder) 34' 45'', True 36' 24''.
Semidiameters: Sun 15' 21'', Moon 16' 6''.
Parallaxes: Sun 1' 0'', Moon 62' 35''.

Since the placeholder position of the Moon surpassed the Sun by 43' 59'': just as the placeholder 34' 45'' is to the excess of the true (1' 39''), so is 43' 59'' to 2' 5''. 
<margin>2.</margin>
The placeholder interval must be increased by this much, so that the Moon is truly in 17° 34' 32'' Pisces, distant from the Node by 10° 36' 33''. 
<margin>3.</margin>
This arc gives a latitude of 58' 29'' and a Reduction of 2' 39'': the Ecliptic position of the Moon is that much closer to the Node, namely in 17° 31' 53'' Pisces.

<margin>4.</margin>
Now with the Sun positioned in 17° Pisces, Tycho orders us to add 4' 15'' to the apparent time or subtract it from the equal time. 
<margin>See chapter 16, page 38.</margin>
Conversely, the difference of Meridians for Graz adds 14 minutes according to the Catalog; but before the Catalog was amended, I was accustomed to add 17' 20'', toward which my mind still inclines. Thus the time will be 0 hours 13 minutes 5 seconds. But on this occasion, I add another 18' 56'' because of the following Precept.

Therefore, Origanus has no more time than 2 hours 12 minutes. But more on this observation elsewhere.

### On the Last and Monthly Equation of 
### Time in Eclipses.

**A**fter all the schemes of the craftsmen have been exhausted, after so many inequalities of the Moon have been brought to light, the star remains stubborn and, rejecting the laws, wanders slightly out of orbit everywhere: but primarily, for a reason confirmed by many examples, it is found to move under the Sun or into the shadow later around the point of the vernal equinox, and earlier around the autumnal equinox, than the calculation explained thus far indicates. But so far, only Eclipses have supplied experiments: what happens to the Moon when it crosses the equinoctial points in the absence of the Sun, no one, as far as I know, has attended to. Therefore, it is premature to inquire into the causes, nor is it the business of this book. In the meantime, therefore, while 
<margin>PRECEPT 171.</margin>
the days bring those causes forth, we shall follow a rule shaped by moderate experience. Having computed the 
<margin>According to Chapter XV.</margin>
time of the Sun on the Ecliptic, and converted it into apparent time, subtract the position of the Sun's Apogee <note>The point in the Sun's apparent orbit furthest from Earth.</note> from the following position of the Moon, or vice versa if it precedes; take this interval into the Table of Lunar Equations, which is found between the 
<margin>Tables, folio 80, 81.</margin>
full degrees of the Year of Eccentricity, and in the same cell noted with lowercase characters, multiply the physical equation eightfold: you will produce the Minutes of the Hour, which, under the name of this monthly equation, are to be further subtracted from the time converted into apparent in the first case; and added in the second case. But if the time of some eclipse has been observed, and from that the position of the Moon is to be computed from the Tables, that time, as apparent, must first be converted into equal time, just as through the customary annual equations, so also through this monthly one, the way being contrary in both cases. Especially in Solar Eclipses, this must be applied:

this monthly correction <note>original: "menstrua æquatio"; a correction factor in lunar theory that varies over the course of a month</note> is such that its effect on the Parallaxes of the Moon is not to be ignored. For when Cancer ♋ or Leo ♌ are rising in our climate <note>Central Europe, specifically Graz</note>, within one-third of an hour <note>20 minutes</note>, the angle of the Orient changes by 2 degrees, and the parallax of latitude by one and a half minutes; in more southern regions, the change is even greater. This produces a difference of nearly one digit <term>digit; a unit of measurement for eclipses equal to one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body</term> on the disk of the Sun. This variety can greatly influence whether the event will occur during the day or the night on Earth.

Let that Solar Eclipse serve as an example. For if I use only Tycho’s correction, the time assumed for calculating the visible position of the Moon at 10:00 AM equal time <note>Mean time, adjusted for the Earth's uniform rotation</note> becomes 10:13 AM apparent time at Graz, with a distance between the centers of 25' 48''. Thus, the beginning of the Eclipse should have been seen 13 minutes earlier, namely at 10:00 AM apparent time. But although the City clock, determined from the altitude of the Sun, was found to be slow, even on that clock the Eclipse began around 10:14 AM, which was truly 10:15 AM <note>10 1/4 hours</note>. Therefore, the Moon arrived at the Sun later than Tycho’s correction of time suggests. But if I also use the monthly correction, having subtracted 17° of Gemini ♊ (the Moon's position) from 6° of Cancer ♋ (the Apogee of the Node ☊), the distance becomes 109 degrees. For an Eccentric Anomaly of the Moon of 109°, the physical part of the correction is listed as 2° 22', which, when multiplied by 8, produces 19 minutes. When these are added to the 10:13 AM apparent time produced by Tycho,
<margin>Precept 170</margin>
the true apparent time at Graz becomes 10:32 AM. Indeed, above, when I calculated the true position of the Moon from 10:00 AM equal time, and the Parallaxes from 10:32 AM apparent time, I found the distance between the centers to be such that the beginning of the Eclipse could have been at 10:26 AM apparent time; this matches the observation.

If the Astronomical correction is used instead of the Tyconic, it mandates subtracting even more than Tycho; thus the monthly correction would become even greater. But not even the third, physical correction of time is sufficient; for it would add only 8 minutes, leaving 9 1/2 minutes still to be added for the monthly correction. But I will deal more with the evidence from other Eclipses of the Sun and Moon in my work *Hipparchus*, as well as with those which are found to disagree with the rule.

### To learn the altitude of the eclipsed luminary.

<margin>PRECEPT 172</margin>
This can be obtained with instruments. But in the absence of those, the rising degree is known through the previous steps, along with its angle and the distance of the eclipsed body from it. When the Logarithms of these are joined, the sum, acting as a Logarithm, shows the arc of the altitude.

### To calculate the inclination of the eclipse to the Vertical circle passing through the center of the eclipsed body.

<margin>PRECEPT 173. Through precept 172</margin>
Through the time at which such or so great an eclipse is to appear, let the altitude of the luminary be sought (if it is not already known); its Antilogarithm, subtracted from the Antilogarithm of the angle of the Orient, leaves the Antilogarithm of the angle by which the circle of Latitude, drawn from the center of the Luminary, is inclined to the vertical circle drawn through the same center of the luminary. This is the first element for the sought inclination. This angle, in the western quadrant of the Ecliptic, is to the right above the Ecliptic, and western from the vertical; to the left below: in the eastern quadrant, it is the opposite.

<column-break/>

<margin>Through precept 152</margin>
Next, from the visible longitude and latitude of the Moon from the Sun, let the distance of the Centers be investigated, which is also useful for other future steps; unless it has been obtained already. Therefore, having subtracted the Logistic Logarithm <note>A specialized logarithm used by Kepler for astronomical ratios</note> of this from the logistic logarithm of the distance in longitude of the Moon from the Sun, there remains the Logarithm of the angle between the same circle of Latitude and the *axis-path* <note>original: "ἀξινείρπον" (axineirpon); the relative path of the Moon's center across the Sun's disk</note>, which is the second element of the sought Inclination; standing toward the setting <note>west</note> of the circle of latitude if the Moon is before the Sun, and toward the rising <note>east</note> if it has passed it by visible motion. If the visible latitude is small, you will use the Logarithm of this more advisedly, so that the complement of the sought angle comes forth. By the composition of both Elements, or the subtraction of one from the other, as the situation requires, the sought Inclination is formed. This often seems absurd at first
<margin>See *Astronomia Pars Optica* chapter 11, *Epitome Astronomiae* page 892.</margin>
glance—namely in a small quantity of eclipse—as the Moon may seem to enter under the sun from the eastern region, and in another Eclipse to exit from the western region, relative to the vertical. The elements are added together if the circle of latitude falls between the Vertical and the line through the centers <note>original: "Diacentron"</note>; one is subtracted from the larger other if the opposite is true; and then the sought Inclination follows the region of the second element, as long as it was larger than the other; and the contrary region, if it was smaller.

Thus in the Eclipse of the year 1598, at the apparent hour at Graz 10:26 AM, with 22° Gemini ♊ rising.

as an Antilogarithm gives 4° 10'. The first element, toward the west, is above the Ecliptic for the Moon in the western Quadrant. And because the beginning of the eclipse was at this moment, and the distance of the centers (owing to the small visible latitude of 0' 30'' North) was nearly equal to the sum of the semi-diameters, I will use the logistic logarithm of the latitude 479000. Subtracting the logistic logarithm of the distance of the centers 64600 from it, the remainder 414400 shows 0° 54' as the Complement of the angle between the line through the centers and the circle of latitude. Thus the second element becomes 89° 6' toward the west, because the Moon is seen in front of the Sun; and above the Ecliptic, because the visible latitude is North. Since therefore both Elements are toward the west, with the arc of latitude between them, they must be added together to make 93° 16'. Thus the beginning of the eclipse should have been seen at the right edge of the Sun, turned only very slightly downward. Indeed, the observation holds that it was seen almost exactly to the right; because in a sudden glance, 3 degrees on the edge of the Sun (divided into 360°) were not noticed.

Similarly, if you calculate the inclination for the apparent hour at Graz 12:47 PM, with 23° Cancer ♋ rising, the first element is found to be 32° 22' toward the west; the other, through the distance of the centers 31' 27'' (the sum of the semi-diameters at the contact when the Eclipse ends) and through the longitude of the Moon from the Sun in the visible Ecliptic of 25' 52'', is calculated as 55° 20' from the circle of Latitude toward the east. Since this does not fall between the others, a subtraction of the elements must be made; there remains 22° 58' from the second element, which was larger here. Therefore, the inclination from the vertical was that much toward the East.

### How the true position of the Moon in its orbit is derived from the exact observation of the beginning or end of a solar eclipse, or from any specific phase.

<margin>PRECEPT 174</margin>
<margin>Through precepts 141, 147</margin>
<margin>Given the Inclination of the Eclipse.</margin>
<margin>Optics, Chapter 11. As in precept 173.</margin>
At the exactly known time of observation, look for the position of the Sun, along with its parallax and semidiameter; likewise, find the position of the Node ☊, along with the parallax and semidiameter of the Moon ☽. These values change slowly, and neglecting the equation of time does not harm them much. If, at the same time, the inclination of the defect <note>The angle or orientation of the "bite" taken out of the Sun's disk</note> was observed—a method of observation I refined in my *Optics* <note>Kepler refers to his 1604 work, *Astronomiae Pars Optica*</note>—then look for its first element, and through the resolution of the next process, find the second element as well. When its logistic logarithm is added to the logistic logarithm of the distance of the centers (which is known from observation), the result is the logistic logarithm of the visible longitude of the Moon from the Sun. This, together with the position of the Sun, gives the visible position of the Moon in the Ecliptic. Therefore, add or subtract the parallax of the Moon's longitude from the Sun in the opposite way than was done before when making the visible position from the true one. In this way, the true position of the Moon in the Ecliptic is established, which is easily reduced to the Orbit through its distance from the Node ☊.

<margin>Through precept 153</margin>
<margin>Through precepts 133, 170</margin>
> As in the next example, imagine the time was exactly observed at 12 hours and 47 minutes, when the Eclipse ended at Graz, together with an inclination of 22° 58'. The position of the Sun is found to be 16° 51' of Pisces ♓, the Node ☊ at 6° 58' of Pisces ♓, and the parallaxes and semidiameters as above. Therefore, through the apparent time and the position of the Sun, the first element is found to be 32' 22'', which, when added to 22° 58' (because it previously had to be subtracted), makes the second element 55° 20'. Its logarithm 19544, combined with the sum of the semidiameters 31' 27'' (because at the end of the Eclipse, this is the distance of the centers) with the logistic value 64595, yields the logistic logarithm 84139, which corresponds to 25' 51'' of longitude of the Moon from the Sun. When this is added to the position of the Sun, it makes the visible position of the Moon 17° 16' 51'' of Pisces ♓, because it is the end of the Eclipse and the Moon has passed the Sun. Add the parallax of the Moon’s longitude from the Sun, 26' 38'', because it projected the Moon to the west; you will find the true position in the Ecliptic to be 17° 43' 29'' of Pisces ♓. And since this is 10° 38' distant from the Node ☊, it gives a reduction <note>A correction factor to account for the tilt of the orbit</note> of 2' 44''. Thus, the position of the Moon in its Orbit, corresponding to this apparent time, is 17° 40' 45'' of Pisces ♓.

<margin>PRECEPT 175.</margin>
<margin>Without the Inclination of the Eclipse.</margin>
### But what if the inclination was not observed at the same time? Then the latitude must be assumed approximately based on the distance of the Sun from the Node, as it involves less uncertainty; in half an hour it does not vary more than 1', and it provides a longitude that is more reliable the smaller the visible latitude is.

<margin>Through precepts 153, 170.</margin>
Therefore, at the moment of observation, seek out the parallaxes of longitude and latitude of the Moon from the Sun, and let the true latitude from the calculation be converted into the visible latitude. When its antilogarithm <note>The value corresponding to a logarithm in Kepler's tables</note> is subtracted from the antilogarithm of the distance of the centers, the antilogarithm of the visible longitude of the Moon from the Sun remains, as above. The rest follows as before.

> For example, because the beginning of this Eclipse was observed at Uraniborg <note>Tycho Brahe's observatory in Denmark</note> at 10 hours and 10 minutes (by a student sent back to the island by Tycho for the sake of this observation), when the Sun was in 16° 44' of Pisces ♓, and distant from the Node ☊ by 9° 46', the Moon—if it were in the position of the Sun—would have had a latitude of 33' 50'' North. But the parallax of the Moon from the Sun is found for this time at Uraniborg to be 5' 12'' of longitude to the west, and 55' 52'' of latitude; thus the visible latitude becomes about 2'. (Which you may correct after finding the true position of the Moon.)

<column-break/>

> This visible latitude, being so small, I say, detracts very little from the distance of the centers of 31' 27'', so that the visible Longitude of the Moon from the Sun becomes about 31 ½'. This, when subtracted from the position of the Sun because the Eclipse is beginning, gives a sufficiently reliable true Ecliptic position of the Moon at 16° 12 ¾' of Pisces ♓.

<margin>See precept 188.</margin>
This is certainly the most certain method of all for observing the position of the Moon, provided there is no doubt about the true position of the Sun, and that it does not fluctuate in the smallest fractions; a suspicion about which there will be a place to speak elsewhere.

### How the difference of Meridians is investigated from the observation of certain phases of a Solar Eclipse in different places.

<margin>PRECEPT 176</margin>
<margin>See the Astronomical Part of Optics, Chapter 11.</margin>
<margin>Through precept 175</margin>
The most certain of all phases are the very beginning and the very end; or if the quantity of the defect was defined with a compass in a ray of light, once the fringe which the width of the aperture casts around it has been wiped away from the ray.

From the observation and its location, at the apparent time in that place, let the true positions of the Moon relative to the Sun be sought. When these are compared with each other, if they are on different sides <note>East or West of the Sun</note>, their sum—or if on the same side, their difference—divided by the true hourly motion of the Moon from the Sun, reveals the corresponding hours and minutes. These should be added to the apparent time of that place where the Moon's position appears earlier. When the time thus changed is compared with the observed time of that place, the difference of the Meridians <note>Geographic longitude</note> will be clear.

<margin>By Logarithms if you please.</margin>
> As in our Eclipse, let the end of the eclipse be observed at Graz exactly at 12 hours and 47 minutes; when the Moon had truly followed the Sun to 52' 29'' of Pisces ♓. But the beginning was observed at Uraniborg at 10 hours and 10 minutes, when the Moon truly preceded the Sun by 26' 8''. The sum is 1 degree 18 ½', which, divided by the hourly motion of the Moon from the Sun of 33' 54'', gives a quotient of 2 hours and 19 minutes. And because at Uraniborg the position of the Moon precedes, add the found time to its time, making it 12 hours and 29 minutes. But at Graz, the Moon occupied that later position at 12 hours and 47 minutes. Therefore, the difference of Meridians would be 18 minutes.

<margin>Precept 57</margin>
This is both the best and most beautiful way of investigating the difference of Meridians, and it far surpasses the other method using Eclipses of the Moon. But as I said in Chapter 16, a conclusion about the smallest details should not be made without some multitude of consensus, especially if the visible latitude becomes large, as it does here at the end; for then the longitude provided by it is less reliable.

### Concerning the finding of the Azimuth or the region of the world in which the eclipsing luminary is viewed.

<margin>PRECEPT 177</margin>
<margin>Epitome of Astronomy, book 3, page 228.</margin>
Ptolemy in the *Quadripartitum* <note>The Tetrabiblos, Ptolemy's work on astrology</note> orders us to consider the regions of the Heaven as well. General methods for inquiring into the Azimuth are handed down in spherical geometry; here we deal only with Eclipses. Let us therefore use what is already necessary for the work. In the Ecliptic there are three points: the Luminary <note>The Sun or Moon</note>, the point culminating in the Meridian, and the Nonagesimal degree <note>The point of the ecliptic 90 degrees from the horizon</note> from the rising. These, connected with the Vertex <note>The Zenith</note>, constitute two triangles; and the common angle at the Nonagesimal is a right angle. Since the arcs of the Horizon—which the Arabs call Azimuths—measure the angles at the vertex, it is clear that the angles of these two triangles at the vertex must be investigated. Therefore, such a precept arises.

<page-num>114</page-num>
<header>RUDOLPHINE TABLES</header>

<margin>Concerning this, see Chapter 13, precept 33.</margin>
Through the apparent time and the position of the Sun, the Nonagesimal <note>The 90th degree of the ecliptic measured from the eastern horizon; it is the highest point of the ecliptic above the horizon</note> from the rising point becomes known, as does its distance from the Vertex <note>The Zenith, or the point directly overhead</note>, from the Culminating point <note>The Midheaven, where the ecliptic crosses the local meridian</note>, and from the Luminary <note>The Sun or Moon</note>. Therefore, subtract the Logarithms of the distances of both the Luminary and the culminating point from the vertex, from the Logarithms of the distances of each of those from the Nonagesimal; the remainders will be the Logarithms of the angles at the vertex. One of these is equal to the Rising Amplitude. These angles—either combined, if the culminating point is found between the two points, or if not, subtracted, the smaller from the larger—form the sought-after **Azimuth** <note>The horizontal direction of a celestial object</note>. Observation or imagining the Sphere will indicate the direction <note>North, South, East, or West</note>.

Thus in an Eclipse: with 23° of Cancer ♋ rising, the Nonagesimal is 23° of Aries ♈; the culminating point is 30° of Pisces ♓; the Luminary is at 17° of Pisces ♓. These are distant from the vertex by 42°, 47° 12', and 52° 48'. Thus, the angles are found to be 32° 40' (the Rising Amplitude) and 46° 21'. By subtracting the former from the latter, the **Azimuth** is 13° 41' from the South toward the West.

### Chapter XXXIII.

### ON THE CONJUNCTIONS AND OPPOSITIONS OF THE OTHER Planets, and on Revolutions <note>original: "exeligmos"</note> and Restorations <note>original: "apocatastasis," meaning the return of a planet to a specific starting position</note>.

<margin>
PRECEPT 178.
Of each planet with the Sun.
</margin>
<margin>Through precepts 7 and 6.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'C' with scrollwork and foliage motifs.</image-desc>
<margin>Tables on pages 100, 101, 102.</margin>
The mean Conjunctions of the six Planets—Jupiter ♃, Saturn ♄, Mars ♂, Venus ♀, and Mercury ☿—each with the Sun, are tracked in this way. At the proposed time, collect the mean motions of the Sun and one of the others. Subtract the position of the faster planet from the position of the slower one, adding 12 signs if necessary. The remaining interval from the lighter to the heavier planet (as the Astrologers say), with the Signs converted into Degrees, should be divided by six to produce the **Minutes of a single full Restoration** <note>original: "Scrupula Restitutionis," a technical term for the fractional part of a planet's return cycle</note>, which should be fewer than 60. With these Minutes, from the Sixty-day Table of days <note>original: "Canon Sexagenario," a table used for calculations in base-60</note> which pertains to any of the "Wanderers" <note>The planets</note>, select the Sixty-day periods, Days, and Minutes—namely, the desired time. If an Opposition is sought, or a conjunction of Venus ♀ or Mercury ☿ when retrograde with the Sun ☉, or of Mercury alone: subtract 30' from the Minutes of the full Restoration, or if that is not possible, add them; then perform the selection from the table.

<margin>Precept 52.</margin>
As in the *Rudolphine Nativity* <note>Kepler likely refers to the calculation of the horoscope of Emperor Rudolph II</note>, the mean motion of Jupiter ♃ was collected as 4 Signs, 6° 14' 22'', and for Saturn ♄ as 11 Signs, 5° 35' 5''. Therefore, the motion of the former as the faster being subtracted from the motion of the latter, there remain 6 Signs, 29° 20' 43'' or 209° etc. A sixth part of these is 34' 53'' 27''', which we call the **Minutes of Restoration**. Therefore, with 34' selected, we get 3 Sixty-day periods, 34' 5'' 7''; with 53'' we get 5' 33'' 59''; with 27''' we get 2' 50''. The sum becomes 3 Sixty-day periods, 39° 51' 56'', that is, 219 Days and 51' 56'' of time. This much time remains until the next mean conjunction of the Sun ☉ and Saturn ♄.

For an opposition, instead of 34' 59'' 27''', one would have used 4' 59'' 27''', after discarding 30.

<margin>Tables on pages 94 and 100.</margin>
The method is nearly the same for the restoration of the Moon ☾ to its Apogee, to the Sun ☉, or to the Node ☊; except that the times for the Quarters of a single Restoration are stored in the tables. Therefore, the interval between the Moon and the other three must be divided: for one, not by 6 but by 1 1/2, so that the Minutes are not for a full Restoration, but for a single Quarter.

<margin>PRECEPT 179.</margin>
For the mean conjunctions ☌ of the 5 Planets and the Node ☊ with each other, to know when any one follows a

<column-break/>

proposed time: look for the conjunction of each with the Sun ☉ that follows most closely, and subtract the time collected for the faster one from the time for the slower one; assuming, if necessary, the time of one full Restoration of the Sun to it, or it to the Sun.

<margin>Of two planets with each other.</margin>
<margin>Tables on pages 100, 101.</margin>
Then scan the individual lines of the two Tables, noting when the areas of each create a difference between them equal to the one that just remained, and in which parts of the numbers. You will achieve this more accurately by a double entry: first by the full Restorations, then by the Minutes, etc. Therefore, whatever times selected from the tables provide this, each is to be added to the time of its own next restoration to the Sun; with the parts of the numbers in which such a great difference was found being subordinated each to its like. In this way, an equal Sum of time will be produced on both sides, which, having passed from the proposed start, will show the two planets in conjunction.

### On Restorations <note>original: "Apocatastasis"</note>, or the finding of the returns of several stars to the same starting point.

<margin>
PRECEPT 180
The Period of conjunction for two.
</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' with intricate vine and petal patterns.</image-desc>
How much time actually intervenes between two close mean conjunctions of the same Planets, you will find thus. If one of the two is the Sun, the times of Restoration are in the tables, except in the Table of the Sun ☉ and Moon ☾; for in that one, the times of the Quarters of Restoration are stored in the tables. Therefore, whenever in the others one descends by one line, in the Lunar Table one must descend by 4 lines, so that the times of these Restorations can be compared: of the Moon ☾ to its Apogee and the Node ☊. If, however, the Sun is not one of the two: look for equal times in the Tables of the two others—namely, the times of the Restorations of the Sun to either one, without noting the number of the Restorations in the margin. Whatever Sum of time is found to be the same in both places, that will define the sought-after Period. Here also is the place for double entry to balance the times more accurately.

<margin>
PRECEPT 181.
The Period of conjunction for many.
</margin>
Finally, when a Restoration <note>Apocatastasis</note> of several moving bodies among themselves occurs, or of their Quadratures <note>90-degree aspects</note> or opposite locations; although it is laborious, these Tables nevertheless provide helpful assistance. At the start, the difference of the Periods should be noted for the sake of Longitude. The shortest is the Moon ☾ to the Node ☊; from there this order follows: Moon ☾ to the Sun ☉/Mercury ☿, Moon ☾ to the Apogee, Moon ☾ to the Sun ☉. The section for these Restorations is separate from the others, because here the Center of the Earth is also considered; for the others, the center is the same as that of the solar body. Of those, the shortest is Venus ♀ to the Sun ☉, then Mars ♂ to the Sun ☉, Mercury ☿ to the Equinox, Jupiter ♃ to the Sun ☉, Saturn ♄ to the Sun ☉, Venus ♀ to Mars ♂, and Jupiter ♃ to Mars ♂.

<margin>Through precept 180.</margin>
Therefore, begin from the shorter Period; look for its time, which is found exactly in its own Table, in the Table of the slower body, and establish the proportion of Restorations on both sides through the marginal numbers, and the time through the tables. In this time—as small as possible—three moving bodies should come together again as closely as possible, or reach Quarters or Oppositions. But if at the first entry there is some remaining difference of times by which the individual bodies are reconciled with the Sun, proceed at the second entry to equate the times of the sixty-fold units in the subsequent parts of the numbers more accurately. For if in this larger Period as well some difference remains; that being multiplied several times with its times...

It transitions from calculating planetary positions to determining the vast periodic cycles of the heavens and the theoretical "Great Year," including Kepler's calculation for the date of the world's creation.</meta>

<page-num>115</page-num>
<header>RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS</header>

through these times and the numbers of the Restorations <note>original: "Restitutionum"; refers to a planet returning to its starting position</note>, a value will eventually grow into the size of the difference of a minor Period. Therefore, it will be corrected if you add or take away one minor period from several major ones; by this method, a third period is established. If you seek the time of this third Period—which is not contained many times within the age of the world—also in the Table of the fourth Moving Body <note>The Sun</note>, which has a slower Restoration to the Sun, you will associate that also with the same Restoration <note>original: "Apocatastasin"; the return of celestial bodies to the same relative positions</note> as closely as possible. However, a discrepancy, if any emerges, is more easily tolerated in a slower moving body—since it is to be removed by the correction of its mean motion—than in a swifter one, which grows into a sensible magnitude more slowly.

<margin>Evolutions of the motions of the Moon</margin>
The ancients labored in reconciling the motions of the Moon among themselves, and they gave the name "Evolution" <note>original Greek: "ἐξελιγμὸς"</note> to the Period. Therefore, the Fourth <note>A "fourth" or "quart" is a tiny mathematical unit: 1/60th of a "third," which is 1/60th of a second</note> of latitude differs from the Fourth of Anomaly <note>The variation in a planet's speed or position due to its elliptical orbit</note> by 5' 8'' 63'''. This difference, when traced down through all the lines of the Tables, does not grow to the size of the time of one Fourth. Therefore, returning to the top line, from 1 Restoration, I make 1, or 60; then the difference also becomes 5° 8' 6''. Thus, by a second entry through 20 Restorations, I find the difference D: 1° 42' 42'', which, added to the previous one, makes the difference D: 6° 50' 49'', almost equal to the time of one Fourth. Therefore, the correction is made by subtracting one Fourth from the slower motion. From this is born the minimum Period of 79 Fourths of Anomaly and 80 Fourths of Latitude, the time of which is 9' 4° <note>minutes and degrees</note>; but for the Anomaly, it now falls short by 2' 30'' 17'''. Therefore, the partner to this period will be that which has 80 Anomaly and 81 Latitude, the time of which is 9' 11°. Here it still exceeds the Anomalistic motion by 2' 37'' 50'''. And because this excess and that deficit are almost equal, one Period corrects the other when taken once. Thus the second period becomes 159 Fourths of Anomaly and 161 Fourths of Latitude, the time of which is 18' 15°, etc., in which it exceeds the Anomalistic motion by 7' 33'''.

Indeed, this sought-after time, found through the other Tables, is found almost in line 3 of the Table for the Tropical year <note>The year measured by the seasons (equinox to equinox)</note>, or for Mars ♂, the Sun ☉, and Saturn ♄. But because neither of these two moving bodies was among the first three, they are not yet reconciled with each other, but those three are reconciled separately among themselves, and these two also separately between themselves.

Nor does the remaining difference allow for infinite multiplication. For since the time is of three years, in 180 years the difference already becomes 7' 33''', and in 1400 years it exceeds a day. But in the motion of Anomaly we cannot lose a day within this time, and in Latitude not even an hour; only the observations of the ancients stand in the way. Therefore, one must proceed to a more exact Period. And because 7' 33''' is contained in 2' 30'' 17''' slightly less than twenty times, a Third Period will be born by multiplying the second by twenty and adding one minor first period, so that the twenty-fold excess of the former obliterates the deficit of the latter. Thus, to the Fourths 3180 and 3220, 79 and 80 are added, becoming 3259 and 3300. The times are collected as 6'' 14' 10'', etc., and it exceeds the Anomalistic by 45''; but through the Julian Table <margin>Tables, p. 102.</margin> reduced to years, they give 61 ½ years.

<column-break/>

Let the Calculator seek this time through the rest of the Tables, to see if perhaps the remaining moving bodies might associate themselves at least by Fourths. If he should show any day within 1700 years that restores the three motions of the Moon (for I say nothing of the other Wanderers <note>The planets</note>) to the Fourths—I do not say the same ones, but various ones—with a tolerable discrepancy: then I will confess the probability of the day of Creation proposed by me <margin>The starting gates <note>original: "Carceres"</note>, from which all the moving bodies rushed into their courses. See precept 76.</margin> has been established by him. That day was in the year 3993 before our era, on the 24th of July in the extended Julian calendar, with the Sun, Moon, the Node of the Moon ☽, Mars, Venus, the Aphelion of Jupiter ♃ <note>The point in orbit furthest from the Sun</note>, the Node of Jupiter, and perhaps also the Aphelion of Jupiter, joined in the solstitial point <note>The point of the Summer Solstice</note>; with Jupiter and the Node of Mercury ☿ in the winter solstice point; with Saturn, the Aphelion of Venus ♀, and the Apogee of the Moon ☽ <note>The point furthest from Earth</note>, and perhaps also the Aphelion of Saturn ♄, in the autumnal equinox; with Mercury, the Apogee of the Sun ☉, the Node of Saturn ♄, the Node of Venus ♀, and perhaps also the Node of Mars ♂, in the vernal equinox; so that only the Aphelion of Mars ♂ out of all of them was set uncertainly between Aries ♈ and Taurus ♉, and indeed in a precisely intermediate place.

### To investigate the Anticipation (πρόεμπτωσιν) of the Equinoxes, the Postponement (μετέμπτωσιν) of the rising of fixed stars, and the Precession of the Equinoxes, or the mean quantity of the Tropical year, in any assumed sum of years.
<margin>PRECEPTS 182 183 184</margin>

Convert the sum of years, by division by 60, into First Sexagesimals <note>Groups of 60 years</note>, the sum of Firsts into Seconds, etc. With these Sexagesimals and single years sought in the margin of the Sexagenary Tables, extract the times under the <margin>As in precepts 77. 78. 79. 80. Tables p. 192.</margin> titles of Julian, Tropical, and Sidereal <note>Year measured by the stars</note> years, and each of them; and having made a suitable addition of the excerpts through various entries, if you subtract the Tropical time from the Julian time, <margin>See Epitome of Astronomy, book 7, p. 927.</margin> the Anticipation <note>original: "πρόεμπτωσις"</note> will remain; if the Julian time from the Sidereal time, the Postponement <note>original: "Μετέμπτωσις"</note>; and finally, if the Tropical from the Sidereal, the Precession, which equals the Anticipation and Postponement joined together. But in calculating the Anticipation and Postponement, take care that the number of years proposed is an even-even number <note>A number divisible by 4</note>.

### Concerning the Restoration of Tropical and Sidereal years, or the Great Celestial Year.

Indeed, you will track the Evolution <note>original: "ἐξελιγμὸς"</note> of Julian, <margin>PRECEPT 185. Through precepts 180 181.</margin> Tropical, and Sidereal years by the method above. You will find that 25,411 Sidereal years are equal to 25,412 Tropical years. But the restoration of Julian and Tropical years is almost twice as slow; as is that of Julian with Sidereal years. Finally, the Restoration <note>original: "Restitutio"</note> of all three into the same starting point requires a monstrous sum of years: which I leave for the calculator to seek.

# PRECEPTS FOR THE FOURTH PART OF THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES.

---

### CHAPTER XXXIV.
### ON THE VARIATION OF THE OBLIQUITY OF THE ECLIPTIC.

---

<margin>
As stated in
Chap. XII,
Precept on page 27.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'C' for the word 'Since', containing a small woodcut illustration of an armillary sphere <note>An early astronomical instrument representing the great circles of the heavens</note>.</image-desc>Since it is a doubtful matter whether the obliquity of the Ecliptic <term>Obliquity of the Ecliptic: The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit, which causes the seasons</term> changes at all over the course of centuries; and if it does change, in what manner and by what amount it occurs: let the Astronomer, when approaching the calculation of the motion of the Planets, know that no delay or impediment will be thrown in his way, even if he should pass over this entire section untouched. He may simply use an obliquity as great as the most excellent craftsmen have measured in our own time, 23° 31' 30", or by our reduced solar parallax <note>original: "Parallaxin"; the apparent displacement of the Sun when viewed from different points on Earth</note>, 23° 30' 30", as if this quantity were constant.
<margin>Reason for the order.</margin>
This is the reason why I have relegated this section to the end of the whole work—a topic which, in the works of Copernicus and the Prutenic Tables, occupies the very entrance-hall, as if it were the chief emblem and boast of the entire work.

<margin>Tables, pp. 103, 104.</margin>
If, however, anyone wishes to attempt this calculation: let him know that five forms of it are proposed in these tables. The first of these follows the reliability of the Observations of Eratosthenes <note>A Greek polymath (c. 276–194 BC) who first measured the Earth's circumference and tilt</note>, whom Hipparchus followed, and whom Ptolemy confirmed by his own observations, as he himself indeed asserts. In shaping this form, I have allowed only a very small amount of leeway in the selection of the Epoch of Creation.

The second form, on the contrary, assumed everything from theoretical reasoning <note>original: "speculationibus à priori"</note>, to which the observations of Eratosthenes and Ptolemy nevertheless provided guidance from afar. The third, fourth, and fifth are mixed; since they could not maintain all parts of the theory according to the said observations, they have retained some parts which seemed to have greater probability in theory, and draw out the remaining parts from the observations of the ancients, joined with archetypal theory, by the necessity of mathematical demonstrations.

Regarding these five forms, therefore, the calculator must carefully attend to which one he proposed to follow at the beginning: for he must proceed along its path all the way to the end of the calculation.

<margin>Mean Ecliptic.</margin>
In all five forms, this is common: it is supposed that around the pole of the "Royal Road" <note>original: "viæ Regiæ"; a poetic term for the Ecliptic path</note>, or mean Ecliptic, there is a certain small circle in which the pole of the temporary Ecliptic moves uniformly against the order of the signs; or at least, that it oscillates back and forth within the diameter of that small circle, which is a small part of the colure of the solstices <note>A great circle passing through the celestial poles and the solstices</note>. This small circle is divided, in the manner of the others, into 360 degrees, etc. The beginning of the numbering starts from the point that is furthest from the pole of the Equator; and the numbering proceeds in the direction preceding the signs. And in this circle thus divided, the Argument of Obliquity <term>Argument of Obliquity: The numerical value or "input" used to determine the specific tilt at a given time</term> is numbered in all five forms.

<margin>

common.

ALTHOUGH the Tables already show the obliquities themselves as calculated in the first, more common form: nevertheless, because there are five forms, I will teach how to calculate what is proposed generally according to all of them, rather than merely extracting the values. For I consider it superfluous to build fivefold Tables of the Prosthaphaereses <term>Prosthaphaeresis: A correction factor added or subtracted to a "mean" or average position to find the "true" position</term> of the Obliquity; since the matter itself is uncertain, as said; and therefore there is either no use for such Tables, or it is very rare. Finally, this business is so arranged that an attentive calculator, observing this precept, can calculate the sought value just as easily without a Table as he could take it from a pre-constructed Table by means of a proportional part.
<margin>
PRECEPT 186.
Tables, p. 103
below.
</margin>
Therefore, write down the Mean Obliquity proper to whichever form you have chosen this time, together with the Radius of the Small Circle. You will find these in the Table of the Obliquity of the Ecliptic, recorded at the bottom of each form.

Then add the Antilogarithm of the Argument of Obliquity to the Logarithm of the appropriate Small Circle: the sum, when sought as a Logarithm in the Canon <note>A standard table of logarithms</note>, shows the Prosthaphaeresis of the Obliquity, which you add to the mean obliquity in the first and last quadrant of the Argument, and subtract in the second and third.

This obliquity, established in either case—if you are dealing with the first form—is perfect and absolute without exception on account of the smallness of its circle; but in the four remaining forms, it is perfect only if the pole of the Ecliptic is oscillating in the diameter of the small circle. But if that pole is supposed to go around the circumference of the small circle, then because of its size in the four later forms, there will be need for some small correction, which is performed as follows.

Add the Logarithm of the Argument of obliquity to the Logarithm of the Small Circle, which is proper to each form. Keep the Sum for use in the following precept, and now look it up in the Table of the Correction of Obliquity under the title "Aggregate"; and add the small correction placed on that line to the obliquity previously found in either case; thus it will be the absolute and perfect obliquity according to each form.
<margin>Tables, p. 104 at the bottom.</margin>

### EXAMPLE.

*For the year of Christ 883, let the obliquity be found according to the fourth form. The Epoch of the year of Christ 800, being the next smaller, gives the Argument 5 Signs 3° 28' 0"; for the remaining 83 years (or the nearest number in the Table for Year 84), it gives 2° 41' 25". The sum becomes the Argument of obliquity 5 Signs 6° 9' 25", or 156° 9'.*
