->To Calculate the Prosthaphaeresis of the Equinoxes.<-

<margin>PRECEPT 187.</margin> If there is truly either no change in the Obliquity of the Ecliptic, or such a change that the pole of the temporary Ecliptic oscillates on the <term>colure</term><note>One of the two principal great circles of the celestial sphere</note> of the solstices—if this is the case, I say, no correction (prosthaphaeresis) for the motion of the Equinoxes needs to be sought. If, however, we suppose that the said Pole travels around the circumference of a small circle according to one of the five forms, then this correction for the motion of the Equinoxes also arises. In the first form, this is shown already computed at intervals of 74 years, during which the Argument of obliquity increases by ten degrees; but it can be sought more precisely and commonly in all forms as follows.

First, have ready: 1. The Argument of Obliquity, 2. The uncorrected Obliquity, 3. The total sum for extracting the small correction. From this total, then, subtract the Logarithm of that uncorrected Obliquity; to the remainder, in turn, add the Antilogarithm of the mean Obliquity. The resulting sum, sought in the Table as a Logarithm, will show the Prosthaphaeresis, which carries the label "to be added" in the first semi-circle of the Argument of Obliquity, and "to be subtracted" in the second.

For example, because the previous total was 519584, and the uncorrected Obliquity was 23° 34' 32", subtract its Logarithm 91640; 427944 remains. To this remainder, add the Antilogarithm of the Mean Obliquity 9237. The sum 437217, sought among the Logarithms of the Table, shows 43' 27", the required correction of the equinoxes according to the fourth form, to which this total and mean Obliquity pertained above. And because the Argument of obliquity is from the first semi-circle (namely 156° 9'), this correction of the Equinoxes must be added. In the first form, however, you see the correction is shown as approximately 27' to be added.

->On which day of any year before or after Christ the equinox occurs.<-

<margin>PRECEPT 188.</margin><margin>Precept 139</margin> Above in Chapter XXX, in the description of the subsidiary Table of the Sun’s motions, you learned in passing how to compute the day of the true equinox; but it was assumed that the equinoctial points creep backward at a uniform rate among the fixed stars. Because the inequality of this <term>Precession</term><note>The slow, "backwards" movement of the equinoxes relative to the stars, which Kepler's contemporaries were still trying to measure accurately</note>

<column-break/>

is uncertain, it is certainly not as great as Copernicus reported. See Tycho Brahe's *Progymnasmata* <margin>page 36 of his book</margin> Volume I. Now in this chapter, since from the five-fold form of Obliquity a corresponding five-fold correction of the Equinoxes arises, a general precept for computing the Day and hour of the Equinox must be provided. Its certainty is to be judged by the specific doctrine of each form.

From the Tables of the mean motions of the Sun, for the given completed years, collect the <margin>By precept 76.</margin> mean motion of the Sun and the position of the <term>Apogee</term><note>The point in the Sun's orbit (now known to be Earth's orbit) furthest from the center</note>, or in its place, the annual <term>Anomaly</term><note>The angle used to find a planet's position in its elliptical orbit</note>. <margin>By precept 79.</margin> Then, to the mean motion, add the mean motion of as many months, days, and hours as needed until the circle is complete (for the spring equinox) or until a half-circle is added (for the Autumn equinox). Thus, the time of the "mean" (average) equinox will be established. Then, using the Sun's Anomaly—either collected or formed through the Apogee and mean motion <margin>As in precept 81.</margin>—let the <margin>By precept 85</margin> Prosthaphaeresis be extracted with its label, and by the same means, the daily and hourly motion of the Sun <margin>By precept 141</margin> from the subsidiary tables. If it is assumed that no correction of the Equinoxes occurs, let the <term>Equation of the Sun</term><note>The difference between the Sun's average and actual position</note> alone be divided by the daily and hourly motion; this will yield the Days, Hours, and minutes to be added to the time of the mean equinox (if the equation was to be subtracted) or subtracted (if it was to be added), so that the time of the "true" equinox is obtained. If, however, some correction of the equinoxes is established, let it be sought according to whichever of the five forms <margin>By precept 186</margin> is preferred, for all are in doubt. Once this correction is established, a compensation must be made in the motion of the Sun, so that what this correction takes away, the change in the mean motion restores in our time. And since the Compensation in the 4th and 5th forms has its own <term>Epoch</term><note>A starting reference point in time</note>, this is always subtracted: <margin>Subscribed at the bottom of page 104.</margin> The Compensation is always Added: the Prosthaphaeresis, like the Equation of the Sun, is sometimes Subtracted, sometimes Added. Therefore, if these four items have the same label, they are joined into one sum; if they differ, the smaller ones of the same label are subtracted from the larger ones, and the remainder is marked with the label of the larger. Finally, let this sum or remainder be divided by the Sun's daily or hourly motion, and the result applied to the time of the mean equinox, using the label opposite to that of the dividend, as before.

For example, consider the equinox of Hipparchus <note>A famous Greek astronomer of the 2nd century BC</note> observed in the year 147 before Christ: we calculate at the beginning of that year the Apogee at 5° 49' 45" in Gemini, and the Sun's mean motion at 9 signs 7° 28' 31". February of a common year adds 1 sign 28° 9' 11", making 11 signs 5° 37' 42". 24 days add 23° 39' 20". This makes 0 signs 11° 29' 17"; the remainder to complete the circle is the motion of 17 hours, 26 minutes, 24 seconds. From this, relative to the Apogee, the Complement of the Anomaly is numbered at 65° 50', which gives an Equation of 1° 5' 52" to be added; however, in the same year 147, the Correction of the Equinoxes is found to be 10' 36" to be subtracted. Conversely, because the year 147 BC is 3,853 years from the Epoch of Creation, through this interval the Compensation of the first form is collected as 11' to be added, without an Epoch. Therefore, having combined the additions and the subtraction, the remainder is 1° 5' 2" 18", which, divided by the daily motion of 58' 10", makes 1 day, 22 hours, 20 minutes, to be subtracted from the time of the mean equinox. Thus, the true equinox in the year 147 occurs on the current day of March 23, at 19 hours, 6 minutes, 24 seconds from noon at Uraniborg, according to this first form of the Correction of the Equinoxes—differing from what we calculate without the correction.

at a minimum: for just as this occurred in the time of Hipparchus and in our own, a <term>Compensation</term><note>Latin: *pensatio*; a mathematical adjustment used to balance discrepancies in orbital calculations</note> is attached to this form, as well as to each of the others.

<margin>A Caution.</margin>
However, by this rule, the days of the equinoxes—as Ptolemy claims to have observed them—are not represented in every respect.

Whatever differences may exist here, whether between the models themselves or from a uniform <term>precession</term><note>The slow, circular wobbling of the Earth’s axis that changes the timing of the seasons</note>, we should not be moved by the authority of Ptolemy. He seems to have erred entirely in the numbering of the days of the Egyptian year, perhaps misled either by Hipparchus’s calculation of the Sun’s motion or by the Roman Calendar and its <term>intercalation</term><note>The insertion of leap days to keep a calendar aligned with the seasons</note>. This conjecture is strengthened by a passage in Censorinus, who reports that in the very same year that Ptolemy last observed the Moon—and subsequently (extraordinary Roman intercalations having already been announced in Egypt) observed both equinoxes—the first day of the Egyptian month of Thoth fell on the 12th day before the Calends of August. It ought to have been on the 13th, if the same pattern of the Julian intercalation had been maintained then as is today, and if the year had not suffered any extraordinary interference from the Priests.

<margin>
See Astronomical Epistles, page 921.
Progymnasmata, Vol 1. pages 32 and 254.
Commentary on Mars, Chapter 69.
</margin>
<margin>
Longimontanus, in "Theories of Astronomy," Book 1, page 33, said not only that he erred in observing, but that he feigned several observations that he had actually computed from Hipparchus.
</margin>
Yet if we hold Ptolemy’s reputation for carefulness in too high a regard to believe he could be deceived by a calculation or the Roman year, we must resort to extremes and say that the equinoxes made a "jump" around Ptolemy's time, which the following centuries up until Proclus had to compensate for. Indeed, I can prove by the most certain evidence of <term>ecliptic</term><note>The apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> observations that the Sun’s approach even to the fixed stars is unequal around its minimum points. If God wills, I shall publish a separate book on this matter.

<margin>
On the contrary, I wrote in the Epitome, page 921, that the Sun's motion fluctuates due to physical causes. See the introduction to the Ephemerides, page 99.
</margin>
By this one observation, the caution of our Tycho is most highly commended as being utterly necessary. For the sake of greater credibility, I shall transcribe it from the book of Origanus published long ago; these are his words:
> *Tycho wished to show an accurate solar motion that responded exquisitely enough to the observations of these times (even if only for a few centuries). For that reason, he does not explain how his equation of time for the calculation of the Sun's motion changes for different eras. He repeatedly warns and insists that others should follow his example and achieve something in this area; **ESPECIALLY SINCE WE DETECT IN THE CELESTIAL BODIES NOT THAT SAME PERPETUITY, STABILITY, AND CONSTANCY OF MOTION WHICH MOST PHILOSOPHERS IMAGINE FOR THEMSELVES IN THE HEAVENS.***

Thus far Origanus. Since this greatest master of astronomical contemplation has affirmed this as a witness, let some philosopher of the Stoic sect go now and try to tear down the faith of our sacred history—which testifies to the Sun’s course being halted or turned backward—by a stubborn presumption about nature.

### On the varying length of the Tropical Year, and on seeking Revolutions.

<margin>
PRECEPT 189.
Tables page 102.
</margin>
The Canon shows the <term>Mean Quantity</term><note>The average or "ideal" value before accounting for specific local variations</note> of any number of <term>Tropical Years</term><note>The time it takes for the Sun to return to the same position in the cycle of seasons, such as from one spring equinox to the next</note> in days, sixty-day units, and fractions. However, two causes vary this in calculation: the first is certain and inherent—the different starting points of the tropics through the year, or as astrologers say, the different roots of the <term>Revolutions</term><note>The completion of one full orbit or seasonal cycle</note>. For the Tropical year is shortest when it begins from the Sun’s <term>Apogee</term><note>The point in the Sun's apparent orbit where it is furthest from Earth</note>; it is longest when it begins from the <term>Perigee</term><note>The point where it is closest to Earth</note>; and it is middling at the mean longitudes, which today are in 6° of Gemini or Sagittarius. The second cause, the <term>Prosthaphaeresis</term><note>A correction added or subtracted to adjust a mean value to a true value</note>
<margin>Found by Precept 186.</margin>

<column-break/>

of the equinoxes, is both uncertain and imperceptible in a small number of years. For if the correction for the equinoxes and the "Compensation" of the stars' motion are equal and of opposite effects, this cause does not change the Tropical year; it is otherwise if they are of the same effect, or if they are opposite but unequal. In the former case the sum of both, and in the latter the difference, changes the length of the Tropical year.

<margin>
Precept 139
Precept 187
Tables page 102.
</margin>
For the sake of the Revolutions, therefore, let the second cause be neglected. If indeed the "Root" or the position of the Sun in the Ecliptic is indicated (to which the Sun must return after some years), you have already learned above how to investigate the time from the subsidiary tables; or even just now: for the process is the same. Simply take the "root" position of the Sun instead of the 0° Aries or 0° Libra positions, and to complete the 12 signs, propose the length of the Sun's position from 0° Aries to be completed. If the position is not given, let it be sought by time, at least to the nearest noon; then add the hours of the root to the hours emerging in the year of the Revolution. This is most advisable, although the Sexagesimal Canons could have multiple uses for other methods.

### How the rest of Astronomy is handled once the Correction of the Equinoxes is accepted and calculated.

<margin>
PRECEPT 190.
Of the fixed stars by general Precept 70.
By Precept 187.
</margin>
FIRST, the positions of the stars must be defined differently. Once the true positions of each have been calculated according to the preceding precepts, first find the Corrections (*Prosthaphaereses*) for the year of our era 1588 in the chosen "Form." If it is labeled "Subtract," add it to the position of the stars (excepting the Sun); if "Add," subtract it. Then find the Correction specific to the year in question, and according to what the label requires, add it in the first semicircle of the Obliquity argument, and subtract it in the second.

<margin>
PRECEPT 191.
As in Precept 188.
</margin>
The Sun must be dealt with differently: first, it is not the Correction for the year 1588 that is used, but in Forms I, IV, and V, its own peculiar arc—placed at the bottom of the "Compensation" table—must be perpetually subtracted. Then, through the interval from the proposed year back to the epoch of 4000 BC, once the argument of obliquity for each form is established, the correction for the equinox must be sought and, according to the label, added or subtracted as with the others. Thirdly, from the same Argument of Obliquity, let the Compensation also be extracted for Forms I, IV, and V, and let it be added according to the label. It does not matter, among these three which share the same label, whether they are added separately or in a heap; or if they are of different labels, whether they affect the position to be corrected separately or by the difference of the larger one.

For example, let the true position of the Sun in the year 1625 be 24° 38' Leo, where the star *Cor Leonis* <note>Regulus, the heart of the Lion</note> is. Let the positions be corrected by the Correction of Form I. Therefore, I extract the 1588 Correction: 17' 13'' to be subtracted (which I would also calculate if I used the Epoch of the argument written at the bottom of Form I for 4000 BC, and then gathered the motion of the Argument through the interval from that time, etc.). Add this to the position of the fixed star, contrary to what the label "Subtract" wants. Now, for the year 1625, the Correction is 19' 25'' to be subtracted, which I subtract. After taking away the 17' 13'', there remain 2' 12'' to be subtracted, so that the position of the fixed star becomes 24° 35' 48'' Leo. But for the Sun's position, I subtract nothing for the year 1588, because nothing is placed at the bottom of the Compensation table in Form I. I do, however, subtract the Correction for the year, namely 19' 25''. Then find the "Compensation" for this year, which is 16' 2'' to be added, which I add. After taking the additions from the subtractions, 3' 23'' remain to be subtracted, and the position of the Sun becomes 24° 34' 37'' Leo.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the "Rudolphine Tables," Johannes Kepler’s masterwork of planetary motion. On the previous page, Kepler discussed the Earth's axial tilt (obliquity) and the historical discrepancies in the timing of the equinoxes. Here, he begins to provide specific mathematical "precepts" or rules for calculating the positions and latitudes of the fixed stars across different eras, comparing his data with that of the ancient astronomer Hipparchus and his own predecessor, Tycho Brahe.</meta>

<page-num>119</page-num>
<header>RUDOLPHINE PRECEPTS.</header>

These things are so arranged because, since it is necessary for the equinoxes of Tycho and Hipparchus to be represented through the motion of the Sun, the positions of these equinoxes—having been introduced through their <term>Prosthaphaeresis</term><note>An "equation of correction" used to account for non-uniform celestial motion; from the Greek for "addition and subtraction."</note>—now depart further from one another in the sphere of the fixed stars. Thus, the Sun’s motion is indeed altered through a <term>Compensation</term><note>A mathematical adjustment to balance discrepancies in orbital calculations.</note> by as much as the difference in the Prosthaphaeresis requires. Nevertheless, the interval between the Sun and the fixed stars for the year 1588 remains the same as that which Tycho established through his observations. Therefore, by the time of Hipparchus, the Sun and the fixed stars are now pulled apart from each other, though by less than Hipparchus was able to achieve by observation; no account was taken for other times, even if the departure is wider.

<margin>Regarding which, see Precept 181.</margin>
In various places, the "prisons" of the Sun's motions—from which they likely broke forth—are also reported. Thus, this Prosthaphaeresis of the equinoxes, being of uncertain reliability yet accepted into the calculation, carries the whole of Astronomy up and down.

<margin>PRECEPT 192. On the sidereal year. Tables, page 102.</margin>
Furthermore, the sidereal year in Forms I, IV, and V is diminished from its mean quantity (which the Canon shows) by as much as if you were to divide the difference of the Compensations at the beginning and end of the proposed sidereal periods by the mean daily motion from the fixed stars.

Now, just as the Prosthaphaeresis of the equinoxes—the daughter of varied <term>Obliquity</term><note>The angle of the Earth's axial tilt relative to its orbit.</note>—has harmed the longitude of the fixed stars, the variation of the Obliquity itself harms the latitude in nearly the same way, so that it cannot remain the same through all ages. Consequently, the inclination at the <term>Limits</term><note>The points of greatest northern or southern distance from the ecliptic.</note> of the planetary paths suffers the same defect.

<margin>PRECEPT 193. On the latitude of fixed stars in different centuries. Tables, page 105 and following. See Chapter XII, pages 26, 27, and Precept 195.</margin>
For if we assume that the obliquity of the Ecliptic does not change, then no change will occur in the latitudes either, and we may use them as perennial values, just as Brahe assigned them to each star for the year 1600 in his Catalog. Sometimes the very purpose or use for which the latitude of a star is sought is such that it suggests one should entirely ignore its variation, even if there were any. But if the calculator is absolutely determined to spend effort on uncertain and unnecessary matters, come, I shall prescribe for him what he should do in full. For there is a twofold method of computing latitude: the first assumes that the pole of the Ecliptic oscillates [librates] on the <term>solstitial colure</term><note>A great circle on the celestial sphere passing through the celestial poles and the two solstices.</note>, suffering no Prosthaphaeresis of the equinoxes. It works like this: for the proposed time, find the position of the longitude of the star or the proposed point, and the obliquity of the Ecliptic according to one of the five forms; subtract from this the obliquity of our own time, if it was smaller. Add the logarithm of the excess to the logarithm of the star’s longitude (or the proposed point) from the equinox, either before or after. The sum sought among the logarithms reveals the "scruples" [minutes of arc] which must be added to Southern latitude in Northern Signs, and to Northern latitude in Southern Signs; but they must be subtracted from Northern latitude in Northern Signs, and from Southern latitude in Southern Signs.

<margin>Through precepts 190, 186.</margin>
<margin>Longomontanus <note>Christian Severin Longomontanus, Tycho Brahe’s former assistant.</note> presents this method in his *Theories*, page 92, just as if the pole of the Ecliptic oscillates on the solstitial colure, even though he meanwhile computes the Prosthaphaeresis of the equinoxes from the circuit of the pole in a small circle (*Theories*, page 88).</margin>
But if the obliquity of our time was greater, subtract in turn the one you found for the proposed time from this one, and with the scruples of latitude elicited, proceed through all cases in the contrary manner to what has just been said.

The second method of computing assumes the Pole of the Ecliptic is carried around in a small circle. Here, one must first compute the Prosthaphaeresis of latitude, not from the customary temporary Ecliptic, but as if from the "mean Ecliptic" or the <term>Royal Road</term><note>Latin: *via regia*; the path of the Sun, or the Ecliptic.</note>, and that at any elongation of the star from the <term>node</term><note>The point where the orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note> of the Ecliptics, not only for the proposed time but also for the year 1600. Then,

<column-break/>

indeed, by comparing the Prosthaphaereses of both times with each other, it is elicited what must be changed in the latitude of the year 1600 so that the latitude for the proposed year is obtained.

<margin>PRECEPT 194.</margin>
Therefore, collect the "argument" of the Obliquity for both the proposed time and the year 1600 AD; having subtracted these arguments from a full circle, give the name "longitude of the Node of the Ecliptics from the equinox" to the remainders for both times. Subtract these elongations of the Node from the longitude of the Star or Point which belongs to that same time (adding a full circle first, if necessary), so that the Elongation of the point from the ascending Node is clear. As long as this is less than a Semicircle, the Prosthaphaeresis is Northern from the Royal Road; but where it exceeds a semicircle, it is Southern. To the logarithms of both these Elongations, add the logarithm of the semicircle of the small circle (which is specific to the form of Obliquity used). The sums, as logarithms, give the Prosthaphaeresis of latitude for both times, indicating what should have been added or subtracted at both times if we knew the latitude of the star from the Royal Road.

If, therefore, both elongations were simultaneously either less or greater than a semicircle, subtract the smaller Prosthaphaeresis from the larger; but if one is less than a semicircle and the other greater, make a sum of the two together. And to the sum always—but to the difference only then, if the Prosthaphaeresis of the proposed time is smaller—apply the title contrary to that which the Prosthaphaeresis of the year 1600 has. But if, with a larger Prosthaphaeresis for the proposed time, the state of both were the same, apply the title to the difference which the Prosthaphaeresis of the year 1600 has. Thus you will have a composite arc with its title, which again must be applied with its own singular caution to the latitudes of the stars which they have for the year 1600. For if its direction is contrary to the latitude, add it; if it is the same, subtract one from the other; the remainder, retaining the state of the whole, will be the latitude of the star for the proposed time.

<margin>Precept 193</margin>
<margin>Precept 194</margin>
For the sake of example, let it be the "Northern Head of Gemini" [the star Castor]: which in the year 1600 is at $14^\circ 40'$ of **Cancer**, with a latitude of $10^\circ 2'$ **North**. I will compute its latitude for the time of Hipparchus, when the star was at $20^\circ 18'$ of **Gemini**. Let the first form of Obliquity be proposed to us, and let the Pole first oscillate on the diameter of the small circle. Suppose the obliquity of the Ecliptic at Hipparchus's time is found to be $23^\circ 51' 30''$. Subtract, therefore, the obliquity of our time, $23^\circ 30' 30''$. The excess, $21' 0''$, gives the logarithm 509805, to which add the logarithm 1440 for the star’s longitude of $80^\circ 18'$. The sum 511245, sought among the logarithms, reveals $20' 56''$. This Prosthaphaeresis is to be subtracted, because the star's latitude is Northern in the Northern sign of Gemini. Therefore, this Prosthaphaeresis being subtracted from $10^\circ 2'$ (the latitude of our time), it leaves $9^\circ 41'$ as its latitude in the time of Hipparchus. Secondly, let the pole go around in a small circle, and let it again be the First Form. We have the longitude of the fixed star also for the proposed time, namely $20^\circ 18'$ in **Gemini**. The argument of the Obliquity in the first form is 339° 30' at Hipparchus's time, and 215° 21' in our time; these being subtracted from 360°, there remains the longitude of the Node of the Ecliptics: $20^\circ 30'$ in **Aries** for Hipparchus, and $154^\circ 39'$ ($24^\circ 39'$ in **Leo**) for us. I subtract these, each from its star position; the Elongation of the star from the Node will be $59^\circ 48'$ for Hipparchus and $320^\circ 2'$ for us. To the logarithms of these, 14586 and 45314, adding the logarithm 562564 of the small circle's semidiameter ($12' 24''$), the sums 577150 and 607878 show Prosthaphaereses of $10' 44''$ **North** and $7' 53''$ **South**, because Hipparchus's elongation was less than a semicircle and ours was greater. Therefore, the Prosthaphaereses are to be joined into one sum, so that it is...

# RUDOLPHINE TABLES

From this we know that around this place of the star at the Ecliptic in Hipparchus’s time, it was among the northern fixed stars, with a latitude closer to the star which, according to this motion of the Pole (which is for the year 1600), is about 18' 37''. And that which is through the <term>libration</term><note>A slow oscillation or "swinging" motion, real or apparent, of a celestial body.</note> of the pole.

In the second form of the poles, let this latitude of Hipparchus be 9° 34', and in the fifth, 9° 39'. Thus, finally, the ancient observations of latitudes are satisfied in some manner.

<margin>PRECEPT 195</margin>
**For a fixed star whose longitude and latitude is given for the year 1600, to investigate the Declination and Right Ascension for any time.**

<margin>Through precept 190</margin>
FIRST, let the longitude of the given star be established for the proposed time, according to one of the five forms of <term>Obliquity</term><note>The angle between the Earth's equator and the ecliptic (the path of the Sun).</note>, which was also applied in the place of the Sun. We shall determine the longitude, and with the latitude—no other than that which is of the year 1600, exactly as if it were perpetually invariable—seek the <term>Declination</term><note>The celestial equivalent of latitude; the distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.</note> and <term>Right Ascension</term><note>The celestial equivalent of longitude; the distance of a star measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</note>. Thus the Declination and Right Ascension will be produced, suitable also for the proposed time.

<margin>Tables page 24. Our Table of Right Ascension and Declination. See Chapter XII. Our Obliquity of the Ecliptic is for all times for the Fixed stars.</margin>
For even if the latitudes of the fixed stars perhaps change, it is by the departure of the Ecliptic itself from the Fixed stars and the Equator: where the Fixed stars, and hence the result of this change, do not agree among themselves: and so the declination, even if it is constructed for all times for the Fixed stars.

<margin>PRECEPT 196</margin>
**On correcting the places of the Planets which Ptolemy observed, so that they can be skillfully compared with the calculation; and vice-versa.**

SINCE Ptolemy holds that point of the fixed stars as the beginning, which the Sun ascends on the day after that day on which we, from these tables, compute the true <term>equinox</term><note>The moment the Sun crosses the celestial equator, making day and night equal length.</note> for that time; Ptolemy’s observation diminishes the degrees by about one degree and 3 minutes. Therefore, either subtract so much from the computed hourly Table, or add it to the places from his observation: so that you may rightly compare modern observations with Ptolemaic ones in the same demonstration. There is no reason, therefore, for you to fear that this error of one degree in the calculation will overflow into Eclipses or other motions of the Planets. For it is a mistake of counting the numbering from a later point: the tenor of the motions remains, despite this mistake, plainly the same.

<column-break/>

<margin>Epitome of Astronomy, Book VII, page 923.</margin>
And it has been said elsewhere: it was possible for the Astronomer of those moving bodies to practice, even if we were plainly to erase that shameful second point of the equinox.

### On the Refractions of the rays of the stars in the air.

I have subjoined a triple Table of <term>Refractions</term><note>The bending of light as it passes through the Earth's atmosphere, making stars appear higher in the sky than they actually are.</note> to the Catalog of Fixed Stars, from Tycho’s *Progymnasmata*; because Gruenperger did the same in his edition of the Fixed Stars. Although the use of the Table does not primarily refer to the calculation of these Tables: as they are not produced for that which the stars undergo in the inconsistent air, but the use is unique in applying observations to the calculation. For if the refracted altitude of a star is observed; by means of the altitude sought in the margin, extract the refraction, and from which thread of a famous example through the observed altitude, so that it becomes true (just as you will remove the <term>parallax</term><note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different positions; here, the difference between the view from the Earth's surface and its center.</note> from the compared altitude, so that it becomes apparent) if the longitude and latitude of the star observed in refraction has already been computed; with the altitude extract the refraction: the angle of the vertical and the Ecliptic must be drawn out into longitude and latitude, and each must be applied to its own fitting place, so that it may be freed from refraction, by that way so that the horizontal position is made from the true place. But beware of assuming the parallax, as I would wish to employ the horizontal parallax to be tested in the hours of the edition. For the proportion of the Horizontal ones to the others is not the same in both places.

<margin>PRECEPT 197.</margin>
<margin>Which precept 133 is the first element.</margin>
<margin>Through precept 133</margin>
I could conveniently give many warnings about this Table, if the method of the work did not stand in the way. These few things, however, seemed to suffice. In the Refractions of the Sun and Moon, continuing up to 45 degrees, Tycho gave something for the mathematician to dispute: for subtle things are not established by observations. However, Tycho assumes different refractions for the Fixed stars, a different trust for himself from that, since he would discern the same process at distinct times, and in distinct times: if perhaps (which he would assume in vain) the varied altitude of the stars from the center of the earth were the cause of the variety. I think the Refractions of the Sun were made larger for this reason, because he did not apply the parallax even though he never detected it, and therefore he thought to remove the refraction besides, as for the most part in the twilight, which depressed him too much and therefore he thought to remove the refraction besides. In the Moon, the excuse is from the air itself, as also in the Sun. For with both the full Moon and by day, the air is chosen for the observations of the Sun; but the Fixed stars, observed in the deep of night and with a most serene sky, remain plainly the same despite this error.

## OF LOGARITHMIC MEASURES. <note>original: *MORVM LOGISTICORVM*. This is a continuation of the phrase "Table of Logarithmic Measures." "Logistics" here refers to the art of calculating with sexagesimal fractions (base 60), the standard for astronomy.</note>

Subtractive values used in Kepler's specific geometric calculations.</note> | Arc of the Quadrant. # CANON of Logarithms and Antilogarithms <note>A "Canon" in this context is a formal table of mathematical rules or values. Kepler used these logarithms—a relatively new invention in his time—to calculate the orbits of planets with unprecedented precision.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the general prosthaphaereses (corrections) of the previous page to a specific mathematical tool: the Canon of Mesologarithms. While the previous tables dealt with orbital distances, this table is used to calculate the latitudes (the north-south deviation from the ecliptic) of the five known planets.</meta>

# Rudolphine Tables

### Part of the TABLE <note>original: "CANONIS." A "canon" in this context is a mathematical table or rule used for calculation.</note> of Mesologarithms <note>Kepler used the term "mesologarithm" to refer to the logarithms of sines. These were revolutionary tools that allowed astronomers to perform complex calculations using addition and subtraction instead of long-form multiplication and division.</note> up to ten Degrees. Primarily for the latitudes of the five Planets.

->Parts or Degrees.<-

# Rudolphine Tables / Table of the Angle of the EAST

->III. Climate. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; IV. Climate. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; V. Climate.<-

# Part One: Common [Tables] 
# Or, Tables of the Altitude of the Nonagesimal <note>The "Nonagesimal" is the point on the ecliptic—the path the Sun follows—that is exactly 90 degrees from where the ecliptic meets the horizon. It is the highest point of the ecliptic in the sky at any given moment and is crucial for calculating how a celestial body's position appears to shift (parallax), especially during eclipses.</note>

# Rudolphine Tables

->### Table of the EASTERN Angle<-

---

->**TEMPERATE ZONE.**<-
<margin>
The [degrees of the] Nonagesimal <note>The Nonagesimal is the point on the ecliptic—the sun's path—that is 90 degrees from the horizon. It is the highest point of the ecliptic currently in the sky.</note> from the ascending semicircle stand in the Eastern Quadrant.
</margin>
<margin>
Arcs beginning from Aries (♈), up to the limits in the areas to be taken, are transposed in the Ecliptic in a reverse-direction; then the opposite begins to rise directly in the [meridian] itself.
</margin>

</insert>

Part One or General [Section].

### ...or of the Altitude of the Nonagesimal.

...the [points] placed rise inversely, beginning in the North itself through the East into the South: and the Nonagesimal <note>The Nonagesimal is the 90th degree of the ecliptic measured from the point currently rising on the eastern horizon; it represents the highest point of the sun's path in the sky at any given moment.</note> from the east is in the following [signs] <note>original: "in consequentia," meaning moving in the natural order of the zodiac signs.</note>, but with respect to the Horizon, from the West through the North into the East. And when the arc ceases to rise in the Meridian itself [in the] North.

<margin>Because the Sun (☉), Venus (♀), and Moon (☾) are perpetually positioned on the Horizon, the Nonagesimal is perpetually [linked] to the Sun, Venus, and Moon. It remains stable, passing through all regions of the horizon forward to the right.</margin>

---

...those placed rise directly, starting from the North itself through the East into the South: and the Nonagesimal is ordered to be taken from the eastern point: it is transposed in the Ecliptic in the following signs, but with respect to the horizon, from the East through the South into the West, then the opposite begins to rise inversely in the North itself.

<meta>This page continues the astronomical data of the Rudolphine Tables, shifting from the calculation of the "Nonagesimal" (the highest point of the ecliptic) seen on page 31 to the "Equation of Time." These tables were essential for converting "apparent time" (measured by the sun's position, as on a sundial) into "mean time" (a steady, uniform time used for precise astronomical calculations).</meta>

These tables allowed astronomers to synchronize solar observations with uniform clock time for any given date or year.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Catalog of Places" from the Rudolphine Tables. The list moves from the letter M through S. The coordinates provide the longitude (expressed as a time difference in hours and minutes) and latitude (expressed as the altitude of the celestial pole). The reference meridian for these tables is Tycho Brahe’s observatory at Uraniborg on the island of Hven. Locations marked "a." (ante) are East of the meridian, while those marked "f." (fere/post) are West.</meta>

To this end should be related, especially for the use of sailors navigating the Ocean, a universal Map of the world consisting of a circular disk and two semicircles, which I am preparing. In it, the primary meridian is the one specific to these Tables [Uraniborg]: the others, distant by full hours toward the west, are marked with S. [West]; while those toward the east are marked with A. [East].

### On the Places aligned with the Meridian of these Tables.

How much uncertainty and how much labor is involved in examining the longitudes of places! I wish to show this by a single example, taken from the middle of Europe. Between ROME and NUREMBERG, in the time of Regiomontanus, there were thought to be 36 Minutes [of time difference]. (Regiomontanus, *On the First Motion*, problem 45). Werner has 32': however, from the beginning of the eclipse on January 18, 1497, observed in both places—at Rome by himself at 5:24 AM, and at Nuremberg by someone unknown at 4:52 AM—28 minutes are gathered. Apianus, in his *Astrolabe*, thought he should choose a middle ground between Regiomontanus and Werner, 34'. Yet Mästlin, Everard, and Origanus stay closer to Werner, setting it at 33'. But Stöffler in his *Calendar*, not paying attention to Werner's observation, set it at 18'; whom Apianus seems to have followed later in his *Caesarean Astronomy*, setting it at 19'. And Magini chose a middle between Apianus's earlier figure and Stöffler’s tradition, setting it at 26'. Schöner in his *Resoluta* has only 12'; which Mercator and Hondius follow in their maps. Stadius in his *Ephemerides* has 15'. Jansson, in his universal map, seems to have descended to 10'. I, trusting rather in the consensus of two observations of Lunar eclipses held in Rome from the years 1616 and 1617, which I also observed in Linz, make Linz 10 minutes further east than Rome, just as much as it is from Uraniborg according to other observations. Thus, for me, Rome and Uraniborg fall under the same Meridian, which is no more than 4 minutes further east than the one for Nuremberg. For its connection with the meridian of Alexandria, etc., see the Instructions.

# SUMMARY OF COMMON ERAS,
## AS MANY AS HAVE COME TO OUR KNOWLEDGE: THEY ARE COMPARED INDIVIDUALLY WITH THEIR YEARS BEFORE OR AFTER THE INCARNATION OF THE WORD;

->*the customary beginnings of the Years in the Months and Days of the Julian year are also assigned,*<-

<image-desc>A vertical decorative divider made of repeated floral ornaments (fleurons) separates the two columns of text.</image-desc>

<margin>
Running before our Era of the Incarnation <note>This column lists dates in years BCE (Before Common Era).</note>
</margin>

**5509, on the Calends of September <note>September 1st</note>**, begin the Years of the World according to the Greeks, in the Patriarchate of Constantinople. They also establish this as the head of the fifteen-year Cycles of Indictions <note>A 15-year tax cycle used in the Roman Empire for dating documents.</note>.

**3761, on the Nones of October <note>October 7th</note>**, begin the Years from Adam, according to the Jews after the time of Christ.

**776, in July**, the first Olympic Contest was celebrated. But the first year of the Olympiad itself begins variously, according to different beginnings of the year among different Nations. For the Macedonians, the first year of the Olympiad (that is, in which the Olympiad was celebrated) began in October of the year 777 before Christ. For many Greek nations, from the Winter Solstice of that ending year 777; for Achaea and Josephus, from April of the year 776; for the Athenians from the very month of the games, namely from June or July.

**The Years of the Founding of Rome**, begin in the month of May, on the *Parilia* <note>An ancient Roman festival of shepherds held on April 21st, though the text notes May here as a variant start</note>, in the year:
**753**, according to Varro and most writers after Augustus, and for the Emperors themselves in the celebration of the Secular Games;
**752**, according to Cato, Tarruntius, the Capitoline Fasti <note>A list of Roman magistrates inscribed on marble in the Forum</note>, Eusebius, Solinus, the Chronologist in Clement, etc.

**747, on February 26th.** The first day of *Thoth* <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, the first month of the Egyptian year, of the Years of Nabonassar <note>original: "Annorum Nabonassari"</note> in wandering solar years: these are used by Ptolemy and other astronomers.

**433, on June 26th.** The beginning of the Nineteen-year Cycles of Meton <note>A cycle of 19 years used to align the solar and lunar calendars</note>, each of which consisted of the same number of moveable Lunar Years: in which the first of the Months was *Hecatombaeon*; and *Poseideon* was doubled in seven years <note>referring to the leap months added to keep the lunar year in sync with the seasons</note>.

**330, on June 28th.** The beginning of the Lunar Periods of Calippus, each of which is 76 years long.

**324, on November 12th.** The first *Thoth* of the Years from the death of Alexander the Great, in wandering Egyptian years. For there are exactly 424 Egyptian years between this and the beginnings of Nabonassar. Ptolemy, Theon, Al-Battani <note>original: "Albategnius"</note>, etc., use these.

**312, in the Springtime**, in the Month of *Nisan*, the beginning of the era of the Greeks or *Chittim*; which the writer of the history of the Maccabees uses in Jewish affairs.

**312, in Autumn**, or the Ides of October <note>October 15th</note>, begins the ERA OF CONTRACTS, the Antiochian Years, used in Councils, supposedly from the rise of that city: likewise the Years of the Edessenes, according to Eusebius; who calls those the YEARS OF THE SELEUCIDS, but beware. The writer of the history of the Maccabees also uses these in the affairs of the Gentiles. The Arabian astronomers after Christ derive them from the fixed Julian Calends of October, extended backward; and they call them the Years of Alexander, the Years of *Dhilkarnajin* <note>The "Two-Horned One," a traditional title for Alexander the Great in Arabic sources</note>. And that Humen the Egyptian Astronomer followed this beginning of the year and this era in his Astronomical Tables is apparent from the words of John of Paris, the translator, which you may see in Calvisius in his *Introduction to Chronology*, folio 83.

<column-break/>

**311, on the Ides of October.** The beginning of the Years according to the Chaldeans in Ptolemy. The Seleucid Kings use these in their letters, which are inserted in the history of the Maccabees. Therefore, I think the name "Seleucid" is proper to these years, contrary to Eusebius.

**285, on the 5th day before the Calends of July <note>June 27th</note>**, begin the Years according to Dionysius the Mathematician, in Ptolemy.

**48, on the 4th day before the Ides of May <note>May 12th</note>**, on the 23rd day of the month *Artemisius*. The Antiochian Years, reckoned from the reception of liberty; which Ignatius, the Patriarch of that place, begins from the first of *Artemisius*. At the same time and from the same point, the INDICTIONS of Caesar also run. Some of the Christians of the East, however, derive them from the Calends of September of the preceding year, at the beginning of the Constantinopolitan Year.

**45, on the Calends of January <note>January 1st</note>**, on a Friday, begin the fixed Julian Years, or the first of the modern Calendar, extended backward according to the restoration of Augustus.
From the same place also begins the era of the Indians, which is of receding Arabic years; according to Niccolò de' Conti the Historian.

**38, on the Calends of January.** The Era of Caesar (Octavian) of Spain begins, common in Church Councils.

**1, on the Calends of January**, begins the great Cycle of 532 years <note>The Victorian/Dionysian cycle combining the 28-year solar and 19-year lunar cycles</note>, whose years Sigebert, Marianus Scotus among the older writers, and others use for the years of the Nativity of Christ; and the numbering from the Nativity by the older Eusebius and Jerome also coincides with this.

<margin>
Running in the Year of the Era of the Incarnation <note>This column lists dates in years AD/CE (Common Era).</note>
</margin>

Since the times of the Merovingian Franks, or at least from Charlemagne, the whole West has used this Era: for which reason the calculation of these Tables is also accommodated to it.
Although the Era is named from the Incarnation, and it properly ought not to begin before the feast of the Annunciation <note>March 25th</note>: others nevertheless give it the name from the Nativity <note>December 25th</note> instead. Thus the head of the Year is manifold. For:

**On the 8th day before the Calends of January <note>December 25th</note>**, at the feast of the Nativity of Christ (from which they are also called Years of the Nativity), Thuanus is the authority that they begin in Rome in the business of the Apostolic Chamber. These make Christ one year older than Dionysius <note>Dionysius Exiguus</note>, the author of the era, does.

**On the Calends of January themselves**, which Julius Caesar, the author of the Calendar, 45 years before this time, wished to be the head of the Year, the users of this era observe even now; namely all succeeding Emperors, the Roman Empire, Germany, and most surrounding Provinces and Kingdoms. This was also established in the kingdom of France by public decree in the year 1564, and it prevailed shortly thereafter, as Thuanus testifies; these RUDOLPHINE TABLES also observe this Head of the Year and of the Era.

**On the 6th day before the Calends of March <note>February 24th</note>**, however, is the Head of the Year in the Cycle of the Sun of these Tables, and in the Computation of the Day of the Week, when we name the days in the Roman manner, counting the Bissextile <note>The leap day</note> on the Calends of March.

# Rudolphine Tables
<meta>catchword: Table Re-</meta>

<margin>Year of Christ 1.</margin> Some Latin Church authorities observe the very Calends of March <note>March 1st</note>; because in their reckonings, this is frequently the Paschal month, as it currently receives the greater part of the Jewish month of Nisan. Several cities throughout Italy follow them in this. The start of the year in the Solar Cycle of these Tables is the same, when we count the days of the month according to common practice, proceeding in a leap year through February 29th. The Venetians, Florentines, Pisans, and several other Italian Republics hold the time of the Vernal Equinox as the head of the year for this era, according to Luca Gaurico <note>An Italian astrologer and bishop (1476–1558).</note>; so did the Germans under Charlemagne, most historians of that age, and the people of Trier even today: as did João de Barros, the Portuguese historian, 100 years ago.

<margin>8th day before the Calends of April <note>March 25th</note>,</margin> the Feast of the Annunciation—that is, the Incarnation—was established as the head of the year by the ancient Church authorities, and by a custom taken from them, even by Christian Kings and Republics. Therefore, according to the Cycle of Dionysius Exiguus <note>Dionysius the Small (c. 470–544), the monk who invented the AD/BC dating system.</note>, from whom this era was born, it was on this day of the first current year that Christ would finally have been conceived in the womb of the Blessed Virgin.

<margin>The Calends of April <note>April 1st</note>,</margin> are held as the beginning of the year by the Clementines, Anastasius of Antioch, Gregory of Tours, and others. For to them, March (or *Dystros* <note>original: "Δύστρ." - the Macedonian month name</note>) is considered the 12th month, and April the 1st; because the Jewish month of Nisan frequently coincided with it in ancient times. The movable Feast of Easter was the head of the year in France before the year 1564, and in England, Florence, and Rome in the Consistory of Cardinals and for ecclesiastical matters, according to Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a French historian.</note>. Hence, for some of the ancients, these years are named from the "Passion of the Lord," an ambiguous title.

<margin>Year of Christ 28.</margin> In October, the Paschal Cycle of Victor of Capua and Victorinus of Aquitaine begins. The years flowing from the beginning of this Cycle are used by some as an Era, under the title "of Grace," namely from the preaching of John; or even under the title "from the Passion," even though that actually occurred later.

<margin>222. Calends of January <note>January 1st, 222 AD</note>.</margin> The 16-year cycles <term>Hekkaedecaëterides</term> <note>A 16-year cycle used to align the lunar and solar calendars.</note> of Hippolytus begin.

<margin>284. 4th day before the Calends of September <note>August 29, 284 AD</note>.</margin> At the beginning of the fixed Egyptian year, the Paschal Cycles of Dionysius of Alexandria begin; as do the Diocletian Years; called the Era of Martyrs, the Era of the Abyssinians, the Ethiopians, the Coptic Era <note>original: "Elkupti"</note>, and also the years of Grace. This era was used by the entire Roman world in place of dating by Consuls until the times of Justinian, according to Scaliger <term>Scal.</term> <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a leading chronologist of the era.</note>. But the Churches of later times, Constantinople and Antioch, being enticed by the proximity of the Calends of September themselves—since they poorly tolerated this ancient three-day anticipation of the Julian Months—began to establish the head of their years on the Roman Calends of September <note>September 1st</note>, as mentioned in the first era; and they intercalate in February, like the Romans, leaving Egypt its own beginning of months and intercalation. John of Paris also seems to have followed this custom in the translation of the astronomical tables of the Egyptian *Humen* <note>Referring to an almanac or set of tables</note>, mentioned above; where he writes, *the Tables were made for the Noon of the city of Antioch, four months before the year of Christ 1143, that is, on the Calends of September of the year 1142.*

<margin>285. Calends of April <note>April 1st</note>,</margin> the Paschal month, was pleasing to the Alexandrian Church as the head of the Diocletian or Martyr era.

<margin>312. 7th day before the Calends of October <note>September 25th</note>.</margin> The beginning of the INDICTIONS of Constantine is held from this day until today in the Courts of the Emperors. But the Greek Emperors and the Church authorities of Constantinople begin them from the Calends of September, the head of their year; with them are Cedrenus, the Arab-

<column-break/>

<margin>Year of Christ</margin> ic Gospel, which writes *Tarik* <note>original: "Tarik" - Arabic for date or history.</note> for Indiction. The Roman Church and the Popes, on the contrary, begin the Indictions from the following Calends of January, 313. Ignatius, Patriarch of Antioch, starts from the Calends of May (or *Artemisius*), in the year 313.

<margin>552. 3rd day before the Ides of August <note>August 11th</note>,</margin> the Era of the Armenians begins: the months are Persian, but fixed, and the intercalation is purely Roman.

<margin>622. July 16th,</margin> Friday. The beginning of the lunar years of the Hegira <note>The migration of Muhammad from Mecca to Medina, marking the start of the Islamic calendar.</note>, which move backward <note>Because it is a lunar calendar, the months rotate through the seasons.</note>, used by the Muhammadan Arabs and Turks.

<margin>632. June 16th,</margin> the years of Yazdegerd the Persian begin, on the Egyptian model, wandering and moving backward.

These are, therefore, the customary eras—that is, both public and for daily use. There are other eras that are either not for daily use, or not public but at least private to individual historians, or of non-ruling cities, and thus not commonly used: to enumerate them would be infinite. First, regarding the Years of the World, among individual historians there are almost as many opinions as there are men, which the reader may seek from the authors themselves. However, the Latins generally count 5199 years until Christ. More recent authors count 1200 years and more, though variously. Following these more closely, I find a placement of the Planets suitable for the beginning, 3993 years before the current era, on August 24th, in mid-summer.

Next, the Alphonsine Tables <note>13th-century astronomical tables named after Alfonso X of Castile.</note> derive the era of the Deluge from the year 3102 before Christ; I derive it from the year 2337. The city of Babylon, from its origin, which was 104 years after the flood (the year 2233 before the era of the Incarnation), counted 1903 years until the surrender to Alexander, beginning in 330 before Christ. Moses, St. Paul, and Eusebius count the years of the Promise from 1941 before the Incarnation; for me, it is 1965. From the Exodus from Egypt, for me, it was counted in the desert as 1535 before Christ. From there, the Books of Kings have 480 years to the founding of the Temple; but St. Paul increases this sum. From the occupation of Peraea, Jephthah counts 300 years to his own time. For me, it is 302 or 303.

<margin>From the division of the Land,</margin> for me, it was 1489 before Christ. From this arise the Jubilees and Sabbatic years, which the Samaritans retain.

<margin>From the founding of the Temple,</margin> for me, it was 999 before Christ; whether this was counted publicly is unknown. But from the capture of the citadel of Sion and the seat of the Kingdom being established in Jerusalem, I demonstrate that Ezekiel counts his 390 years until the preaching of Jeremiah; and the remaining 40 until the kingdom and city were destroyed, for me, 606 before Christ; which they held as the first year of captivity: from which the 70th year was the Return, in the year 537 BC.

<margin>The years of the fall of Troy,</margin> the return of the Heraclidae, and other notable events for which there are Canons of Eratosthenes—see these in the works of chronologists.

Furthermore, the first of men necessarily counted the years of his own age, whom the others imitated. Thus, in the 600th year of Noah's life, Moses records the Deluge. Most nations imitated this in counting the years of their leaders, judges, Kings, and Emperors. Here it should be noted that it cannot be shown that the year of the Jews, however named, had any other beginning after the Exodus than the month of the new crops. Thus, the same year frequently occurs as the last of a predecessor and the first of a successor.

<margin>But today</margin> Empires are reckoned from their own initial days, as are other events. Thus they begin the Era of Alfonso from June 1st, in the year of the Incarnation 1252. Thus in the year 1582, on the 15th/5th of October, the years of the Gregorian Correction begin. Finally, on August 28th/18th, 1619, begin the years of the reign of FERDINAND II, August Emperor of the Romans, King of Hungary and Bohemia.

> In the Year of Christ 632. The first day of Farvardin falls on June 16, coinciding with the Egyptian month Choeac; likewise the other Persian months coincide with the other Egyptian months in order, except for the single month of Aderma, which began on the 6th day of the Egyptian month Mesori, having the Wahak or the Epagomenae <note>Intercalary days added to the end of the year to align it with the solar cycle.</note> before it, as they followed the Egyptian Mesori. Therefore the Arab astronomer Aben <note>Likely referring to Ibn al-Haytham or a similar source.</note> sets it at 35 days.

Before Christ in the Year 3993, on the 24th of July, at 0 hours, 33 minutes, 26 seconds. The Mean Sun was at 0 degrees, 0 minutes, 0 seconds of Cancer. The Apogee at 0 degrees, 0 minutes, 0 seconds of Taurus. The North Pole of the World was above the end of the tail of the Lesser Bear [Ursa Minor], the Southern Pole was under the Hydra; the equinoctial point of the Zodiac, or 0 Aries: that which in the year 1600 was numbered as 19 degrees, 13 minutes, 36 seconds of Pisces, between the horns of Taurus. The other equinoctial point, or 0 Libra, which in the year 1600 was numbered as 19 degrees, 13 minutes, 36 seconds of Virgo; in which very degree, or nearly so, on October 9 (or September 29), 1604, were Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, followed immediately the next day by the rising of the most brilliant new star <note>The Supernova of 1604, often called Kepler's Star.</note>, at 17 degrees, 43 minutes of Sagittarius, with a Latitude of 1 degree, 55 minutes North; thus marking the equinox of Creation.

<note>A "Canon" in this context is a mathematical table. "Sexagenarius" refers to the sexagesimal (base-60) system used here to break down degrees into incredibly precise fractions.</note>

Rudolphine Tables

## SATURN
### HIGHEST OF THE SUPERIOR PLANETS
<note>In the geocentric and early heliocentric models, the "Superior Planets" were those outside Earth's orbit: Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. Saturn was the "highest" because it was the most distant known planet from the Sun.</note>

->Stationary Limits of JUPITER.<-
<note>These are the mathematical conditions under which Jupiter appears to stop its normal eastward motion and begin moving "backward" (retrograde), or vice versa.</note>

| In Anomaly of the Eccentric <note>The position of the planet in its elliptical orbit.</note> | Angle of First Commutation <note>The angle between the Sun and the planet as seen from Earth when it first becomes stationary.</note> | Angle of Second Commutation <note>The angle when the planet returns to direct motion.</note> |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **0** | **123. 57** | **124. 54** |
| **90** | **126. 22** | **126. 24** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **180** | **128. 15** | **127. 15** |
| **270** | **125. 38** | **125. 41** |

The depth of the Sun below the Horizon at the moments of JUPITER’s morning emergences <note>original: "Emersionum"; this is the heliacal rising, when the planet first becomes visible in the morning before sunrise.</note> and evening occultations <note>original: "occultationum"; the heliacal setting, when the planet is lost in the Sun's glare in the evening.</note>, according to PTOLEMY, must be 10 Degrees.

The depth of the Sun below the horizon at the moments of the morning appearances <note>original: "Emersionum." The moment a planet first becomes visible in the dawn sky after being obscured by the Sun's light.</note> and evening disappearances <note>original: "occultationum." <summary>This page contains the mathematical tables for determining the latitude of Mars and the precise angles at which it begins and ends its retrograde (backward-looking) motion. It concludes with an observation from Ptolemy regarding the visibility of Mars during dawn and twilight.</summary>

--- Page 214 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the tables of Mars to those of Venus. Following the structure of the Rudolphine Tables, Kepler provides the "Epochs"—starting positions for specific years—and the "Mean Motions," which show how far the planet travels over various increments of time (days, hours, months). These allow an astronomer to calculate the planet's position for any date in history.</meta>

66 Rudolphine Tables

<summary>This page contains primary astronomical tables for Venus, listing its epoch positions for centuries across history and its mean motion per day, hour, and month. These values, calculated for Tycho Brahe's Uraniborg meridian, are the building blocks for determining the planet's location at any given time.</summary>
<keywords>Venus, mean motion, epochs, aphelion, ascending node, Uraniborg, Rudolphine Tables, planetary orbits</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the tables for the planet Venus. Having provided the "Epochs" (starting positions) on the previous page, Kepler now provides the "Mean Motions." These tables allow a calculator to determine how much the planet, its aphelion, and its nodes have moved over a specific number of years, which is then added to the Epoch value.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the specific calculations for the planet Venus within Kepler’s Rudolphine Tables. Following the "Mean Motions" on the previous page, which show where the planet would be if its orbit were a perfect circle, this page provides the "Equations." These are the mathematical corrections required to account for the planet's actual elliptical orbit and the varying speeds at which it travels.</meta>

# TABLE of the Latitudes of VENUS.

| Arg. of Lat. <note>The "Argument of Latitude" is the angle used to determine how far a planet has moved from the point where its orbit crosses the ecliptic (the nodes).</note> | Inclination <note>The angular distance of the planet north or south of the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note> Deg. ## Terms of the Stations of VENUS.
<note>Stations are the points in a planet's orbit where it appears to stand still before moving in retrograde (backward) or direct (forward) motion.</note>

| In Eccentric Anomaly. | First Commutation Angle. | Second Angle of Change. | | In Ecc. Anom. | First Commutation Angle. | Second Angle of Change. | | In Eccentric Anomaly. | First Commutation Angle. | Second Angle of Change. |

---

The depth of the Sun below the Horizon at the times of the evening appearances and the morning disappearances of <term>Venus</term>, according to PTOLEMY, is 5 degrees. In evening disappearances and morning appearances, it is less; even though at those times, <term>Venus</term>, like the Moon, is diminished in light. Because of this, <term>Venus</term> is sometimes seen for two or three days at once in both the morning and evening, emerging in the morning before it is hidden in the evening. Thus, this planet has this unique quality among the other planets, and shares it with the Moon: that around certain maximum elongations <note>The angular distance between the Sun and a planet as viewed from Earth.</note>, it needs no depth of the Sun below the Horizon to show itself, but provides a view of itself even during the day for several hours.

> Before Christ 3993, on July 24, at 0 hours, 33 minutes, 26 seconds of equal time at Uraniborg, <note>Uraniborg was the observatory of Tycho Brahe on the island of Hven.</note> the **Moon** in its mean motion was at 22° 57' 2'' of Gemini [♊]. > The Moon was indeed centrally conjoined with the Sun in true motion, so that there was a total eclipse in Ethiopia at 27° 56' 17'' of Gemini [♊].

<summary>This page presents the specific astronomical corrections (equations) for the Moon's orbit, organized by the Eccentric Anomaly from 0 to 90 degrees. These tables allowed astronomers to adjust the Moon's average position to find its true position in the sky using Kepler's physical laws and logarithms.</summary>

'Quadrature' means the Node is 90 degrees away from the Sun. The 'Reduction' is a mathematical correction used to account for the fact that the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to the Earth's orbit around the Sun.</note>

Part 3.

<summary>This page contains base-60 sexagesimal tables for the mean motions of the Moon, covering its elongation from the Sun, its anomaly (position in its elliptical orbit), and its latitude relative to the ecliptic. These tables provide the mathematical foundation for predicting the Moon's position by breaking down its motion into highly precise fractional increments.</summary>

# THE RUDOLPHINE TABLES

-> CYCLE OF ENCOUNTERS <note>original: *Obviationum*; refers to the meeting or conjunction of celestial bodies</note> of the Mean Sun and the Ascending Node of the Moon in a Period: the minor period consisting of 372 Julian years and 2 days, and the major period consisting of exactly 2828 Julian years. It is established that in the first year of this Period, the conjunction (☌) of the Sun (☉) and the Node (☊) <note>An eclipse can only occur when the Sun is near one of the two points where the Moon's orbit crosses the Earth's orbit (the nodes).</note> occurs at the very moment of midnight which begins the first of January, although none of the possible Epochs or starting points holds this exactly. The days, however, are understood to be "current days," spanning from the preceding midnight to the following midnight. <-

Constructed tables <note>original: "Tab. ficti", likely referring to mean or calculated motions rather than observed ones.</note>

<note>Glossary of technical terms used in these tables:</note>
<term>Canon</term>: A formal table or set of rules for calculation.
<term>Lunar Motions</term>: The calculated movement of the moon across the sky.
<term>Periods of Anomaly</term>: The time it takes for the moon to return to the same point in its elliptical orbit (usually apogee to apogee).
<term>Apogee</term>: The point in the moon's orbit where it is farthest from the Earth.
<term>Node</term>: The two points where the moon's orbit intersects the ecliptic (the sun's apparent path).
<term>Signs and Degrees</term>: A method of measuring the 360° circle of the zodiac, divided into 12 "signs" of 30° each.

<summary>This page presents a detailed astronomical table for calculating the position of the Moon's apogee and its nodes over a vast timeframe, ranging from individual years to 12,000 years. It provides the data necessary to account for the "anomaly"—the Moon's varying speed along its elliptical path—and the retrograde motion of its orbital nodes.</summary>
<keywords>lunar motion, anomaly, apogee, lunar nodes, astronomical tables, time measurement, zodiac signs, mean motion</keywords>

# Part Three.

...which was or will be, as if in an empty month: with the fictitious hourly table, the proposed time for the Syzygies <note>original: "Syzygiis Luminarium". The syzygy refers to the alignment of the Sun, Earth, and Moon, occurring at New Moon and Full Moon.</note> of the Luminaries is found if you add the Monthly Equations <note>original: "Æquationes Menstruas". These are periodic corrections applied to the Moon's mean motion to account for gravitational variations throughout the month.</note>.

<note>Parallax is the apparent displacement of the Moon against the stars due to the observer's position on Earth. Semidiameter is the half-width of the Moon's visible disk. These values change as the Moon moves from Apogee (farthest) to Perigee (nearest).</note>

> Although the Diameter of the Moon has been quite elegantly derived by demonstration from Archetypal causes <note>Kepler refers to his geometric theories of cosmic harmony</note>; observations nevertheless frequently require a larger value; perhaps because the height of the Lunar atmosphere is so great that the demonstrated solidity of the globe is increased all around by one minute <note>original: "Scrupulo"</note>, or one and a half, or even more, according to the variety of physical causes.

> The Moon also, when directly overhead <note>original: "verticalis"</note>, can appear half a minute <note>original: "sc." - scrupulo</note> larger than when on the Horizon.

# ECLIPSE LIMITS

| | | Lunar Eclipses | | Solar Eclipses | |
|:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |
| | | **☾ at Apogee** | **at Perigee** | **☾ at Apogee** | **at Perigee** |
| **Sun in** | **Apogee** | 10.46 | 12. 0 | 15.58 | 17.12 |
| | **Perigee** | 10.40 | 11.54 | 16. 4 | 17.19 |

These limits are adapted to the "fictitious" or first-equated motion of the Moon <note>A calculation baseline used in these tables</note>, not to the mean motion nor to the true motion in every respect. Similarly, they apply to the mean motion of the Node, and to the maximum Inclination of the limit, which is presupposed everywhere: because this changes very little in the 18 days before and after the meeting <note>conjunction</note> of the Sun and the Node. The demonstrative semidiameter of the Moon is also presupposed, not physically enlarged.

<summary>This page presents mathematical tables for lunar latitude, reduction, parallax, and size, essential for calculating eclipses. Kepler also provides "Eclipse Limits" to determine if a lunar or solar eclipse will occur based on the distance of the Sun and Moon from their orbital nodes.</summary>

<note>The footer of the table serves as a guide for shifting decimals. Because this is a base-60 (sexagesimal) system, the same numbers can represent different values depending on their position—much like how "10" can mean ten ones or one ten. By following the symbols at the bottom (~, ', '', etc.), a calculator can use these same digits to determine values for hundreds or thousands of years.</note>

<summary>This page contains numerical tables used to calculate the mean motion of the Earth's axial tilt (obliquity of the ecliptic) and its weighting relative to the stars over periods of up to 12,000 years. It also includes a correction table for fine-tuning these long-term astronomical observations.</summary>

<insert>
Regarding stars 23 and 24, in my copy I find the sign ♉ <note>Taurus</note> enclosed in a circle. Whether that was from the original, or added by me during the transcription, I do not remember. Certainly, there was reason for doubt, because star 23 greatly exceeds the boundaries of the Swan and approaches the Little Horse <note>Equuleus</note>. Indeed, star 26 with the index numbers of 7 seems to be the same. But I demonstrate my good faith to astronomers by sharing this copy. In entries 12 and 14, I followed the consensus of my copy with that of Longomontanus <note>Christian Longomontanus, Tycho Brahe's chief assistant.</note>. That is what I always looked to.

> a.b. *Discussions concerning the fixed stars primarily make use of the Heart of the Lion <note>original: "cor Leonis," known today as the star Regulus</note> and the Ear of Grain of the Virgin <note>original: "spicam Virginis," known today as the star Spica</note>. Copernicus acted unwisely because he calculated the precession of the Equinoxes from the first star of Aries, whose location in Ptolemy is rough <note>original: "ὁλοσχερὴς" (holoscheres) – meaning broad or approximate</note>; for he counts from it to Spica 170° 0', and to the Heart of the Lion 115° 50'. When Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe</note> discovered that the former was 170° 39' and the latter 116° 40', he chose another star outside the constellation figure to avoid calculating precession from a false position or confusing astronomers with double or triple precessions starting from the same fixed star. This was the Bright star above the head <note>The star Hamal</note>, although I believe that in the original human imagination, it was attributed to the other horn.*

<summary>This page lists the coordinates and brightness of stars in Pegasus, Andromeda, the Triangle, Berenice's Hair, and Aries. It includes a significant note by Kepler debating the "zero point" of the celestial coordinate system used by Ptolemy, Copernicus, and Tycho Brahe.</summary>

The Rudolphine Tables

Therefore, in the year 1600, the equinoctial point precedes Tycho's Principal <note>The "Principal" likely refers to the star used as the primary reference point in Tycho Brahe's catalog.</note> by 32° 6', the first star of the constellation by 27° 37', and the position attributed to it by Ptolemy by 26° 47' or 26° 58'. These latter two precessions of Tycho should be compared with the Copernican ones, not the former. See Tycho’s *Progymnasmata*, Volume I, pages 194, 226, and following.

->*by Tycho Brahe.*<-

->## Second Class<-

This class EMBRACES THOSE FIXED STARS WHICH Tycho omitted from the ancient catalog of Hipparchus, as repeated and amended by Ptolemy. It pleases me to call these **SEMI-TYCHONIC**: for I have reduced them—having sought them from the codex of Ptolemy, using also the version by George of Trebizond published at Tübingen 76 years ago by Schreckenfuchs—to the year 1600. I did this by adding to the longitude positions provided by Ptolemy an arc equal to what Tycho added to a nearby bright star; and by either adding or subtracting as many minutes from the latitude as the obliquity of the Ecliptic is believed to have been greater in any given place under Ptolemy: yet in such a way that the calculation of a nearby round number was maintained.

Moreover, I thought it better here to follow the Greek text of Ptolemy more closely than [the versions used by] others—the Prutenic Tables, Copernicus, and the Alphonsines—who seem to have followed the Arabic version of the *Almagest*; so that by this means there might be an opportunity for comparing the versions...

<summary>This page concludes the primary catalog of 1,000 fixed stars by Tycho Brahe, covering southern constellations like Sirius, Argo Navis, and Centaurus. It also introduces the "Semi-Tychonic" stars—ancient data from Ptolemy that Kepler updated to the year 1600 for completeness.</summary>
<keywords>Tycho Brahe, Sirius, Procyon, Argo Navis, Hydra, Centaurus, Semi-Tychonic stars, Ptolemy, Hipparchus, George of Trebizond, Schreckenfuchs, Almagest, star magnitude</keywords>

# Part Four.

...to provide information: and because it is uncertain whether the Arabs corrected anything in those Ptolemaic records, or whether all the diversity of versions arose from the negligence of transcribers. There are a few to which I have applied my hand, either in my book on the star of the Serpentarius <note>original: *de stella Serpentarij*; referring to Kepler's 1606 work on the supernova in Ophiuchus</note> or elsewhere, which I have expressed in an ancient character for the sake of warning.

In TAURUS. Observation of the Pleiades.

Its frequent approach to the Moon and its use in very ancient observations make it of great importance. Therefore, Tycho lists only 4; and yet I do not find the first of them in the Observations. Also, my manuscript has 23° 50' instead of 23° 13' 1/2, which Bayer's marking confirms. It seems Ptolemy was allowed a longitude so small that he even displaces the boundaries of the Pleiades to 1° 30', and thus uses it in the observations of Timocharis; yet these do not support such a value. The same Ptolemy, starting from a quadrilateral, fails in his enumeration, adding one fourth star on the outside. Yet there are 7, which Galileo expresses in the *Sidereal Messenger* <note>original: *Nuncio*; Galileo's 1610 book reporting his telescopic discoveries</note>. But my markings from very different times, relying on three of Tycho's stars, agree closely enough with these numbers; as if it should be read thus in Ptolemy:

| The southern end of the leading side <note>original: τὸ νότιον πέρας τῆς ἡγουμένης πλευρᾶς</note> | 23.50 | ♉ | 4. 13 | |

| The one leading it, frequently failing <note>to be seen</note> <note>original: ὁ ἡγούμενος αὐτῇ συχνὰ ἐκλείπων</note> | 24. 0 | ♉ | 4.26 | |
| The one following the Pleiades <note>original: ὁ ἑπόμενος τῇ πλειάδι</note> | 24.47 | ♉ | 3.55 | |

But if the Pleiades were a "Raft" and contained by a single quadrilateral, even in the last one, the observed altitude exceeds the calculation. It is entirely right that there is one <note>sum of the 3rd column argues this, for they are 33</note>. And the Magnitude of the first is reported as 1, and the third as 6, since the bright star of the Pleiades is not smaller than that; hence the seventh is of the 3rd Magnitude in ♉.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the "Fixed Stars" from the Rudolphine Tables. Having previously covered the constellations known to the ancients, it now transitions to the southern constellations, which were largely unknown to European astronomers until the age of exploration.</meta>

# Rudolphine Tables
# Third Class of Fixed Stars.

## XII. COMPRISING CELESTIAL IMAGES WHICH ARE NOT AT ALL VISIBLE FROM OUR NORTHERN TEMPERATE ZONE.

Johann Bayer, in his *Uranometria* <note>Bayer’s landmark 1603 star atlas</note>, attributes these to Amerigo Vespucci, Andrea Corsali, and Pedro de Medina, the first among Europeans to see them; he asserts they were first corrected to astronomical standards by Petrus Theodori <note>Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser, a Dutch navigator whose observations formed the basis for these southern constellations</note>. Indeed, Jacobus Bartsch of Lusatia <note>Kepler’s son-in-law and a talented astronomer</note>—an industrious young man long celebrated for his great merits regarding the celestial globe—recently sent these to me from Augsburg to Ulm, cast into numbers and charts. This was a small flower plucked from the *Christian Uranography* of Schiller <note>Julius Schiller, who attempted to replace pagan constellations with Christian ones</note>, whose edition Bartsch is hastening according to the author's final wishes. Bartsch has promised that he would hereafter publish most perfect charts for an eighteen-inch globe, including the ancient figures, which is better suited to Tycho Brahe's original plan.

# TRIPLE TABLE OF REFRACTIONS,
->**Confirmed by the long and manifold Observations of TYCHO BRAHE,** primarily in the **SOUND** <note>the Øresund strait</note>, where the Baltic Sea flows into the German Ocean: but also partly in the Imperial Fortress of **BENATKY** in the Kingdom of Bohemia. The air was chosen for this purpose, as clear as could be. <note>Refraction is the bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere; Tycho was the first to rigorously account for how this makes stars near the horizon appear higher than they actually are.</note><-
